fullMarks: For a fluid mosaic model answer, begin with the lipid bilayer, then explain that proteins are embedded in it and that lipids and proteins can move laterally. Include how carbohydrates are joined to proteins or lipids.
For cell wall questions, describe its support, strength, protection and shape functions, then name the layers of the plant cell wall and their materials.
For nucleus questions, name the nuclear envelope, nuclear pores, nucleoplasm, nucleoli and chromatin; explain that DNA contains genes and controls cell activities.

For lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum answers, clearly distinguish RER (ribosomes; protein synthesis) from SER (lipid metabolism, transport and detoxification), then explain lysosomal digestion and waste breakdown.
For Golgi complex questions, explain cisternae and how the apparatus modifies proteins from rough ER, packs them into vesicles, and stores or transports them for secretion.
For chloroplast questions, name the double membrane, grana, thylakoids, stroma, photosynthetic pigments, DNA and ribosomes; connect chlorophyll and light energy to photosynthesis.
For turgor pressure, write the sequence: water-filled large vacuole presses outwards on the cytoplasm and cell wall; the cell becomes turgid, helping it maintain its shape.
When a question asks you to describe a structure, draw a clear, large diagram if useful and label the named parts accurately; finish with a sentence linking the structure to its function.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying the cell membrane is fully permeable. Fix: State that it is selectively-permeable and controls which molecules can pass.
Mistake: Mixing up rough and smooth ER. Fix: RER has ribosomes and serves in protein synthesis; SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid metabolism, transport and detoxification.
Mistake: Saying cristae are the fluid inside mitochondria. Fix: Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane; the fluid-like material is the matrix.
Mistake: Describing chromatin and chromosomes as unrelated structures. Fix: State that chromatin condenses into thick chromosomes when a cell starts dividing.
Mistake: Saying plant cells have many small temporary vacuoles like animal cells. Fix: Most mature plant cells have one large central vacuole; animal cells may have many small temporary vacuoles.

Mistake: Naming only cellulose as the material of every plant cell-wall layer. Fix: Match materials to layers: the primary wall includes cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the middle lamella contains magnesium, calcium and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.

shortTheory.question: What are the main functions of the cell membrane?
shortTheory.answer: It is selectively-permeable. It allows very few molecules to pass through it while blocks many other molecules.

shortTheory.question: What key role does the Golgi apparatus play in eukaryotic cells?
shortTheory.answer: It modifies proteins coming from rough ER and packs them into small membrane-bound sacs called Golgi vesicles.These sacs are kept in cell or are transported to exterior in the form of secretions.

shortTheory.question: How do lysosomes contribute to the cell's functioning?
shortTheory.answer: Lysosomes also have enzymes for breaking cellular wastes. They also engulf the damaged organelles and break them. Lysosomes can store certain molecules for later use.

shortTheory.question: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?
shortTheory.answer: These folds are called cristae (singular: crista). They increase the surface area for respiration.

shortTheory.question: How are chromatin and chromosomes related?
shortTheory.answer: When a cell starts dividing, its chromatin condenses and takes the shape of thick chromosomes.

shortTheory.question: How would you define a stem cell?
shortTheory.answer: Such unspecialized cell that has the ability to make a variety of specialized cell types is called stem cell.

steps.why: The cell cycle begins with G1 after the previous M phase has ended.
steps.text: After M phase, the cell enters G1, where it grows and makes proteins and organelles.

steps.why: DNA replication is the defining event of S phase.
steps.text: In S phase, the DNA of each chromosome is replicated, and each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

steps.why: G2 provides further growth and checks and preparation before mitosis.
steps.text: In G2, the cell grows further, produces proteins needed for division, checks for DNA damage, and prepares for mitosis.

steps.text: In M phase, the cell divides into two daughter cells.

example.question: Describe the sequence of events in the cell cycle from G1 to cell division.
example.answer: The cell grows in G1, copies its DNA in S, prepares for division in G2, and divides during M phase.

explain.title: What is the cell cycle?
explain.body: The textbook defines it as: “It is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.” The cell cycle has two main phases: interphase and the mitosis phase.

explain.title: Interphase: most of the cell cycle
explain.body: Interphase lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle. The cell performs its life functions and prepares for the next division. It consists of G1, S, and G2 phases.

explain.title: G1 and S phases
explain.body: G1 is also called the growth phase: the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and makes enzymes needed in S phase. In S phase, the DNA of each chromosome is copied. Each chromosome then consists of two sister chromatids, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.

explain.title: G2, M, and G0 phases
explain.body: In G2, the cell grows further, makes proteins for division, checks for DNA damage, and prepares for mitosis. After interphase, M phase divides the cell into two daughter cells. Some cells enter G0 and stop dividing while carrying out specialized functions; neurons may remain there indefinitely, while epithelial cells continue to divide.

mistakes: Do not say that the chromosome number doubles in S phase; the DNA is copied, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Do not confuse G1 and G2: G1 is the first growth phase, while G2 follows DNA replication and includes preparation for division.
Do not say that every cell enters G0; the textbook notes that some cells, such as epithelial cells, continue to divide without entering G0.
Do not describe interphase as a resting phase; the cell performs life functions, grows, copies DNA, and prepares for division.

yourTurn.question: How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?
solution: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator.
A ring of microfilaments contracts and the furrow moves inward, pinching the parent cell into two.
In plant cells, Golgi apparatus makes vesicles that move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast.
The plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane, resulting in two daughter cells.
yourTurn.answer: Animal cells divide by an inward-moving furrow; plant cells form a phragmoplast from Golgi vesicles, which grows outward.

steps.why: Naming the two major parts gives the structure for describing the complete process.
steps.text: There are two major phases of mitosis i.e. karyokinesis and cytokinesis.

steps.why: Prophase starts the nuclear division by making chromosomes visible and forming spindle fibres.
steps.text: During prophase, the thread-like chromatin material condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.

steps.why: Metaphase is identified by chromosome alignment along the cell equator.
steps.text: The chromosomes attached with spindle fibres arrange themselves along the equator of the cell.

steps.why: The separation and movement of sister chromatids are the main events of anaphase.
steps.text: The chromosome's sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles of the cell.

steps.why: Telophase rebuilds the nuclei around the separated chromosome sets.
steps.text: In this phase, new nuclear envelope forms around each set of separated chromosomes and nucleolus reforms.

steps.why: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm after the nucleus has divided.
steps.text: Cytokinesis is the division of cytoplasm.

example.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
example.answer: Karyokinesis occurs through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm to form two daughter cells.

explain.title: What mitosis does
explain.body: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell. It occurs in the somatic cells of eukaryotes.

explain.title: The two major parts
explain.body: There are two major phases of mitosis i.e. karyokinesis and cytokinesis. Karyokinesis means the division of the nucleus. Cytokinesis is the division of cytoplasm.

explain.title: The four phases of karyokinesis
explain.body: In prophase, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down. In metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres and line up at the equator. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles. In telophase, new nuclear envelopes form, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.

explain.title: Cytokinesis in animal and plant cells
explain.body: In animal cells, a furrow develops at the equator and a ring of microfilaments contracts, pinching the cell into two. In plant cells, Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to form a plate called phragmoplast; it grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane.

explain.title: Why mitosis matters and what can go wrong
explain.body: Mitosis supports growth, cell replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction. If mitosis is not properly regulated, cells may divide uncontrollably and form tumours. Tumours that invade other tissues are malignant tumours (cancer); spreading of disease is called metastasis.

mistakes: Do not say mitosis halves the chromosome number: each daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
Do not mix up anaphase and metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase, while sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
Do not confuse karyokinesis with cytokinesis: karyokinesis is division of the nucleus, while cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm.
Do not describe plant cytokinesis as an inward-moving cleavage furrow; the book describes Golgi vesicles forming a plate that grows outward.
Do not call every tumour cancer: a tumour that stays in its original location is benign; a tumour that invades other tissues is malignant.

recap.question: In which phase is the DNA of each chromosome replicated?
recap.answer: S phase; the DNA is replicated, and the total number of chromosomes remains the same.

recap.question: A cell has copied the DNA of each chromosome, but the total number of chromosomes has not changed. Which phase has just occurred?
recap.answer: S phase

For significance, cover both maintaining chromosome number and bringing genetic diversity.
Marks are often awarded for correct phase names and their key events; do not confuse homologous chromosome separation in anaphase-I with sister chromatid separation in anaphase-II.

yourTurn.question: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
solution: Crossing over exchanges portions of chromosomes between non-sister chromatids.
This creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes.
Each chromosome in the gametes carries a unique set of genes.
When diverse gametes combine, they contribute to genetic diversity.
yourTurn.answer: Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes, so gametes carry unique sets of genes. This contributes to genetic diversity.

yourTurn.question: What are sister chromatids, and when do they separate in meiosis?
solution: Sister chromatids are the two chromatids of one chromosome.
During anaphase-II, spindle fibres pull sister chromatids apart toward opposite poles.
yourTurn.answer: Sister chromatids are the two chromatids of one chromosome. They separate during anaphase-II.

steps.why: The division has four named phases, so first place them in the correct order.
steps.text: Meiosis-I consists of prophase-I, metaphase-I, anaphase-I and telophase-I.

steps.why: Pairing and exchange are the distinctive events to identify in prophase-I.
steps.text: In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads, and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.

steps.why: The tetrads must line up before the homologous chromosomes can separate.
steps.text: In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator.

steps.why: This is the reduction division: homologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids, separate.
steps.text: In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes move toward opposite poles; each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.

steps.why: Nuclear reformation and cytokinesis complete the first division.
steps.text: In telophase-I, nuclear envelopes reform, chromosomes uncoil, and cytokinesis produces two haploid daughter cells.

example.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
example.answer: Meiosis-I pairs homologous chromosomes and allows crossing over, aligns tetrads at the equator, separates homologous chromosomes, and ends with two haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: What meiosis does
explain.body: It is the type of cell division in which each daughter cell receives half the number of chromosomes as compared to the parent cell. In meiosis, a diploid parent cell divides to produce four haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: Diploid and haploid
explain.body: Diploid means the cells in which chromosomes are in pairs (homologous pairs) while haploid means the cells with half number of chromosomes i.e., cells with no pairs of chromosomes.

explain.title: The first division
explain.body: In meiosis-I, the homologous chromosomes in a diploid cell separate and so two haploid daughter cells are produced. In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair, form tetrads and can exchange portions by crossing over.

explain.title: The second division
explain.body: Meiosis-II closely resembles mitosis. Sister chromatids separate during anaphase-II, and the process ends with four haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: Why meiosis matters
explain.body: Meiosis helps maintain chromosome number across generations and contributes to genetic diversity. Non-disjunction can make gametes with more or fewer chromosomes than normal.

mistakes: Do not say sister chromatids separate in anaphase-I; homologous chromosomes separate then, while sister chromatids separate in anaphase-II.
Do not confuse synapsis (pairing of homologous chromosomes) with crossing over (exchange of chromosome portions).
Do not say meiosis produces two daughter cells in total; meiosis-I produces two cells, and meiosis-II results in four.
Do not call the daughter cells diploid; they have half the parent cell’s chromosome number and are haploid.
When describing genetic diversity, explain that crossing over creates new gene combinations.

recap.question: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate?
recap.answer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

recap.question: During which phase do chromosomes attached to spindle fibres arrange along the cell equator?
recap.answer: Metaphase

examTips: A short question may ask you to compare chromosome number, daughter-cell number, cell type, or crossing-over in mitosis and meiosis.
For a comparison, write both sides clearly: for example, “same as the parent” for mitosis and “reduced by half” for meiosis.
For a question about meiosis-I phases, use the order prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I and state the event in each phase.
Marks are often awarded for the correct event and its phase; do not name an event without naming the phase.
For significance of meiosis, include haploid gametes, maintenance of chromosome number, and variation.

hints: Think about the chromosome number in the daughter cells.

yourTurn.question: How does meiosis differ from mitosis in terms of chromosome number?
solution: In mitosis, the chromosome number in daughter cells remains the same as in the parent cell.
In meiosis, the chromosome number is reduced by half.
yourTurn.answer: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same as the parent cell; meiosis reduces it by half.

hints: Think of the exchange that happens in prophase I.
Non-sister chromatids exchange segments, producing variations.
yourTurn.question: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
solution: During prophase I, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange their segments in crossing-over.
This produces variations.
yourTurn.answer: Crossing-over exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, producing variations.

steps.why: The comparison starts by showing that mitosis involves only one division.
steps.text: Mitosis: A parent cell divides only once; two daughter cells are produced.

steps.why: This gives the corresponding number of divisions and daughter cells for meiosis.
steps.text: Meiosis: A parent cell undergoes two divisions; four daughter cells are produced.

steps.why: Chromosome number is one of the main differences between the divisions.
steps.text: Mitosis: Chromosome number in daughter cells remains the same as the parent cell.

steps.why: Meiosis reduces chromosome number, in contrast with mitosis.
steps.text: Meiosis: The chromosome number is reduced by half in daughter cells.

steps.why: Crossing-over distinguishes meiosis and explains the occurrence of variation.
steps.text: Mitosis: Variations are not generated; no crossing over occurs during prophase.

steps.why: This completes the comparison by giving the meiosis-side feature.
steps.text: Meiosis: Variations occur due to crossing-over; crossing-over occurs during prophase.

example.question: Compare mitosis and meiosis in terms of number of divisions, daughter cells, chromosome number, and crossing-over.
example.answer: Mitosis has one division and produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent; it does not involve crossing-over. Meiosis has two divisions and produces four daughter cells with half the chromosome number; crossing-over occurs and variations are produced.

explain.title: What the two divisions share
explain.body: DNA replication occurs during interphase (S phase) before both divisions. Both divisions also involve chromosome condensation, spindle formation, and the stages prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. Cytokinesis occurs at the end of both divisions.

explain.title: How many cells are made
explain.body: In mitosis, a parent cell divides once and produces two daughter cells. In meiosis, a parent cell undergoes two divisions and produces four daughter cells.

explain.title: How chromosome number changes
explain.body: In mitosis, the chromosome number in daughter cells remains the same as the parent cell. In meiosis, the chromosome number is reduced by half in daughter cells.

explain.title: Pairing and crossing-over
explain.body: In mitosis, homologous chromosomes do not form pairs and crossing-over does not occur. In meiosis, homologous chromosomes form pairs and crossing-over occurs during prophase. This helps produce variations.

explain.title: Where and why they occur
explain.body: Mitosis occurs in somatic cells and supports growth, development, and maintenance. Meiosis occurs in germ line cells and produces gametes in animals and spores in plants for sexual reproduction.

explain.title: When sister chromatids separate
explain.body: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase in mitosis. In meiosis, they separate during anaphase II; homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase I.

mistakes: Do not say meiosis produces two daughter cells; it produces four.
Do not say the chromosome number stays the same in meiosis; it is reduced by half.
Do not confuse homologous chromosomes separating in anaphase I with sister chromatids separating in anaphase II.
Do not say crossing-over occurs in mitosis; it occurs in prophase of meiosis.
When describing metaphase, distinguish a single chromosome aligning in mitosis from homologous pairs aligning in meiosis.
Do not forget to state the phase when naming an event in a question about meiosis-I.

recap.question: What separates during anaphase-I?
recap.answer: Homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase-I.

recap.question: What is the result of meiosis, according to this section?
recap.answer: Four haploid cells

rubric.how: Mention growth of the cell.

As a result, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

examTips: Short questions often ask for one phase, function or difference; use the exact stage name and a clear defining event.
Long questions commonly ask you to describe mitosis, meiosis-I, cytokinesis or the significance of a process. Organize the answer by phase or by separate points.
For mitosis, keep the order prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Correct stage names and events earn marks.
For a diagram question, draw clear cells and chromosomes, and label structures such as chromosomes, spindle fibres, equator, poles and nuclear membrane where relevant.
Use precise comparisons: meiosis-I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis-II separates sister chromatids. Crossing over occurs in prophase-I.

Therefore, chromosomes duplicate in the S phase.

steps.why: Prophase begins mitosis by making chromosomes visible and organizing the spindle.
steps.text: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes. The spindle forms and the nuclear membrane breaks down.

steps.why: Metaphase is identified by chromosome alignment at the cell's equator.
steps.text: Metaphase: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes, which line up at the equator of the cell.

steps.why: The separation and movement of sister chromatids define anaphase.
steps.text: Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.

steps.why: Telophase restores two nuclei, one around each chromosome set.
steps.text: Telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles, and nuclear membranes reform around the two sets.

steps.why: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to complete cell division.
steps.text: Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, forming two daughter cells.

example.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis. Include a labelled diagram if required.
example.answer: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes. The spindle forms and the nuclear membrane breaks down. Metaphase: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes, which line up at the equator of the cell. Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell. Telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles, and nuclear membranes reform around the two sets. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, forming two daughter cells. Diagram description: Draw four simple cells in sequence, labelled Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase and Telophase. Show condensed chromosomes and spindle formation in prophase; chromosomes along the equator with spindle fibres in metaphase; separated chromatids moving towards opposite poles in anaphase; and two reforming nuclei in telophase. Label chromosomes, spindle fibres, equator, poles and nuclear membrane where visible.

explain.title: Interphase prepares the cell
explain.body: Interphase includes G1, S and G2. The cell grows and carries out its activities in G1, replicates DNA in S, and prepares for division in G2.

explain.title: Mitosis makes matching cells
explain.body: Mitosis is nuclear division in somatic cells. Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase lead to two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.

explain.title: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm
explain.body: Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two. Plant cells form a cell plate that develops into a new cell wall.

explain.title: Meiosis reduces chromosome number
explain.body: Meiosis has two divisions. Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis-I, reducing chromosome number; sister chromatids separate in meiosis-II.

explain.title: Meiosis creates variation
explain.body: Crossing over in prophase-I and independent assortment create new genetic combinations. Meiosis produces haploid cells and helps maintain a species' chromosome number after fertilization.

mistakes: Do not say DNA replication happens in mitosis; it occurs in the S phase before cell division.
Do not confuse metaphase, when chromosomes line up, with anaphase, when chromatids separate.
In meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids remain together until meiosis-II.
Do not say mitosis halves chromosome number; it normally preserves it.
Do not describe plant cytokinesis as a cleavage furrow; plants form a cell plate.
Crossing over occurs in prophase-I of meiosis, not ordinary mitotic prophase.

recap.question: How many divisions occur in meiosis, and when do sister chromatids separate?
recap.answer: Meiosis has two divisions; it separates sister chromatids during anaphase II.

recap.question: Which result is characteristic of meiosis?
recap.answer: Four daughter cells with half the parent chromosome number

solutions.question: Enlist the events that occur during the G1 phase of interphase?
steps: The cell grows in size during the G1 phase.
The cell carries out its normal metabolic activities.
The cell synthesizes proteins and produces organelles.
The cell prepares for DNA replication in the S phase.
solutions.answer: During G1, the cell grows, performs normal activities, makes proteins and organelles, and prepares for DNA replication.

solutions.question: What is the main purpose of the S phase in the cell cycle?
steps: During the S phase, DNA is replicated.
Each chromosome is duplicated to form two identical sister chromatids.
solutions.answer: The S phase duplicates the cell’s DNA, forming two sister chromatids for each chromosome.

solutions.question: During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?
steps: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase of mitosis.
They move towards opposite poles of the cell.
solutions.answer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

solutions.question: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
steps: During prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair with each other.
Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding segments of DNA; this exchange is called crossing over.
Crossing over produces new combinations of genes in the resulting cells.
solutions.answer: Crossing over creates new combinations of genes and increases genetic variation.

solutions.question: What is the role of spindle fibres in mitosis?
steps: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes at their centromeres.
They move the chromosomes or sister chromatids towards opposite poles of the cell.
solutions.answer: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes and move them towards opposite poles during mitosis.

solutions.question: How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?
steps: In an animal cell, the cell membrane pinches inward to form a cleavage furrow, which divides the cytoplasm.
In a plant cell, a cell plate forms between the two daughter nuclei and develops into a new cell wall.
solutions.answer: Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow, whereas plant cells form a cell plate that develops into a new cell wall.

solutions.question: What is the difference between prophase of mitosis and prophase-I of meiosis-I?
steps: In prophase of mitosis, chromosomes condense; homologous chromosomes do not pair, and crossing over does not occur.
In prophase-I of meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes pair to form bivalents.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase-I.
solutions.answer: Unlike mitotic prophase, prophase-I includes pairing of homologous chromosomes and crossing over.

solutions.question: How does meiosis differ from mitosis in terms of chromosome number?
steps: In mitosis, the chromosome number in the daughter cells remains the same as in the parent cell.
In meiosis, the chromosome number is reduced to half in the daughter cells.
solutions.answer: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number, while meiosis reduces it to half.

solutions.question: What are the key events of anaphase in mitosis?
steps: The centromeres divide, separating the sister chromatids.
The spindle fibres pull the separated chromatids towards opposite poles of the cell.
Each chromatid is now considered a daughter chromosome.
solutions.answer: During anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell.

solutions.question: What is the function of the centrosome during cell division?
steps: The centrosome duplicates and the two centrosomes move towards opposite poles of the cell.
They organise the spindle fibres that attach to chromosomes and help move them during cell division.
solutions.answer: The centrosome organises the spindle fibres that move chromosomes during cell division.

solutions.question: What are sister chromatids, and when do they separate in meiosis?
steps: Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of a chromosome joined together at the centromere.
They separate during anaphase II of meiosis.
solutions.answer: Sister chromatids are identical chromosome copies joined at the centromere; they separate during anaphase II.

solutions.question: How is mitosis related to the process of regeneration?
steps: Regeneration is the process by which an organism replaces or regrows lost or damaged body parts.
Mitosis produces new cells for this process.
The new cells grow and develop into the cells and tissues needed to replace the lost or damaged part.
solutions.answer: Mitosis produces the new cells needed for regeneration of lost or damaged body parts.

solutions.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
steps: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
The nucleolus and nuclear membrane disappear, and spindle fibres form as the centrioles move towards opposite poles of the cell.
Metaphase: Chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at their centromeres and arrange themselves at the equator of the cell.
Anaphase: The centromeres divide, and the sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
Telophase: Chromatids reach the poles and become chromosomes; they uncoil, the spindle fibres disappear, and new nuclear membranes and nucleoli form around each set of chromosomes.
Mitosis produces two daughter nuclei containing the same number and kinds of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.
solutions.answer: Mitosis proceeds through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, producing two genetically identical daughter nuclei.

solutions.question: Describe cytokinesis in animal and plant cells.
steps: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells after nuclear division.
In an animal cell, the cell membrane constricts inwards at the middle, forming a cleavage furrow.
The cleavage furrow deepens until the cytoplasm is divided and two daughter cells are separated.
In a plant cell, vesicles gather at the equator and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outwards until it joins the existing cell wall and separates the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.
solutions.answer: Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow, while plant cells divide by formation of a cell plate; both processes separate the daughter cells.

solutions.question: Describe the significance of mitosis.
steps: Mitosis is responsible for the growth of an organism by increasing the number of cells.
It replaces worn-out or damaged cells and helps in the repair of tissues.
It enables regeneration of lost or damaged body parts in some organisms.
It is a means of asexual reproduction in many organisms.
It maintains the chromosome number and genetic similarity in the daughter cells.
solutions.answer: Mitosis is important for growth, repair, replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction, while maintaining chromosome number.

solutions.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
steps: Prophase I: Chromosomes become visible, and each chromosome consists of two chromatids joined at a centromere.
Homologous chromosomes pair with each other to form pairs called bivalents.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments of genetic material; this process is called crossing over.
The nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear, and spindle fibres form.
Metaphase I: Homologous chromosome pairs arrange themselves at the equator of the cell, and spindle fibres attach to their centromeres.
Anaphase I: Homologous chromosomes separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
The centromeres do not divide, so the sister chromatids of each chromosome remain attached.
Telophase I: The chromosomes reach the poles, and the cell divides to form two haploid cells; each chromosome still consists of two chromatids.
solutions.answer: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair and may exchange segments, then separate to opposite poles while their centromeres remain undivided, forming two haploid cells.

solutions.question: Describe the significance of meiosis.
steps: Meiosis produces haploid cells by reducing the chromosome number to half.
It maintains the constant chromosome number of a species from one generation to the next when fertilization restores the diploid number.
It produces genetic variation through crossing over and the independent assortment of chromosomes.
solutions.answer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates genetic variation, helping maintain the chromosome number of a species across generations.

solutions.question: What role might mistakes in the cell cycle checkpoints play in the emergence of cancer?
steps: Cell-cycle checkpoints normally control whether a cell can proceed to the next stage and help prevent the division of cells with damaged DNA.
If mistakes in these checkpoints allow abnormal cells to continue dividing, they may divide uncontrollably.
The resulting mass of abnormal cells may form a tumour and can lead to cancer.
solutions.answer: Faulty cell-cycle checkpoints can allow abnormal cells to divide uncontrollably, leading to tumour formation and cancer.

solutions.question: Why do skin cells divide continuously throughout an organism's existence, but nerve and muscle cells permanently exit the cell cycle?
steps: Skin cells are continually lost or damaged, so they keep dividing to replace them and repair the tissue.
Nerve and muscle cells become highly specialised for their functions.
These specialised cells permanently leave the cell cycle and do not normally divide.
solutions.answer: Skin cells divide to replace lost or damaged cells, whereas specialised nerve and muscle cells permanently leave the cell cycle.

definitions.text: It is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.
Many cells stop dividing and start performing their specific functions. This phase is called G0 phase.
Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell.
Karyokinesis means the division of the nucleus.
It is the division of cytoplasm.
It is the type of cell division in which each daughter cell receives half the number of chromosomes as compared to the parent cell.
Diploid means the cells in which chromosomes are in pairs (homologous pairs)
haploid means the cells with half number of chromosomes i.e., cells with no pairs of chromosomes.
They pair up in a process called synapsis.
Each pair of homologous chromosomes is called tetrad.
Each chiasma is the site for crossing over i.e., exchange of portions of chromosomes between non-sister chromatids.
During meiosis-I, chromosomes separate while during meiosis-II sister chromatids separate. It is called disjunction.
Sometimes non-disjunction occurs. Due to it, the daughter cells (gametes) receive more or less than the normal number of chromosomes.
If the tumors remain in their original location, they are called benign.
If they migrate and invade other tissues, they are called malignant tumors (cancer).
It is called metastasis(spreading of disease).

In mitosis answers, distinguish karyokinesis (nuclear division) from cytokinesis (cytoplasm division); do not leave cytokinesis out.

mistakes: Mistake: Saying that DNA replication doubles the chromosome number in S phase. Fix: State that DNA is copied and each chromosome has two sister chromatids, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Mistake: Saying sister chromatids separate in anaphase-I. Fix: In anaphase-I homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids separate in anaphase-II.
Mistake: Confusing homologous chromosomes with sister chromatids. Fix: Homologous chromosomes pair in prophase-I; sister chromatids are the two copies joined at one centromere.
Mistake: Describing plant cytokinesis as a cleavage furrow. Fix: Animal cells form a furrow; plant cells form a cell plate from vesicles.
Mistake: Writing that crossing over happens in mitosis. Fix: Identify crossing over as an event of prophase-I of meiosis.
Mistake: Listing mitosis stages but forgetting cytokinesis. Fix: After telophase, state how the cytoplasm divides to produce two daughter cells.

shortTheory.question: Enlist the events that occur during the G1 phase of interphase.
shortTheory.answer: During this phase cell makes proteins and organelles and so grows in size. Cell also makes enzymes that are required in S phase for the replication of DNA.

shortTheory.question: What is the main purpose of the S phase in the cell cycle?
shortTheory.answer: During this phase, the DNA of each chromosome is replicated (copied). It results in the duplication of chromosomes (each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids). The total number of chromosomes in cell remains the same.

shortTheory.question: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
shortTheory.answer: Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes. Each chromosome in the gametes carries a unique set of genes.

shortTheory.question: What is the role of spindle fibres in mitosis?
shortTheory.answer: The spindle fibres attached with chromosomes pull toward the poles. Due to this pulling, the chromosome's sister chromatids separate.

shortTheory.question: How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?
shortTheory.answer: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator. At this furrow, the cytoplasm has a ring of microfilaments. The ring contracts and the furrow moves inward. In this way parent cell is pinched into two. In plant cells, Golgi apparatus makes vesicles. These vesicles move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast. The plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane. The result is two daughter cells.

shortTheory.question: What are sister chromatids, and when do they separate in meiosis?
shortTheory.answer: Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. In anaphase-II, spindle fibres pull sister chromatids apart toward opposite poles.

writtenQuestions.text: Explain the levels of organization in multicellular organism. How does each level contribute to the overall functioning of an organism?
modelAnswer: Atoms are the smallest unit of matter that maintain the property of an element.
Atoms combine to form molecules.
Molecules combine in specific ways to make organelles, each specialized for a particular function.
Organelles assemble and interact to make cells, the smallest units with characteristics of life.
Similar cells work together in tissues to perform specific functions.
Related tissues work together in organs to perform specific functions.
Multiple organs work together in organ systems to perform related functions.
Organ systems together make an organism.
Each higher level combines the activities of lower levels to perform increasingly complex functions.
Answer: Atom → molecule → organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

explain.title: The levels build on one another
explain.body: Organization starts with atoms and becomes more complex at each level: molecules, organelles, cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and organisms.

explain.title: Cells and tissues
explain.body: A cell is the smallest unit with characteristics of life. A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform one or more specific functions.

explain.title: Organs and organ systems
explain.body: An organ is made of related tissues working together. An organ system consists of multiple organs working together to perform related functions.

explain.title: Emergent properties
explain.body: When parts interact at a higher level, they can create functions that the separate parts cannot perform alone. For example, different heart tissues work together so the heart can pump blood.

explain.title: Examples in plants and animals
explain.body: In animals, the heart is an organ and the circulatory system is an organ system. In plants, a leaf is an organ, while the root system and shoot system are organ systems.

mistakes: Do not place tissue before cell: similar cells combine to form a tissue.
Do not define an organ as a group of similar cells; an organ consists of related tissues.
Do not confuse an organ system with an organ: an organ system contains multiple organs.
Do not leave out organelle when writing the complete sequence from atom to organism.
Do not describe emergent properties as functions of separate parts alone; they arise from the parts interacting.

explain.body: An organ is made of tissues that work together for a particular function. The textbook defines an organ system this way: “An organ system consists of organs that work together to perform essential functions.” In plants, the two main systems are the root system and the shoot system.

explain.title: A leaf is a complex organ
explain.body: The textbook states: “In plants, leaf is a complex organ made of various related tissues.” Epidermal tissue forms the outer layer. Mesophyll tissue lies between the two epidermises and is the site of photosynthesis. Vascular tissue contains xylem and phloem.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe the tissue composition of the stomach. How does each tissue contribute to the digestive function of the stomach?
modelAnswer: The inner wall of the stomach is made up of glandular epithelial tissue.
It secretes mucus, which protects the inner wall from acid, and gastric juice containing pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid.
Connective tissue lies beneath the epithelial tissue; it provides structural support and contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
There are three smooth muscle layers: outer longitudinal, middle circular, and inner oblique.
These muscles contract and relax to mix food with gastric juice.
The outer connective tissue encircles and supports the stomach.

explain.body: “Various organs are present in human body, each with specific functions.” For example, “The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood throughout the body.” The lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, and the brain coordinates organs, thinking, and decision-making.

explain.title: The stomach is made of tissues
explain.body: “Stomach is an important organ of the digestive system. It is responsible for the partial digestion of proteins. It also stores food.” Its epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice; connective tissue provides support; and smooth muscle layers mix food with gastric juice.

explain.title: Organ systems work through their organs

The digestive system digests food and absorbs it; the respiratory system exchanges gases; the nervous system coordinates and controls body functions; and the blood circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products.

writtenQuestions.text: What is homeostasis, and why is it important for organisms?
modelAnswer: Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in the external environment.
It is important because cells function properly only when conditions such as temperature, pH, and the concentrations of salts, glucose and oxygen are kept in the normal range.

writtenQuestions.text: How does the human body maintain a stable internal temperature?
modelAnswer: When body temperature rises above normal, the temperature-regulating centre in the brain sends a message to sweat glands.
Sweating occurs and, as sweat evaporates, heat is lost and body temperature falls towards normal.
When body temperature falls, the centre sends a message to muscles, causing shivering.
Shivering generates heat and raises body temperature towards normal.

The urinary system eliminates waste materials from the body.
It also regulates water and salt balance in body tissues.
In this way, it helps maintain blood volume, blood pressure and pH levels.

explain.title: What homeostasis means
explain.body: Homeostasis is defined as the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment of the body despite changes in the external environment. Temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar and pH are examples of conditions the body regulates.

explain.title: Why homeostasis matters
explain.body: Cells work properly only when conditions around them, such as temperature, pH, and the concentrations of salts, glucose and oxygen, stay in the normal range.

explain.title: Temperature responses
explain.body: When body temperature rises, sweating causes heat loss as sweat evaporates. When temperature falls, shivering generates heat. Both responses help bring body temperature towards normal.

explain.title: Systems work together
explain.body: Several organ systems help maintain homeostasis. The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate activities; the respiratory system supplies oxygen and expels carbon dioxide; and the cardiovascular system helps regulate temperature and pH while carrying necessary substances to cells.

explain.title: Other system roles
explain.body: The digestive system distributes nutrients to cells. The urinary system eliminates wastes and regulates water and salt balance. The integumentary system protects the body and helps regulate temperature through sweating.

mistakes: Defining homeostasis only as keeping the body warm; it also involves conditions such as blood pressure, blood sugar and pH.
Saying that sweating generates heat; evaporation of sweat causes heat to be lost.
Forgetting to explain shivering when asked how temperature is controlled.
Listing organ systems without stating how each one contributes to homeostasis.
Confusing the roles of systems: the respiratory system supplies oxygen and expels carbon dioxide, while the cardiovascular system carries substances to cells.

steps.why: Begin by defining the internal balance that the question asks about.
steps.text: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions in an organism.

example.question: Q5.9. Define homeostasis and explain its importance. Discuss how different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
example.answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions in an organism. It is important because cells and organs need suitable conditions to function properly. Different organ systems work together: the digestive system supplies nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, the circulatory system transports materials, and the excretory system removes wastes. Their coordinated actions help maintain stable internal conditions.

explain.title: Organisation from small to large
explain.body: The order is cell → tissue → organ → organ system. Cells with similar functions form tissues; different tissues work together in organs; organs cooperate in organ systems.

explain.title: Tissues perform specialised jobs
explain.body: Animal tissues include epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissues. Plant tissues include epidermal tissue, mesophyll, xylem, and phloem. Their structures suit their functions.

explain.title: The stomach digests food
explain.body: Stomach epithelial tissue produces mucus, pepsinogen, and hydrochloric acid. Connective tissue supports the stomach and contains blood vessels and nerves. Smooth muscle churns food and mixes it with digestive juices.

explain.title: The leaf captures and transports materials
explain.body: Palisade mesophyll carries out most photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas exchange. Xylem brings water to the leaf, phloem carries food, and the epidermis protects the leaf.

explain.title: Organs and systems cooperate
explain.body: Plant roots anchor and absorb water and minerals, while shoot organs support photosynthesis, transport, and reproduction. In humans, organ systems cooperate to provide needed materials and remove wastes.

explain.title: Homeostasis keeps conditions stable
explain.body: Homeostasis means maintaining stable internal conditions. Systems such as the respiratory, circulatory, digestive, and excretory systems work together so cells and organs can function properly.

mistakes: Reversing the order of tissue and organ in the organisation hierarchy.
Saying xylem transports food or phloem transports water; xylem transports water and minerals, while phloem transports food.
Confusing palisade and spongy mesophyll: palisade mainly carries out photosynthesis, while spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas exchange.
Listing stomach tissues without explaining what each does.
Defining homeostasis without explaining why it matters or how organ systems help maintain it.
Describing only one side of a comparison question instead of giving a difference between both terms.

recap.answer: Sweating helps lose heat, so body temperature falls towards normal.

recap.answer: The body maintains a stable internal environment despite external changes.

solutions.question: Enlist the levels of organization from cells to organ systems.
steps: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system
solutions.answer: Cells are organized into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems.

solutions.question: What are the major roles of the epithelial tissue present in the stomach?
steps: The epithelial tissue forms the inner lining of the stomach and protects its wall from gastric juices.
It secretes mucus, which protects the stomach lining, and gastric juice, which helps in the digestion of food.
solutions.answer: Stomach epithelium protects the stomach wall and secretes mucus and gastric juice.

solutions.question: How do the smooth muscles contribute to the stomach’s function?
steps: The smooth muscles in the stomach contract and relax to churn and mix food with gastric juices.
Their contractions also push the partly digested food towards the small intestine.
solutions.answer: Smooth muscles churn food with gastric juices and move it towards the small intestine.

solutions.question: What is the function of the palisade mesophyll in the leaf?
steps: Palisade mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts.
They absorb light and carry out most of the photosynthesis in the leaf.
solutions.answer: Palisade mesophyll carries out most of the photosynthesis in the leaf.

solutions.question: What is the role of the shoot system in plants?
steps: The shoot system consists of the stem, leaves, buds, flowers and fruits.
It supports the plant and bears its leaves and reproductive structures.
Leaves make food by photosynthesis, while flowers take part in reproduction.
solutions.answer: The shoot system supports the plant, bears its leaves and reproductive structures, and helps in food-making and reproduction.

solutions.question: What is homeostasis, and why is it important for organisms?
steps: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment in an organism despite changes in the external environment.
It is important because cells and their enzymes function properly only when internal conditions remain within suitable limits.
solutions.answer: Homeostasis keeps an organism’s internal environment stable so its cells and enzymes can function properly.

solutions.question: How does the human body maintain a stable internal temperature?
steps: The hypothalamus in the brain monitors the temperature of the blood and helps regulate body temperature.
When the body is too warm, sweat glands produce sweat and skin blood vessels widen; evaporation of sweat and increased blood flow to the skin help lose heat.
When the body is too cold, skin blood vessels narrow to reduce heat loss, and muscles may shiver to produce heat.
solutions.answer: The hypothalamus helps maintain body temperature by coordinating sweating and widening of skin blood vessels when hot, and shivering and narrowing of skin blood vessels when cold.

solutions.question: Differentiate between the following: Tissue and organ
steps: Tissue: A group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.
Organ: A structure made of different tissues working together to perform a particular function.
Example: In the stomach, epithelial, muscular and other tissues work together as an organ.
solutions.answer: A tissue is a group of similar cells performing a function, whereas an organ is made of different tissues working together.

solutions.question: Differentiate between the following: Root system and shoot system
steps: Root system consists of roots, usually growing below the ground; shoot system consists of the stem, leaves, buds, flowers and fruits, usually growing above the ground.
Roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts; the shoot supports the plant and carries out functions such as photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.
Roots generally do not have nodes, internodes or leaves; the stem of the shoot has nodes and internodes and bears leaves and buds.
solutions.answer: The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals, while the shoot system bears the above-ground parts and performs functions such as support, photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.

solutions.question: Differentiate between the following: Epidermal and mesophyll tissue
steps: Epidermal tissue forms the outer covering of a plant and protects it from injury and water loss.
Epidermal cells are usually closely packed; the epidermis may have a waxy cuticle and stomata for gas exchange and water loss.
Mesophyll tissue is present inside the leaf, between the upper and lower epidermis.
Mesophyll cells contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis; spaces between some mesophyll cells also allow gas exchange.
solutions.answer: Epidermal tissue covers and protects the plant, while mesophyll tissue inside the leaf performs photosynthesis and allows gas exchange.

solutions.question: Differentiate between the following: Palisade and spongy mesophyll
steps: Palisade mesophyll is found below the upper epidermis of the leaf.
Its cells are elongated and closely packed, and contain many chloroplasts; it is the main site of photosynthesis.
Spongy mesophyll is usually found below the palisade mesophyll, toward the lower epidermis.
Its cells are irregular and loosely arranged, with large air spaces between them; these spaces help in the exchange of gases.
Spongy mesophyll cells also contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis.
solutions.answer: Palisade mesophyll has closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells for photosynthesis, while spongy mesophyll has loosely arranged cells and air spaces that aid gas exchange.

solutions.question: Explain the levels of organization in multicellular organism. How does each level contribute to the overall functioning of an organism?
steps: In multicellular organisms, cells are organized into levels: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems and the organism.
Cells are the basic structural and functional units of an organism; specialized cells perform particular functions.
A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.
An organ consists of different tissues working together to perform specific functions.
An organ system consists of organs working together to perform major functions of the body.
All organ systems work in coordination to maintain the life of the organism.
solutions.answer: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems; coordinated organ systems make up and maintain the multicellular organism.

solutions.question: What is a tissue level? Explain plant and animal tissues.
steps: The tissue level is the level of organization in which similar cells work together to perform a particular function.
Plant tissues are groups of plant cells with a common structure and function; they are broadly classified as meristematic and permanent tissues.
Meristematic tissues consist of actively dividing cells and bring about plant growth.
Permanent tissues consist of mature cells that perform specific functions, such as protection, support, storage and transport.
Animal tissues are groups of specialized cells that work together to perform particular functions.
The main types of animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.

Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces and lines cavities; connective tissue supports and connects body parts; muscular tissue contracts to produce movement; nervous tissue receives and transmits messages.
solutions.answer: The tissue level is a group of similar cells working together; plant tissues include meristematic and permanent tissues, while the main animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

solutions.question: Describe the tissue composition of the stomach. How does each tissue contribute to the digestive function of the stomach?
steps: The wall of the stomach is made of epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.
Epithelial tissue lines the stomach and contains glands that secrete gastric juice; mucus helps protect the lining from the acidic juice.
Connective tissue supports and binds the stomach tissues and contains blood vessels that supply them.
Muscular tissue in the stomach wall contracts to churn and mix food with gastric juice and move it through the digestive tract.
Nervous tissue controls and coordinates the activities of the stomach.
solutions.answer: In the stomach, epithelial tissue secretes gastric juice and protects the lining, connective tissue supports and supplies it, muscular tissue churns and moves food, and nervous tissue coordinates activity.

solutions.question: Describe the tissue composition of the leaf. How does each tissue contribute to the functions of the leaf?
steps: The leaf is composed mainly of epidermal, mesophyll and vascular tissues.
The upper and lower epidermis protect the leaf; the cuticle helps reduce water loss, and stomata allow gas exchange.
Mesophyll tissue lies between the epidermal layers. Palisade mesophyll contains many chloroplasts and is the main site of photosynthesis.
Spongy mesophyll has air spaces that allow gases to move through the leaf; its cells also carry out photosynthesis.
Vascular tissue occurs in the veins of the leaf. Xylem transports water and mineral salts to the leaf, while phloem transports the food made in the leaf to other parts of the plant.
solutions.answer: Epidermal tissue protects the leaf and enables gas exchange, mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, and vascular tissue transports water, minerals and food.

solutions.question: How do the organ systems come together to form the human body?
steps: The human body is organized into cells, tissues, organs and organ systems.
Different tissues combine to form organs, and organs that work together form an organ system.
The organ systems perform different functions but work in coordination with one another.
For example, the digestive system breaks down food and absorbs nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system transports oxygen and nutrients to body cells.
Together, the organ systems maintain the activities and life of the human body.
solutions.answer: Different organs form organ systems, and the coordinated work of all organ systems performs the functions needed to maintain the human body.

solutions.question: Describe the roles of the digestive system and the excretory system in homeostasis.
steps: The digestive system breaks down complex food into simple, soluble substances that can be absorbed into the blood.
The absorbed nutrients are transported to body cells and used for energy, growth and repair.
Undigested food is removed from the body as faeces; this helps prevent unwanted material from accumulating.
The excretory system removes metabolic wastes from the body.
The kidneys filter the blood and remove urea, excess water and salts to form urine.
By regulating the amount of water and salts in the body and removing wastes, these systems help maintain a stable internal environment.
solutions.answer: The digestive system supplies useful nutrients, while the excretory system removes wastes and regulates water and salts; together they help maintain homeostasis.

solutions.question: Explain the functions of various plant organs.
steps: Roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts; some roots also store food.
The stem supports the plant and bears leaves, flowers and fruits.
The stem transports water and mineral salts from roots to leaves and carries prepared food from leaves to other parts of the plant.
Leaves make food by photosynthesis.
Leaves exchange gases with the air through stomata and lose water vapour by transpiration.
Flowers are the reproductive organs of flowering plants; after fertilisation, they develop into fruits and seeds.
The fruit protects the seeds and may help in their dispersal.
Seeds can germinate to produce new plants.
solutions.answer: Roots absorb and anchor; stems support and transport; leaves make food, exchange gases and transpire; flowers reproduce; fruits protect seeds.

solutions.question: Describe the structure and function of the plant root system.
steps: The root system consists of the primary root and its branches, which spread through the soil.
The root tip is protected by a root cap, which protects the growing region as the root pushes through the soil.
Behind the root cap is the region of cell division, where cells divide to produce new cells.
The region of elongation is where the new cells increase in length, making the root grow.
In the region of maturation, cells differentiate into different tissues; root hairs arise from its outer cells.
Root hairs increase the surface area for absorption of water and mineral salts from the soil.
The cortex lies between the outer layer and the central vascular tissues; it helps conduct water and may store food.
The vascular tissues include xylem and phloem. Xylem transports water and mineral salts, while phloem transports prepared food.
The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and mineral salts from the soil.
solutions.answer: The root has a cap and regions of cell division, elongation and maturation; root hairs absorb water and minerals, while cortex and vascular tissues conduct or store materials.

solutions.question: Define homeostasis and explain its importance. Discuss how different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
steps: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body.
It is important because cells and enzymes function properly only when internal conditions, such as temperature, water and chemical levels, are kept within suitable limits.
The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide.
The circulatory system transports oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries carbon dioxide and other wastes away from them.
The digestive system supplies nutrients and water to the blood, while the excretory system removes wastes and helps regulate water and salts.
The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate and regulate the activities of body organs in response to changes.
Thus, organ systems work together to keep the internal environment suitable for the body's cells.
solutions.answer: Homeostasis maintains a constant internal environment; coordinated organ systems regulate conditions and supply cells while removing wastes.

solutions.question: Describe how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together to maintain homeostasis of oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body.
steps: The respiratory system takes oxygen from the air into the lungs and removes carbon dioxide from the body.
In the lungs, oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is breathed out.
The circulatory system carries oxygen in the blood from the lungs to body cells.
Oxygen moves from the blood into cells, where it is used in cellular respiration to release energy from food.
Cells produce carbon dioxide during cellular respiration.
The blood carries carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli and is exhaled.
In this way, the respiratory and circulatory systems work together to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, helping maintain the body's internal balance.
solutions.answer: The lungs add oxygen to the blood and remove carbon dioxide; the blood delivers oxygen to cells and carries their carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

solutions.question: How does the structure of epithelial tissue relate to its function in different parts of the body?
steps: Epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells that cover the body surface, line internal organs and cavities, and form glands.
The thin, flat cells of squamous epithelium allow rapid diffusion; for example, it lines the air sacs of the lungs where gases are exchanged.
Cuboidal epithelial cells are suited to secretion and absorption; they occur in kidney tubules and in some glands.
Columnar epithelial cells line parts of the digestive tract, where they help in absorption and secretion.
Ciliated epithelial cells have hair-like cilia; in the respiratory tract, the cilia move mucus and trapped particles towards the throat.
Glandular epithelial cells are specialised for secretion and form glands.
Stratified epithelium has several layers of cells and protects parts exposed to wear, such as the skin and the lining of the mouth.
solutions.answer: Epithelial cell shape, layers and special features suit its location: squamous cells diffuse, cuboidal and columnar cells absorb or secrete, cilia move mucus, and stratified layers protect.

solutions.question: Evaluate the importance of organ systems working in harmony and predict the consequences of a failure in one system on the others.
steps: Organ systems work in harmony to maintain homeostasis and ensure that all body cells receive what they need and that wastes are removed.
For example, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, the circulatory system carries it to cells, and the excretory system helps remove wastes and regulate water and salts.
Because organ systems depend on one another, failure of one system can disturb the functions of other systems.
If the respiratory system fails, less oxygen reaches the blood; the circulatory system then delivers less oxygen to cells, reducing cellular respiration and energy release.
If the circulatory system fails, oxygen and nutrients cannot reach body cells effectively, and carbon dioxide and other wastes cannot be carried away.
If the excretory system fails, wastes and excess water or salts may build up in the body and disrupt the internal environment.
Therefore, the failure of one organ system can affect other systems and may threaten the survival of the whole organism.
solutions.answer: Organ systems cooperate to maintain homeostasis; failure of one disrupts the others, limits supply or waste removal, and can threaten the organism's survival.

definitions.text: Atoms are the smallest unit of matter that maintain the property of an element For example; carbon, hydrogen, oxygen.
Atoms combine to form molecules which can have entirely different properties than the atoms they contain. For example; water, protein, nucleic acid.

Molecules combine in specific ways and make the subcellular level i.e., organelle. Each organelle is specialized to do a particular function. For example; mitochondria are responsible for cellular respiration and ribosomes are specialized for protein synthesis.

When organelles assemble and interact with each other, they make cell – the smallest unit with characteristics of life. They can carry out life activities and can also reproduce. Unicellular organisms are made of only one cell while multicellular organisms are made of many cells.
A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform one or more specific functions.
An organ is a structure made up of related tissues working together to perform specific functions.
An organ system consists of multiple organs that work together to perform related functions.
An organism is a living entity that can function independently on behalf of proper functioning of its organ systems. Examples include humans and trees.

fullMarks: For levels of organization, write the sequence in order: cell → tissue → organ → organ system. If the question asks for the wider sequence, begin at atom and continue through organism.
For a tissue-versus-organ answer, define each clearly first, then give the key difference: a tissue is similar cells working together; an organ is related tissues working together.

For the stomach, name each layer and give its role: epithelial tissue, connective tissue, smooth muscle tissue, and outer connective tissue. Include mucus protection and gastric juice in the epithelial role.
For the leaf, describe epidermal, mesophyll, and vascular tissues separately. Explain that xylem carries water and minerals to the leaf, while phloem carries sugars away from it.
When drawing or labelling a leaf, label the cuticle, upper and lower epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, guard cells, stoma, xylem, and phloem accurately.
For plant-organ questions, state the function of each organ clearly: roots anchor and absorb; stems support and transport; leaves photosynthesise and transpire; flowers reproduce.
For homeostasis, give its definition first, then explain why stable internal conditions matter to cells. Keep examples such as sweating, shivering, or insulin linked to the change they help correct.
mistakes: Writing the levels in the wrong order. Fix: learn the sequence from simple to complex: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
Describing an organ as a group of similar cells. Fix: similar cells form a tissue; an organ contains related tissues working together.
Saying that stomach muscle tissue secretes gastric juice. Fix: epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice; smooth muscles mix food with the gastric juice.
Mixing up xylem and phloem. Fix: xylem carries water and minerals to leaf cells; phloem transports sugars from leaf cells.
Saying that spongy mesophyll is tightly packed. Fix: palisade cells are tightly packed and elongated; spongy cells are loosely arranged with air spaces.
Leaving out the purpose of homeostasis after giving its definition. Fix: state that stable conditions allow cells to function properly, and include a suitable example if asked.

explain.title: What biomolecules are
explain.body: The molecules produced by organisms are called biomolecules or biological molecules. They include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). They are mostly large in size and are called macromolecules.

explain.title: Where they are found and what they do
explain.body: Biomolecules occur in different cell locations and have different roles. Carbohydrates provide and store energy; proteins can act as enzymes, form structures, and control cellular traffic; lipids store energy, insulate against heat, and form part of cell membranes. DNA carries genetic information, while RNA carries information from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

explain.title: Biomolecules in dry mass
explain.body: Biomolecules make 93% of the dry mass of protoplasm. The remaining 7% comprises vitamins and inorganic substances. Of the listed biomolecules, proteins make up 50%, nucleic acids 18%, carbohydrates 15%, and lipids 10%.

explain.title: Metabolism
explain.body: All the chemical reactions that occur in an organism are collectively called metabolism. Anabolism combines simpler substances to form complex substances and uses energy. Catabolism breaks complex molecules down into simpler ones and releases energy.

explain.title: Biochemistry and molecular biology
explain.body: Biochemistry is the study of the chemical processes that occur within living organisms. Molecular biology is the study of the structure and function of the biomolecules.

mistakes: Do not confuse anabolism with catabolism: anabolism builds complex substances, while catabolism breaks them down.
Do not say that anabolism releases energy; it uses energy, whereas catabolism releases energy.
Do not mix up the dry-mass percentages: proteins are 50%, nucleic acids 18%, carbohydrates 15%, and lipids 10%.
Do not confuse the role of DNA with that of RNA: DNA carries genetic information, while RNA carries information from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

explain.title: Carbohydrates and their classes
explain.body: “Carbohydrate” means ‘hydrated carbons’. They are the organic compounds in which the ratio of H and O is 2:1 (same as in water). They are also known as “Saccharides” (meaning sugar). They have the general formula Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ where n is the number of carbon atoms. There are three classes of carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.

explain.title: Monosaccharides
explain.body: Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are made of single sugar molecule. They are easily soluble in water and have sweet taste. They may have 3 to 7 carbon atoms. Pentoses (5 C) and hexoses (6 C) are most common. Ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses; glucose, fructose, and galactose are hexoses.

explain.title: Disaccharides and polysaccharides
explain.body: Disaccharides are made of two monosaccharides units. They are less soluble in water and are less sweet in taste. Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose; maltose is made of two glucose molecules. Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharides units. They are insoluble in water and are tasteless. Examples include starch, glycogen, cellulose, and chitin.

explain.title: Sources and functions
explain.body: Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy. Glucose is used by cells to produce energy through cellular respiration. Dietary fibre contains indigestible carbohydrates e.g., cellulose. It helps for the proper bowel movements. Ribose and deoxyribose are essential parts of RNA and DNA respectively. Plants convert monosaccharides to disaccharides like sucrose for transport. Cellulose supports plant cells and ultimately the whole plant.

mistakes: Do not confuse sucrose with maltose: sucrose is glucose plus fructose, while maltose is two glucose molecules.
Do not call starch a disaccharide; it is a polysaccharide.
Do not say all carbohydrates are sweet or soluble: polysaccharides are tasteless and insoluble in water.
When giving a role for cellulose, distinguish its structural support in plants from its role as dietary fibre in bowel movements.
Do not mix up plant starch and animal glycogen: starch is stored in plants, while glycogen is mainly stored in the liver and muscles.

writtenQuestions.text: Discuss the functions of proteins.
modelAnswer: Proteins are an important part of all cell membranes.
Some proteins, such as collagen and keratin, make almost whole structures of cartilage, hair and nails.
Enzymes are proteins that catalyse all biochemical reactions occurring in organisms.
Some proteins are hormones that regulate body processes.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Actin and myosin are the main components of muscle cells and are responsible for muscular contractions.
Fibrin makes blood clot to prevent the loss of blood after an injury.
Antibodies defend the body against harmful pathogens.

explain.title: The amino-acid structure
explain.body: An amino acid is an organic molecule made of an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen group (H) and a side group (R) which are attached to a central carbon atom. The R group varies: glycine has H, while alanine has CH₃.

explain.title: Essential and non-essential amino acids
explain.body: Essential amino acids: These are the 09 amino acids which cannot be synthesized by our body and are supplied by foods. Non-essential amino acids: These are 11 amino acids that can be synthesised in our bodies.

explain.title: Protein sources and functions
explain.body: Good sources include meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses and beans. Proteins form cell membranes and body structures; enzymes catalyse biochemical reactions; some proteins act as hormones; haemoglobin transports oxygen; actin and myosin help muscular contractions; fibrin helps blood clot; and antibodies defend against pathogens.

explain.title: Why lipids matter

explain.title: Nucleotides are the units of nucleic acids
explain.body: Your textbook defines them this way: “Nucleic acids are the biomolecules that are composed of units called nucleotides. A nucleotide is made up of three components:” Those components are pentose sugar, nitrogenous base and phosphate group (PO₄).

explain.title: DNA has a double helix structure
explain.body: “DNA is made of deoxyribonucleotides (de-oxy-ribo-nucleotides).” Its sugar is deoxyribose, and its bases are adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. The two strands coil around each other. A pairs with T, while C pairs with G.

explain.title: DNA carries hereditary information
explain.body: The nucleotide sequence in DNA determines the order of amino acids during protein synthesis. A segment of DNA that determines the synthesis of a protein is called a gene. DNA is also passed from one generation to the next.

explain.title: RNA helps in protein synthesis
explain.body: “RNA is single-stranded. Its strand consists of ribonucleotides.” These contain ribose and may have adenine, uracil, cytosine or guanine. mRNA carries information to ribosomes, tRNA transfers amino acids, and rRNA forms structural and functional parts of ribosomes.

mistakes: Do not mix up the sugars: DNA has deoxyribose, while RNA has ribose.
