steps.why: Start by identifying the two strands and the overall DNA shape.
steps.text: DNA is made of two long nucleotide strands twisted around one another to form a double helix.

steps.why: The backbone and bases describe how each strand is arranged.
steps.text: Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and nitrogenous bases directed towards the inside.

steps.why: Complementary pairing explains how the two strands are held together and how the sequence is matched.
steps.text: The bases on the two strands pair specifically by hydrogen bonds.

steps.why: The first specific complementary pair must be named accurately.
steps.text: Adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T).

steps.why: The second specific pair completes the base-pairing rule.
steps.text: Cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G).

example.question: Q6.5. Explain the double helix structure of DNA, and discuss the base pairing in this structure.
example.answer: DNA consists of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each strand has a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and bases on the inside. Adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine.

explain.title: Carbohydrates
explain.body: Monosaccharides are single sugar units; disaccharides have two joined sugar units; polysaccharides have many. Carbohydrates provide energy, store energy and can build structures such as plant cell walls.

explain.title: Proteins
explain.body: Proteins are made from amino acids. Their functions include structure, growth and repair, enzyme action, transport, defence, movement and blood clotting.

explain.title: Lipids
explain.body: Many fats and oils are triglycerides made from glycerol and three fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.

explain.title: Nucleic acids
explain.body: DNA stores genetic information. Its two strands form a double helix with complementary base pairs A–T and C–G. RNA includes mRNA, tRNA and rRNA and helps make proteins.

explain.title: Water and food
explain.body: Water dissolves and transports substances and provides a medium for cellular reactions. Food nutrient values are estimates and can change with serving size, ingredients and cooking.

mistakes: Do not confuse a single sugar (monosaccharide) with a many-unit polysaccharide.
Do not say humans digest cellulose; it provides structural support in plants and is dietary fibre for humans.
Do not confuse the roles of proteins: haemoglobin transports oxygen, antibodies defend against pathogens, and enzymes help reactions.
Do not describe unsaturated fatty acids as having no double bonds; that describes saturated fatty acids.
Do not swap DNA base pairs: adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine.
When drawing structures, include all required parts and labels; a list of names alone may not earn the drawing marks.
For nutrition comparisons, do not compare values on different serving-size bases without converting them.

recap.question: What is the name of the process in which a DNA nucleotide sequence is copied into mRNA?
recap.answer: Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA sequence; translation uses the mRNA sequence at a ribosome to form a protein.

recap.question: Which statement best describes a gene?
recap.answer: A segment of DNA with a specific nucleotide sequence carrying information for a protein

solutions.question: What are the main functions of carbohydrates in the body?
steps: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy for the body.
They provide energy for the activities of cells and tissues.
Excess carbohydrates are stored in the body for later use.
Some carbohydrates, such as cellulose, provide structural support in plants.
solutions.answer: Carbohydrates provide energy, can be stored for later use, and may have a structural role.

solutions.question: How do the three group of carbohydrates differ in taste?
steps: Monosaccharides and disaccharides are sweet in taste.
Polysaccharides are generally tasteless.
solutions.answer: Monosaccharides and disaccharides are sweet, while polysaccharides are generally tasteless.

solutions.question: Name two common monosaccharides and two disaccharides.
steps: Two common monosaccharides are glucose and fructose.
Two common disaccharides are sucrose and lactose.
solutions.answer: Monosaccharides: glucose and fructose; disaccharides: sucrose and lactose.

solutions.question: Which monosaccharides make a sucrose molecule?
steps: A sucrose molecule is made up of one glucose molecule and one fructose molecule.
solutions.answer: Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose.

solutions.question: Give an example of a storage polysaccharide in plants.
steps: Starch is a storage polysaccharide in plants.
solutions.answer: Starch is a storage polysaccharide in plants.

solutions.question: Define amino acid and draw its structure.
steps: An amino acid is the basic unit of proteins.
Each amino acid has a central carbon atom bonded to an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen atom, and a variable side group (R).
Draw the structure: H₂N–CH(R)–COOH.
solutions.answer: An amino acid is the basic unit of proteins, with the general structure H₂N–CH(R)–COOH.
solutions.figure: Draw a central carbon atom bonded to an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen atom (H), and a variable side group (R). The general structure is H₂N–CH(R)–COOH.

solutions.question: What are the basic components of lipids? Draw their structures.
steps: Lipids are made up of glycerol and fatty acids.
Glycerol has three carbon atoms, each associated with a hydroxyl group (–OH).
Draw glycerol: HO–CH₂–CH(OH)–CH₂–OH.
A fatty acid consists of a long hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl group (–COOH).
Draw a fatty acid: R–COOH, where R represents the long hydrocarbon chain.
solutions.answer: The basic components of lipids are glycerol and fatty acids.
solutions.figure: Draw glycerol as HO–CH₂–CH(OH)–CH₂–OH. Draw a fatty acid as R–COOH, showing a long hydrocarbon chain (R) attached to a carboxyl group (COOH).

solutions.question: What are the types of RNA? Write their functions.
steps: There are three types of RNA: messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
Messenger RNA carries genetic information from DNA to the ribosome.
Transfer RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis.
Ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosomes, where proteins are made.
solutions.answer: mRNA carries genetic information, tRNA carries amino acids, and rRNA forms part of ribosomes.

solutions.question: Briefly describe the function of DNA.
steps: DNA stores hereditary information in the form of genes.
It passes this information from parents to offspring and controls the activities of the cell by directing the synthesis of proteins.
solutions.answer: DNA stores and transmits hereditary information and directs protein synthesis.

solutions.question: Write a comprehensive note on the structures and roles of the three classes of carbohydrates.
steps: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; many have hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2:1.
They are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides according to the number of sugar units.
Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and cannot be broken down into smaller sugars. Examples are glucose, fructose and ribose.
Glucose is an important source of energy for cells; ribose is a component of RNA and ATP.
Oligosaccharides contain a small number of monosaccharide units; disaccharides contain two units joined by a glycosidic bond.
Examples of disaccharides are sucrose (glucose and fructose), maltose (two glucose units) and lactose (glucose and galactose).
Disaccharides provide energy; sucrose is also the main sugar transported in plants.
Polysaccharides are large molecules made of many monosaccharide units joined together.
Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants, while glycogen stores carbohydrate in animals, especially in the liver and muscles.
Cellulose forms plant cell walls and provides structural support; it is not digested by humans.
solutions.answer: The three classes of carbohydrates are monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are single sugar units, such as glucose, fructose and ribose; they provide energy or form parts of other molecules. Oligosaccharides contain a few sugar units; examples include sucrose, maltose and lactose, which provide energy, and sucrose is transported in plants. Polysaccharides contain many sugar units; starch stores food in plants, glycogen stores it in animals, and cellulose provides structural support in plant cell walls.

solutions.question: Discuss the functions of proteins.
steps: Proteins are important components of cell membranes and other cell structures; they help in the growth and repair of body tissues.
Many proteins act as enzymes and speed up chemical reactions in cells.
Some proteins act as hormones and help regulate body functions.
Antibodies are proteins that defend the body against disease-causing organisms.
Some proteins transport substances; for example, haemoglobin transports oxygen in blood.
Proteins can also provide energy when required.
solutions.answer: Proteins perform structural, enzymatic, regulatory, defensive and transport functions, and can also provide energy.

solutions.question: What are fatty acids? Explain their types.
steps: Fatty acids are long chains of carbon and hydrogen atoms with a carboxyl group (–COOH) at one end.
They combine with glycerol to form fats and oils.
Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-to-carbon double bonds and carry the maximum number of hydrogen atoms; they are commonly found in animal fats and are often solid at room temperature.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more carbon-to-carbon double bonds; they are commonly found in plant oils and are often liquid at room temperature.
Unsaturated fatty acids with one double bond are monounsaturated; those with more than one are polyunsaturated.
solutions.answer: Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl group (–COOH) at one end. They combine with glycerol to form fats and oils. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-to-carbon double bonds and are often found in solid animal fats. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds; they are often found in liquid plant oils and may be monounsaturated or polyunsaturated.

solutions.question: Describe the basic structure of fats and oils. Explain how lipids play role in energy storage.
steps: A fat or oil molecule is generally made of one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acid molecules.
The fatty acids are joined to glycerol by ester bonds; such a molecule is called a triglyceride.
Fats and oils are lipids and are insoluble in water.
Lipids store energy in a concentrated form and provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates.
Stored fats can be broken down when the body needs energy.
solutions.answer: Fats and oils are triglycerides made of glycerol and three fatty acids; they serve as concentrated energy stores.

solutions.question: Explain the double helix structure of DNA, and discuss the base pairing in this structure.
steps: A DNA molecule consists of two long polynucleotide strands twisted around each other to form a double helix.
The sugar and phosphate groups form the outer backbone of each strand, while nitrogenous bases face inward.
The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
Adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T), and guanine (G) pairs with cytosine (C).
Thus, the sequence of bases on one strand determines the complementary sequence on the other strand.
solutions.answer: DNA is a double helix with two complementary strands in which A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

solutions.question: Explain how the information in DNA is converted to RNA and then to proteins.
steps: The information for making a protein is present in the sequence of bases in DNA.
During transcription, a complementary messenger RNA (mRNA) copy of the required DNA information is made.
The mRNA carries this information from the nucleus to a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
During translation, the ribosome reads the mRNA code; transfer RNA (tRNA) brings the corresponding amino acids.
The amino acids are joined in the order specified by the mRNA to form a protein.
solutions.answer: DNA information is transcribed into mRNA, which is translated at a ribosome into a protein.

solutions.question: Evaluate the importance of water in the functioning of biomolecules.
steps: Water is a major component of living cells and provides a medium in which many biochemical reactions take place.
Water dissolves many substances, allowing them to be transported within organisms and to take part in reactions.
Water participates in some chemical reactions, including the breakdown of large molecules by hydrolysis.
Its properties help maintain a stable temperature in organisms and their surroundings.
Water is therefore essential for the structure and functioning of cells and biomolecules.
solutions.answer: Water acts as a reaction medium and solvent, supports transport and chemical reactions, and helps maintain stable conditions for biomolecules.

solutions.question: Find the amount/ percentage of carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats and water in the following food product and compare them with each other: Roti(40gm), Burger, Cucumber, Egg, Rice(100gm), Potato fries(100gm),Carrot
steps: The values below are approximate; actual amounts vary with the recipe and method of preparation.
For comparison, foods without a stated weight are taken as 100 g edible portions. Rice is taken as cooked rice, and burger as a typical plain burger.
Roti (40 g): carbohydrates ≈ 19.5 g (48.8%); proteins ≈ 3.8 g (9.5%); fats ≈ 1.5 g (3.8%); water ≈ 14.3 g (35.8%).
Burger (100 g): carbohydrates ≈ 30 g (30%); proteins ≈ 12 g (12%); fats ≈ 10 g (10%); water ≈ 45 g (45%).
Cucumber (100 g): carbohydrates ≈ 3.6 g (3.6%); proteins ≈ 0.7 g (0.7%); fats ≈ 0.1 g (0.1%); water ≈ 95.2 g (95.2%).
Egg, whole (100 g edible portion): carbohydrates ≈ 0.7 g (0.7%); proteins ≈ 12.6 g (12.6%); fats ≈ 9.5 g (9.5%); water ≈ 76.2 g (76.2%).
Cooked rice (100 g): carbohydrates ≈ 28.2 g (28.2%); proteins ≈ 2.7 g (2.7%); fats ≈ 0.3 g (0.3%); water ≈ 68.4 g (68.4%).
Potato fries (100 g): carbohydrates ≈ 41.4 g (41.4%); proteins ≈ 3.4 g (3.4%); fats ≈ 14.1 g (14.1%); water ≈ 39.1 g (39.1%).
Carrot (100 g): carbohydrates ≈ 9.6 g (9.6%); proteins ≈ 0.9 g (0.9%); fats ≈ 0.2 g (0.2%); water ≈ 88.3 g (88.3%).

Comparison: cucumber contains the most water, while roti has the highest carbohydrate percentage among these estimates. Egg is richest in protein by percentage, and potato fries are highest in fat. The burger values can vary considerably with its ingredients.
solutions.answer: Cucumber contains the most water; roti has the highest carbohydrate percentage, egg the highest protein percentage, and potato fries the highest fat percentage among these approximate values.

definitions.text: Biochemistry is the study of the chemical processes that occur within living organisms (e.g., photosynthesis, cellular respiration).
Molecular biology is the study of the structure and function of the biomolecules (e.g., carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids).
The molecules produced by organisms are called biomolecules or biological molecules.
All the chemical reactions that occur in an organism are collectively called metabolism.
Anabolism is the type of metabolism in which simpler substances are combined to form complex substances. Energy is used in these reactions.
Catabolism is the type of metabolism in which complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones. Energy is released in these reactions.
They are the organic compounds in which the ratio of H and O is 2:1 (same as in water).
Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are made of single sugar molecule. They are easily soluble in water and have sweet taste.
They are made of two monosaccharides units. They are less soluble in water and are less sweet in taste.
Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharides units. They are insoluble in water and are tasteless.
They are defined as the polymers of amino acids.
Amino acids are the organic molecules that join in specific number and sequence to make proteins.
Essential amino acids: These are the 09 amino acids which cannot be synthesized by our body and are supplied by foods.
Non-essential amino acids: These are 11 amino acids that can be synthesised in our bodies.
An amino acid is an organic molecule made of an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen group (H) and a side group (R) which are attached to a central carbon atom:
Lipids are organic compounds that are insoluble in water but are soluble in organic solvents (e.g., alcohol, ether, benzene).
Glycerol is an alcohol having 3 carbon atoms. Each carbon has a hydroxyl group.
Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains with carboxyl group (COOH) at the end.
Saturated fatty acids have internal carbon atoms bonded with maximum number of hydrogen atoms. They do not have double bonds between carbon atoms. Saturated fatty acids are solid at room temperature.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds between carbon atoms. They are liquid at room temperature.
Fats and oils are the most familiar lipids. They contain one glycerol and three fatty acids.
Nucleic acids are the biomolecules that are composed of units called nucleotides.
A nucleotide is made up of three components:
The segment of DNA in which the sequence of nucleotides determines the synthesis of a protein (polypeptide chain) is called a gene.
RNA is single-stranded. Its strand consists of ribonucleotides. A ribonucleotide contains ribose sugar instead of deoxyribose.
The process of making mRNA copy of DNA is called transcription.
The ribosome reads this sequence and joins specific amino acids to form a protein. This step is known as translation.

fullMarks: For the three carbohydrate groups, state the number of sugar units first, then solubility and taste; include one correct example if the question asks for structures or roles.
For an amino-acid drawing, show a central carbon attached to NH₂, COOH, H and R, and label all four groups clearly.
For lipid structures, distinguish glycerol from fatty acids; show three fatty acids in fats and oils, but two fatty acids and a phosphate group in a phospholipid.

When explaining fatty-acid types, mention the carbon-to-carbon bonds and the state at room temperature: saturated has no double bonds and is solid; unsaturated has one or more double bonds and is liquid.
For DNA, write the two strands and double-helix arrangement, then state A–T and C–G pairing and the correct hydrogen-bond counts.

mistakes: Mistake: Saying polysaccharides are sweet or water-soluble. Fix: They are tasteless and insoluble in water.
Mistake: Confusing the storage polysaccharides of plants and animals. Fix: Starch is stored in plants; glycogen is mainly stored in the liver and muscles of animals.
Mistake: Drawing an amino acid without its R group or central carbon. Fix: Attach NH₂, COOH, H and R to the same central carbon.
Mistake: Saying saturated fatty acids have double bonds. Fix: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-to-carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.
Mistake: Drawing fats and oils with only two fatty acids. Fix: Show one glycerol and three fatty acids; two fatty acids plus phosphate describes a phospholipid.
Mistake: Pairing adenine with cytosine, or giving the wrong bond count. Fix: A pairs with T using two hydrogen bonds; C pairs with G using three.
Mistake: Mixing up transcription and translation. Fix: Transcription copies DNA information into mRNA; translation uses mRNA at a ribosome to make a protein.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.2: How do the three group of carbohydrates differ in taste?
shortTheory.answer: Monosaccharides have sweet taste. Disaccharides are less sweet in taste. Polysaccharides are tasteless.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.3: Name two common monosaccharides and two disaccharides.
shortTheory.answer: Two common monosaccharides are glucose and fructose. Two disaccharides are sucrose and maltose.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.5: Give an example of a storage polysaccharide in plants.
shortTheory.answer: Starch is a storage polysaccharide found in plants.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.6: Define amino acid and draw its structure.
shortTheory.answer: An amino acid is an organic molecule made of an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen group (H) and a side group (R) which are attached to a central carbon atom. Structure: H₂N—C(H)(R)—COOH.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.8: What are the types of RNA? Write their functions.
shortTheory.answer: Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the genetic information from DNA to the ribosomes during protein synthesis. Transfer RNA (tRNA) transfers specific amino acids to the ribosomes, ensuring the correct sequence during protein synthesis. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) constitutes the structural and functional components of ribosomes, the cellular machinery for protein synthesis.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.9: Briefly describe the function of DNA.
shortTheory.answer: DNA contains the hereditary information. This information is in the form of a sequence of nucleotides. This sequence determines the order of amino acids during protein synthesis. During reproduction, DNA is passed from one generation to the next.

writtenQuestions.text: Define metabolism. Differentiate between catabolism and anabolism.
modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions that occur within an organism to sustain life.
Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones, releasing energy.
Anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and consumes energy.

explain.title: Metabolism
explain.body: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions that occur within an organism to sustain life. It has two subsets: catabolism and anabolism.

explain.title: Catabolism
explain.body: Catabolism involves the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler ones, releasing energy in the process. Cellular respiration and lipolysis are examples.

explain.title: Anabolism
explain.body: Anabolism involves building up complex molecules from simpler ones. This process consumes energy. Photosynthesis and protein synthesis are examples.

mistakes: Do not reverse the definitions: catabolism breaks down, while anabolism builds up.
Do not say that anabolism releases energy; it consumes energy.
When giving an example, make sure it matches the process: lipolysis is catabolism, while protein synthesis is anabolism.
Include the energy change as well as the change in molecules when differentiating the two processes.

explain.title: Enzymes are catalysts
explain.body: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed. They can therefore act as catalysts without becoming the products of the reactions.

explain.title: Enzymes have a particular structure
explain.body: Enzymes are predominantly proteins and have a three-dimensional globular structure. This structure allows them to form active sites that can bind specifically to substrates.

explain.title: Enzymes are specific
explain.body: An enzyme is specific to the reaction it catalyses and to the nature of its substrate. For example, amylase specifically catalyses the breakdown of starch into simple sugars.

explain.title: Enzymes can need cofactors
explain.body: Some enzymes need additional non-protein molecules called cofactors to be fully active. Prosthetic groups bind tightly, while coenzymes bind loosely and may be released during the reaction.

explain.title: Enzymes work in different places and uses
explain.body: Intracellular enzymes operate within cells; extracellular enzymes are secreted outside cells. Enzymes may also work one after another in a reaction sequence and are used in food, paper, detergent, and fermentation industries.

mistakes: Do not say that enzymes are consumed during the reactions they catalyse.
Do not confuse a substrate with an enzyme: the substrate is the molecule that undergoes the enzyme-controlled reaction.
Do not mix up intracellular enzymes, which work within cells, with extracellular enzymes, which are secreted outside cells.
Do not reverse prosthetic groups and coenzymes: prosthetic groups bind tightly; coenzymes bind loosely and may be released.

explain.title: Metabolism has two directions

explain.title: Enzymes are biological catalysts

explain.title: Substrate concentration affects reaction rate

explain.title: Inhibitors reduce enzyme action

solutions.question: Define metabolism. Differentiate between catabolism and anabolism.
steps: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions taking place in the body of an organism.
Catabolism is the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler molecules, releasing energy.
Anabolism is the synthesis of complex molecules from simpler molecules, requiring energy.
solutions.answer: Metabolism includes all chemical reactions in an organism; catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy, while anabolism builds molecules and requires energy.

solutions.question: Which type of metabolism demands input of energy? Give an example.
steps: Anabolism demands an input of energy.
For example, the synthesis of proteins from amino acids is an anabolic reaction.
solutions.answer: Anabolism requires energy; for example, the synthesis of proteins from amino acids.

solutions.question: Define an enzyme. What is its role in metabolism?
steps: An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up in the reaction.
Enzymes regulate and speed up the metabolic reactions in living organisms.
solutions.answer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up metabolic reactions without being used up.

solutions.question: What is the active site of enzyme? State its importance in enzyme specificity.
steps: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
The shape of the active site is complementary to a particular substrate.
This makes an enzyme specific: it acts only on its particular substrate.
solutions.answer: The active site binds a particular substrate, giving the enzyme its specificity.

solutions.question: Provide an example of a specific enzyme-substrate pair.
steps: Amylase acts on starch.
solutions.answer: Amylase and starch.

solutions.question: What is the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity?
steps: As substrate concentration increases, the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases.
The rate reaches a maximum when all the enzyme active sites are occupied.
After this point, adding more substrate does not increase the reaction rate.
solutions.answer: Increasing substrate concentration increases enzyme activity until all active sites are occupied; then the rate remains constant.

solutions.question: Provide two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH.
steps: Pepsin works best in an acidic medium, at about pH 2.
Trypsin works best in an alkaline medium, at about pH 8.
solutions.answer: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2, while trypsin has an optimum pH of about 8.

solutions.question: What do you mean by optimum temperature and pH?
steps: The optimum temperature is the temperature at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.
The optimum pH is the pH at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.
solutions.answer: Optimum temperature and pH are the conditions at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.

solutions.question: Which type of enzyme inhibitors inhibit the enzymes without attaching to the active site?
steps: Non-competitive inhibitors inhibit enzymes without attaching to the active site.
They bind to another part of the enzyme and change the shape of its active site, so the substrate cannot bind properly.
solutions.answer: Non-competitive inhibitors bind away from the active site and alter its shape.

solutions.question: Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibition.
steps: Competitive inhibitors have a shape similar to the substrate and compete with it for the enzyme’s active site.
Their binding prevents the substrate from binding; increasing the substrate concentration can reduce their effect.
Non-competitive inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site.
This changes the shape of the active site and reduces enzyme activity; increasing the substrate concentration does not overcome their effect.
solutions.answer: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site, whereas non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the active site’s shape.

solutions.question: Describe the characteristics of enzymes.
steps: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
Most enzymes are proteins.
Enzymes are specific: each enzyme acts on a particular substrate or catalyses a particular reaction.
They are not used up during reactions and can be used again.
Enzymes work effectively in small amounts.
Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and an optimum pH at which it works fastest.
solutions.answer: Enzymes are specific protein biological catalysts that can be reused and work best at an optimum temperature and pH.

solutions.question: Describe how temperature extremes can inhibit enzyme activity and lead to enzyme denaturation.
steps: At low temperatures, enzyme and substrate molecules move slowly, so fewer successful collisions occur and the reaction rate decreases.
As temperature rises, molecules move faster and the reaction rate increases up to the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
Above the optimum temperature, heat disrupts the bonds that maintain the enzyme’s shape.
The active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits; the enzyme is denatured and its activity decreases or stops.
Very low temperatures usually slow enzyme activity but do not denature the enzyme.
solutions.answer: Low temperatures slow enzyme activity, while high temperatures can denature the enzyme by changing the shape of its active site.

solutions.question: How does pH affect enzyme activity?
steps: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest.
A change in pH from the optimum reduces the enzyme’s activity.
Very high or very low pH can alter the enzyme’s shape, including the active site, so the substrate cannot bind properly.
At extreme pH, the enzyme may be denatured and stop working.
solutions.answer: Enzymes work best at their optimum pH; extreme pH can change the active site and denature the enzyme.

solutions.question: Describe the factors that affect the activity of enzymes.
steps: Temperature: As temperature rises, enzyme activity increases up to an optimum temperature. Above the optimum, the enzyme’s shape changes (it is denatured), so its activity decreases or stops. Low temperature slows enzyme activity.
pH: Each enzyme works best at a particular optimum pH. A pH above or below this value changes the enzyme’s shape and reduces its activity; extreme pH can denature the enzyme.

Substrate concentration: Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate of the enzyme-controlled reaction while enzyme molecules are available. The rate reaches a maximum when all the enzyme molecules are occupied by substrate.
Enzyme concentration: Increasing enzyme concentration increases the reaction rate when sufficient substrate is available, because more enzyme molecules can act on the substrate.
Inhibitors: Inhibitors reduce or stop enzyme activity by interfering with the enzyme’s action.
solutions.answer: Enzyme activity is affected by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration and inhibitors.

solutions.question: Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.
steps: In the Lock-and-Key model, the active site has a fixed shape that exactly fits a particular substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; the reaction occurs and the products are released.
In the Induced Fit model, the active site is not an exact rigid fit before binding.
When the substrate binds, the enzyme changes shape slightly so that the active site fits the substrate more closely.
Both models explain enzyme specificity and the formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.
solutions.answer: The Lock-and-Key model has a fixed active site that fits the substrate, while the Induced Fit model has an active site that changes shape to fit it.

definitions.text: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions that occur within an organism to sustain life.
Catabolism involves the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler ones, releasing energy in the process.
Anabolism involves building up complex molecules from simpler ones. This process consumes energy.
Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed in the process.
Some RNA molecules also act as enzymes. Such RNA is called ribozyme.
Intracellular enzymes operate within cells e.g., enzymes of cellular respiration.
Extracellular enzymes are secreted outside the cells to catalyse reactions e.g., enzymes secreted by the cells of stomach walls into stomach cavity for the digestion of food.
Many enzymes require additional non-protein molecules to be fully active. Such non-protein molecules are called cofactors.
Inorganic cofactors include metal ions like iron and magnesium ions.
Prosthetic groups tightly bind with the enzymes.
Coenzymes loosely bind to the enzyme and may be released during the reaction.
An enzyme has one or more pockets or clefts on its surface. These are called active sites. The active sites are directly involved in catalysis.
Each enzyme works at maximum rate at a specific temperature called optimum temperature.
They show maximum activity at a specific pH, called their optimum pH.

At high substrate concentration, all active sites of the enzymes are occupied. In this condition, any more substrate molecules do not find free active sites. This state is called saturation of active sites and reaction rate does not increase.
Certain substances, called enzyme inhibitors, bind to enzyme and decrease its activity. This phenomenon is known as enzyme inhibition.
Some inhibitors resemble the enzyme’s substrate. They compete with the substrate to attach to the active site of enzyme.
Some enzyme inhibitors do not have similarity to the substrate. They do not attach to the active site of enzyme. Rather, they attach to some other location of enzyme.

definitions.term: Lock and Key Model of Enzyme Action
definitions.text: According to it, the active site of enzyme has a fixed structure. The substrate molecule fits precisely into it to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
According to this model, the active site of enzyme is not rigid. When substrate interacts with the enzyme, its active site is reshaped to perform its function.

A standard comparison question with clear differences in binding sites.
A broad, standard long question that can be answered in organised points.
Tests the temperature curve, loss of structure, and denaturation.

A standard comparison that may require a labelled sequence or diagram.

fullMarks: For metabolism questions, define metabolism first, then clearly contrast breakdown with energy release (catabolism) against building larger molecules using energy (anabolism).
For enzyme characteristics, organise the answer into clear points: protein nature, globular structure, specificity, location of action, cofactors, and examples.
For enzyme-action questions, write the steps in order: substrate meets active site, enzyme-substrate complex forms, reaction occurs, products are released, and the enzyme remains available.
When comparing the two enzyme models, state that the lock-and-key active site has a fixed structure, while the induced-fit active site changes shape when the substrate interacts with it.

For temperature and pH answers, state the effect on enzyme activity and explain why: excess heat disrupts bonds and the globular structure; pH changes can affect ionization of amino acids at the active site.

For graphs, label both axes and show the correct trend: a temperature curve peaks at optimum temperature, a pH curve peaks at optimum pH, and a substrate-concentration curve levels off when active sites are occupied.

For inhibition questions, identify where each inhibitor binds and what happens next: competitive inhibitors block the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the enzyme’s shape.
mistakes: Writing that enzymes are used up in reactions. Fix: state that enzymes speed up reactions without being consumed.
Mixing up catabolism and anabolism. Fix: catabolism breaks complex molecules down and releases energy; anabolism builds complex molecules and consumes energy.
Saying an induced-fit active site is fixed. Fix: explain that it is reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
Claiming that substrate concentration raises the reaction rate forever. Fix: explain that the rate levels off once all active sites are occupied.
Saying high temperature always speeds up an enzyme. Fix: activity rises only up to a point; well above the optimum, heat can denature the enzyme and sharply reduce activity.
Swapping the pH examples. Fix: pepsin works in acidic conditions, while trypsin works in alkaline conditions.
Confusing the binding sites in inhibition. Fix: competitive inhibitors block the active site; non-competitive inhibitors attach elsewhere and change the enzyme’s shape.

shortTheory.question: Define an enzyme. What is its role in metabolism?

shortTheory.question: Give two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH values.
shortTheory.answer: For example, pepsin in stomach works in acidic medium (pH 1.5 to 2.0) while trypsin in small intestine works in alkaline medium (pH 7 to 8).

shortTheory.question: What do you mean by optimum temperature and optimum pH?
shortTheory.answer: Each enzyme works at maximum rate at a specific temperature called optimum temperature. They show maximum activity at a specific pH, called their optimum pH.

shortTheory.answer: Some inhibitors resemble the enzyme’s substrate. They compete with the substrate to attach to the active site of enzyme. explain.title: What ATP is
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “Cells use a special energy currency for their reactions. This currency is a nucleotide called adenosine triphosphate (ATP).” ATP has three subunits: adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.

explain.title: How ATP releases energy
explain.body: The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds. When the outer phosphate bond breaks, inorganic phosphate (Pi) separates, ATP becomes ADP, and energy is released. Breaking one phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.

explain.title: How ATP is made again
explain.body: Cells get energy from the oxidation of food. They use this energy to combine ADP with Pi and form ATP. Your textbook summarizes: “ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and is broken down during energy-consuming processes.”

explain.title: Why ATP is called an energy currency
explain.body: ATP transfers energy between metabolic reactions. A cell can make ATP when energy is available, then break it down when a process needs energy.

mistakes: Do not say that ATP is made of adenine and phosphate only; include ribose and all three phosphate groups.
Do not say the whole ATP molecule breaks apart when energy is released; the outer phosphate bond breaks, forming ADP and Pi.
Do not confuse ATP with ADP: ATP has three phosphate groups, while ADP has two.
Do not omit the energy value or give the wrong unit: the section states about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.

explain.title: What photosynthesis means
explain.body: Your textbook defines photosynthesis as: “Photosynthesis is the synthesis of glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight (and chlorophyll), with oxygen as a by-product.” In simple terms, organisms use light to make food from raw materials.

explain.title: The two phases
explain.body: Photosynthesis has light reactions and dark reactions. Light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. Dark reactions take place in the stroma of the chloroplasts.

explain.title: What happens in the light reactions
explain.body: Chlorophyll absorbs light and releases high-energy electrons. Their energy helps produce ATP. Light also breaks water, releasing oxygen. Electrons and hydrogen ions are used to reduce NADP to NADPH.

explain.title: What happens in the dark reactions
explain.body: Carbon dioxide combines with 5-carbon compounds. The resulting unstable 6-carbon compounds split into 3-carbon compounds. ATP and hydrogen from NADPH help make 3-carbon carbohydrates, which are used to make glucose and regenerate the 5-carbon compounds.

explain.title: Pigments absorb light
explain.body: Your textbook defines pigments as: “Pigments are the substances that absorb visible light. Different pigments absorb light of different wavelengths (colours).” Chlorophyll-a is the main pigment; chlorophyll-b and carotenoids are accessory pigments.

hints: Recall the three stages in order.

yourTurn.question: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
solution: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: glucose is broken into two pyruvic acid molecules, with two ATP and two NADH formed.
When oxygen is available, pyruvic acid moves to the mitochondrial matrix and is converted into acetyl coenzyme-A.
In the Krebs cycle, acetyl coenzyme-A is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide, forming ATP, NADH and FADH₂.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner membranes of mitochondria; electron flow releases energy used to make ATP.
At the end of the chain, electrons and hydrogen ions combine with oxygen to form water.

steps.why: Glycolysis is the first stage and occurs in the cytoplasm.
steps.text: In the first step, glucose (6C) is broken into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C), with two ATPs and two NADH.

steps.why: When oxygen is available, pyruvic acid proceeds from the cytoplasm to the mitochondrial matrix.
steps.text: Pyruvic acid moves to the matrix of mitochondria and is converted into acetyl coenzyme-A, carbon dioxide and NADH.

steps.why: This stage completely oxidizes acetyl coenzyme-A and makes energy-rich compounds.
steps.text: In the Krebs cycle, acetyl coenzyme-A is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide, forming ATP, NADH and FADH₂.

steps.why: This final stage uses electron energy to make ATP and oxygen to form water.
steps.text: On the inner membranes of mitochondria, electrons pass through an electron transport chain and release energy used to make ATP; electrons and hydrogen ions combine with oxygen to form water.

explain.title: Cellular respiration releases energy
explain.body: Organisms get energy by breaking the C-H bonds of food. For this purpose, they carry out the oxidation of food inside cells. This oxidation of food is called cellular respiration. The most common food used by cells to get energy is glucose.

explain.title: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen
explain.body: Cellular respiration occurring in the presence of oxygen is called aerobic respiration. It is the complete oxidation of glucose with maximum release of energy.

explain.title: Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen
explain.body: Cellular respiration that occurs in the absence of oxygen is called anaerobic respiration. In anaerobic respiration, glucose is incompletely oxidized with less amount of energy released.

explain.title: Fermentation has two forms
explain.body: During alcoholic fermentation, pyruvic acid is further broken down into alcohol and CO₂. During lactic acid fermentation in skeletal muscles, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid.

explain.title: Aerobic respiration has three main steps
explain.body: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm. The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. The electron transport chain occurs on the inner membranes of mitochondria and uses released energy to make ATP.

mistakes: Do not confuse aerobic respiration, which occurs in the presence of oxygen, with anaerobic respiration, which occurs in its absence.
Do not say that glycolysis requires oxygen; the section states that oxygen is not required.
Do not mix up fermentation products: yeast forms ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, while skeletal muscles form lactic acid.
Do not put the Krebs cycle in the cytoplasm; it occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
Do not put the electron transport chain in the mitochondrial matrix; it occurs on the inner mitochondrial membranes.
When explaining the electron transport chain, do not omit that oxygen combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

solution: ATP means adenosine triphosphate; ADP means adenosine diphosphate.

ADP gains a phosphate group and energy to become ATP again.
yourTurn.answer: ATP means adenosine triphosphate and ADP means adenosine diphosphate. ATP transfers usable energy for cellular activities; ADP can gain a phosphate group and energy to become ATP again.

example.question: Q8.1. Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
example.answer: ATP is the chief energy currency of cells: it releases usable energy when its terminal phosphate group is removed, and it can be regenerated from ADP.

explain.title: ATP transfers usable energy
explain.body: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) can release usable energy when its terminal phosphate group is removed, forming ADP. Cells use this energy for activities such as movement, active transport and building molecules. ADP can gain phosphate to become ATP again.

explain.title: Photosynthesis stores energy
explain.body: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light. Light reactions take place in thylakoids and split water, releasing oxygen. Dark reactions take place in the stroma and use carbon dioxide and energy-rich products to make glucose.

explain.title: Respiration releases energy
explain.body: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose and transfers some of its energy to ATP. Glycolysis begins in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration continues in mitochondria and produces most ATP through the electron transport chain.

explain.title: Oxygen makes aerobic respiration possible
explain.body: In aerobic respiration, oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain and water forms. Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

explain.title: Anaerobic respiration yields less energy
explain.body: Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and yields a net 2 ATP per glucose. Animal cells produce lactic acid; yeast produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.

Do not say oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide; it is released when water is split.

Do not give 4 ATP as the net yield of anaerobic respiration: the net profit is 2 ATP per glucose.
Do not leave out oxygen from the aerobic respiration equation or put it in the anaerobic definition.
In ATP answers, explain both energy release (ATP to ADP) and regeneration (ADP to ATP).

recap.answer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen.

solutions.question: Write the importance of oxidation-reduction reactions.
steps: Oxidation-reduction reactions involve the transfer of electrons from one substance to another.
These reactions are important in cellular metabolism because they transfer energy during processes such as photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
solutions.answer: Oxidation-reduction reactions transfer electrons and energy during important metabolic processes.

solutions.question: What do ATP and ADP mean? What are the roles of these molecules for the cellular metabolism?
steps: ATP means adenosine triphosphate; ADP means adenosine diphosphate.
ATP and ADP are energy-carrying molecules present in cells.
ATP stores energy and supplies it for cellular activities when it changes into ADP and phosphate.
ADP can be changed back into ATP by adding a phosphate group, using energy released during respiration.
solutions.answer: ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate and ADP for adenosine diphosphate; ATP stores and supplies energy for cellular activities by breaking down into ADP and phosphate, while ADP can be converted back into ATP.

solutions.question: Write down the word equation for photosynthesis.
steps: Carbon dioxide + water —(sunlight and chlorophyll)→ glucose + oxygen
solutions.answer: Carbon dioxide + water —(sunlight and chlorophyll)→ glucose + oxygen

solutions.question: Why is chlorophyll important for photosynthesis?
steps: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy from the Sun.
This light energy is used to carry out photosynthesis.
solutions.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs the light energy needed for photosynthesis.

solutions.question: How is oxygen produced during photosynthesis?
steps: During the light reactions of photosynthesis, water molecules are split using light energy.
Oxygen is released as a by-product of this splitting of water.
solutions.answer: Oxygen is produced when water molecules are split during the light reactions of photosynthesis.

solutions.question: Which organisms carry out photosynthesis? Which cell organelle is responsible for the absorption of light for photosynthesis?
steps: Photosynthesis is carried out by green plants, algae and some bacteria.
Chloroplasts are the cell organelles that absorb light for photosynthesis.
solutions.answer: Green plants, algae and some bacteria carry out photosynthesis; chloroplasts absorb the light.

solutions.question: State the main purpose of cellular respiration?
steps: The main purpose of cellular respiration is to release energy from food, especially glucose, for cellular activities.
solutions.answer: Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose for cellular activities.

solutions.question: State the equation (in words or symbols) for aerobic respiration.
steps: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP)
solutions.answer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP)

solutions.question: Write a brief note on the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration.
steps: Oxygen is used in aerobic respiration to break down glucose completely.
It combines with hydrogen to form water, allowing the release of energy.
Carbon dioxide and water are the end products of aerobic respiration.
solutions.answer: Oxygen enables the complete breakdown of glucose during aerobic respiration, releasing energy and producing carbon dioxide and water.

solutions.question: Define anaerobic and aerobic respiration.
steps: Respiration is the breakdown of food, especially glucose, in cells to release energy.
Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of food in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of food in the absence of oxygen to release energy.
solutions.answer: Respiration is the breakdown of food to release energy; aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen, whereas anaerobic respiration occurs in its absence.

solutions.question: What are the end products of anaerobic respiration in animals and yeast?
steps: In animals, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
solutions.answer: Animals produce lactic acid; yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

solutions.question: How do muscles respond to oxygen deficiency during intense exercise?
steps: During intense exercise, the muscles may not receive enough oxygen for their energy needs.
Muscle cells then respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid.
The accumulation of lactic acid can cause muscle fatigue and cramps.
solutions.answer: When oxygen is deficient, muscles respire anaerobically, producing lactic acid that may cause fatigue and cramps.

solutions.question: List ways in which respiratory energy is used in the body.
steps: Energy from respiration is used for muscle contraction and movement.
It is used for active transport of substances across cell membranes.
It is used to make new molecules and for growth and repair.
It is used in cell division and other activities of cells.
solutions.answer: Respiratory energy powers movement, active transport, synthesis, growth, repair, and cell division.

solutions.question: Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
steps: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the chief energy currency of all cells.
Energy released during respiration is stored in ATP and can be supplied to cellular activities when needed.
When ATP breaks down by hydrolysis into ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and inorganic phosphate, energy is released.
ADP combines with phosphate, using energy, to form ATP again.
solutions.answer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the chief energy currency of all cells; it supplies energy when it breaks down by hydrolysis into ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and phosphate.

solutions.question: Outline the processes involved in photosynthesis?
steps: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts of green cells, where chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
Light energy is converted into chemical energy.
Water molecules are split into hydrogen and oxygen using light energy; oxygen is released.
Hydrogen combines with carbon dioxide to form glucose, storing chemical energy in the food.
The overall process can be represented as: carbon dioxide + water — light and chlorophyll → glucose + oxygen.
solutions.answer: In photosynthesis, chlorophyll absorbs light and converts its energy into chemical energy; water is split into hydrogen and oxygen, oxygen is released, and hydrogen combines with carbon dioxide to form glucose.

solutions.question: Write a note on the intake of carbon dioxide and water by plants
steps: Carbon dioxide enters the leaves from the air through small openings called stomata.
Water is absorbed from the soil by the roots, mainly through root hairs.
The water is transported from the roots to the leaves through xylem vessels.
solutions.answer: Plants take in carbon dioxide through leaf stomata and absorb water through their roots, which transport it to the leaves.

solutions.question: Explain the types and importance of anaerobic respiration.
steps: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen, releasing a small amount of energy.
In yeast, glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide; this process is called alcoholic fermentation.
Alcoholic fermentation is used in baking, because carbon dioxide makes dough rise, and in brewing, to produce alcoholic drinks.
In muscle cells during strenuous exercise, glucose is converted into lactic acid when the oxygen supply is insufficient; this is lactic acid fermentation.
Lactic acid fermentation also occurs in certain bacteria and is used to make yoghurt and other fermented milk products.
solutions.answer: The two types of anaerobic respiration are alcoholic fermentation, in which yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide (used in baking and brewing), and lactic acid fermentation, in which muscle cells or certain bacteria convert glucose into lactic acid (important in strenuous exercise and used to make yoghurt and other fermented milk products).

solutions.question: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
steps: Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen. Glucose is first broken down into pyruvic acid by glycolysis in the cytoplasm; a small amount of ATP and NADH is formed.
Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondrion and is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing carbon dioxide and producing NADH.

Acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix. It is oxidized through a series of reactions; carbon dioxide is released, a small amount of ATP is formed, and NADH and FADH₂ are produced. Oxaloacetate is regenerated so the cycle can continue.
NADH and FADH₂ carry high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Energy from electron transfer is used to make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with hydrogen to form water. Thus, glucose is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide and water, with ATP released.
solutions.answer: In aerobic respiration, glycolysis in the cytoplasm forms pyruvic acid. In the mitochondrion, pyruvic acid is converted to acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle. The Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and forms a small amount of ATP and the electron carriers NADH and FADH₂; these carriers supply electrons to the electron transport chain. Electron transfer drives ATP formation, and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.

solutions.question: Compare the processes of respiration and photosynthesis.
steps: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water.
Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts containing chlorophyll; respiration begins in the cytoplasm and its later stages occur in mitochondria.
Photosynthesis requires light and stores energy in glucose; respiration does not require light and releases energy from glucose.
Photosynthesis occurs in green cells; respiration occurs in all living cells.
Thus, the raw materials and products of the two processes are broadly opposite.
solutions.answer: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts of green cells and requires light to use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, storing energy; respiration occurs in all living cells, begins in the cytoplasm and continues in mitochondria, uses glucose and oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, and releases energy without requiring light.

solutions.question: How does the structure of ATP enable it to store and release energy efficiently?
steps: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) consists of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
Energy is associated with the bonds between its phosphate groups, especially the bond to the terminal phosphate.
When the terminal phosphate is removed by hydrolysis, ATP forms ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and inorganic phosphate, releasing energy for cellular activities.
ADP can be converted back into ATP by the addition of a phosphate group using energy from respiration or photosynthesis.
solutions.answer: ATP’s three phosphate groups allow energy to be stored in their bonds; hydrolysis removes the terminal phosphate to form ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing energy, and energy from respiration or photosynthesis can add the phosphate back.

definitions.text: Bioenergetics is the study of energy transformations in living organisms.
In oxidation, molecule loses electrons.
In reduction, it gains electrons.
Cells use a special energy currency for their reactions. This currency is a nucleotide called adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
Photosynthesis is the synthesis of glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight (and chlorophyll), with oxygen as a by-product.
Pigments are the substances that absorb visible light.
This oxidation of food is called cellular respiration.
Cellular respiration occurring in the presence of oxygen is called aerobic respiration.
Cellular respiration that occurs in the absence of oxygen is called anaerobic respiration.
During anaerobic respiration in bacteria and yeast etc. pyruvic acid is further broken down into alcohol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂. This type of anaerobic respiration is called alcoholic fermentation.

During anaerobic respiration in the skeletal muscles of humans and other animals, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃). This type of anaerobic respiration is called lactic acid fermentation.
It is a coenzyme. One form of this coenzyme also carries phosphate. It is called NADP.

fullMarks: For redox answers, state both electron changes clearly: oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. Then link electron flow to ATP production.

For ATP, give its full name, identify its three parts (adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups), and explain that breaking the outer phosphate bond releases energy while ADP can be joined with Pᵢ to make ATP.
For photosynthesis, write the word or symbol equation first, then describe light reactions in thylakoids and dark reactions in the stroma. Do not say that dark reactions take place only at night.

In a photosynthesis mechanism answer, include chlorophyll absorbing light, electron transport and ATP formation, water splitting and oxygen release, NADPH formation, and carbon dioxide reduction to make glucose.

For respiration, distinguish the processes by oxygen requirement, completeness of glucose oxidation, products, site and energy yield. The chapter’s comparison gives 36 ATP for aerobic and 2 ATP for anaerobic respiration.

For long answers on aerobic respiration, organise the steps in order: glycolysis in cytoplasm; Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. State the main products or outcomes of each.
When drawing a mechanism diagram, use arrows in the correct direction and label the key substances and sites. For written equations, balance the coefficients and include the final products.
mistakes: Writing that oxidation gains electrons or reduction loses electrons. Fix: oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains them.
Saying ATP is made by breaking ATP. Fix: ATP breakdown releases energy; cells make ATP by combining ADP with Pᵢ using energy.
Saying oxygen in photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide. Fix: water is broken during the light reaction and oxygen is released.
Putting light reactions in the stroma or dark reactions on thylakoids. Fix: light reactions occur on thylakoid membranes; dark reactions occur in the stroma.
Mixing up fermentation products. Fix: animal skeletal muscles produce lactic acid; yeast produces ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Describing anaerobic respiration as complete oxidation or assigning it 36 ATP. Fix: it is incomplete oxidation without oxygen and the chapter’s table gives 2 ATP as the net profit.
Listing the aerobic stages without their locations or in the wrong order. Fix: glycolysis—cytoplasm; Krebs cycle—mitochondrial matrix; electron transport chain—inner mitochondrial membrane.

shortTheory.question: Write the importance of oxidation-reduction reactions.
shortTheory.answer: Oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions are fundamental to the metabolism of organisms. In these reactions, electrons are transferred between molecules. This electron flow is essential for generating energy in the form of ATP during processes like cellular respiration and photosynthesis.

shortTheory.question: What do ATP and ADP mean? What are the roles of these molecules for the cellular metabolism?
shortTheory.answer: This currency is a nucleotide called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). In common energy reactions only the outer P-P high-energy bond breaks. When this happens, ATP becomes ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and one Pᵢ is released. Cells store this energy by combining ADP with Pᵢ to form ATP. So, we can summarize that ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and is broken down during energy-consuming processes. In this way ATP transfers energy between metabolic reactions.

shortTheory.question: Why is chlorophyll important for photosynthesis?
shortTheory.answer: Pigments absorb sunlight and convert it into chemical energy for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll-a absorbs light of blue and red wavelengths. When a pigment absorbs light, reactions occur in it and its electrons are released. The high energy electrons pass through electron transport chain and their energy is used for the formation of ATP and for reducing NADP to NADPH.

shortTheory.question: How is oxygen produced during photosynthesis?
shortTheory.answer: Light also breaks water molecule. Oxygen is released while hydrogen atoms give electrons to chlorophyll and become hydrogen ions.

shortTheory.question: Which organisms carry out photosynthesis? Which cell organelle is responsible for the absorption of light for photosynthesis?
shortTheory.answer: Autotrophic organisms (plants, algae, some bacteria) use inorganic raw materials to prepare their organic food. Light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.

shortTheory.question: Define anaerobic and aerobic respiration.
shortTheory.answer: Cellular respiration occurring in the presence of oxygen is called aerobic respiration. Cellular respiration that occurs in the absence of oxygen is called anaerobic respiration.

shortTheory.question: What are the end products of anaerobic respiration in animals and yeast?
shortTheory.answer: During anaerobic respiration in the skeletal muscles of humans and other animals, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃). During anaerobic respiration in bacteria and yeast etc. pyruvic acid is further broken down into alcohol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂.

shortTheory.question: How do muscles respond to oxygen deficiency during intense exercise?
shortTheory.answer: When skeletal muscles of humans work hard (during exercise etc.) but oxygen supply is not sufficient to fulfil the demand, the skeletal muscles carry out anaerobic respiration to get energy.

explain.title: Nutrition and nutrients
explain.body: Nutrition means the processes in which food is prepared or obtained and converted into body substances for growth and energy. Nutrients are the substances required by organism for energy, growth, repair, and maintenance.

explain.title: Mineral nutrients
explain.body: Mineral nutrients are special chemical elements absorbed from soil that are essential for plants to grow. Plants need these materials, in addition to the materials used in photosynthesis, to make other biomolecules.

explain.title: Two groups of minerals
explain.body: The minerals which are required in larger quantities are called macronutrients, for example carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, potassium, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, and magnesium. The minerals which are required in lower quantities are called micronutrients, for example iron, molybdenum, boron, copper, manganese, zinc, chlorine, and nickel.

explain.title: Nitrogen and magnesium
explain.body: Nitrogen is a necessary part of proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. Roots absorb nitrogen in the form of nitrates. Magnesium is part of chlorophyll and activates many plant enzymes; roots absorb it in ionic form (Mg²⁺).

explain.title: Chlorosis
explain.body: A shortage of nitrogen or magnesium can cause chlorophyll to become insufficient and leaves to turn yellow. This yellowing is called chlorosis. The plant moves nitrogen or magnesium from older to younger leaves, so yellowing is seen in old leaves first.

mistakes: Do not swap the definitions: macronutrients are needed in larger quantities; micronutrients are needed in lower quantities.
Do not say that nitrogen is absorbed as magnesium ions; the section says roots absorb nitrogen as nitrates and magnesium as Mg²⁺.
Do not describe magnesium as only an enzyme activator; it is also a component of chlorophyll.
Use chlorosis for yellowing due to insufficient chlorophyll, not as the name for a mineral nutrient.

yourTurn.question: Differentiate between: i. Xylem and phloem
solution: Xylem transports water and salts.
Phloem transports food.
yourTurn.answer: Xylem transports water and salts; phloem transports food.

hints: Begin with the root hairs and say how they absorb salts and water.
Then trace the route through the root tissues to the xylem.
yourTurn.question: Explain the internal structure of root and describe the uptake of salt and water by root.
solution: The epidermis is the outermost covering of the root and is a single layer of cells.
Many epidermal cells have root hairs that extend into the spaces among soil particles.
Root hairs have a large surface area and are in direct contact with soil water.
Root hairs take in more salts by active transport.
Water moves from soil to root hairs by osmosis because the soil water has a lower concentration of salts than the root hairs.
Water with dissolved salts moves from the root hairs to the other cells of the epidermis, then through the cortex, endodermis and pericycle.
Water from the pericycle moves into the root xylem, from where it is transported to the xylem of the stem.
yourTurn.answer: Root hairs absorb salts by active transport and water by osmosis. Water and dissolved salts pass through the epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle into the xylem.

steps.why: Root hairs are the first structures to contact soil water and their large surface area helps absorption.

example.question: Explain the internal structure of root and describe the uptake of salt and water by root.

explain.title: The transport tissues
explain.body: In all land plants except mosses and liverworts, xylem and phloem carry materials. Xylem transports water and salts, while phloem transports food.

explain.title: Passive transport
explain.body: Passive Transport: It is the movement of ions or molecules across cell membrane from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. This movement does not require energy. Diffusion and osmosis are examples of passive transport.

explain.title: Active transport
explain.body: Active Transport: It is the movement of ions or molecules across cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, using energy. Root hairs take in more salts by active transport.

explain.title: Osmosis
explain.body: Osmosis: It is the movement of water molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration. This movement does not require energy. In the root, water moves from soil into root hairs by osmosis.

explain.title: The route through a root
explain.body: Root hairs take in water and salts from the soil. Water passes through the epidermis and cortex to the endodermis, then to the pericycle and into the xylem.

mistakes: Do not swap the roles of xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and salts; phloem transports food.
Do not say salts enter root hairs by osmosis; the section says salts enter by active transport.
Do not say water enters root hairs by active transport; it enters by osmosis.
Do not leave out the route through cortex, endodermis and pericycle in a long answer.
Do not stop the route at the pericycle; state that water moves into the xylem.

steps.why: Potassium uptake raises the solute concentration in the guard cells.
steps.text: During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport.

steps.why: The higher solute concentration draws water into the guard cells by osmosis.
steps.text: Water moves from epidermal cells into guard cells by osmosis.

steps.why: Turgid guard cells bend so that their inner sides move apart.
steps.text: The guard cells become turgid; their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens.

steps.why: In the evening, the change in potassium ions and glucose concentration leads to water leaving the guard cells.
steps.text: Potassium ions move back to epidermal cells, and water moves out of the guard cells.

steps.why: When guard cells lose turgor, their inner sides touch and close the opening.
steps.text: The guard cells lose turgor, their inner sides touch and the stoma closes.

example.question: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
example.answer: During daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells, water follows by osmosis and the turgid guard cells open the stoma. In the evening, potassium ions and water leave the guard cells; they lose turgor and the stoma closes.

explain.title: What transpiration means
explain.body: The loss of water in the form of vapours from plant surface is called transpiration. Water can leave through stomata in leaves, the cuticle on the leaf epidermis, or lenticels in the stems of some plants.

explain.title: How water vapour leaves a leaf
explain.body: Water moves from xylem into the cell walls of mesophyll cells. It evaporates from the moist walls into the leaf’s air spaces, then moves towards the stomata and passes into the outside air. Most transpiration occurs through stomata and is called stomatal transpiration.

explain.title: How stomata open and close
explain.body: Stomata open and close because the turgor pressure of their guard cells changes. In daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells by active transport; water follows by osmosis, making the guard cells turgid and opening the stoma. In the evening, potassium ions move back to epidermal cells and water leaves, so the guard cells lose turgor and the stoma closes.

explain.title: Why transpiration matters and what affects it
explain.body: Transpiration is a necessary evil: it creates a pull on water columns in the xylem, helping transport water and salts from roots to leaves. Higher temperature and wind increase transpiration, while higher humidity lowers it. Leaves with more surface area transpire more, and in most plants the lower leaf surface transpires more because it has more stomata.

mistakes: Do not say that guard cells open because water leaves them; water enters them by osmosis during daytime, making them turgid.
Do not reverse the evening events: potassium ions and water move out of guard cells, and the stoma closes.
Do not write that humidity increases transpiration; higher humidity lowers its rate.
Do not give only the effect of temperature or wind: include the reason given in the section.
Do not confuse transpiration with only stomatal water loss; water can also leave through the cuticle and lenticels.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

steps.why: The upward movement in the leaf creates tension throughout the connected column.

example.question: How does water lost from a leaf result in water being pulled upwards through the plant?
example.answer: Water loss from mesophyll cells draws more water from the xylem. Movement in the leaf xylem creates tension in the continuous water column, pulling the whole column upwards.

explain.title: What is transpirational pull?
explain.body: Roots cannot push absorbed water to the leaves. Transpiration from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force on water in the roots, called transpirational pull.

explain.title: How does the pull reach the roots?
explain.body: A continuous water column extends through xylem from leaves to stem to roots. When water moves up in the leaf xylem, it creates tension in the entire column, which is pulled upwards.

explain.title: Why does the water column stay continuous?
explain.body: The section gives three reasons: attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels, and adhesion of water molecules to the walls of xylem vessels.

explain.title: The route of water
explain.body: Water is pulled upwards through xylem from roots, through the stem, and towards the leaves. Water lost by mesophyll cells is replaced by water entering from xylem vessels.

mistakes: Do not say that roots push the absorbed water upwards; the section says leaves apply the pulling force.

Do not describe the water column as moving downwards; the tension pulls it upwards.

writtenQuestions.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

steps.why: Sucrose is loaded into phloem at the site supplying food.
steps.text: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.

steps.why: The increased solute concentration causes water to enter the sieve tubes.
steps.text: Water flows into sieve tubes from nearby xylem by osmosis.

steps.why: Water entering the sieve tubes raises their fluid pressure and pushes food solution along.

steps.why: Unloading food and water at the sink lowers pressure there, maintaining flow from source to sink.

explain.title: What is translocation?
explain.body: “We know that inside the plant body, food is transported from one part to the other through phloem tissue.” This movement of food is called translocation. In most plants, glucose is converted into sucrose for transport.

explain.title: Sources and sinks
explain.body: “The sources include photosynthetic tissues (e.g. mesophyll of leaves) and storage tissues (e.g. roots). Sinks include the sites of food utilization (e.g. growing tips of roots and stems) and the storage tissues.” A source supplies food; a sink uses or stores it.

explain.title: Pressure flow mechanism
explain.body: “The mechanism of the transport of food in plants is called pressure flow mechanism.” At the source, sucrose loading causes water to enter the sieve tubes by osmosis, raising fluid pressure.

explain.title: Food moves towards the sink
explain.body: “Due to higher fluid pressure at the source than the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.” At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water moves into the xylem, lowering the pressure.

explain.title: Xylem and phloem differ
explain.body: “Xylem is a one-way passage for water and salts (from roots to leaves). Phloem is a two-way passage for food.” Food direction depends on supply and demand at sources and sinks.

mistakes: Do not say that food travels in xylem; food is transported through phloem.
Do not describe phloem as one-way; it is a two-way passage, with movement depending on sources and sinks.
Do not mix up active transport and osmosis: sucrose is actively transported, while water moves by osmosis.
Do not say water enters the sieve tubes at the sink; at the sink, water moves from sieve tubes into the xylem.
Do not leave out the pressure difference: higher pressure at the source drives bulk flow towards the sink.
