yourTurn.question: Describe the process of gaseous exchange in plants
solution: Gaseous exchange in plants occurs through the body surface.
The epidermis of roots, stems and leaves allows gases to exchange between the inner cells and the environment; a thick cuticle over some parts also allows exchange.
In leaves and young stems, gases move in and out through stomata; inside the plant body, gases are exchanged between cells and air.
In woody stems, bark does not allow gaseous exchange, so special pores called lenticels allow exchange with the environment.
During daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
yourTurn.answer: Gases exchange through the plant surface; leaves and young stems use stomata, while woody stems use lenticels. During daytime leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

hints: Find the pore type named for woody stems.
Stomata are in leaves and young stems; lenticels are in bark.
yourTurn.question: Differentiate between: v. Lenticular transpiration and stomatal transpiration
solution: Stomatal transpiration occurs through stomata, mainly in leaves and young stems.
Lenticular transpiration occurs through lenticels present in the bark of woody stems.
yourTurn.answer: Stomatal transpiration occurs through stomata in leaves and young stems; lenticular transpiration occurs through lenticels in the bark of woody stems.

steps.text: Gaseous exchange in plants occurs through the body surface.

steps.why: This identifies the openings used in leaves and young stems.

steps.why: Woody stems have bark, so the answer must name the special pores that allow exchange there.

example.question: Describe the main routes of gaseous exchange in a plant and state how gas exchange differs during day and night.
example.answer: Plants exchange gases through their surfaces. Leaves and young stems use stomata, while woody stems use lenticels. During daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen; at night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Gas exchange changes between day and night
explain.body: During the daytime, all plant cells carry out cellular respiration while green parts also carry out photosynthesis. In photosynthesis, they use carbon dioxide and release oxygen. At night, photosynthesis does not occur, but respiration continues: plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Plant surfaces allow gases to pass
explain.body: “In plants, the gaseous exchange between body and the environment occurs through the surface.” The epidermis of roots, stems and leaves allows exchange between inner cells and the environment. A thick cuticle over some parts also allows gas exchange.

explain.title: Stomata serve leaves and young stems
explain.body: “In leaves and young stems, the air moves in and out through the stomata present in epidermis.” Inside the plant body, gaseous exchange occurs between cells and air.

explain.title: Lenticels serve woody stems
explain.body: “In woody stems, the entire surface is covered by bark. Gaseous exchange cannot occur through bark.” Special pores in the bark, called lenticels, allow gaseous exchange with the environment.

mistakes: Do not say that photosynthesis continues at night; respiration continues, but there is no photosynthesis.
Do not confuse stomata with lenticels: stomata occur in leaves and young stems, while lenticels occur in woody-stem bark.
Do not write that gases pass through the bark itself; the bark does not allow gaseous exchange.
When describing daytime exchange, state both directions: carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves.
When describing nighttime exchange, state both directions: oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves.

recap.question: Why does food flow from the source towards the sink?

steps.why: Guttation releases liquid water as droplets, unlike transpiration, which removes water as vapour.
steps.text: In guttation, water leaves as droplets.

steps.why: The location of the small pores is a defining feature given for guttation.
steps.text: The droplets pass through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves.

steps.why: Dew is formed outside the leaf by condensation, so it is not guttation.
steps.text: Water droplets formed by condensation of water vapour from the air are dew, not guttation.

example.question: A student sees water droplets at the tips of a grass plant's leaves at night. Explain whether this is guttation or dew.
example.answer: It is guttation if the droplets are released through pores at the leaf tips; dew forms by condensation of water vapour from the air on the leaf surface.

explain.title: Extra gases
explain.body: During the day, plants use the carbon dioxide produced in cellular respiration for photosynthesis. At night, when photosynthesis is not occurring, carbon dioxide becomes a waste product. Plants release this excess carbon dioxide through their general surfaces and stomata. Excess oxygen from photosynthesis is released into the atmosphere through the stomata.

explain.title: Extra water
explain.body: Plants remove extra water in two ways. During the day, they remove it by transpiration, which may be stomatal, cuticular or lenticular. Some plants, such as grasses, use guttation at night: water droplets pass through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves.

explain.title: Guttation is not dew
explain.body: Guttation is water released from a plant through pores at leaf tips or edges. Dew means the water drops on the surface of leaves formed by the condensation of water vapours present in the air.

explain.title: Other metabolic wastes
explain.body: Some plants store wastes as harmless crystals or keep them in leaves that later fall. Some excrete wastes through special pores by applying force. Rubber plants excrete latex, Acacia (keekar) trees excrete gums, coniferous trees excrete resins, and ladyfinger excretes mucilage.

mistakes: Do not say that guttation and dew are the same: guttation is released through leaf pores, but dew forms by condensation of water vapour in the air.
Do not confuse the examples: rubber plant excretes latex, keekar excretes gum, coniferous trees excrete resin, and ladyfinger excretes mucilage.
When describing guttation, include that droplets pass through pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Do not write that plants remove all extra water only by transpiration; some plants also use guttation.

yourTurn.answer: Hydrophytes live in freshwater or wet soil and absorb water through their whole surface. Xerophytes live in extremely dry environments and have deep roots, few stomata, and a thick waxy cuticle; some store water in succulent organs.

steps.why: The habitat tells us which plant type the example describes.
steps.text: A cactus lives in an extremely dry environment, so it is a xerophyte.

steps.text: It has deep roots to absorb water from almost dry soil.

steps.why: A thick cuticle and few stomata reduce water loss.
steps.text: Its body surface has very few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle.

steps.text: It may store water in a soft, juicy specialized stem or root called a succulent organ.

example.question: Explain how a cactus is adapted to live in an extremely dry environment.
example.answer: A cactus is a xerophyte. It has deep roots to absorb water from almost dry soil, very few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle to reduce water loss, and it may store water in succulent organs.

explain.title: Mesophytes live in moderate conditions
explain.body: “Mesophytes are the terrestrial plants which are adapted to survive in moderate environment that are neither too dry nor too wet.” They have well-developed roots and a cuticle, and they can keep stomata closed to reduce water loss.

explain.title: Hydrophytes live in wet places
explain.body: “Hydrophytes live in freshwater (ponds, and lakes etc.) or in wet soil.” They absorb water through their whole surface. Many have broad floating leaves with many upper-surface stomata, through which extra water moves out.

explain.title: Xerophytes cope with dry places
explain.body: “Xerophytes live in extremely dry environments (deserts).” Deep roots help them absorb water from almost dry soil. Few stomata and a thick waxy cuticle reduce water loss. Some store water in succulent organs.

explain.title: Halophytes cope with salty places
explain.body: “Halophytes live in habitats with salty waters (e.g. sea or salty marshes).” Water tends to move out of their hypotonic bodies into the hypertonic environment. They absorb salts to make their bodies hypertonic, so water does not move out of their cells. Excess salt can be stored in cells or excreted through salt glands on leaves.

mistakes: Do not mix up hydrophytes, which live in freshwater or wet soil, with halophytes, which live in salty habitats.
Do not say xerophytes have many stomata; the section says their body surface has very few stomata.
Do not call a succulent organ a leaf; it is a specialized stem or root that stores water.
Do not say halophytes absorb salts to make water leave their cells. The salt adjustment makes their bodies hypertonic so water does not move out.
When describing hydrophytes, include the upper surfaces of broad floating leaves as the location of many stomata.

recap.question: How is guttation different from dew formation?

steps.why: Sugar loading at the source begins the pressure-flow process.
steps.text: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is loaded into the phloem.

steps.why: More sucrose lowers the phloem's water potential, drawing water into it.
steps.text: Water enters the phloem from nearby xylem by osmosis.

steps.why: Water entry creates the pressure needed to move phloem sap.
steps.text: The entry of water raises the pressure in the phloem at the source.

steps.why: The pressure difference drives dissolved food from the source to a sink.
steps.text: Phloem sap moves down the pressure gradient towards a sink.

steps.why: Removing sugar and water at the sink helps maintain the pressure difference.
steps.text: At the sink, sucrose is unloaded for use or storage and water moves out of the phloem.

steps.why: A labelled schematic makes the source-to-sink direction clear in a board answer.
steps.text: Diagram description: Draw a leaf labelled source connected by a phloem tube to a root or fruit labelled sink; show sucrose loading and water entering from xylem at the source, pressure-driven flow towards the sink, and sucrose unloading with water leaving at the sink.

example.question: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism.
example.answer: At the source, sucrose loading draws water into phloem from xylem by osmosis. This creates high pressure, which drives phloem sap towards a sink. Sucrose is unloaded at the sink and water moves out, maintaining the pressure gradient.

explain.title: Mineral nutrition
explain.body: Plants need mineral elements for growth and life processes. Macronutrients are needed in large amounts, while micronutrients are needed in small amounts. Nitrogen helps plants make amino acids and proteins; magnesium is needed for chlorophyll.

explain.title: Roots absorb water and minerals
explain.body: Root hairs provide a large surface area for absorption. Water enters root cells by osmosis, while mineral ions are absorbed mainly by active transport. The ions and water move through root tissues towards the xylem.

explain.title: Transpiration and stomata
explain.body: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial parts of a plant. Guard cells regulate the stomatal pore. When guard cells take up water they become turgid and open the pore; when they lose water they become flaccid and close it.

explain.title: Transport through xylem and phloem
explain.body: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral salts from roots towards leaves, helped by transpiration pull. Phloem carries food, mainly sucrose, from sources to sinks. In pressure flow, sugar loading draws water into phloem and creates pressure for flow.

explain.title: Gaseous exchange and excretion
explain.body: Gases move mainly by diffusion through stomata and lenticels. Plants can remove extra water by transpiration and guttation, store wastes in tissues that are shed, and release wastes as gums, resins or latex.

mistakes: Do not confuse osmosis with active transport: osmosis moves water across a selectively permeable membrane, while active transport moves substances using energy.
Do not say that phloem carries water from roots to leaves as its main job; that is the main role of xylem.
Do not describe transpiration and guttation as the same: transpiration loses water vapour, while guttation releases liquid droplets.
When explaining stomatal movement, do not stop at saying guard cells open and close; include water movement and the change between turgid and flaccid states.
Do not claim that high humidity increases transpiration. It lowers the water-vapour gradient and usually reduces transpiration.
In pressure flow, do not say that food moves because of gravity; explain the pressure gradient from source to sink.

recap.question: Why do halophytes absorb salts?
recap.answer: A halophyte absorbs salts to make its body hypertonic, so water does not move out of its cells.

recap.question: Which description best identifies a mesophyte?
recap.answer: A plant adapted to moderate conditions

solutions.question: Define mineral nutrition in plants.
steps: Mineral nutrition is the process by which plants absorb and use mineral nutrients for their growth and development.
solutions.answer: Mineral nutrition is the absorption and use of mineral nutrients by plants for growth and development.

solutions.question: Define macronutrients and micronutrients and give examples.
steps: Macronutrients are mineral nutrients required by plants in large amounts.
Examples of macronutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
Micronutrients are mineral nutrients required by plants in very small amounts.
Examples of micronutrients are iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum and chlorine.
solutions.answer: Macronutrients are needed in large amounts, while micronutrients are needed in very small amounts; nitrogen and magnesium are examples of macronutrients, and iron and zinc are examples of micronutrients.

solutions.question: State the roles of nitrogen and magnesium in plants.
steps: Nitrogen is needed for the formation of proteins and other important compounds in plants.
Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and is therefore essential for photosynthesis.
solutions.answer: Nitrogen is needed to form proteins, while magnesium is a component of chlorophyll.

solutions.question: Define transpiration and its types.
steps: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
The three types of transpiration are stomatal transpiration, cuticular transpiration and lenticular transpiration.
Stomatal transpiration occurs through stomata, cuticular transpiration through the cuticle, and lenticular transpiration through lenticels.
solutions.answer: Transpiration is water loss as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant; its types are stomatal, cuticular and lenticular transpiration.

solutions.question: How is the transpirational pull important in plants?
steps: Transpirational pull is the suction force produced by transpiration from the leaves.
It helps in the upward movement of water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to the leaves through the xylem.
solutions.answer: Transpirational pull helps transport water and dissolved mineral salts upward from the roots to the leaves.

solutions.question: Transpiration is the loss of water from plants. Is it a harmful phenomenon? If no, what is its importance?
steps: No, transpiration is not wholly harmful; it is an important process in plants.
It produces transpirational pull, which helps in the upward transport of water and dissolved mineral salts from roots to leaves.
It also helps cool the plant.
solutions.answer: Transpiration is important because it aids the upward transport of water and mineral salts and cools the plant.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: i. Xylem and phloem
steps: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to the aerial parts of the plant.
Phloem transports prepared food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Xylem tissue is mainly made up of dead cells, whereas phloem tissue is mainly made up of living cells.
solutions.answer: Xylem transports water and minerals upward and is mainly made of dead cells; phloem transports food and is mainly made of living cells.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: ii. Transpiration and guttation
steps: Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant in the form of water vapour; guttation is the loss of water in the form of liquid droplets.
Transpiration occurs mainly through stomata, and also through the cuticle and lenticels; guttation occurs through hydathodes, usually at the edges or tips of leaves.
Transpiration usually occurs during the day, whereas guttation commonly occurs at night or early in the morning.
Transpiration is caused by evaporation of water, whereas guttation is caused by root pressure.
solutions.answer: Transpiration is loss of water vapour mainly through stomata, while guttation is loss of liquid water through hydathodes, usually due to root pressure.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: iii. Hydrophytes and halophytes
steps: Hydrophytes are plants that grow in water or in waterlogged places; halophytes are plants that grow in salty soils or water.
Hydrophytes have little or no need to conserve water, whereas halophytes have adaptations that help them live in salty surroundings.
Floating hydrophytes commonly have stomata on the upper surface of their leaves; halophytes may remove excess salts through special glands.
solutions.answer: Hydrophytes grow in water, whereas halophytes grow in salty habitats and have adaptations to tolerate or remove excess salt.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: iv. Hydrophytes and xerophytes
steps: Hydrophytes are plants adapted to live in water or waterlogged places; xerophytes are plants adapted to live in dry habitats.
Hydrophytes generally have reduced roots and supporting tissues, while xerophytes commonly have well-developed roots to absorb water from dry soil.
Hydrophytes may have thin or absent cuticles; xerophytes have adaptations such as a thick cuticle and reduced leaves to reduce water loss.
Floating hydrophytes commonly have stomata on the upper surface of their leaves; xerophytes usually have fewer or sunken stomata.
solutions.answer: Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic habitats, whereas xerophytes are adapted to dry habitats and conserve water.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: v. Lenticular transpiration and stomatal transpiration
steps: Stomatal transpiration is the loss of water vapour through stomata, mainly in leaves.
It is the chief type of transpiration and its rate is regulated by the opening and closing of stomata.
Lenticular transpiration is the loss of water vapour through lenticels in woody stems.
It occurs continuously and is not regulated by guard cells.
solutions.answer: Stomatal transpiration occurs through stomata and is regulated by guard cells; lenticular transpiration occurs through stem lenticels and is continuous.

solutions.question: How do the plants of rubber and keekar excrete their wastes?
steps: The rubber plant excretes its waste in the form of latex.
Keekar excretes wastes in the form of gum.
solutions.answer: Rubber excretes latex, while keekar excretes gum.

solutions.question: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
steps: When guard cells absorb water by osmosis, they become turgid and their curved walls bend away from each other.
The stomatal pore opens, allowing gaseous exchange and the loss of water vapour.
When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid and their walls move towards each other.
The stomatal pore closes, reducing the loss of water vapour.
solutions.answer: Stomata open when guard cells become turgid and close when they become flaccid.

solutions.question: Explain the internal structure of root and describe the uptake of salt and water by root.
steps: The outermost layer of a root is the epidermis. Some epidermal cells grow out to form root hairs, which increase the surface area for absorption.
Inside the epidermis is the cortex, made of loosely arranged cells with spaces between them. Water and dissolved mineral salts pass through the cortex towards the centre of the root.
The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex and surrounds the vascular tissues.
Just inside the endodermis is the pericycle. The vascular tissues, xylem and phloem, are present in the central part of the root.
Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis, moving from a region of higher water concentration in the soil to a region of lower water concentration in the cell sap.
Mineral salts are absorbed from the soil as ions. Root cells take up many mineral ions by active transport, using energy.
Water and mineral ions pass through the root tissues to the xylem. The xylem transports them upwards to the stem and leaves.
solutions.answer: The root has an epidermis with root hairs, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and central xylem and phloem; root hairs absorb water by osmosis and mineral ions mainly by active transport, and the xylem carries them upwards.

solutions.question: Describe temperature, wind and humidity as the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
steps: Temperature: An increase in temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and usually increases the rate of transpiration.
Wind: Wind removes the moist air surrounding a leaf, maintaining a steep water-vapour gradient and increasing transpiration.
Humidity: High humidity reduces the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air, so transpiration decreases; low humidity increases it.
solutions.answer: Higher temperature and wind generally increase transpiration, while higher humidity decreases it.

solutions.question: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
steps: Root hairs absorb water from the soil by osmosis and mineral salts by absorption, often involving active transport.
Water and dissolved mineral salts move through the root tissues and enter the xylem.
The xylem carries water and salts upwards from the roots to the stem and leaves.
Evaporation of water from the leaves creates a transpiration pull that draws water upwards through the xylem.
Cohesion between water molecules and their adhesion to the xylem walls help maintain the continuous water column.
Root pressure also helps push water upwards through the xylem.
solutions.answer: Water and mineral salts enter the root and move upwards through the xylem, aided mainly by transpiration pull and also by root pressure.

solutions.question: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
steps: Food, mainly sucrose, is transported through the phloem from a source, such as a leaf where food is made, to a sink, such as a growing or storage part of the plant.
At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes of the phloem from surrounding cells.
The increased concentration of sucrose in the phloem lowers its water potential.
Water enters the phloem from the nearby xylem by osmosis.
The entry of water produces high pressure in the phloem at the source.
At the sink, sucrose is unloaded from the phloem and is used or stored. This raises the water potential of the phloem there.
Water moves out of the phloem and returns to the xylem, creating lower pressure at the sink.
The pressure difference between the source and the sink drives the movement of phloem sap along the sieve tubes from source to sink. This is called the Pressure Flow Mechanism.
solutions.answer: Sugar loading at the source causes water to enter the phloem by osmosis and builds pressure; sugar unloading at the sink causes water to leave and lowers pressure, so the pressure difference drives food through the phloem from source to sink.

solutions.question: How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
steps: Plants lose extra water mainly by transpiration through the stomata of leaves.
Liquid water may also be removed as droplets through hydathodes at the margins or tips of leaves; this process is called guttation.
Excess salts and other wastes may be stored in leaves, bark or fruits, which are later shed.
Some plants also remove wastes in substances such as gums, resins and latex.
solutions.answer: Plants remove extra water by transpiration and guttation, and get rid of salts and other wastes by storing or secreting them and shedding waste-containing parts.

solutions.question: Describe the process of gaseous exchange in plants
steps: Plants have no specialised respiratory organs; gases are exchanged mainly by diffusion through stomata in leaves, lenticels in woody stems and the surface of roots.
Air enters the leaf through open stomata and diffuses through the intercellular spaces to and from the mesophyll cells.
During photosynthesis, carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf and oxygen diffuses out; during respiration, oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide is released.
Guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomata, helping control gaseous exchange and water loss.
Roots exchange gases with the air spaces between soil particles; oxygen diffuses into the roots and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
solutions.answer: Plants exchange gases by diffusion through stomata, lenticels and root surfaces. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves during photosynthesis; respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Guard cells regulate stomatal opening.

solutions.question: Describe the mechanisms/adaptations in plants for excretion of wastes.
steps: Plants do not have specialised excretory organs; wastes are removed or stored in different ways.
Gaseous wastes diffuse out through stomata in leaves and lenticels in stems.
Extra water is lost by transpiration and may also be removed by guttation through hydathodes.
Some wastes are stored in vacuoles or in leaves, bark and old xylem.
Wastes such as gums, resins and latex may be secreted.
Waste-containing leaves and bark are shed, removing the stored wastes from the plant.
solutions.answer: Plants excrete wastes by diffusion, water loss, secretion and storage in parts that are later shed.

solutions.question: Explain osmotic adjustments in in hydrophytes, xerophytes and halophytes.
steps: Osmotic adjustment is the adjustment of the solute concentration of cells to help a plant absorb or retain water in its habitat.
Hydrophytes live in abundant water. Their cells generally have dilute cell sap and do not need a high solute concentration to absorb water.
Xerophytes live in dry habitats. They maintain a concentrated cell sap, which lowers the water potential of their cells and helps them absorb and retain water.
Halophytes live in soils with a high salt concentration. They accumulate salts, especially in cell vacuoles, or produce other dissolved solutes in their cells.
This raises the solute concentration of halophyte cells and helps them take up water from salty soil while limiting the harmful effects of salts in the cytoplasm.
solutions.answer: Hydrophytes generally have dilute cell sap, xerophytes maintain concentrated cell sap to absorb and retain water, and halophytes accumulate salts in vacuoles or other solutes to take up water from salty soil.

solutions.question: Why do plants transpire more on a windy day compared to a humid one?
steps: Wind removes the moist layer of air that collects around the surface of leaves.
This maintains a steep difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the surrounding air, so water vapour diffuses out faster.
Humid air already contains much water vapour, so the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air is smaller.
Therefore, transpiration is generally faster on a windy day than on a humid day.
solutions.answer: Wind increases transpiration by removing moist air around leaves, while humid air reduces the water-vapour gradient and slows it.

definitions.text: Nutrition means the processes in which food is prepared or obtained and converted into body substances for growth and energy.
Nutrients are the substances required by organism for energy, growth, repair, and maintenance.
Such materials are called mineral nutrients. These are special chemical elements absorbed from soil that are essential for the plants to grow.
The minerals which are required in larger quantities are called macronutrients e.g. carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, potassium, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, and magnesium.
The minerals which are required in lower quantities are called micronutrients e.g. iron, molybdenum, boron, copper, manganese, zinc, chlorine, and nickel.
Transport means the movement of substances such as water, nutrients, hormones, and waste products within an organism.
It is the movement of ions or molecules across cell membrane from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. This movement does not require energy.
It is the movement of ions or molecules across cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, using energy.
It is the movement of water molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration. This movement does not require energy.
The loss of water in the form of vapours from plant surface is called transpiration.
The pulling force in leaves is created by the transpiration of water from their surfaces. Therefore, it is called transpirational pull.
According to pressure flow mechanism, dissolved food flows from a source to a sink.

fullMarks: For root uptake, write the route in order: root hair → epidermis → cortex → endodermis → pericycle → xylem. Explain that salts enter root hairs by active transport and water enters by osmosis.

For stomatal opening and closing, describe both stages in order: potassium ions enter by active transport, water enters by osmosis and guard cells become turgid; later potassium ions and water move out, guard cells lose turgor and the stoma closes.
For water transport, name transpiration pull and explain the continuous xylem water column. Include attraction between water molecules, the narrow xylem vessels, and adhesion of water to xylem walls.

For pressure flow, identify source and sink first. Then explain sucrose loading, water entering phloem by osmosis and raising pressure, sucrose unloading at the sink, and water returning to xylem so pressure falls.

When comparing processes or plant types, use paired points that clearly distinguish both sides. For example, transpiration releases water vapour through plant surfaces, while guttation releases water droplets through pores at leaf tips or edges.

In gaseous exchange answers, distinguish day from night: during daytime green parts photosynthesise as well as respire; at night photosynthesis stops and respiration continues. Mention stomata, root and leaf surfaces, and lenticels in woody stems.

For long answers about plant structures or processes, draw a neat, relevant labelled diagram where useful. For root uptake, label root hair, epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, xylem and phloem; for food transport, label source, sink, phloem, sieve tube, companion cell and xylem.
mistakes: Mixing up active transport and osmosis: state that salts enter root hairs by active transport, while water enters by osmosis.
Saying xylem carries food or phloem carries water and salts: remember that xylem transports water and salts, while phloem transports food.
Describing transpiration as only water loss: explain that it also creates the pull that helps move water and salts from roots to leaves.
Leaving out the potassium-ion step in stomatal opening: mention active transport of K⁺ into guard cells before water enters by osmosis.
Confusing guttation with dew: guttation releases water droplets through pores at leaf tips or edges; dew forms when water vapour in the air condenses on leaves.
Saying food moves in only one direction through phloem: explain that its direction depends on source and sink, and phloem can transport food in two directions.
Confusing hydrophytes and halophytes: hydrophytes live in freshwater or wet soil, while halophytes live in salty habitats.

shortTheory.question: Define macronutrients and micronutrients and give examples.
shortTheory.answer: The minerals which are required in larger quantities are called macronutrients e.g. carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, potassium, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, and magnesium. The minerals which are required in lower quantities are called micronutrients e.g. iron, molybdenum, boron, copper, manganese, zinc, chlorine, and nickel.

shortTheory.question: Define transpiration and name its types.
shortTheory.answer: The loss of water in the form of vapours from plant surface is called transpiration. This loss may occur through stomata in leaves, through the cuticle present on leaf epidermis, or through special openings called lenticels present in the stems of some plants. The three types are stomatal transpiration, cuticular transpiration, and lenticular transpiration.

shortTheory.question: How is the transpirational pull important in plants?
shortTheory.answer: Although transpiration is the loss of water from plant but, yet it creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem tissue of leaves, stem and root. This pull is responsible for the transport of water and salts from root to leaves.

shortTheory.question: Transpiration is the loss of water from plants. Is it harmful? If not, what is its importance?
shortTheory.answer: Transpiration is a necessary evil. Although transpiration is the loss of water from plant but, yet it creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem tissue of leaves, stem and root. This pull is responsible for the transport of water and salts from root to leaves.

shortTheory.question: Differentiate between xylem and phloem.
shortTheory.answer: Xylem is responsible for the transport of water and salts while phloem is responsible for the transport of food.

shortTheory.question: How do the plants of rubber and keekar excrete their wastes?
shortTheory.answer: For example, rubber plant excretes latexes, Acacia (keekar) tree excretes gums.

modelAnswer: The thick walls of fungal spores help them tolerate unfavourable conditions.

steps.why: DNA must be copied so that each daughter bacterium can receive DNA.
steps.text: The bacterial DNA replicates.

steps.why: The copied DNA molecules are moved towards the two sides of the cell.
steps.text: The daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides.

steps.why: The cell begins to divide into two parts.
steps.text: The cell membrane pinches in.

steps.why: A wall forms between the two developing cells.
steps.text: A new cell wall is synthesized in the middle.

steps.why: These stages produce two cells with the same genetic information.
steps.text: Two identical daughter bacteria are produced.

example.question: Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
example.answer: Two identical daughter bacteria are produced.

explain.title: Asexual reproduction
explain.body: Asexual reproduction does not involve the fusion of gametes. Its offspring are genetically identical to the parent. Binary fission, budding, spore formation, and vegetative propagation are methods described in this section.

explain.title: Binary fission and budding
explain.body: In bacterial binary fission, DNA replicates, the copies move to opposite sides, and the cell separates to form two daughter bacteria. Protists such as Amoeba divide their nucleus before their cytoplasm. In budding, a part of the parent grows out as a bud; it may separate or remain attached. Yeast and hydra reproduce by budding.

explain.title: Spore formation
explain.body: Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells. Fungi produce them in sac-like structures called sporangia. The sporangium releases mature spores, which germinate when conditions become favourable. Some bacteria form endospores inside the cell in unfavourable conditions.

explain.title: Vegetative propagation
explain.body: Vegetative propagation makes a new plant from a vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of its parent. It takes less time than sexual reproduction, and its offspring are genetically identical to the parent. It may happen naturally or through human methods.

explain.title: Natural structures in plants
explain.body: Stolons grow horizontally above the ground; tubers are fleshy underground stems with eyes; rhizomes grow horizontally below ground; bulbs have fleshy leaves; and corms do not. Suckers are shoots from the base of a plant or its underground roots. Modified Bryophyllum leaves have buds at their margins that can grow into new plants.

mistakes: Do not confuse a stolon with a rhizome: a stolon grows above the ground, while a rhizome grows below it.
Do not call potato eyes roots; they are buds.
Do not say that a corm has fleshy leaves. A bulb has fleshy leaves; a corm does not.
Do not reverse the stages of binary fission: in Amoeba, the nucleus divides before the cytoplasm.
Do not say that spores germinate in unfavourable conditions; they germinate when conditions are favourable.
Do not confuse natural vegetative propagation, which happens on its own, with artificial propagation, in which humans use plant parts.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation allows many new plants to be produced in a short time.
The new plants are exactly like the parent plant, so its useful characteristics are passed on.
However, the offspring do not have genetic differences.
They are equally sensitive to environmental changes and prone to the same diseases or pests.

yourTurn.question: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
solution: Vegetative propagation allows many new plants to be produced in a short time.
The new plants are exactly like the parent plant, so its useful characteristics are passed on.
However, the offspring do not have genetic differences.

example.question: Explain cutting and give examples of plants grown from stem and root cuttings.
example.answer: A cutting is a piece of stem or root cut from a plant and used to grow a new plant. Roses and grapevines are grown from stem cuttings; sweet potato is grown from root cuttings.

explain.title: Artificial propagation
explain.body: Artificial propagation includes the methods in which humans produce new plants by using the vegetative parts of plants. The section names cutting, grafting and tissue culture as techniques.

explain.title: Cutting
explain.body: In some plants, a piece of stem or root can grow into a new plant. Roses and grapevines are examples of stem cuttings, while sweet potato is an example of a root cutting.

explain.title: Grafting
explain.body: Grafting joins a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of a second plant. It can combine beneficial characteristics of two plants and is used for many commercial fruit trees and ornamental plants.

explain.title: Advantages and disadvantage
explain.body: Vegetative propagation can produce many plants quickly and keeps useful characteristics because the new plants are like the parent. But the offspring have no genetic differences, so they may share sensitivity to environmental changes and the same diseases or pests.

mistakes: Do not define cutting as joining two plants; joining plant parts describes grafting.
Do not say grafting uses a whole seed. It joins a bud or small stem to the roots or stems of another plant.
Do not give only benefits when asked for advantages and disadvantages; include the lack of genetic differences and shared vulnerability.
Do not confuse stem cuttings with root cuttings: roses and grapevines are stem-cutting examples, while sweet potato is a root-cutting example.
Do not say vegetative offspring have genetic differences; the section states they are identical.

writtenQuestions.text: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within embryo sac of a flower.
modelAnswer: The diploid megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores.

Inside it, mitosis forms eight haploid nuclei.
Two nuclei migrate to the centre and fuse to form a fusion nucleus.
One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the egg cell.

The female gametophyte is the embryo sac in the ovule.
It contains an egg cell and a fusion nucleus.

In questions on the embryo sac, include meiosis, four megaspores, the one surviving megaspore, mitosis, the fusion nucleus, the egg, and the seven-cell result.
For flower-part questions, match each whorl with its components and function where asked; use the terms anther, filament, ovary, style, and stigma precisely.

steps.why: The flowering plant itself is the diploid generation that begins this cycle.
steps.text: The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.

steps.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make haploid spores.
steps.text: The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.

steps.why: The male and female spores develop into their respective gametophytes.
steps.text: Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.

steps.why: Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, where the pollen tube can form.
steps.text: Pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.

steps.why: The pollen tube carries the two sperms to the embryo sac.
steps.text: The pollen tube grows towards the ovule and carries two sperms into the embryo sac.

steps.why: The two sperm fusions form the zygote and the endosperm-forming nucleus.
steps.text: One sperm fuses with the egg to form a zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus.

steps.why: These changes lead to a seed that can grow into the next sporophyte.
steps.text: The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.

example.question: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
example.answer: The diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores; these develop into gametophytes that make gametes. Fertilization forms a zygote, which develops into the next sporophyte.

explain.title: Alternation of generations
explain.body: The major groups of plants have two type generations during sexual reproduction which come one after the other. These are sporophyte generation and gametophyte generation. The sporophyte generation produces spores which grow and make the new gametophyte generation. The gametophyte generation produces gametes which unite and make the new sporophyte generation. This phenomenon is called alternation of generations.

explain.title: Flower parts
explain.body: The four concentric whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens), and gynoecium (carpels). A stamen has an anther and a filament. A carpel has an ovary, style, and stigma.

explain.title: Male and female gametophytes
explain.body: The microspore undergoes mitosis and forms a pollen grain, the male gametophyte. The ovule contains a megaspore mother cell; after meiosis and further development, one megaspore forms the female gametophyte, or embryo sac.

explain.title: Pollination and double fertilization
explain.body: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma. The pollen tube carries two sperms into the embryo sac. One fuses with the egg to form a zygote, and the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.

explain.title: Seed and fruit formation
explain.body: After fertilization, the zygote develops into an embryo and the triploid nucleus develops into endosperm tissue. The ovule matures into a seed and the ovary changes into a fruit.

mistakes: Do not confuse pollination with fertilization: pollination is pollen transfer from anther to stigma; fertilization is the fusion of gametes or nuclei.
Do not swap the male and female gametophytes: the pollen grain is male and the embryo sac is female.
Do not say both sperms fuse with the egg. One fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus.
Do not confuse the ovary and ovule after fertilization: the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
Do not call the fusion nucleus triploid before sperm fusion; the sperm fuses with it to produce the triploid nucleus.
When describing embryo-sac development, include that only one of the four megaspores remains alive.

recap.question: What is one difference between cutting and grafting?
recap.answer: Cutting uses a cut piece of stem or root to grow a new plant. Grafting joins plant parts so they grow as one plant.

recap.question: What is a cutting in artificial propagation?
recap.answer: A piece of stem or root cut from a plant and used to grow a new plant

modelAnswer: Spores can be dispersed widely to new places.
They can withstand harsh or unfavourable conditions.
When conditions become favourable, they germinate or resume growth to form new organisms.
writtenQuestions.followUp: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.

rubric.description: State that spores are small or readily dispersed to new places.
rubric.why: Explains how spores help organisms reach new places.
rubric.how: Mention wide dispersal, such as by air or other agents.

rubric.description: State that spores resist harsh conditions and can grow when conditions improve.
rubric.why: Explains how spores improve survival and allow growth later.
rubric.how: Mention survival in adverse conditions and later germination or growth.

examTips: Short questions commonly ask for a definition, a sequence, a function, or a difference between two structures. Use the exact textbook terms such as runner, rhizome, pollen grain and embryo sac.
For a process question, earn marks by writing the steps in order. In binary fission, show DNA replication, cell elongation, formation of a septum and two daughter bacteria.
For comparisons, use paired points so the examiner can clearly see the difference between the two terms.
Long questions on the flower life cycle and embryo-sac development need the sequence and the correct ploidy terms: haploid (n), diploid (2n) and triploid (3n).
For a flower diagram question, label each pointer neatly and use a straight line that touches the structure being named. Common labels include stigma, style, ovary, anther, filament, petal and sepal.

hints: First identify the horizontal stem as aboveground or underground.
Describe where roots and shoots form and name the example plant.
yourTurn.question: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.
solution: A runner is a horizontal aboveground stem.
It grows out from the parent plant.
Roots and shoots develop at the runner's nodes.
The rooted nodes grow into new plants, as in strawberry.
yourTurn.answer: Roots and shoots form at nodes of a horizontal aboveground runner and grow into new plants, as in strawberry.

steps.why: The starting cell must copy its genetic material before it can divide.
steps.text: The bacterial DNA replicates, producing two copies.

steps.why: Cell growth separates the copies so each daughter cell can receive DNA.
steps.text: As the cell grows and elongates, the DNA copies move apart.

steps.why: The inward-growing cell boundary makes the division between the two DNA copies.
steps.text: The cell membrane and wall grow inward between the copies, forming a septum.

steps.why: This is the final outcome of binary fission.
steps.text: The cell separates into two genetically identical daughter bacteria.

example.question: Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
example.answer: Bacterial DNA replicates; the cell elongates; a septum forms between the DNA copies; the cell divides into two genetically identical daughter bacteria.

explain.title: Asexual reproduction
explain.body: Asexual reproduction needs one parent and does not involve the fusion of gametes. Binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, and spore formation in fungi are examples. The offspring are usually genetically similar to the parent.

explain.title: Spores and survival
explain.body: Fungi produce spores that can be dispersed and can germinate in suitable conditions. Some bacteria form thick-walled endospores in harsh conditions. Protective spores can remain dormant until conditions become favourable.

explain.title: Vegetative propagation
explain.body: New plants can grow from vegetative parts such as stems, roots or leaves. Runners and stolons grow above the ground; rhizomes, tubers, bulbs and corms are underground structures. People can also use methods such as cuttings, grafting and layering.

explain.title: Flower structure and gametophytes
explain.body: The four flower whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens) and gynoecium or carpel (stigma, style and ovary). The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac inside the ovule is the female gametophyte.

explain.title: Fertilization and plant generations
explain.body: A pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries male gametes to the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus: this is double fertilization. The embryo develops in the seed, and the seed grows into a new sporophyte plant.

mistakes: Do not call a rhizome an aboveground stem: it is underground; a runner or stolon is aboveground.
Do not confuse the male and female gametophytes: pollen grain is male, and the embryo sac is female.
Do not say that the endosperm is diploid: it is triploid (3n) in flowering plants.
In double fertilization, one male gamete fuses with the egg, while the other fuses with the fusion nucleus; the egg is not fertilized by two male gametes.
When describing spore formation, distinguish survival in harsh conditions from germination, which occurs in suitable conditions.
For binary fission, do not omit DNA replication or the formation of two daughter bacteria.

recap.question: What are the male and female gametophytes in flowering plants?
recap.answer: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

recap.question: Which flower whorl contains the stamens?
recap.answer: Androecium

solutions.question: Write a short note on budding in yeast.
steps: A small outgrowth, called a bud, appears on the yeast cell.
The nucleus divides by mitosis, and one daughter nucleus moves into the bud.
The bud grows and may separate from the parent cell to form a new yeast cell. Sometimes it remains attached, forming a chain of cells.
solutions.answer: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding: a bud grows on the parent cell, receives a daughter nucleus and forms a new cell.

solutions.question: Write a short note on spore formation in fungi.
steps: In fungi, spores are produced in structures called sporangia, usually present at the tips of hyphae.
When the sporangium matures, it releases the spores.
Under favourable conditions, a spore germinates and grows into a new hypha, which develops into a fungus.
solutions.answer: Fungi reproduce by forming spores in sporangia; the released spores germinate under favourable conditions to form new hyphae.

solutions.question: What are the advantages of spore formation in fungi and bacteria?
steps: A large number of spores can be produced, helping fungi reproduce and spread.
Spores are light and can be carried by air or other means to new places.
Their thick protective walls help them survive unfavourable conditions.
Bacterial endospores also have protective coverings that help bacteria survive unfavourable conditions, such as heat and lack of water.
solutions.answer: Spores are numerous, readily dispersed and protected by resistant walls, helping fungi and bacteria survive and spread.

solutions.question: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.
steps: A runner is a horizontal stem that grows along the ground surface.
Roots and shoots develop at the nodes of the runner.
Each rooted node can grow into an independent plant, as in strawberry and grass.
solutions.answer: Runners produce new plants when roots and shoots grow from their nodes.

solutions.question: State how potatoes reproduce through tubers.
steps: A potato tuber is an underground stem that stores food.
The small depressions on a tuber, called eyes, are buds.
When a tuber is planted, buds in its eyes sprout and grow into shoots; roots also develop, forming a new plant.
solutions.answer: Potatoes reproduce vegetatively from the buds, or eyes, on their underground tubers.

solutions.question: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
steps: Advantages: Vegetative propagation is a rapid method of producing new plants.
The new plants are genetically similar to the parent and retain its desirable characters.
It is useful for plants that do not produce viable seeds.
Disadvantages: There is little or no genetic variation among the offspring.
Diseases present in the parent plant may be passed to the new plants.
solutions.answer: Vegetative propagation is rapid and preserves desirable characters, but produces little variation and can pass diseases to offspring.

solutions.question: Name the four whorls present in a flower and also tell the components of each whorl.
steps: A flower has four whorls arranged from the outside towards the centre.
Calyx: made up of sepals, which usually protect the flower bud.
Corolla: made up of petals, which are often coloured and attract pollinators.
Androecium: the male whorl, made up of stamens; each stamen consists of an anther and a filament.
Gynoecium (pistil): the female whorl, made up of one or more carpels; a carpel has a stigma, style and ovary, and the ovary contains ovules.
solutions.answer: The four whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens: anther and filament) and gynoecium or pistil (carpels: stigma, style and ovary containing ovules).

solutions.question: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within embryo sac of a flower.
steps: Inside the ovule, a diploid megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Three megaspores degenerate, while the remaining functional megaspore develops into the embryo sac.
The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically three times, producing eight haploid nuclei.
Three nuclei move to the micropylar end; one forms the egg cell and the other two form the synergids.
Three nuclei move to the opposite, chalazal end and form the antipodal cells.
The remaining two nuclei lie in the centre of the embryo sac and are called polar nuclei.
solutions.answer: One functional megaspore divides three times to form an eight-nucleate embryo sac; one nucleus forms the egg cell and two central nuclei form the polar nuclei.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Asexual and sexual reproduction
steps: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent; sexual reproduction usually involves two parents.
In asexual reproduction, no gametes are formed and no fertilization takes place; in sexual reproduction, male and female gametes fuse during fertilization.
Asexual reproduction produces offspring that are usually genetically identical to the parent; sexual reproduction produces offspring with variations.
solutions.answer: Asexual reproduction needs one parent and no gamete fusion, whereas sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes and produces variation.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Binary fission in bacteria and amoeba
steps: In bacteria, the DNA replicates and the cell divides into two; bacteria do not have a distinct nucleus.
In Amoeba, the nucleus first divides into two, followed by division of the cytoplasm.
Bacterial division occurs by formation of a dividing partition; in Amoeba, the cell constricts and separates into two daughter cells.
solutions.answer: Bacteria divide without a distinct nucleus, while in Amoeba the nucleus divides first and the cytoplasm divides afterwards.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Stolon and rhizome
steps: A stolon is a horizontal stem that grows along the soil surface; a rhizome is a horizontal stem that grows underground.
Stolons produce roots and shoots at their nodes; rhizomes have nodes and produce roots below and aerial shoots above the ground.
Example of a stolon: strawberry; example of a rhizome: ginger.
solutions.answer: A stolon is a surface-growing horizontal stem, while a rhizome is an underground horizontal stem.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Bulb and corm
steps: A bulb is an underground shoot with a short stem surrounded by fleshy leaves that store food; a corm is a swollen underground stem that stores food.
The fleshy leaves of a bulb store food; the solid stem of a corm stores food and is covered by dry, scaly leaves.
Example of a bulb: onion; example of a corm: gladiolus.
solutions.answer: A bulb stores food in fleshy leaves around a short stem, while a corm stores food in a swollen, solid stem.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Cutting and grafting
steps: In cutting, a piece of a plant, usually a stem, is planted in soil and develops roots and shoots to form a new plant.
In grafting, a stem piece (scion) from a desired plant is joined to the rooted stem (stock) of another plant.
Cutting produces a new plant from the planted piece; grafting joins parts of two plants so they grow as one plant.
solutions.answer: Cutting grows a new plant from a planted plant part; grafting joins a scion to the stock of another plant.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Vegetative propagation and artificial propagation
steps: Vegetative propagation is the formation of new plants from vegetative parts such as roots, stems or leaves.
Vegetative propagation may occur naturally or may be carried out artificially.
Artificial propagation is carried out by humans using methods such as cutting, grafting, layering or tissue culture.
solutions.answer: Vegetative propagation produces plants from vegetative parts; artificial propagation is the human-controlled method of doing so.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Male and female gametophytes
steps: The male gametophyte in a flowering plant is the pollen grain, which develops in the anther and produces male gametes.
The female gametophyte is the embryo sac, which develops inside the ovule and contains the egg cell.
The male gametophyte is carried to the stigma in the pollen grain; the female gametophyte remains inside the ovule.
solutions.answer: The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, while the female gametophyte is the embryo sac inside the ovule.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Calyx and corolla
steps: Calyx is the outermost floral whorl and is made up of sepals; corolla is the floral whorl inside the calyx and is made up of petals.
Sepals are usually green and protect the flower in the bud stage; petals are often brightly coloured and attract insects for pollination.
solutions.answer: The calyx is the sepal whorl that protects the flower bud, while the corolla is the petal whorl that often attracts pollinators.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: Stamen and carpel
steps: Stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower; carpel is the female reproductive part.
A stamen consists of an anther and a filament; a carpel consists of a stigma, style and ovary.
The anther produces pollen grains; the ovary contains ovules, which contain the female gametes.
The stigma receives pollen grains; the filament supports the anther. The style connects the stigma to the ovary.
solutions.answer: Stamen: male flower part, made of anther and filament; the anther produces pollen grains. Carpel: female flower part, made of stigma, style and ovary; the ovary contains ovules.

solutions.question: Label the given diagram of flower.
Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
steps: In binary fission, the DNA of a bacterial cell replicates.
The cell elongates, and the two DNA copies move apart.
The cell membrane and cell wall grow inward between the two DNA copies, forming a partition.
The parent cell divides into two daughter cells, each with a copy of the DNA.
The daughter bacteria are genetically identical to the parent cell, except for any mutations.
solutions.answer: In binary fission, a bacterium copies its DNA and divides into two daughter bacteria, each receiving one copy.

solutions.question: What do you mean by vegetative propagation? Differentiate among different plant structures modified for vegetative propagation.
steps: Vegetative propagation is a type of asexual reproduction in which a new plant develops from a vegetative part of the parent, such as a stem, root or leaf, rather than from a seed.
Runners are slender stems that grow horizontally along the ground; buds at their nodes form new plants, for example in strawberry.
Rhizomes are horizontal underground stems with nodes and buds; they produce shoots and roots, for example in ginger.
Stem tubers are swollen underground stems that store food; their buds, called eyes, can grow into new plants, for example in potato.
Bulbs are short underground stems surrounded by fleshy food-storing leaves; a bud can develop into a new plant, for example in onion.
Corms are short, solid, swollen underground stems that store food and produce new shoots, for example in gladiolus.
Suckers arise from the base or underground part of a parent stem and grow into separate plants, for example in banana.
Some plants also propagate from roots or leaves; for example, sweet potato can grow from roots and Bryophyllum can form plantlets on its leaves.
Plants formed by vegetative propagation are usually genetically similar to the parent plant.
solutions.answer: Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction from vegetative parts of a parent plant. Modified structures include runners (horizontal stems, e.g. strawberry), rhizomes (horizontal underground stems, e.g. ginger), stem tubers (swollen stems with eyes, e.g. potato), bulbs (short stems with fleshy leaves, e.g. onion), corms (solid swollen underground stems, e.g. gladiolus) and suckers (shoots from the plant base, e.g. banana). Roots and leaves can also produce new plants, as in sweet potato and Bryophyllum.

solutions.question: Describe the ways by which humans can grow new plants by using the vegetative parts of the parent plants?
steps: Humans use artificial vegetative propagation to produce plants from stems, roots or leaves of a parent plant.
In cutting, a piece of stem, root or leaf is cut from the parent and planted in moist soil; it develops roots and shoots and grows into a new plant.
In layering, a low branch is bent to the ground and covered with soil while still attached to the parent. After roots develop, the rooted part is cut off and planted separately.
In grafting, a shoot or twig (scion) from a desired plant is joined to the rooted stem (stock) of another plant. The two parts unite and grow as one plant.
In tissue culture, small pieces of plant tissue are grown under sterile conditions on a nutrient medium; they develop into many new plants.
solutions.answer: New plants can be grown by cutting, layering, grafting and tissue culture. Cutting roots a detached plant part; layering roots a branch while it remains attached and then separates it; grafting joins a scion to a stock; tissue culture grows many plants from small pieces of tissue in sterile nutrient medium.

solutions.question: Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.
steps: Sporophyte is the diploid (2n) generation of a plant that develops from the zygote and produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Gametophyte is the haploid (n) generation that develops from a spore and produces gametes by mitosis.
The sporophyte produces spores, which grow into gametophytes; this allows the life cycle to alternate between diploid and haploid generations.
The gametophyte produces male and female gametes. Their fusion at fertilisation forms a diploid zygote.
The zygote develops into an embryo and then a new sporophyte, completing the cycle.
solutions.answer: The sporophyte is the diploid generation that produces haploid spores by meiosis. The gametophyte is the haploid generation that develops from spores and produces gametes. Fertilisation joins gametes to form a diploid zygote, which develops into the sporophyte.

solutions.question: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
steps: The visible flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.
In the anthers, diploid cells undergo meiosis to form haploid microspores. Each microspore develops into a pollen grain, the male gametophyte.
In an ovule, a diploid cell undergoes meiosis to form haploid megaspores; one develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell.
After pollination, a pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries the male gametes to the ovule.
Fertilisation forms a diploid zygote, which develops into an embryo. The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary usually develops into a fruit.
When the seed germinates, the embryo grows into a new diploid sporophyte plant; thus, sporophyte and gametophyte generations alternate.
solutions.answer: The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte. Meiosis in the anther and ovule produces haploid microspores and a megaspore; these develop into the male gametophyte (pollen grain) and female gametophyte (embryo sac). After pollination, the pollen tube carries male gametes to the ovule. Fertilisation forms a diploid zygote, which develops into an embryo in a seed. The seed germinates into a new sporophyte, completing alternation of generations.

solutions.question: Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
steps: A diploid megaspore mother cell in the nucellus of the ovule undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Three megaspores degenerate, and the remaining functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions to form eight haploid nuclei.
Three nuclei move to the micropylar end and form the egg cell and two synergids.
Three nuclei move to the chalazal end and form three antipodal cells.
The remaining two nuclei lie in the centre of the embryo sac as polar nuclei.
Thus, the mature embryo sac has seven cells and eight nuclei.
solutions.answer: The embryo sac develops from one functional megaspore and consists of seven cells and eight nuclei: an egg cell, two synergids, three antipodals and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

solutions.question: Why are spores considered an adaptation for survival in harsh environmental conditions?
steps: Spores have thick protective walls that help them withstand unfavourable environmental conditions.
They can remain dormant during harsh conditions and germinate when conditions become favourable.
solutions.answer: Spores survive harsh conditions because their thick protective walls help them remain dormant until conditions become favourable.

solutions.question: How do asexual and sexual reproduction contribute differently to genetic diversity of plant populations?
steps: In asexual reproduction, offspring are produced from one parent and are usually genetically identical to the parent, so little or no genetic variation is produced.
In sexual reproduction, male and female gametes fuse. Their hereditary material combines, producing variation among offspring and increasing genetic diversity in the population.
solutions.answer: Asexual reproduction produces little or no genetic variation, whereas sexual reproduction produces variation and increases genetic diversity.

solutions.question: How does the pollen tube facilitate the process of fertilization in flowering plants?
steps: After pollination, a pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube.
The pollen tube grows down through the style to the ovule in the ovary.
It carries the male gametes to the embryo sac, where a male gamete fuses with the egg cell to bring about fertilization.
solutions.answer: The pollen tube carries the male gametes from the pollen grain through the style to the ovule, where fertilization occurs.

definitions.text: The reproduction that does not involve the fusion of gametes is called asexual reproduction.
The reproduction that involves the fusion of male and female gametes is called sexual reproduction.
Binary fission means division in to two.
During budding, a part of the parent organism grows out from its body. This part is called a bud.
Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells.
It is a methods of asexual reproduction in plants. In this method, new plant is produced from the vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of the parent plant.
Natural vegetative propagation is a process where plants reproduce on their own, using structures like stems, roots, or leaves.
Artificial vegetative propagation means the processes in which humans use the vegetative parts of plants for their reproduction by methods like cuttings, grafting, or layering.
It is a horizontal stem that grows above the ground. A stolon has nodes where new leaves and roots grow.
It is fleshy stem that grows underground. It has “eyes” which are actually its buds.
It is a horizontal stem that grows below the ground. It has nodes where new leaves and roots grow.
It is a very short stem that grows underground. It has bud and fleshy leaves.
It resembles the bulb but does not have fleshy leaves. Almost all of a corm consists of stem, with a few brown non-functional leaves on the outside.
Suckers are new shoots that emerge from the base of the parent plant or from its underground roots. These shoots grow into new plants while still attached to the parent.
Such a piece of stem or root that are cut from a plant and used to grow new plant is called cutting.
Grafting is the joining of two or more plant parts of the same type to form a single plant.
The sporophyte generation produces spores which grow and make the new gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte generation produces gametes which unite and make the new sporophyte generation.
This phenomenon is called alternation of generations.
The receptacle is the swollen tip of a flower stalk where all the floral parts (are attached. It serves as the base that supports the flower's structure.
It is the outermost whorl. It is made of green leaf-like sepals. Sepals protect the inner parts of a developing flower before it opens.
It is the second whorl and made of petals. Most flowers have coloured petals.
It is the third whorl and is made of male reproductive structures called stamens. Each stamen consists of an anther and a filament.
It is the innermost whorl made of the female reproductive structures called carpels. A carpel consists of three parts.
It is called pollination i.e. the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.
The transfer of pollens from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant is called self-pollination.
The transfer of pollens from the anther of one plant to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. is called cross-pollination.
This process of the fusion of two sperms (one with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus) is called double fertilization.
This process is known as parthenocarpy.
The resulting structure, which contains seven cells (one egg cell, one fusion nucleus, and five non-functional cells), is the female gametophyte or embryo sac.
The resulting two-celled structure is a pollen grain, which is the male gametophyte.

formulas.formula: Sporophyte (2n) → meiosis → spores (1n) → gametophyte (1n) → gametes (1n) → fertilization → zygote (2n) → sporophyte (2n)
formulas.use: Use to show alternation of generations; n means a chromosome-set count, so it is dimensionless and has no SI unit.
Use for fusion of haploid nuclei to form a diploid nucleus, such as the egg and sperm forming a zygote; n is a dimensionless chromosome-set count.
Use for the second sperm fusing with the fusion nucleus to form the triploid endosperm nucleus; n is a dimensionless chromosome-set count.

fullMarks: For binary fission, write the stages in order: bacterial DNA replicates, daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides, the membrane pinches in, a new cell wall forms in the middle, and two identical daughter bacteria result.
For vegetative structures, identify whether each is above or below ground, describe the relevant buds or nodes, and add an example plant where asked.
For artificial propagation, define cutting and grafting separately, explain how each is done, and include examples such as roses or grapevines for cuttings and fruit trees for grafting.
For flower questions, list all four whorls in order from outermost to innermost, then give each whorl’s components; label anther, filament, stigma, style, ovary, petal and sepal clearly on a diagram.

For embryo-sac development, show the number and ploidy of the starting cell and products: one diploid megaspore mother cell, four haploid megaspores, one surviving megaspore, then eight haploid nuclei; finish with the egg, fusion nucleus and five non-functional cells.

For the flowering-plant life cycle, connect the stages with arrows and include meiosis, mitosis, pollination, fertilization, seed formation and the next sporophyte; keep 1n, 2n and 3n labels accurate.

When explaining double fertilization, state what each sperm fuses with and what each product becomes: egg forms the zygote and then embryo; fusion nucleus forms the endosperm nucleus and then endosperm.
End each explanation by directly answering the question, and use the book’s terms such as microspore, megaspore, gametophyte, sporophyte and embryo sac accurately.
mistakes: Mixing up a stolon and a rhizome. Fix: a stolon is a horizontal stem above ground; a rhizome is a horizontal stem below ground.
Writing that potato is a root tuber. Fix: the chapter describes a tuber as a fleshy underground stem, and potato eyes are buds.
Saying bulbs and corms both have fleshy leaves. Fix: a bulb has fleshy leaves; a corm does not.
Confusing cutting with grafting. Fix: a cutting is a piece of stem or root used to grow a plant; grafting joins plant parts to form one plant.
Calling the pollen grain the female gametophyte or the embryo sac the male gametophyte. Fix: pollen grain is male; embryo sac is female.
Giving the wrong products of double fertilization. Fix: one sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus.
Leaving out the ploidy or the number of embryo-sac products. Fix: include four haploid megaspores, one surviving megaspore, eight haploid nuclei, and the final seven-cell structure.

shortTheory.question: Write a short note on budding in yeast.
shortTheory.answer: This method is very common in yeast (a unicellular fungus). During budding, a part of the parent organism grows out from its body. This part is called a bud. When the bud has grown big, it may separate from parent body or may remain attached.

shortTheory.question: Write a short note on spore formation in fungi.
shortTheory.answer: Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells. Most fungi (e.g. Rhizopus: bread mold) produce spores in special sac-like structures called sporangia (Singular: sporangium). When spores are mature, the sporangium bursts and spores are released. Spores can tolerate unfavourable conditions due to their thick walls. When favourable conditions are available, the spores germinate to produce new fungus.

shortTheory.question: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.
shortTheory.answer: Stolon (runner): It is a horizontal stem that grows above the ground. A stolon has nodes where new leaves and roots grow. The leaves grow upwards and roots grow down. In this way, a new plant is formed at the node. Strawberry reproduces by using its stolon.

shortTheory.question: State how potatoes reproduce through tubers.
shortTheory.answer: Tuber: It is fleshy stem that grows underground. It has “eyes” which are actually its buds. Eyes can grow into new plants. Potatoes reproduce by tubers.

shortTheory.question: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
shortTheory.answer: Vegetative propagation allows to produce many new plants in a short time. The new plants are exactly like the parent plant, so they all have the same good characteristics. This means useful qualities, like good fruit or strong growth, are passed on to the next generation. Plants produced through vegetative propagation do not have genetic differences. In other words, all the offspring are identical. Due to it, they are equally sensitive to environmental changes and prone to the same diseases or pests.

shortTheory.question: Name the four whorls present in a flower and tell the components of each whorl.
shortTheory.answer: Calyx: It is the outermost whorl. It is made of green leaf-like sepals. Corolla: It is the second whorl and made of petals. Androecium: It is the third whorl and is made of male reproductive structures called stamens. Each stamen consists of an anther and a filament. Gynoecium: It is the innermost whorl made of the female reproductive structures called carpels. A carpel consists of three parts: ovary, style and stigma.

shortTheory.question: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within the embryo sac.
shortTheory.answer: The ovule acts as megasporangium. It contains a diploid megaspore mother cell which undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores. Only one megaspore remains alive. Inside megaspore, eight haploid nuclei are formed by mitosis. Two nuclei migrate to the center and fuse to form a fusion nucleus. One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the female gamete i.e., egg cell.

shortTheory.question: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction.
shortTheory.answer: The reproduction that does not involve the fusion of gametes is called asexual reproduction. The offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical to the parents. On the other hand, the reproduction that involves the fusion of male and female gametes is called sexual reproduction. In sexual reproduction, the offspring have variations among themselves and with the parents.
