explain.title: Mean
explain.body: The mean, also known as the average, is the sum of all the values in a data set divided by the number of values. It represents the central value of a data set.

explain.title: Median
explain.body: The median is the middle value of a data set when the values are arranged in ascending or descending order. If the number of values is odd, the median is the middle value. If the number of values is even, the median is the average of the two middle values.

explain.title: Finding the median
explain.body: Arrange the data in ascending order first. For an odd number of values, use position (n + 1)/2. For an even number of values, average the values at positions n/2 and n/2 + 1.

explain.title: Mode
explain.body: The mode is the value that appears most frequently in a data set. A data set may have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all.

explain.title: Finding the mode
explain.body: Count the frequency of each value in the data set. The value with the highest frequency is the mode. If two or more values share the highest frequency, they are all modes; if every value occurs equally often, there is no mode.

Dividing the sum by the wrong number of values when calculating the mean.
Assuming a data set always has a mode; it can have more than one mode or no mode.
Giving a mode without checking which value has the highest frequency.

solutions.question: Explain the importance of biostatistics in the field of public health. Provide examples of how it is used to inform public health decisions.
steps: Biostatistics is the application of statistical methods to biological and health-related data.
It helps public health workers collect, organize, present, analyse and interpret information about the health of a population.
It is used to measure the frequency and distribution of diseases, such as their incidence and prevalence, and to identify changes or patterns over time.
It helps identify possible risk factors by comparing health information from different groups of people.
It is used to assess whether public health programmes, treatments or preventive measures are effective.
The results help public health authorities make evidence-based decisions, set priorities and distribute health services and resources.
For example, health authorities can analyse reports of influenza cases from different areas to identify an outbreak and decide where to send vaccines and medical staff.
They can also compare infection rates before and after a vaccination campaign to assess whether the campaign has reduced disease.
solutions.answer: Biostatistics analyses health data to identify disease patterns, evaluate health programmes and guide evidence-based public health decisions; for example, influenza case data can help locate outbreaks and direct vaccines and staff to the areas most in need.

solutions.question: Discuss the differences between mean, median, and mode. Include examples where each measure is most appropriate to use.
steps: The mean is the arithmetic average of a set of values. It is calculated by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values.
Example: for 2, 3 and 4, mean = (2 + 3 + 4) ÷ 3 = 3.
The mean is most appropriate for numerical data that are fairly evenly distributed and do not contain extreme values, because extreme values can greatly affect it.
The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order. If there is an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle values.
Example: for 2, 3, 4 and 100, the median = (3 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3.5.
The median is most appropriate for skewed data or data with extreme values, such as household incomes, because it is less affected by unusually high or low values.
The mode is the value or category that occurs most often in a data set.
Example: in 1, 2, 2, 3, the mode is 2. For categories, the most frequently reported blood group is the mode.
The mode is most appropriate for identifying the most common value or category, especially when the data are categorical, such as the most popular fruit.
solutions.answer: The mean is the arithmetic average, the median is the middle value in ordered data, and the mode is the most frequent value or category; use the mean for balanced numerical data, the median for data with extreme values, and the mode for the most common value or category.

notes.answer: Biology is the science of life. Its major fields are Zoology, Botany, and Microbiology, and its sub-fields focus on particular structures, processes, organisms, or relationships.

notes.checkAnswer: Taxonomy.

notes.title: Biology and other sciences
notes.answer: Biology is linked with other sciences because their principles and methods help us understand living organisms and biological processes.
notes.explanation: Biology connects with other sciences when their ideas or methods are used to study living things. For example, physics helps explain how muscles and joints work, while statistics helps analyse biological data.
notes.simple: Different sciences help us study different parts of life: its chemicals, movement, data, locations, useful products and economic value.
examples: Using bacteria to produce insulin is an example of Biotechnology.
Studying how climate change affects where organisms live is an example of Biogeography.
steps: Identify the science or method being used.
Connect it to what is being studied about living organisms.
Name the related branch of Biology.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch studies the distribution of living organisms in different geographical regions?
notes.checkAnswer: Biogeography.

notes.title: Careers In Biology
notes.answer: Biology can lead to careers such as medicine and surgery, dentistry, pharmacology, physiotherapy, agriculture, forestry, biotechnology and forensics.
notes.explanation: Biology can lead to many careers. Each career has its own kind of work and may require a specific degree or course.
notes.simple: Studying Biology can prepare you for work with people, animals, plants, health, or biological information.
examples: Dentists diagnose and treat dental diseases and perform surgeries; they get a 4-year BDS degree.
Agricultural scientists improve farming practices and crop production; a 4-year BS degree in Agriculture is required.
steps: Choose a career related to Biology.
Learn what work people in that career do.
Check which degree or course is required.
notes.checkQuestion: What degree is necessary to become a forester?
notes.checkAnswer: A 4-year BS degree in Forestry is necessary.

notes.title: Quranic Instructions to Study Life
notes.answer: The verse in Sura Al-Ambia says that every living thing was made from water.
notes.explanation: The section presents Quranic verses that encourage reflection on the origin and development of living things. It mentions water, human development, and differences in how animals move.
notes.simple: The section asks us to think about what the Quran says about living things: their connection with water, how humans develop, and how animals move.
examples: The verse in Sura Al-Ambia says, “We made every living thing from water.”
The verse in Sura An-Nur describes animals that creep on their bellies, walk on two legs, or walk on four.
steps: Read the verse and note its main idea.
Connect the idea to the living things or process described in the section.
State the verse’s meaning clearly, without adding details not given in the text.
notes.checkQuestion: According to the verse quoted from Sura Al-Ambia, what were living things made from?
notes.checkAnswer: The verse says that every living thing was made from water.

notes.title: Science as a Collaborative Field
notes.answer: Science is collaborative when researchers from different disciplines work together to solve complex problems.
notes.explanation: Scientists from different fields can combine their knowledge and skills to investigate problems that are too complex for one field alone. For example, cancer research may involve biologists, geneticists, pharmacologists and statisticians.
notes.simple: A difficult scientific problem can be solved more effectively when specialists from different fields work together.
examples: The Human Genome Project brought together researchers in molecular biology, genetics, informatics and computer science to sequence and map the human genome.
Climate change research brings together atmospheric science, ecology, economics and sociology.
steps: Identify the scientific problem.
Name the different fields that can contribute.
Explain how their different expertise helps investigate or solve the problem.
Give a textbook example, such as the Human Genome Project or cancer research.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two groups of specialists involved in cancer research.
notes.checkAnswer: Oncologists and biologists are two groups of specialists involved in cancer research.

notes.title: Scientific Method
notes.answer: The scientific method is the ordered process used to investigate a scientific problem: recognition of a problem, observation, hypothesis, deduction, experiments, and results.
notes.explanation: The scientific method is a set of steps scientists use to investigate a problem. They make observations, suggest a testable hypothesis, work out what should happen if it is true, test it with experiments, and report the results.
notes.simple: A scientist asks a question, makes a possible explanation, tests it fairly, and shares what happened.
steps: Recognize and define the scientific problem.
Make observations and study previous research.
Propose a hypothesis that matches the observations and can be tested.
Make a deduction: predict what should happen if the hypothesis is true.
Perform experiments to test the hypothesis.
Collect and summarize results, then share the findings.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the six steps of the scientific method in order.
notes.checkAnswer: Recognition of a problem, observation, hypothesis, deduction, experiments, and results.

notes.title: From Hypothesis to Theory and Law
notes.answer: A theory that is proved again and again by experiments becomes a law or principle.
notes.explanation: A hypothesis that is supported by experiments can lead to a theory. Scientists continue to test theories, and a theory proved repeatedly by experiments becomes a law or principle.
notes.simple: Test an idea, test it again, and use the results to build scientific explanations.
examples: The theory of evolution explains how species change over time through natural selection.
Hardy-Weinberg law and Mendel’s laws of inheritance are examples of biological laws.
steps: Experiments prove a hypothesis correct.
Scientists use the supported hypothesis to make further hypotheses.
When the new hypotheses are also proved, the original hypothesis becomes a theory.
Scientists keep testing the theory and try to disprove it.
If experiments prove it again and again, it becomes a law or principle.
notes.checkQuestion: According to your textbook, what can a theory become if experiments prove it again and again?
notes.checkAnswer: Experiments support hypotheses; repeated testing can lead to a theory and then a law or principle.

notes.title: How scientists investigated malaria
notes.answer: Mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium and are involved in the spread of malaria.
notes.explanation: Biologists used observations, hypotheses, deductions and experiments to investigate malaria. Their evidence showed that Plasmodium causes malaria and that mosquitoes transmit it.
notes.simple: Scientists noticed clues, made a possible explanation, and tested it. Their experiments showed that mosquitoes carry Plasmodium and can pass it on.
examples: Laveran found Plasmodium in the blood of a malarial patient.
Ross found that infected mosquitoes could transmit malaria to healthy sparrows.
steps: Observe clues about malaria.
Suggest a hypothesis.
Make a deduction from the hypothesis.
Test the deduction with an experiment.
Use the results to judge the hypothesis.
notes.checkQuestion: What did Ross's experiments show about mosquitoes?
notes.checkAnswer: Ross found Plasmodium multiplying in mosquitoes and showed that infected mosquitoes transmitted malaria to healthy sparrows.

notes.title: Branches of Biology and the Scientific Method
notes.answer: Biology is the study of life, and the scientific method uses observations, hypotheses, deductions, and experiments to investigate biological questions.
notes.explanation: Biology is the study of life. It has many branches because living things can be studied in different ways: by their structure, functions, development, relationships, and classification. Scientists use observations, hypotheses, deductions, and experiments to investigate questions.
notes.simple: Biology studies living things. Its branches help us focus on one kind of question at a time. The scientific method is a careful way to test possible answers.
examples: Genetics studies heredity and variation.
Physiology studies the functions of living organisms and their parts.
steps: Observe a problem or pattern.
Form a hypothesis that could explain it.
Make deductions from the hypothesis.
Test the deductions with experiments.
Analyse the results and decide whether the hypothesis is supported.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch studies the functions of living organisms and their parts?
notes.checkAnswer: Physiology

notes.title: Biodiversity
notes.answer: Biodiversity is the variety of organisms in a particular area.
notes.explanation: Biodiversity describes the variety of organisms in a particular area. It is measured by counting the different kinds of organisms and considering the variation within each kind. Biodiversity is important because it supports ecosystem stability, helps regulate climate, provides natural resources, and supports industries.
notes.simple: Biodiversity means how many different kinds of living things live in a place, and how much they vary.
examples: A tropical region has more biodiversity than a polar region.
Plants and algae absorb carbon dioxide, helping to keep the climate balanced.
steps: Identify the area being discussed.
Consider the number of different kinds of organisms there.
Also consider the variation within each kind.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the term for the variety of organisms in a particular area?
notes.checkAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of organisms in a particular area.

notes.title: Why do biologists classify organisms?
notes.answer: Classification is the process in which organisms are divided into groups and subgroups on the basis of similarities and differences found in them.
notes.explanation: Classification groups organisms by their similarities and differences. This makes them easier to study and helps biologists understand their relationships.
notes.simple: Classification is like sorting things into groups. Organisms with things in common are put together, so they are easier to study.
examples: Biologists can group organisms with similar physical characteristics together.
Genetic similarities and differences can help biologists understand similarities and differences in organisms’ structures and functions.
steps: Look for similarities and differences among organisms.
Use these features to place organisms into groups and subgroups.
Study the groups to identify organisms and understand their relationships.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one reason biologists classify organisms?
notes.checkAnswer: It groups organisms by similarities and differences so they are easier to study.

notes.title: Taxonomic ranks: broad groups to specific groups
notes.answer: The highest rank is domain; the lowest rank is species.
notes.explanation: Taxonomic ranks arrange organisms in levels, from the broadest group, domain, to the most specific group, species. Each level is divided into smaller, related groups.
notes.simple: Think of classification as sorting organisms into groups that get smaller and more specific at each step.
examples: In the table in your textbook, a human belongs to the domain Eukarya and the species Homo sapiens.
For plants and fungi, the rank corresponding to phylum is called division.
steps: Start with the broadest rank: domain.
Move down through kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family and genus.
Finish with species, the lowest rank.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the highest and lowest taxonomic ranks.
notes.checkAnswer: Domain, kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus, species.

notes.title: History of Classification
notes.answer: Classification developed from two kingdoms to three kingdoms, then five kingdoms, and later three domains.
notes.explanation: Classification systems changed as scientists learned more about organisms. Aristotle grouped life into plants and animals. Later systems added kingdoms to deal with organisms that did not fit well, and Woese added domains above kingdoms.
notes.simple: Scientists changed the classification system as they learned more about how organisms are alike and different.
examples: Haeckel added Protista for Euglena-like organisms.
Woese divided organisms into the domains Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
steps: Remember the order: two kingdoms, three kingdoms, five kingdoms, then three domains.
Connect each system with its scientist: Aristotle, Haeckel, Whittaker and Woese.
Recall what changed: new groups were added to classify organisms more clearly.
notes.checkQuestion: Who proposed the three-kingdom system, and when?
notes.checkAnswer: Ernst Haeckel proposed the three-kingdom system in 1866.

notes.title: Three Domains of Living Organisms
notes.answer: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
notes.explanation: Living organisms are grouped into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes, but their cell walls differ. Eukarya includes organisms with cells that have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
notes.simple: Think of domains as the broadest groups of living organisms. Archaea and Bacteria have prokaryotic cells; Eukarya has eukaryotic cells.
examples: Methanogens belong to Archaea.
Yeast belongs to Eukarya.
steps: Remember the three names: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
For Archaea, remember that their cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan and some live in extreme environments.
For Bacteria, remember that their cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
For Eukarya, remember that its cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the three domains of living organisms?
notes.checkAnswer: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

notes.title: The four kingdoms of Domain Eukarya
notes.answer: The four kingdoms are Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
notes.explanation: Domain Eukarya contains four kingdoms in this section: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. They differ in how their members are organised, obtain food, and in the materials of their cell walls.
notes.simple: To identify a eukaryote's kingdom, check whether it is unicellular or multicellular, how it gets food, and whether it has a cell wall—and what that wall is made of.
examples: Yeast belongs to Kingdom Fungi.
Amoeba belongs to Kingdom Protista.
steps: Protista includes unicellular, colonial, filamentous or simple multicellular eukaryotes.
Fungi absorb food from decaying matter and have cell walls made of chitin.
Plantae are multicellular autotrophs with cellulose cell walls.
Animalia are multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and have no cell walls.
notes.checkQuestion: To which kingdom does yeast belong?
notes.checkAnswer: Kingdom Fungi.

notes.title: Viruses and classification
notes.answer: Viruses are acellular and lack the characteristics of the three domains of life, so they are not included in the classification system.
notes.explanation: Viruses are acellular particles at the borderline of living and non-living. They contain DNA or RNA inside a protein coat, cannot carry out metabolism, and need a host organism to make proteins and increase in number. They are not placed in the classification system because they lack the characteristics of the three domains of life. Prions consist only of protein, while viroids consist only of circular RNA.
notes.simple: A virus is not made of cells and cannot do everything a living organism does by itself. It must use a host to make more viruses, so it does not fit into the three-domain classification of life.
examples: A bacteriophage is a virus that attacks bacteria.
An influenza virus is another example of a virus.
steps: Check whether the particle is made of cells: viruses are acellular.
Check whether it can carry out metabolism: viruses cannot run metabolism.
Remember that viruses use a host to make proteins and increase in number.
Conclude that viruses lack the characteristics of the three domains of life, so they are not included in the classification system.
notes.checkQuestion: Why are viruses not included in the classification system?
notes.checkAnswer: They are acellular and lack the characteristics of the three domains of life.

notes.title: Binomial Nomenclature
notes.answer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of scientific naming in which each organism's name has two parts: its genus name followed by its species name.
notes.explanation: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-part scientific name. The first part names its genus and the second part names its species. This standard name is used worldwide, helping biologists communicate clearly even when they speak different languages.
notes.simple: Each organism gets a two-word scientific name: first its genus, then its species.
examples: Onion — *Allium cepa*
Human being — *Homo sapiens*
steps: Write the genus name first, beginning with a capital letter.
Write the species name second, beginning with a small letter.
Use italics when printing the scientific name.
If handwriting the name, underline its two parts separately.
notes.checkQuestion: In *Panthera tigris*, which word is the genus name?
notes.checkAnswer: The genus name comes first and begins with a capital letter; the species name comes second and begins with a small letter.

notes.title: Biodiversity and classification
notes.answer: The taxonomic ranks from broadest to most specific are Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
notes.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms. Biologists classify organisms into groups using shared features. The Linnaean ranks go from the broadest, domain, to the most specific, species. Scientific names use two words: genus followed by species.
notes.simple: Classification is like sorting living things into labelled groups, from very large groups down to very specific ones.
examples: Humans are named Homo sapiens: Homo is the genus and sapiens is the species.
The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
steps: Identify the organism’s features, such as its cell type and number of cells.
Use shared characteristics to place it in the correct domain and kingdom.
Continue through the taxonomic ranks from broad to specific.
Give the organism a two-word scientific name: genus first, species second.
notes.checkQuestion: Write the taxonomic ranks from broadest to most specific.
notes.checkAnswer: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

notes.title: 3.1 Cell
notes.answer: The cell is the basic unit of life.
notes.explanation: Living things are made of cells. Cells carry out the functions needed for life. Most cells are too small to see without a microscope, although a few are large enough to see with the naked eye.
notes.simple: Cells are tiny building blocks that make up living things and do the work needed to keep them alive.
examples: The ostrich egg cell is large enough to be seen with the naked eye.
A cell is like a city: different structures do different jobs, while the nucleus directs the cell's activities.
steps: Remember that the cell is the basic unit of life.
Explain that living organisms are made of cells.
Add that cells carry out the functions necessary for life.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the basic unit of life?
notes.checkAnswer: Cells are the building blocks of living organisms and carry out the functions needed for life.

notes.title: Cell structures and their functions
notes.answer: Cell structures have different features and functions. For example, the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell, while the nucleus directs cellular activities.
notes.explanation: A cell has structures that each perform particular jobs. Some provide support or control what enters and leaves; others store materials, make proteins, or help the cell move. Knowing each structure’s location and function helps you explain how a cell works.
notes.simple: Think of a cell as a tiny working unit. Its parts have different jobs, like protecting it, controlling it, or moving materials.
examples: The cell wall gives plant cells strength and support.
The nucleus contains DNA and directs cell activities.
steps: Identify the cell structure named in the question.
Recall its key feature or location.
State its function clearly, using the textbook’s terms.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the channels in plant cell walls that allow molecules to pass between adjacent cells called?
notes.checkAnswer: Plasmodesmata are channels in cell walls that allow molecules to pass between adjacent cells.

notes.title: Structural advantages of plant and animal cells
notes.answer: The large central vacuole.
notes.explanation: Plant and animal cells have structures suited to their jobs. Plant cell walls support and protect cells, chloroplasts make food, and large vacuoles help keep cells firm. Animal cells have structures such as centrioles and lysosomes, and their lack of a rigid cell wall lets them change shape.
notes.simple: Cell structures are parts with particular jobs. Plant cells have structures that help them stay supported and make food. Animal cells have structures that help with cell division, cleanup, and movement.
examples: A plant cell wall supports and protects the cell.
A sperm cell uses its flagellum to move toward the egg.
steps: Identify the structure named in the question.
State its job using the textbook's wording.
Link that job to the advantage it gives the cell.
notes.checkQuestion: Which plant cell structure provides turgor pressure that helps maintain cell shape?
notes.checkAnswer: The large central vacuole stores water, nutrients, and waste products. It provides turgor pressure that maintains cell shape.

notes.title: Cell Specialization
notes.answer: A red blood cell carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues.
notes.explanation: In multicellular organisms, different cells have different structures and jobs. Specialization helps each cell do its job well, and division of labour lets cells and cell parts work together.
notes.simple: Cells are like a team: each kind has a shape and parts suited to a particular job.
examples: Mesophyll cells absorb light for photosynthesis.
Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues.
steps: Cells formed by cell division are initially similar.
They undergo specialization or differentiation and develop special sizes, structures, and metabolic features.
Their features suit particular jobs, such as photosynthesis, movement, or carrying oxygen.
Different cell types work together in a multicellular organism.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one job of a red blood cell?
notes.checkAnswer: Mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts for photosynthesis; their shape and arrangement help absorb light.

notes.title: Stem cells
notes.answer: Stem cells are undifferentiated or unspecialized cells that can differentiate into specific cells.
notes.explanation: Stem cells are unspecialized cells. They can make new cells that differentiate into particular specialized cell types. Some stem cells remain in the body and help maintain or repair tissues.
notes.simple: A stem cell is a cell that has not yet become a particular kind of cell. It can develop into specific cell types.
examples: Skin stem cells help in wound healing.
Bone marrow stem cells differentiate to make different types of blood cells and immune cells.
steps: Identify a stem cell as an unspecialized or undifferentiated cell.
State that it can differentiate into specific cells.
notes.checkQuestion: How would you define a stem cell?
notes.checkAnswer: Stem cells are undifferentiated or unspecialized cells that can differentiate into specific cells.

notes.title: Cell structures and their functions
notes.answer: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.
notes.explanation: A cell has structures that perform different jobs. The nucleus controls cell activities and contains genetic material. Organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes, the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes each have special roles. In multicellular organisms, cells can become specialized to perform particular functions.
notes.simple: A cell is like a small team: each part has its own job, and the parts work together.
examples: Mitochondria release energy during cellular respiration.
Mesophyll cells in leaves make glucose by photosynthesis.
steps: Identify the cell structure named in the question.
Recall the main job of that structure.
Connect its job to the needs of the whole cell.
notes.checkQuestion: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis?
notes.checkAnswer: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

notes.title: The Cell Cycle: Growth, DNA Copying and Division
notes.answer: The cell cycle is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.
notes.explanation: The cell cycle is an ordered series of events in which a eukaryotic cell grows, copies its DNA, and divides into two daughter cells. Interphase includes G1, S, and G2. In G0, some cells stop dividing to carry out special functions.
notes.simple: A cell grows, copies its DNA, prepares, and then divides. Some cells pause dividing in G0.
examples: In S phase, the DNA is copied, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Neurons can remain in G0 for an indefinite period, while epithelial cells continue to divide.
steps: After M phase, the cell enters G1 and grows.
In S phase, the cell copies its DNA.
In G2 phase, the cell grows further and prepares for division.
In M phase, the cell divides into two daughter cells.
Some cells may leave the cycle and enter G0.
notes.checkQuestion: In which phase is the DNA of each chromosome replicated?
notes.checkAnswer: S phase; the DNA is replicated, and the total number of chromosomes remains the same.

notes.title: Mitosis: making two matching cells
notes.answer: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell.
notes.explanation: Mitosis makes two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. It has two major parts: karyokinesis, the division of the nucleus, and cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.
notes.simple: Mitosis is like copying a cell: the copied chromosomes are shared between two new cells, so each new cell has the same chromosome number as the original.
examples: When skin cells are replaced, mitosis makes new cells that are exact copies of older cells.
In Hydra, mitosis helps a bud grow into a new individual.
steps: First, the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Then, cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
The result is two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
notes.checkQuestion: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate?
notes.checkAnswer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

notes.title: Meiosis: making haploid cells
notes.answer: Meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells from one diploid parent cell.
notes.explanation: Meiosis makes four haploid cells from one diploid parent cell. In meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes separate; in meiosis-II, sister chromatids separate. For example, crossing over exchanges portions of non-sister chromatids, while non-disjunction can give gametes too many or too few chromosomes.
notes.simple: Meiosis is a two-division process that makes four cells, each with half the parent cell’s chromosome number.
examples: Crossing over can produce new combinations of genes.
If chromosomes fail to separate properly, non-disjunction may produce gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes.
steps: In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over can occur.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate into two haploid sets.
In meiosis-II, sister chromatids separate.
At the end, four haploid daughter cells are formed.
notes.checkQuestion: What separates during anaphase-I?
notes.checkAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase-I.

notes.title: Comparing Mitosis and Meiosis
notes.answer: Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. Meiosis produces four daughter cells with half the chromosome number.
notes.explanation: Mitosis has one division and makes two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent. Meiosis has two divisions and makes four daughter cells with half the parent cell’s chromosome number. Crossing-over occurs in meiosis and helps produce variation.
notes.simple: Mitosis makes two similar cells. Meiosis makes four cells with half the chromosome number, and crossing-over can make them varied.
examples: If a parent cell has 8 chromosomes, mitosis produces daughter cells with 8 chromosomes each.
If a parent cell has 8 chromosomes, meiosis produces daughter cells with 4 chromosomes each.
steps: Check how many divisions take place: one in mitosis and two in meiosis.
Compare the number of daughter cells: two in mitosis and four in meiosis.
Compare chromosome numbers: unchanged in mitosis and reduced by half in meiosis.
Look for crossing-over: it occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.
Remember that sister chromatids separate in mitosis and in anaphase II of meiosis.
notes.checkQuestion: How many divisions occur in meiosis, and when do sister chromatids separate?
notes.checkAnswer: Meiosis has two divisions; it separates sister chromatids during anaphase II.

notes.title: The cell cycle and cell division
notes.answer: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. Meiosis produces cells with half the chromosome number and contributes to genetic variation.
notes.explanation: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in which a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides. Mitosis makes two genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number; meiosis makes cells with half the chromosome number and creates genetic variation.
notes.simple: A cell first grows and copies its DNA. Then it divides. Mitosis makes two matching cells; meiosis makes cells with half the chromosomes.
examples: In the S phase, DNA is copied so each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
In mitosis, sister chromatids separate during anaphase. In meiosis, homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis-I and sister chromatids separate in meiosis-II.
steps: Interphase: the cell grows during G1, copies DNA during S, and prepares for division during G2.
Mitosis: the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm divides to form two daughter cells.
Meiosis: two nuclear divisions produce cells with half the original chromosome number; crossing over helps create variation.
notes.checkQuestion: When do sister chromatids separate in mitosis?
notes.checkAnswer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase of mitosis; in meiosis they separate during anaphase-II.

notes.title: Levels of organization
notes.answer: The levels from simplest to most complex are atom, molecule, organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism.
notes.explanation: Living things are organized from small, simple parts to larger, more complex levels. Parts at each level work together, so higher levels can do things their separate parts cannot do alone.
notes.simple: Small parts join together to make bigger parts. When the parts work together, the bigger structure can do more.
examples: Muscle cells work together to form muscle tissue, which can contract and generate force.
Different tissues in the heart work together so the heart can pump blood.
steps: Atoms combine to form molecules.
Molecules combine to form organelles.
Organelles work together in cells.
Similar cells form tissues.
Related tissues form organs.
Organs work together in organ systems.
Organ systems together make an organism.
notes.checkQuestion: What level comes after tissue?
notes.checkAnswer: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems.

notes.title: Plant organs and organ systems
notes.answer: Plants have a root system and a shoot system. The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and salts; the shoot system includes stems, branches, leaves, and flowers and enables processes such as photosynthesis and reproduction.
notes.explanation: A plant organ is made of tissues that work together. Plant organs also work together in two main systems: the root system and the shoot system.
notes.simple: Roots work mostly below the ground. Stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits make up the shoot system, mostly above the ground.
examples: A leaf is an organ: its tissues work together in photosynthesis, gas exchange, and transport.
Roots anchor a plant and absorb water and minerals; the stem supports other organs and transports materials.
steps: Name the organ or system.
State which tissues or organs it includes, if needed.
Give its main function using the textbook's terms.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the two main organ systems in plants and give one role of each.
notes.checkAnswer: The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals; the shoot system includes stems, branches, leaves, and flowers.

notes.title: Human Organs and Organ Systems
notes.answer: Smooth muscle tissue.
notes.explanation: The stomach is an organ made of different tissues. Its epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice, while its smooth muscle layers contract and relax to mix food with gastric juice. Organ systems are groups of organs that work together to perform important body functions.
notes.simple: An organ is made of tissues working together. An organ system is made of organs working together.
examples: The stomach is an organ in the digestive system.
The respiratory system includes the lungs, trachea, and bronchi.
steps: Identify the organ or organ system being asked about.
Name the relevant tissue or organs.
State what they do and how that helps the body.
notes.checkQuestion: Which stomach tissue contracts and relaxes to mix food with gastric juice?
notes.checkAnswer: The epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice, and the smooth muscles mix food with gastric juice.

notes.title: Homeostasis: keeping the body's conditions stable
notes.answer: Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment of the body despite changes in the external environment.
notes.explanation: Homeostasis keeps the conditions inside the body stable enough for cells and organs to work properly. The body responds to changes, such as a rise in temperature or blood glucose, and brings conditions back towards normal.
notes.simple: Homeostasis is the body's way of keeping its inside conditions steady, even when things change outside or inside the body.
examples: When body temperature rises, sweat evaporates from the skin and heat is lost.
When blood glucose rises after drinking juice, insulin lowers it towards normal.
steps: A change occurs, such as body temperature rising above normal.
The body detects the change and sends signals to the organs that can respond.
Sweat glands secrete sweat.
As sweat evaporates, heat is lost and body temperature falls towards normal.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens when body temperature rises above normal?
notes.checkAnswer: Sweating helps lose heat, so body temperature falls towards normal.

notes.title: How living things are organised
notes.answer: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system
notes.explanation: A multicellular organism is organised in levels, from cells to organ systems. Different tissues and organs work together, and organ systems cooperate to keep the organism alive and its internal conditions stable.
notes.simple: Small parts join together in an organised way. Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs work together in organ systems.
examples: In a stomach, epithelial tissue produces secretions, while smooth muscle mixes food.
In a leaf, mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, while xylem transports water.
steps: Cells with similar functions group together to form tissues.
Different tissues combine to form an organ.
Organs that work together form an organ system.
Organ systems work together to maintain the organism.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the correct order from cells to organ systems?
notes.checkAnswer: Cells form tissues; tissues form organs; organs form organ systems.

notes.title: Biomolecules and metabolism
notes.answer: Biomolecules are molecules produced by organisms. Metabolism is the total of the chemical reactions in an organism.
notes.explanation: Biomolecules are molecules made by organisms. They help build cells and carry out life processes. Metabolism includes all the chemical reactions in an organism: anabolism builds complex substances, while catabolism breaks them down.
notes.simple: Cells contain different kinds of large molecules. Some provide or store energy, some build cell structures, and some carry genetic information. The chemical reactions happening in an organism are called metabolism.
examples: Proteins make up 50% of the dry mass of protoplasm.
Anabolism combines simpler substances to form complex substances.
steps: Remember the four main groups: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
Use the table to connect each biomolecule with its location and function.
For metabolism, distinguish building (anabolism) from breaking down (catabolism).
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to complex molecules during catabolism?
notes.checkAnswer: Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy.

notes.title: The three classes of carbohydrates
notes.answer: A disaccharide is made of two monosaccharide units.
notes.explanation: Carbohydrates are grouped by how many sugar units they contain. Monosaccharides have one unit, disaccharides have two, and polysaccharides have hundreds to thousands. Their taste and solubility also differ.
notes.simple: Think of sugar units like building blocks: one block is a monosaccharide, two joined blocks are a disaccharide, and a very long chain is a polysaccharide.
examples: Glucose is a monosaccharide; sucrose is a disaccharide.
Starch is a polysaccharide found in plants.
steps: Look for how many sugar units the carbohydrate contains.
One unit means monosaccharide; two units mean disaccharide; a very large number means polysaccharide.
Use taste and solubility as extra clues: monosaccharides are sweet and easily soluble, disaccharides are less sweet and less soluble, and polysaccharides are tasteless and insoluble.
notes.checkQuestion: How many monosaccharide units make up a disaccharide?
notes.checkAnswer: Monosaccharides are single sugar molecules; disaccharides contain two monosaccharide units; polysaccharides contain hundreds to thousands of monosaccharide units.

notes.title: Proteins: building blocks and jobs
notes.answer: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Their functions include forming cell structures, catalysing biochemical reactions, regulating body processes, transporting oxygen, enabling muscle contraction, clotting blood and defending against pathogens.
notes.explanation: Proteins are polymers made from amino acids. Amino acids have a central carbon attached to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and an R group. The R group differs between amino acids. Proteins have many roles, including building structures, catalysing reactions, transporting oxygen and defending the body.
notes.simple: Proteins are like long chains made from amino-acid units. The different amino acids and their order help make different proteins with different jobs.
examples: Glycine has H as its side group.
Alanine has CH₃ as its side group.
steps: Identify the amino acid units as the building blocks of proteins.
Remember that the R group varies between amino acids.
Link a protein to its function: for example, haemoglobin transports oxygen.
Use examples from the text to support your answer.
notes.checkQuestion: Which part of an amino acid differs between glycine and alanine?
notes.checkAnswer: The R group (side group).

notes.title: Lipids: fats, oils and membranes
notes.answer: Lipids include fats, oils and phospholipids. Fats and oils contain glycerol and three fatty acids; phospholipids contain glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group.
notes.explanation: Lipids do not dissolve in water, but they dissolve in some organic solvents. Many lipids are made from glycerol and fatty acids. Fats usually contain saturated fatty acids and are solid at room temperature; oils contain unsaturated fatty acids and are liquid at room temperature. For example, animal fats are usually solid, while olive oil is liquid.
notes.simple: Think of glycerol as a small backbone. Fatty acids attach to it to make many lipids. The type of fatty acid helps determine whether a fat is solid or an oil is liquid at room temperature.
examples: Animal fats are examples of fats containing saturated fatty acids.
Olive oil is an example of an oil containing unsaturated fatty acids.
steps: Remember that glycerol has three carbon atoms, each with a hydroxyl group.
A fatty acid has a long hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl group (COOH) at the end.
Identify saturated fatty acids by their carbon-to-carbon single bonds; they are solid at room temperature.
Identify unsaturated fatty acids by one or more carbon-to-carbon double bonds; they are liquid at room temperature.
Remember the structures: fats and oils have one glycerol and three fatty acids; phospholipids have one glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of fatty acid is found in fats that are solid at room temperature?
notes.checkAnswer: Saturated fatty acids.

notes.title: Nucleic Acids: DNA and RNA
notes.answer: Nucleic acids are made of nucleotides. DNA carries hereditary information, and RNA helps with protein synthesis.
notes.explanation: Nucleic acids are built from nucleotides. DNA stores hereditary information, while different types of RNA help use that information to make proteins.
notes.simple: Think of DNA as information written in a sequence of bases. RNA helps carry and use that information so a protein can be made.
examples: A nucleotide contains a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group.
In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine; cytosine pairs with guanine.
steps: A nucleotide has a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group.
DNA has deoxyribose and the bases A, T, C and G.
RNA has ribose and the bases A, U, C and G.
mRNA carries information, tRNA transfers amino acids and rRNA forms part of ribosomes.
notes.checkQuestion: Which bases pair in DNA, and how many hydrogen bonds are between each pair?
notes.checkAnswer: Adenine pairs with thymine using two hydrogen bonds, and cytosine pairs with guanine using three hydrogen bonds.

notes.title: How DNA instructions make a protein
notes.answer: DNA → mRNA by transcription; mRNA → protein at a ribosome by translation.
notes.explanation: A gene is a sequence of DNA nucleotides that carries information for making a specific protein. The sequence is copied into mRNA by transcription. The mRNA goes to a ribosome, where its sequence is used to join amino acids into a protein. This is translation.
notes.simple: DNA keeps the instructions. A copy of the instructions travels to a ribosome, which uses them to make a protein.
examples: DNA gene → mRNA: transcription.
mRNA → amino acids joined into a protein at a ribosome: translation.
steps: A gene is a specific sequence of DNA nucleotides that carries information for making a specific protein.
The DNA sequence is copied into messenger RNA (mRNA). This is transcription.
The mRNA carries its nucleotide sequence to a ribosome.
The ribosome reads the mRNA sequence and joins specific amino acids to make a protein. This is translation.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the name of the process in which a DNA nucleotide sequence is copied into mRNA?
notes.checkAnswer: Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA sequence; translation uses the mRNA sequence at a ribosome to form a protein.

notes.title: Biomolecules: the main ideas
notes.answer: Biomolecules are molecules in living things, including carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
notes.explanation: Biomolecules are important molecules in living things. Carbohydrates mainly provide energy, proteins have many roles including growth and repair, lipids store energy and form membranes, and nucleic acids store and use genetic information. Water is the medium in which many of these processes occur.
notes.simple: Living things contain different kinds of molecules. Each kind has a particular job, such as providing energy, building structures, or carrying instructions.
examples: Glucose is a monosaccharide used in respiration to release energy.
DNA stores genetic information; RNA helps use that information to make proteins.
steps: Carbohydrates include sugars and starches; they are a major energy source.
Proteins are made from amino acids and perform many structural and functional jobs.
Most lipids are made from fatty acids and glycerol; they store energy and help form cell membranes.
DNA stores inherited information. RNA helps use that information to make proteins.
Water dissolves many substances and provides a medium for reactions in cells.
notes.checkQuestion: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
notes.checkAnswer: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine; DNA contains thymine instead of uracil.

notes.title: Metabolism: breaking down and building up
notes.answer: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions that occur within an organism to sustain life.
notes.explanation: Metabolism includes all the chemical reactions that keep an organism alive. Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy. Anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and uses energy.
notes.simple: Catabolism breaks things down and releases energy. Anabolism builds things up and needs energy.
examples: Cellular respiration breaks glucose into carbon dioxide and water to get energy.
Photosynthesis joins carbon dioxide and water to make glucose using sunlight.
steps: Identify whether complex molecules are being broken down or built up.
If they are broken down into simpler ones, the process is catabolism and releases energy.
If simpler molecules are joined to form complex ones, the process is anabolism and consumes energy.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of metabolism builds complex molecules and uses energy?
notes.checkAnswer: Anabolism requires energy input; photosynthesis is an example.

notes.title: Enzymes: catalysts with specific jobs
notes.answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions without being consumed.
notes.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they speed up reactions in living organisms without being used up. Their shape gives them an active site that binds particular substrates, so enzymes are specific. Some enzymes also need cofactors to work fully.
notes.simple: An enzyme is like a reusable helper: it speeds up a particular reaction, then can be used again.
examples: Amylase catalyses the breakdown of starch into simple sugars.
Protease enzymes help remove protein stains from clothes.
steps: A substrate binds to the enzyme’s matching active site.
The enzyme speeds up the reaction.
The product is released, and the enzyme is not consumed.
notes.checkQuestion: Which enzyme breaks down starch into simple sugars?
notes.checkAnswer: Amylase breaks down starch into simple sugars.

notes.title: How Enzymes Act
notes.answer: The induced fit model.
notes.explanation: An enzyme acts on a substrate at its active site. In the lock-and-key model, the active site has a fixed structure. In the induced fit model, the active site changes shape when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
notes.simple: The active site is the part of an enzyme where the substrate fits and the reaction happens. The two models explain whether that site stays fixed or changes shape.
examples: Lock-and-key: a substrate fits into a fixed active site.
Induced fit: the active site reshapes when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
steps: Identify the enzyme's active site.
Describe how the substrate interacts with that site.
State whether the active site is fixed or reshaped.
Explain that the enzyme catalyzes the reaction and the product is released.
notes.checkQuestion: In which model is the active site reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme?
notes.checkAnswer: The lock-and-key model has a fixed active site; in the induced fit model, the active site is reshaped.

notes.title: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
notes.answer: The activity of an enzyme is affected by temperature, pH and substrate concentration.
notes.explanation: Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration. Each enzyme has conditions where it works best. Too much heat or a big change in pH can reduce its activity, while adding substrate increases the rate only until all enzyme active sites are occupied.
notes.simple: Enzymes work best under particular conditions. If the conditions are not right, they work more slowly or may stop working.
examples: Most human enzymes work fastest at about 37°C.
Pepsin works in an acidic medium, while trypsin works in an alkaline medium.
steps: At a suitable temperature, increasing temperature makes molecules move more and the reaction rate rises.
Above the optimum temperature, heat breaks bonds in the enzyme and its globular structure is lost.
A pH change can affect amino acids at the enzyme's active site and slow or stop the enzyme.
Increasing substrate concentration raises the reaction rate until all active sites are occupied.
Once all active sites are occupied, extra substrate does not increase the reaction rate.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the reaction rate when all enzyme active sites are occupied?
notes.checkAnswer: The rate increases at first, then levels off when all active sites are occupied.

notes.title: How enzyme inhibitors work
notes.answer: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches somewhere other than the active site and changes the enzyme’s shape.
notes.explanation: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete for the enzyme’s active site. Non-competitive inhibitors attach somewhere else on the enzyme; this changes the enzyme’s shape and its active site, so the substrate cannot fit.
notes.simple: An inhibitor slows or blocks an enzyme. It either blocks the active site directly or changes its shape from another place.
examples: An antibiotic can act as a competitive inhibitor of a bacterial enzyme.
Mercury can act as a non-competitive inhibitor.
steps: Check whether the inhibitor resembles the substrate.
If it competes for the active site, it is competitive inhibition.
If it attaches elsewhere and changes the enzyme’s shape, it is non-competitive inhibition.
notes.checkQuestion: Where does a non-competitive inhibitor attach?
notes.checkAnswer: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches somewhere other than the active site and changes the enzyme’s shape.

notes.title: Enzymes: how they work and what affects them
notes.answer: A competitive inhibitor binds to the enzyme’s active site.
notes.explanation: This chapter covers metabolism, enzyme structure and specificity, factors affecting enzyme activity, and inhibition. The exercise text provided here contains Sections A–C; no Section D questions were supplied.
notes.simple: An enzyme is a protein that helps a chemical reaction happen faster. Its active site fits a particular substrate, rather like a shape fitting into a matching space.
examples: Amylase acts on starch.
Pepsin works best in an acidic environment, while trypsin works best in an alkaline environment.
steps: A substrate binds to the enzyme’s active site.
The enzyme helps convert the substrate into product or products.
The products leave, and the enzyme can be used again.
Temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors can affect the rate.
notes.checkQuestion: Where does a competitive inhibitor bind to an enzyme?
notes.checkAnswer: A competitive inhibitor binds to the enzyme’s active site and blocks the substrate from binding.

notes.title: ATP: the cell’s energy currency
notes.answer: ATP is a nucleotide that stores and transfers usable energy for cell activities.
notes.explanation: ATP is a nucleotide made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups. The bonds between its phosphate groups are high-energy bonds. When the outer phosphate bond breaks, ATP becomes ADP, inorganic phosphate (Pi) separates, and about 7.3 kcal of energy per mole is released. Cells use energy from food to join ADP and Pi and make ATP again. For example, ATP can break down to release energy for a cell process, while energy from food can be used to rebuild ATP.
notes.simple: ATP is like a small energy packet. Breaking off its outer phosphate releases energy, and cells can use energy from food to attach a phosphate again.
examples: ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi + energy (7.3 kcal/mole)
ADP + H₂O → AMP + Pi + energy (7.3 kcal/mole)
steps: ATP is made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
Breaking the outer phosphate bond releases energy and forms ADP and Pi.
Cells use energy from food to combine ADP and Pi and make ATP again.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the products when ATP reacts with water and its outer phosphate bond breaks?
notes.checkAnswer: Adenosine triphosphate

notes.title: Photosynthesis
notes.answer: Photosynthesis is the synthesis of glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight (and chlorophyll), with oxygen as a by-product.
notes.explanation: Photosynthesis is how plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. It happens in two phases: light reactions in the thylakoid membranes and dark reactions in the stroma. Chlorophyll absorbs light, and the light reactions make ATP and NADPH for the dark reactions.
notes.simple: Plants use light to make food. The light reactions capture energy, and the dark reactions use that energy to make carbohydrates.
examples: Light reactions release oxygen when light breaks water molecules.
In the dark reactions, carbon dioxide is used to make carbohydrates.
steps: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
The light reactions use light energy to make ATP and NADPH and release oxygen from water.
The dark reactions use ATP and hydrogen from NADPH to reduce carbon dioxide and make carbohydrates.
The carbohydrates are used to make glucose.
notes.checkQuestion: Where do the light and dark reactions of photosynthesis take place?
notes.checkAnswer: Light reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes; dark reactions occur in the stroma.

notes.title: Cellular Respiration
notes.answer: Cellular respiration is the oxidation of food inside cells to release energy.
notes.explanation: Cellular respiration releases energy by oxidizing food inside cells. With oxygen, glucose is completely oxidized and releases more energy; without oxygen, glucose is incompletely oxidized and releases less energy. The main stages of aerobic respiration are glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain.
notes.simple: Cells release energy from food. Oxygen allows more energy to be released; without enough oxygen, cells release less.
examples: In yeast, pyruvic acid is converted into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.
In hard-working muscles when oxygen is insufficient, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid.
steps: In glycolysis, one glucose molecule is broken into two pyruvic acid molecules in the cytoplasm.
When oxygen is available, pyruvic acid is converted into acetyl coenzyme-A and enters the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix.
The Krebs cycle produces carbon dioxide, ATP, NADH and FADH₂.
In the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membranes, electrons release energy used to make ATP; oxygen combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.
notes.checkQuestion: Where does glycolysis occur, and does it need oxygen?
notes.checkAnswer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen.

notes.title: Bioenergetics: energy in living things
notes.answer: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, and cellular respiration releases energy from glucose for cell activities.
notes.explanation: Cells need a steady supply of usable energy. In this chapter, ATP links the energy released by respiration to the work cells perform, while photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose.
notes.simple: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose. Respiration releases energy from glucose, and ATP carries usable energy around the cell.
examples: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
steps: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy during photosynthesis.
Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
Respiration breaks down glucose and transfers some of its energy to ATP.
With oxygen, aerobic respiration produces much more ATP than anaerobic respiration.
Without enough oxygen, cells can use anaerobic respiration, which produces less ATP.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the main purpose of cellular respiration?
notes.checkAnswer: ATP is the cell’s usable energy carrier; ADP can gain a phosphate group to become ATP.

notes.title: Mineral Nutrition in Plants
notes.answer: Plants absorb mineral nutrients from soil. Macronutrients are needed in larger quantities, and micronutrients are needed in lower quantities. Nitrogen is a component of proteins and chlorophyll. Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and activates many enzymes.
notes.explanation: Plants need mineral nutrients from the soil to make important substances and grow. Macronutrients are needed in large quantities, while micronutrients are needed in small quantities. Nitrogen is used to make proteins and chlorophyll; magnesium is part of chlorophyll.
notes.simple: Plants take useful minerals from the soil. They need some minerals a lot and others only a little.
examples: Potassium is a macronutrient because plants need it in larger quantities.
Iron is a micronutrient because plants need it in lower quantities.
steps: Classify a mineral by how much of it plants need.
If plants need it in larger quantities, it is a macronutrient.
If plants need it in lower quantities, it is a micronutrient.
Recall that nitrogen is a component of proteins and chlorophyll.
Recall that magnesium is a component of chlorophyll.
notes.checkQuestion: State one role of nitrogen and one role of magnesium in plants.
notes.checkAnswer: Nitrogen is needed for proteins and chlorophyll; magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and activates many enzymes.

notes.title: How roots take in water and salts
notes.answer: Root hairs absorb salts by active transport and water by osmosis. Water and dissolved salts then pass through the root to the xylem.
notes.explanation: Water and mineral salts enter the root mainly through root hairs. Root hairs take in salts by active transport, and water follows by osmosis. The water and dissolved salts then pass through the root towards the xylem.
notes.simple: Root hairs take in salts, and water moves in after them. The water and salts travel through the root to the xylem.
examples: Root hairs take salts in by active transport.
Water moves from soil into root hairs by osmosis.
steps: Root hairs touch the soil water and provide a large surface area.
Root hairs take in salts from the soil by active transport.
Water moves from soil into root hairs by osmosis.
Water and dissolved salts pass through the epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle.
Water moves from the pericycle into the root xylem.
notes.checkQuestion: How do root hairs absorb salts and water from the soil?
notes.checkAnswer: Root hairs absorb salts by active transport; water enters by osmosis.

notes.title: Transpiration and stomata
notes.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapours from the plant surface. It occurs through stomata, the cuticle and lenticels.
notes.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant’s surface. Most water vapour leaves through stomata. Guard cells open or close the stomata by changing their turgor, and factors such as temperature, wind and humidity affect how quickly water is lost.
notes.simple: Plants lose water vapour, mostly through tiny openings in their leaves. Wind usually speeds up this loss; high humidity slows it down.
examples: On a windy day, moving air carries away humid air around leaves, so more water can evaporate.
When guard cells take in potassium ions, water enters them by osmosis and the stoma opens.
steps: Water moves from the xylem into the cell walls of mesophyll cells.
Water evaporates from the moist walls into the air spaces in the leaf.
Water vapours move towards the stomata and pass to the outside air.
During daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells, water follows by osmosis, and the guard cells become turgid so the stoma opens.
In the evening, potassium ions and water move out of guard cells; they lose turgor and the stoma closes.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does wind speed up transpiration?
notes.checkAnswer: Wind carries away humid air around the leaves, allowing more water to evaporate.

notes.title: How water moves upwards in plants
notes.answer: Transpirational pull is the pulling force created by transpiration from leaf surfaces; it pulls water upwards through the xylem.
notes.explanation: Water evaporating from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull. This pull draws water upwards through the continuous water column in the xylem, from roots to leaves.
notes.simple: Leaves lose water, and that loss pulls more water up from the roots through the xylem.
examples: When mesophyll cells lose water, more water enters them from the xylem.
As water moves up through the leaf xylem, tension pulls the water column upwards through the stem and roots.
steps: Water is lost from the leaf surfaces by transpiration.
Mesophyll cells lose water, so more water enters them from the xylem.
The water column in the xylem is continuous from leaves through the stem to the roots.
Movement of water in the leaf xylem creates tension in the whole column.
This tension pulls the water column upwards.
notes.checkQuestion: What creates the pulling force that moves water upwards in a plant?
notes.checkAnswer: Transpiration from leaf surfaces creates the pull.

notes.title: How food moves through a plant
notes.answer: Food moves through phloem from a source to a sink because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink.
notes.explanation: Food is transported through phloem. In most plants, it travels as sucrose from a source, where food is available, to a sink, where food is used or stored. Loading sucrose at the source draws water into the phloem and raises its pressure. At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water leaves the phloem, lowering its pressure. This pressure difference drives the flow of food.
notes.simple: Think of food flowing through phloem from where it is supplied to where it is needed or stored. Water pressure helps push it along.
examples: A mesophyll cell in a leaf can be a source; a growing root tip can be a sink.
A root storing food can be a source when it supplies food, or a sink when it receives food for storage.
steps: At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes.
Water enters the sieve tubes from nearby xylem by osmosis.
The fluid pressure rises at the source, pushing food solution towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded and water moves into the xylem by osmosis.
The pressure is lower at the sink, so food flows in bulk from the higher-pressure source towards it.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does food flow from the source towards the sink?
notes.checkAnswer: Food moves in phloem from higher pressure at the source towards lower pressure at the sink.

notes.title: Gaseous Exchange in Plants
notes.answer: Plants exchange gases through their surfaces. Leaves and young stems mainly use stomata, while woody stems use lenticels.
notes.explanation: Plants exchange gases with their environment through their surfaces. Leaves and young stems use stomata, while woody stems use lenticels because their bark does not allow gaseous exchange.
notes.simple: Plants exchange gases through openings or surfaces. In daylight, photosynthesis changes which gases leaves exchange with the environment; at night, respiration continues without photosynthesis.
examples: During daytime, leaves take in carbon dioxide from the environment and release oxygen.
At night, plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
steps: Remember that respiration happens in plant cells during both day and night.
During the day, green parts also carry out photosynthesis.
Stomata in leaves and young stems allow gases to move in and out.
Lenticels allow gaseous exchange through the bark of woody stems.
notes.checkQuestion: Which special pores allow gaseous exchange through the bark of woody stems?
notes.checkAnswer: Lenticels

notes.title: How Plants Excrete Wastes
notes.answer: Plants excrete gases through surfaces and stomata, extra water by transpiration or guttation, and other wastes by storing or excreting them.
notes.explanation: Plants get rid of extra gases, water and other metabolic wastes in different ways. They release gases through surfaces and stomata, remove water by transpiration or guttation, and may store or excrete other wastes.
notes.simple: Excretion is how a plant gets rid of substances it does not need. It can release them, store them, or keep them in leaves that later fall.
examples: Grass can release water droplets from the tips or edges of its leaves at night by guttation.
Rubber plants excrete latex, while keekar trees excrete gum.
steps: Plants release excess carbon dioxide and oxygen through their general surfaces and stomata.
Plants remove extra water by transpiration during the day or by guttation at night.
Plants may store wastes as harmless crystals or in leaves that later fall.
Some plants excrete wastes through special pores, such as latex, gum, resin or mucilage.
notes.checkQuestion: How is guttation different from dew formation?
notes.checkAnswer: Guttation is the release of water droplets through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves. Dew forms when water vapour in the air condenses on the leaf surface.

notes.title: How plants adjust to their habitats
notes.answer: There are four types based on habitat: mesophytes, hydrophytes, xerophytes, and halophytes.
notes.explanation: Plants adjust how they take up, keep, or lose water according to their habitat. For example, a cactus stores water in succulent organs, while a water lily removes extra water through stomata on its leaves.
notes.simple: Plants living in different places use different ways to manage water and salts.
examples: A cactus is a xerophyte with a succulent stem.
A water lily is a hydrophyte with broad floating leaves.
steps: Identify the plant's habitat: moderate, wet, very dry, or salty.
Match the habitat to the plant type: mesophyte, hydrophyte, xerophyte, or halophyte.
State the adaptation that helps the plant manage water or salts.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do halophytes absorb salts?
notes.checkAnswer: A halophyte absorbs salts to make its body hypertonic, so water does not move out of its cells.

notes.title: Plant physiology: uptake, transport and excretion
notes.answer: Water enters root cells by osmosis.
notes.explanation: Plants need mineral nutrients, water and gases to grow. Roots absorb water and mineral salts, xylem carries them upwards, and phloem transports food. Transpiration helps pull water through a plant, while plants also use several ways to remove or store wastes.
notes.simple: Roots take in water and minerals, leaves exchange gases and lose water vapour, and transport tissues move water and food around the plant.
examples: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts.
On a windy day, moving air removes moist air from around leaves, so transpiration usually increases.
steps: Root hairs absorb water from the soil by osmosis and mineral salts by diffusion or active transport, depending on the salt and conditions.
Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral salts from roots towards the leaves.
Water evaporates from leaf surfaces and exits mainly through stomata; this loss is transpiration.
Transpiration creates a pull that helps draw water upwards through xylem.
Phloem transports dissolved food, mainly sucrose, from sources to sinks by pressure flow.
notes.checkQuestion: How does water enter root cells?
notes.checkAnswer: Water moves into root cells by osmosis; mineral salts may enter by active transport.

notes.title: Types of Asexual Reproduction
notes.answer: Vegetative propagation is a method of asexual reproduction in plants in which a new plant is produced from the vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of the parent plant.
notes.explanation: Asexual reproduction makes new organisms without the fusion of gametes. In plants, vegetative propagation makes a new plant from a root, stem, or leaf. Some plants also reproduce by binary fission, budding, or spores.
notes.simple: A new plant can grow from a part of its parent, such as a stem or leaf, without seeds.
examples: A potato can grow a new plant from the buds, called eyes, on its tuber.
A strawberry can form a new plant at a node on its stolon.
steps: Identify the method: binary fission, budding, spore formation, or vegetative propagation.
For vegetative propagation, name the plant part or structure involved.
Give the textbook example if the question asks for one.
notes.checkQuestion: What is a stolon?
notes.checkAnswer: A horizontal stem that grows above the ground.

notes.title: Growing plants from plant parts
notes.answer: Cutting grows a new plant from a cut piece of stem or root; grafting joins a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of another plant.
notes.explanation: Artificial propagation is when people grow new plants using parts of a plant, such as stems or roots. Cutting and grafting are two common methods. These methods can preserve useful characteristics, but the new plants have little genetic variation.
notes.simple: People can make new plants from plant parts instead of seeds. A piece can be planted, or parts of two plants can be joined.
examples: Roses and grapevines can be grown from stem cuttings.
Sweet potato can be grown from root cuttings.
steps: For cutting, cut a piece of stem or root from a plant and use it to grow a new plant.
For grafting, attach a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of a second plant.
Remember that grafting can combine beneficial characteristics of two plants.
Remember that vegetative propagation produces plants identical to the parent, so they share the same strengths and weaknesses.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one difference between cutting and grafting?

notes.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
notes.answer: The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, and the female gametophyte is the embryo sac.
notes.explanation: In flowering plants, the diploid sporophyte makes haploid spores. These grow into small gametophytes, which make gametes. After fertilization, a diploid zygote develops into a new sporophyte.
notes.simple: The plant makes spores, spores grow into tiny structures that make gametes, and the joined gametes start a new plant.
examples: A pollen grain is the male gametophyte.
The embryo sac is the female gametophyte.
steps: The diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Spores grow into haploid male and female gametophytes.
The male gametophyte makes sperms; the female gametophyte contains the egg and fusion nucleus.
Pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.
One sperm fuses with the egg to form a zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form the endosperm nucleus.
The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
