notes.checkAnswer: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

notes.title: Reproduction in Plants: Main Ideas
notes.answer: The pollen tube carries the male gametes towards the embryo sac.
notes.explanation: Plants can reproduce without seeds by using spores or vegetative parts, and sexually by producing gametes in flowers. In flowering plants, pollen carries the male gametes and the ovule contains the female gametophyte. Fertilization forms a seed, which can grow into a new sporophyte plant.
notes.simple: A plant can make a new plant from a plant part, or make seeds after fertilization. Flowers help make the male and female cells needed for seed formation.
examples: A potato tuber can grow into a new potato plant.
A pollen tube carries male gametes to the embryo sac in an ovule.
steps: Identify whether reproduction is asexual or sexual.
For asexual reproduction, look for one parent and no fusion of gametes.
For sexual reproduction in flowering plants, follow pollen to the ovule.
Remember that fertilization forms the embryo and endosperm, and the ovule develops into a seed.
notes.checkQuestion: Which structure carries the male gametes from a pollen grain towards the embryo sac?
notes.checkAnswer: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

notes.title: Introduction to Biostatistics
notes.answer: Biostatistics applies statistical methods to biological sciences and helps people use biological and health data.
notes.explanation: Biostatistics uses statistical methods to help study biological and health-related questions. It helps researchers plan studies, analyse data, interpret results, predict outcomes, and support public health decisions.
notes.simple: Biostatistics is statistics used in biology and health.
examples: Analysing COVID-19 rates can help guide vaccination campaigns.
Comparing wheat yields can help researchers assess different varieties and farming practices.
steps: Plan a study so that it collects relevant and sufficient data.
Analyse the data to find trends, correlations, and patterns.
Interpret the results so they can guide decisions.
Use current data to predict outcomes and plan actions.
notes.checkQuestion: What can biostatistics help public health officials do with data about disease rates?
notes.checkAnswer: Biostatistics is a branch of statistics that applies statistical methods to biological sciences.

notes.title: Mean, Median, and Mode
notes.answer: Mean = sum of all data points divided by number of data points; median = the middle value after ordering; mode = the most frequent value.
notes.explanation: Mean, median, and mode describe the centre or most common value in a data set. Find the mean by adding all the values and dividing by how many there are. Find the median after arranging the values in order. Find the mode by checking which value occurs most often.
notes.simple: Mean is the sharing-out average, median is the middle after sorting, and mode is the value that occurs most often.
examples: For 2, 4, 6, the mean is (2 + 4 + 6)/3 = 4.
For 2, 4, 6, the median is 4, and there is no mode because no value repeats.
steps: For the mean, add all the data values and divide by the number of values.
For the median, arrange the values in ascending order.
If there are an odd number of values, take the middle value; if there are an even number, average the two middle values.
For the mode, count how often each value appears and choose the value or values with the highest frequency.
notes.checkQuestion: Find the median of 2, 10, 4, 8.
notes.checkAnswer: The values in order are 2, 4, 8, 10. The two middle values are 4 and 8, so the median is (4 + 8)/2 = 6.

notes.title: Reading and making a bar chart
notes.answer: A bar chart represents data using bars of different heights or lengths to compare categories.
notes.explanation: A bar chart uses bars to show the values of different categories, so you can compare them quickly.
notes.simple: Each category gets a bar. The bar’s height shows that category’s value.
examples: If Species A has 15 plants, its bar reaches 15 on the value axis.
If Species D has 25 plants, its bar is taller than the bar for Species A.
steps: Arrange the categories and their values.
Draw and label the x-axis and y-axis.
Choose a suitable scale with equal intervals.
Draw equal-width bars, spaced evenly, to the correct values.
Label each bar with its category and value.
notes.checkQuestion: What does the height of a bar show?
notes.checkAnswer: The value of the corresponding category.

notes.title: Biostatistics and ways to summarise data
notes.answer: Biostatistics applies statistical methods to biological sciences. Mean, median, mode, and bar charts help describe and interpret data.
notes.explanation: Biostatistics applies statistical methods to biological sciences. It helps organise and understand data so people can make informed decisions, for example in public health. The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value when the data is ordered; and the mode is the most frequently occurring value. A bar chart uses bars to show the values of different categories.
notes.simple: Biostatistics helps us use data about living things and health. Mean is the average, median is the middle, and mode is the most common value.
examples: For 2, 4, 6, the mean is (2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = 4.
For 3, 5, 5, 8, the median is (5 + 5) ÷ 2 = 5 and the mode is 5.
steps: Order the values from smallest to largest when finding the median.
For an odd number of values, select the single middle value; for an even number, average the two middle values.
To find the mean, add all values and divide by the number of values.
To find the mode, identify the value or values occurring most frequently.
For a bar chart, place categories on the horizontal axis and show each category's value with a bar.

Incorrect: the species name begins with a small letter.

quiz.stem: In *Apis cerana*, what is *cerana*?
rationales: Incorrect: *Apis cerana* is the scientific name, not a common name.
Incorrect: *Apis* is the genus name.
Correct: the second part, *cerana*, is the species name.
Incorrect: *cerana* is the species part of a scientific name, not a rank above domain.

quiz.stem: Why is binomial nomenclature useful when biologists speak different languages?
options: So each region can choose a different scientific name
So the name is the same worldwide and biologists can communicate clearly
So the organism's common name is always in English
So the scientific name tells the organism's habitat
rationales: Incorrect: the scientific name is intended to be standard, not different in each region.
Correct: one standard scientific name supports clear communication across languages.
Incorrect: scientific names are not required to be common names in English.
Incorrect: the two-part name identifies genus and species, not necessarily habitat.

quiz.stem: Which statement explains why scientific names can avoid confusion between regions?
options: Because the words are taken from Latin and the name is standard worldwide
Because every organism has the same common name
Because Latin names are changed in every country
Because scientific names are based on local languages
rationales: Correct: Latin-based scientific names are standard worldwide, unlike varying common names.
Incorrect: common names can vary from place to place and can cause confusion.
Incorrect: scientific names are intended to remain the same worldwide.
Incorrect: the rules specify Latin words, rather than local-language names.

quiz.stem: Which rule applies to the scientific name of an organism?
options: The same scientific name may be used for two different organisms.
Every scientific name must have three parts.
Every scientific name should be unique.
The species name always comes before the genus name.
rationales: Incorrect: the same scientific name cannot be used for two different organisms.
Incorrect: a scientific name has two parts.
Correct: each scientific name should be unique.
Incorrect: the genus name always comes first.

quiz.stem: Which is a shortcoming of common names described in this section?
options: Common names are always based on scientific definitions.
A common name may be used for several different organisms.
Common names are the same in every region.
Common names always show an organism's genus and species.
rationales: Incorrect: the section says common names have no scientific basis.
Correct: one common name, such as “blue bell,” may be used for different organisms.
Incorrect: common names may differ between regions and countries.
Incorrect: common names do not provide the two scientific-name parts.

quiz.stem: The process of cellular respiration occurs in:
rationales: The nucleus does not serve as the main site of cellular respiration.
Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic cellular respiration.
Ribosomes synthesize proteins rather than carry out cellular respiration.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages molecules rather than carry out cellular respiration.

quiz.stem: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is primarily involved in the synthesis of:
rationales: Proteins are primarily synthesized by ribosomes, especially those on rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is primarily involved in lipid synthesis.
Carbohydrates are not the primary product synthesized by smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
Nucleic acids are synthesized by enzymes rather than by smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

quiz.stem: Ribosomes are composed of:
rationales: Ribosomes are made of ribosomal RNA and proteins.
DNA is not a structural component of ribosomes.
Carbohydrates and lipids are not the primary components of ribosomes.
Ribosomes contain RNA, but carbohydrates are not their other main component.

quiz.stem: What is the primary function of ribosomes?
rationales: Energy production is primarily associated with mitochondria, not ribosomes.
Ribosomes translate messenger RNA to synthesize proteins.
Lipid synthesis is primarily associated with smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
DNA synthesis is carried out by enzymes, not ribosomes.

quiz.stem: Which cell organelle is involved in packaging and modifying proteins?
rationales: The nucleus stores genetic material and does not primarily package and modify proteins.
Mitochondria primarily produce cellular energy rather than package and modify proteins.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins.
The endoplasmic reticulum helps synthesize and transport proteins, but the Golgi apparatus is the primary packaging and modification organelle.

quiz.stem: Which cell organelle is responsible for breaking down waste materials?
rationales: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages molecules rather than breaking down cellular waste.
The nucleus contains genetic material and does not primarily break down waste.
Mitochondria produce energy and do not primarily digest waste materials.
Lysosomes contain enzymes that break down waste and cellular materials.

quiz.stem: Which of the following cell structures is involved in maintaining cell shape?
rationales: The cytoskeleton helps maintain cell shape and provides structural support.
Centrioles organize microtubules and help with cell division, but are not the primary structures maintaining cell shape.
The nucleus contains genetic material and is not the main structure responsible for cell shape.
Lysosomes digest cellular materials rather than maintain cell shape.

quiz.stem: Which specialized region of the nucleus is responsible for ribosome assembly?
rationales: The nucleoplasm is the fluid inside the nucleus, not the main site of ribosome assembly.
The nucleolus is the nuclear region where ribosomal subunits are assembled.
Chromatin is DNA associated with proteins and is not the site of ribosome assembly.
Chromatin is DNA associated with proteins and is not the site of ribosome assembly.

quiz.stem: What is the main function of the nuclear pores?
options: Control of pH of the cell
rationales: Nuclear pores do not primarily regulate cell division.
Nuclear pores do not control the pH of the cell.
Protein synthesis occurs at ribosomes, not at nuclear pores.
Nuclear pores regulate the movement of molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm.

quiz.stem: Which of the following cellular structures is found in animal cells and helps in cell division?
rationales: The cell membrane surrounds the cell but is not the specialized structure that helps organize cell division.
Centrioles, found in many animal cells, help organize the spindle during cell division.
Plasmodesmata are channels between plant cells, not structures in animal cells.
Vacuoles are storage compartments and are not the animal-cell structure that helps organize division.

quiz.stem: Which sub-cellular organelle plays a crucial role in energy production within the cell?
rationales: The endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes and transports molecules but is not the main site of energy production.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages molecules rather than produce most cellular energy.
Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP through aerobic respiration.
Lysosomes digest cellular materials rather than produce energy.

quiz.stem: In a multicellular plant, which cell type is responsible for the production of glucose?
rationales: Xylem primarily transports water and minerals rather than produce glucose.
Phloem primarily transports sugars and other products rather than produce glucose.
Epidermal cells primarily protect the plant and generally are not the main photosynthetic cells.
Mesophyll cells carry out most photosynthesis in leaves, producing glucose.

quiz.stem: Which organelle can double its number by itself?
rationales: Ribosomes are assembled from components and do not independently double their number as organelles.
Lysosomes are formed through cellular membrane trafficking and do not independently replicate.
Mitochondria contain their own DNA and can grow and divide to increase their number.
The Golgi apparatus does not independently replicate by dividing.

quiz.stem: Which of these are present on the surface of rough endoplasmic reticulum?
rationales: Ribosomes attached to its surface give rough endoplasmic reticulum its characteristic appearance.
Lysosomes are separate organelles and are not attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum surface.
Mitochondria are separate organelles rather than structures on the rough endoplasmic reticulum surface.
Vacuoles are separate membrane-bound compartments and are not attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum surface.

quiz.stem: According to your textbook, what is a cell?
options: A part found only in plants
rationales: This is correct: your textbook defines the cell as the basic unit of life.
This is incorrect: cells are the units that form living organisms.
This is incorrect: a cell is a unit, not a group of organs.
This is incorrect: plants and animals are both made of cells.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the role of cells in living organisms?
options: They are the building blocks of living organisms.
They are found only in the largest animals.
They cannot carry out life functions.
They are made only by plants.
rationales: This is correct: your textbook compares cells to the building blocks of a house.
This is incorrect: living things of many sizes are made of cells.
This is incorrect: cells carry out functions necessary for life.
This is incorrect: animals and humans are also made of cells.

quiz.stem: Which statement about the size of cells agrees with the section?
options: Most cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye.
All cells are visible without a microscope.
Cells can be seen only in plants.
Cells are always smaller than bacteria.
rationales: This is correct: most cells cannot be seen with the naked eye.
This is incorrect: the section says most cells are too small to see unaided.
This is incorrect: cells occur in plants, animals and other living things.
This is incorrect: the section does not make this comparison.

quiz.stem: Which example does your textbook give of a cell large enough to be seen with the naked eye?
rationales: This is correct: the ostrich egg cell is one of the examples given.
This is incorrect: this is not an example listed in the section.
This is incorrect: this is not an example listed in the section.
This is incorrect: this is not an example listed in the section.

quiz.stem: In the cell-city comparison, what role is compared to a city's government?
options: It directs the cell's activities by giving instructions.
It acts as a waste disposal unit.
It forms the roads that transport materials.
It produces all the energy in the cell.
rationales: This is correct: the nucleus directs cell activities by giving instructions.
This is incorrect: the city comparison associates waste disposal with structures that remove or break down waste.
This is incorrect: roads and delivery services are compared with structures that process and transport materials.
This is incorrect: the comparison says some structures produce energy but does not identify them as the city's government.

quiz.stem: Why are cells essential to living things?
options: Cells carry out the functions necessary for life.
Cells are visible to the naked eye in every organism.
Only large organisms are made of cells.
Cells have no role in keeping organisms functioning.
rationales: This is correct: cells carry out the functions necessary for life.
This is incorrect: most cells are too small to see with the naked eye.
This is incorrect: every living thing, from a bacterium to a whale, is made of cells.
This is incorrect: cells help keep living things alive and functioning.

quiz.stem: Which layer holds together the primary walls of adjacent plant cells?
rationales: Correct: the middle lamella holds together the primary walls of adjacent cells.
The primary wall is a cellulose-rich wall layer, but it is not the layer joining adjacent cells.
The secondary wall may be made on the inner side of a primary wall in some plant cells.
The cell membrane surrounds the cytoplasm; it does not hold adjacent primary walls together.

quiz.stem: What is the cell wall of fungi made of?
rationales: Peptidoglycan makes up the cell wall of prokaryotes.
Correct: fungal cell walls are made of chitin.
Cellulose is found in plant cell walls and the cell walls of algae.
Tubulin is a protein that makes up microtubules.

quiz.stem: Which structure forms a double-membrane boundary around the nucleus?
rationales: Nucleoplasm is the jelly-like material inside the nucleus.
The nucleolus is a small body inside the nucleus where ribosomes are assembled.
Correct: the nuclear envelope is the double membrane around the nucleus.
Chromatin is thread-like material made of DNA and proteins inside the nucleus.

quiz.stem: What happens to chromatin when a cell starts dividing?
options: The nucleus moves to the centre
The nuclear envelope becomes the cell wall
rationales: In mature plant cells, a large central vacuole can push the nucleus to the side; this is not what happens to chromatin during cell division.
Correct: chromatin condenses and takes the shape of thick chromosomes.
The nucleolus is where ribosomes are assembled; it does not become a vacuole.
The nuclear envelope does not become the cell wall.

quiz.stem: What is the membrane of a plant vacuole called?
rationales: Correct: the membrane of a plant vacuole is called the tonoplast.
A crista is a fold of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion.
A centriole is an organelle involved in forming spindle fibres and basal bodies.
Cisternae are the flattened sacs that make up the Golgi apparatus.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares cilia and flagella?
options: Long and always present in pairs
rationales: Correct: cilia are short and usually numerous, while flagella are longer and fewer.
Flagella are longer but are usually fewer, not numerous.
Cilia are usually numerous, not few.
Flagella are longer and fewer; they are not always present in pairs.

quiz.stem: What material makes the rigid plant cell wall described in this section?
rationales: Correct: the section states that plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
Incorrect: protein is not named as the material of the plant cell wall in this section.
Incorrect: starch is not named as the material of the plant cell wall in this section.
Incorrect: the section says cellulose, not chitin, makes the plant cell wall.

quiz.stem: What is the main advantage of chloroplasts in plant cells?
rationales: Incorrect: making spindle fibres is the role of centrioles in animal cells.
Incorrect: storing water and nutrients is a role of the large central vacuole.
Correct: chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, helping plants produce food.
Incorrect: breaking down waste materials is a role of lysosomes.

quiz.stem: How does the large central vacuole help maintain a plant cell's shape?
options: It allows direct communication between cells.
rationales: Incorrect: centrioles make spindle fibres during cell division.
Correct: the large central vacuole provides turgor pressure that maintains cell shape.
Incorrect: plasmodesmata allow direct communication and transport between plant cells.
Incorrect: lysosomes break down waste materials.

quiz.stem: Which plant cell structures allow direct communication and transport of substances between cells?
rationales: Incorrect: centrioles make spindle fibres during cell division.
Correct: plasmodesmata are channels for communication and transport between plant cells.
Incorrect: chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy.
Incorrect: flagella are involved in movement, such as the movement of sperm cells.

quiz.stem: What is the advantage of centrioles in animal cells?
options: They ensure accurate distribution of chromosomes during cell division.
They let plant cells produce food.
rationales: Correct: centrioles make spindle fibres, ensuring accurate chromosome distribution during cell division.
Incorrect: turgor pressure is provided by the large central vacuole in plant cells.
Incorrect: lysosomes, rather than centrioles, break down waste materials.
Incorrect: chloroplasts allow plants to produce food through photosynthesis.

quiz.stem: Which animal cell structures contain enzymes that break down waste materials?
rationales: Correct: lysosomes contain enzymes that break down waste materials and contribute to cellular cleanup and recycling.
Incorrect: chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
Incorrect: plasmodesmata connect plant cells for communication and transport.
Incorrect: centrioles make spindle fibres for cell division.

quiz.stem: What advantage do animal cells gain from lacking a rigid cell wall?
options: They make chemical energy from light.
rationales: Correct: without a rigid cell wall, animal cells can change shape easily, helping with movements.
Incorrect: converting light energy into chemical energy is the role of chloroplasts.
Incorrect: turgor pressure is provided by the large central vacuole in plant cells.
Incorrect: centrioles make spindle fibres, not the lack of a cell wall.

quiz.stem: Which structure propels a sperm cell toward the egg?
rationales: Correct: the section gives the sperm cell's flagellum as the structure that propels it toward the egg.
Incorrect: the large central vacuole stores materials and provides turgor pressure in plant cells.
Incorrect: plasmodesmata connect plant cells for communication and transport.
Incorrect: a rigid cell wall supports and protects plant cells; it does not propel sperm.

quiz.stem: Which feature helps mesophyll cells perform photosynthesis?
options: To absorb light energy for photosynthesis
To transport water through the stem
To carry oxygen around the body
rationales: Correct: mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts with chlorophyll to capture light energy.
Incorrect: water transport through a plant is not the stated function of mesophyll cells.
Incorrect: red blood cells, not mesophyll cells, carry oxygen around the body.
Incorrect: mesophyll cells are in leaves and do not protect the heart.

quiz.stem: How do root hair cells help a plant?
options: They increase the root's surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
They carry nerve impulses away from the cell body.
They pump blood through the heart.
rationales: Correct: root hairs increase surface area, helping roots absorb water and minerals from soil.
Incorrect: guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomata; root hairs do not close them.
Incorrect: axons carry nerve impulses away from a neuron's cell body.
Incorrect: cardiac muscle contractions help pump blood, not root hair cells.

quiz.stem: Which muscle cells are branched, striated, and found in the heart walls?
rationales: Incorrect: skeletal muscle cells are long and striated and are attached to bones.
Correct: cardiac muscle cells are branched and striated and occur in the heart walls.
Incorrect: smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped and non-striated.
Incorrect: mesophyll cells are green leaf cells specialized for photosynthesis.

quiz.stem: Which part of a neuron carries nerve impulses away from the cell body?
rationales: Incorrect: dendrites receive nerve impulses and transmit them to the cell body.
Correct: axons carry nerve impulses away from the cell body.
Incorrect: root hairs absorb water and minerals from soil.
Incorrect: stomata are openings in leaves regulated by guard cells.

quiz.stem: What is an advantage of the biconcave disk shape of a red blood cell?
options: They provide more surface area to absorb and release oxygen.
They allow the cell to contract.
They increase the cell's ability to transmit nerve impulses.
They form extensions that absorb minerals from soil.
rationales: Correct: the biconcave shape provides more surface area for absorbing and releasing oxygen.
Incorrect: contraction is a specialized function of muscle cells.
Incorrect: neurons transmit nerve impulses; this is not the function of red blood cell shape.
Incorrect: root hair cells form extensions that absorb water and minerals.

quiz.stem: Which is one of the specialized functions of liver cells?
rationales: Correct: liver cells help detoxify toxic substances.
Incorrect: neurons transmit nerve impulses.
Incorrect: mesophyll cells are specialized for photosynthesis.
Incorrect: skeletal muscle contractions move the skeleton.

quiz.stem: What does division of labour within a cell mean?
options: Each organelle carries out a distinct function needed for the cell.
All organelles perform exactly the same task.
Only the nucleus contributes to cell survival.
Organelles work only in multicellular organisms.
rationales: Correct: different organelles carry out distinct functions that contribute to the cell's survival and functioning.
Incorrect: organelles have different functions rather than all doing the same task.
Incorrect: the textbook describes several organelles contributing to cell survival, not only the nucleus.
Incorrect: organelles perform their functions within cells, including cells of single-celled organisms.

quiz.stem: What is the main specialized function of red blood cells?
options: They are specialized to carry oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.
They contract to move food through the alimentary canal.
They make extensions that absorb water from soil.
They receive nerve impulses and send them to the cell body.
rationales: Correct: red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues.
Incorrect: smooth muscle cells in the alimentary canal contract to move food forward.
Incorrect: root hair cells absorb water and minerals from soil.
Incorrect: dendrites receive nerve impulses and transmit them to the cell body.

quiz.stem: Which description best defines a stem cell?
options: A specialized cell that cannot make new cells
An unspecialized cell that can differentiate into specialized cells
A cell found only in the skin
rationales: This is not the section's definition of a stem cell.
This is correct because stem cells are unspecialized and can differentiate into specialized cells.
Stem cells are found in different parts of the body, not only in the skin.
Carrying oxygen is a function of red blood cells, not the definition of a stem cell.

quiz.stem: Which cell is described as the earliest stem cell in development?
rationales: The zygote is identified as the earliest stem cell.
A red blood cell is a specialized cell, not the earliest stem cell.
A nerve cell is a specialized cell that develops from stem-cell lineages.
A muscle cell is a specialized cell that develops from stem-cell lineages.

quiz.stem: What do adult stem cells in the gut and bone marrow regularly do?
options: They produce new tissues for maintenance and repair.
They transport carbon dioxide to the lungs.
They make the primary cell wall.
rationales: This is correct: they regularly divide to produce new tissues for maintenance and repair.
Transporting carbon dioxide is a function of red blood cells.
The section does not describe stem cells as making the primary cell wall.
Photosynthesis is carried out by chloroplasts, not adult stem cells.

quiz.stem: What is one role of stem cells present in the skin?
options: They produce gametes in every tissue.
They carry oxygen from the lungs.
rationales: This is correct: skin stem cells help in wound healing.
The section does not say that skin stem cells produce gametes in every tissue.
Carrying oxygen from the lungs is a function of red blood cells.
The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus and is not formed by skin stem cells.

quiz.stem: What can stem cells present in the liver help the liver do?
options: They help the liver repair after damage.
They make the liver carry nerve impulses.
They turn all liver cells into bone cells.
They stop all cell division in the liver.
rationales: This is correct: liver stem cells help the liver repair after damage.
Nerve impulses are transmitted by neurons, not by the liver.
The section does not say that liver stem cells turn liver cells into bone cells.
The text describes repair and cell production, not stopping all cell division.

quiz.stem: What do bone marrow stem cells differentiate to make?
options: Different types of blood cells and immune cells
rationales: This is correct: bone marrow stem cells make different types of blood cells and immune cells.
Bone marrow stem cells do not make only skin cells according to the section.
Bone marrow stem cells do not make only muscle cells according to the section.
Bone marrow stem cells do not make only nerve cells according to the section.

quiz.stem: Which statement about stem cells that remain in the body is correct?
options: They can divide and differentiate into specific cells as the body needs them.
They can only divide before birth.
They can become only one kind of cell throughout the body.
They cannot help repair damaged tissue.
rationales: This is correct: these stem cells can divide and differentiate as the body needs them.
The section says stem cells remain in different body parts throughout life.
The section describes stem cells differentiating into specific cells, including different blood and immune cells.
The section says stem cells can regenerate damaged tissue under the right conditions.

quiz.stem: What may stem cells do under the right conditions?
options: They can help regenerate damaged tissue under the right conditions.
They make every cell in the body divide at the same rate.
They replace the need for specialized cells.
rationales: This is correct: stem cells can regenerate damaged tissue under the right conditions.
The section does not say stem cells control the division rate of every cell.
Stem cells in skin help in wound healing, rather than preventing it.
Stem cells differentiate into specialized cells; they do not replace the need for them.

quiz.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?
rationales: M phase is primarily for chromosome separation and cell division, not maximum growth.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, rather than when maximum cell growth occurs.
G1 phase is the main growth phase in which the cell increases in size and carries out normal functions.
G2 phase involves further growth and preparation for mitosis, but maximum growth generally occurs in G1.

quiz.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?
rationales: Mitosis separates duplicated chromosomes but does not duplicate them.
G1 phase is mainly for cell growth and preparation for DNA synthesis.
G2 phase follows DNA duplication and prepares the cell for mitosis.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, duplicating the chromosomes.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of mitosis?
options: It results in genetically identical daughter cells.
The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells.
It results in the formation of two daughter cells.
rationales: Mitosis commonly occurs in somatic cells.
Mitosis normally produces daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell and each other.
Mitosis preserves the chromosome number rather than halving it, so this is not a characteristic of mitosis.
Mitosis followed by cytokinesis results in two daughter cells.

quiz.stem: At which stage of mitosis chromosomes line up in the centre?
rationales: In prophase, chromosomes condense and the spindle begins to form, but chromosomes have not yet lined up at the centre.
In metaphase, chromosomes align at the cell’s equatorial plane.
In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles.
In telophase, chromosomes are at the poles and new nuclei begin to form.

quiz.stem: If you observe a cell in which nuclear membrane is reforming around two sets of chromosomes, what stage of cell cycle is this?
rationales: Anaphase is when sister chromatids move apart, before the nuclear membranes reform.
Telophase is when nuclear membranes reform around the two chromosome sets.
Prophase involves chromosome condensation and breakdown of the nuclear envelope, not its reformation.
Metaphase is when chromosomes align at the cell’s centre.

quiz.stem: How does the centrosome contribute to mitosis?
rationales: The centrosome does not initiate DNA replication; DNA replication occurs during S phase.
The centrosome organizes microtubules to form the mitotic spindle.
The nuclear envelope reforms around chromosomes during telophase and is not formed by the centrosome.
Organelle duplication is not the centrosome’s role in mitosis.

quiz.stem: Centrosomes make mitotic spindle in:
rationales: Animal cells typically use centrosomes to organize the mitotic spindle.
Most higher plant cells lack centrosomes and organize their spindle through other microtubule-organizing sites.
Prokaryotic cells do not undergo mitosis and do not have centrosomes.
This is not true of all cells because plant and prokaryotic cells do not use centrosomes to make a mitotic spindle.

quiz.stem: An organism has 4 pairs of chromosomes. After meiosis-I, how many chromosomes and chromatids will be present in each daughter cell?
rationales: Each daughter cell has half the original chromosome number after meiosis I, so it does not have 8 chromosomes.
A starting cell with 8 chromosomes produces cells with 4 duplicated chromosomes after meiosis I, amounting to 8 chromatids per cell.
Each of the 4 chromosomes still consists of two sister chromatids after meiosis I, so there are 8 chromatids, not 4.
Each daughter cell has 4 chromosomes after meiosis I, not 8.

quiz.stem: Which event is unique to meiosis but not mitosis?
rationales: DNA replication occurs before both mitosis and meiosis.
Chromosomes align during both mitosis and meiosis, although the details differ.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.
Nuclear division occurs in both mitosis and meiosis.

quiz.stem: Why is meiosis-II necessary after meiosis-I?
rationales: Chromosomes are replicated before meiosis I, and meiosis II does not include another round of DNA replication.
The chromosome number is reduced during meiosis I, not meiosis II.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids that remained joined after meiosis I.
Genetic recombination mainly occurs through crossing over during prophase I, not meiosis II.

quiz.stem: A cell has copied the DNA of each chromosome, but the total number of chromosomes has not changed. Which phase has just occurred?
rationales: G1 is mainly a growth and preparation phase before DNA replication.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, while the chromosome number remains the same.
G2 follows DNA replication and includes further growth and preparation for division.
M phase is the division phase, not the phase in which DNA is copied.

quiz.stem: During which phase does a cell make proteins and organelles and grow in size?
rationales: G1 is the growth phase in which the cell makes proteins and organelles.
S phase is primarily for DNA replication.
G2 includes further growth and production of proteins needed for cell division.
G0 is a phase in which some cells stop dividing to perform specialized functions.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes interphase?
options: The cell prepares for division and goes through growth and DNA replication.
The cell copies its DNA for the first time after division.
rationales: Interphase includes growth, preparation, and DNA replication before division.
Some cells stop dividing in G0, but this does not describe interphase.
Sister chromatids separate during cell division, not interphase.
DNA is replicated in S phase, which is part of interphase, but this option does not describe all of interphase.

quiz.stem: Which option gives the usual order of the main cell-cycle phases?
rationales: The phases proceed through G1, S, G2, and then M.
S occurs after G1, and M occurs after G2, so this order is incorrect.
G2 follows S, and M follows G2, so this order is incorrect.
G1 begins after M, so this sequence does not give the usual order.

quiz.stem: Which event is most closely associated with G0 phase?
options: The cell grows and prepares for DNA replication.
The cell checks for DNA damage and prepares for mitosis.
The cell stops dividing to carry out a specialized function.
rationales: Growth and preparation for DNA replication are associated with G1.
DNA replication occurs in S phase.
Checking for DNA damage and preparing for mitosis are associated with G2.
In G0, some cells leave the cycle and stop dividing, often to perform specialized functions.

quiz.stem: Which statement about interphase is correct?
options: It lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle.
It is the phase in which the cell divides into two daughter cells.
It is the only phase in which cells perform life functions.
It is the phase in which the cell permanently stops all functions.
rationales: Interphase lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle.
The division into daughter cells occurs in the M phase.
Cells perform life functions during interphase, but it is not stated to be the only phase in which life functions occur.
G0 is associated with stopping division, not permanently stopping all cell functions.

quiz.stem: During which phase do chromosomes attached to spindle fibres arrange along the cell equator?
rationales: Prophase is when chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
Metaphase is correct because chromosomes arrange along the equator to form the metaphase plate.
Anaphase is when sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles.
Telophase is when new nuclear envelopes form around the separated chromosome sets.

quiz.stem: Which event occurs during anaphase of mitosis?
rationales: The nuclear envelope breaks down during prophase.
Sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles during anaphase.
The nucleolus reforms during telophase.
A cleavage furrow moves inward during cytokinesis in animal cells.

quiz.stem: What is the division of the cytoplasm called?
rationales: Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus.
Cytokinesis is correct because it is the division of the cytoplasm.
Metaphase is a phase of karyokinesis, not the division of cytoplasm.
Regeneration is the formation of new body parts, not a cell-division phase.

quiz.stem: Which event is associated with cytokinesis in plant cells?
options: The cell forms a cleavage furrow.
The cell makes a phragmoplast from Golgi vesicles.
Chromosomes line up at the equator.
rationales: A cleavage furrow forms in animal cells during cytokinesis.
In plant cells, Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to form a plate called a phragmoplast.
Plant cells do not have centrosomes; their mitotic spindle forms from spindle fibres in the cytoplasm.
Chromosomes line up at the equator during metaphase, not during plant-cell cytokinesis.

quiz.stem: Which event takes place during telophase?
options: Chromosomes line up along the equator.
rationales: During telophase, both sets of chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Centrosomes duplicate and migrate during prophase.
Chromosomes line up along the equator during metaphase.
Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

quiz.stem: What is the chromosome-number outcome of mitosis?
options: The daughter cells have half the parent cell's chromosome number.
The daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
Only one daughter cell is formed.
The daughter cells receive no chromosomes.
rationales: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number; that is associated with meiosis.
Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
Mitosis produces two daughter cells, not one.
The chromosomes are distributed between the daughter cells; they do not both receive none.

quiz.stem: What can happen if sister chromatids fail to separate during anaphase?
options: A cell receives both sister chromosomes while the other receives none.
The chromosomes line up at the equator.
The cell forms a cleavage furrow.
rationales: If sister chromatids fail to separate, one daughter cell may receive both sister chromosomes and the other none.
Chromosome alignment at the equator is a normal event of metaphase.
Nucleolus reformation is a normal event of telophase.
A cleavage furrow is a normal feature of cytokinesis in animal cells.

quiz.stem: What is a tumour called if it migrates and invades other tissues?
rationales: A benign tumour remains in its original location.
A malignant tumour is correct because it can migrate and invade other tissues.
A metaphase plate is the arrangement of chromosomes at the cell equator.
A phragmoplast is a plate formed during cytokinesis in plant cells.

quiz.stem: What is the result of meiosis, according to this section?
rationales: This is not the result stated for meiosis.
Correct: meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells.
Meiosis produces haploid, not diploid, daughter cells.
Meiosis produces four daughter cells, not two.

quiz.stem: What is the pairing of homologous chromosomes called?
rationales: Correct: homologous chromosomes pair up in a process called synapsis.
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm.
Crossing over is the exchange of portions between non-sister chromatids.
Disjunction is the separation of chromosomes or sister chromatids.

quiz.stem: What is a tetrad?
rationales: A chromosome consists of sister chromatids, but a tetrad is a pair of homologous chromosomes.
Correct: each pair of homologous chromosomes is called a tetrad.
Four daughter cells are produced by meiosis, but they are not a tetrad.
Two haploid sets form after homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase-I.

quiz.stem: During which phase of meiosis-I do homologous chromosomes move toward opposite poles?
rationales: Homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs during prophase-I.
Tetrads align at the equator during metaphase-I.
Correct: homologous chromosomes separate toward opposite poles during anaphase-I.
Nuclear envelopes reform around the haploid sets during telophase-I.

quiz.stem: Which event occurs during anaphase-II?
rationales: Chromosomes replicate before meiosis, not during anaphase-II.
Homologous chromosomes pair during prophase-I.
Correct: spindle fibres pull sister chromatids apart during anaphase-II.
Tetrads align during metaphase-I, not anaphase-II.

quiz.stem: What is it called when chromosomes fail to separate properly during meiosis?
rationales: Crossing over is an exchange of chromosome portions between non-sister chromatids.
Cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm.
Correct: failure of chromosomes to separate properly is called non-disjunction.
Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes.

quiz.stem: Why does meiosis help maintain chromosome number across generations in animals?
options: They restore chromosome number in the zygote
They stop the zygote from dividing
They cause homologous chromosomes to pair
rationales: Correct: gametes have half the chromosome number, and their joining restores the original number in the zygote.
The zygote receives a full set of chromosomes when the gametes join.
The zygote undergoes mitosis many times as it develops.
Pairing of homologous chromosomes occurs during prophase-I, not when gametes join.

quiz.stem: What may happen to gametes because of non-disjunction?
options: One gamete receives more or fewer chromosomes than normal
All gametes receive identical combinations of genes
rationales: Correct: non-disjunction can cause gametes to receive more or fewer than the normal number of chromosomes.
The section does not say non-disjunction makes all gametes genetically identical.
Chromosomes do not duplicate during meiosis-II.
A zygote formed from such gametes may develop, although the offspring may have severe medical problems.

quiz.stem: Which result is characteristic of meiosis?
options: Two daughter cells with the parent chromosome number
Four daughter cells with half the parent chromosome number
Four daughter cells with the parent chromosome number
Two daughter cells with half the parent chromosome number
rationales: This describes the usual result of mitosis, not meiosis.
This is correct: meiosis involves two divisions and produces four cells with half the chromosome number.
Meiosis produces four daughter cells, but their chromosome number is reduced by half.
Meiosis produces four daughter cells, not two.

quiz.stem: According to the comparison in your textbook, where does meiosis occur?
rationales: Somatic cells are associated with mitosis in the comparison.
This is correct: meiosis occurs in germ line cells.
The comparison does not say meiosis occurs in all cells.
Nerve cells are not identified as the site of meiosis.

quiz.stem: During which stage of meiosis do sister chromatids separate?
rationales: Prophase is not the stage when sister chromatids separate.
Metaphase is when chromosomes or chromosome pairs align, not when sister chromatids separate.
In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes are pulled apart.
This is correct: sister chromatids separate during anaphase II.

quiz.stem: Which event in the comparison is identified as a source of variation in meiosis?
rationales: This is correct: variations occur due to crossing-over.
Cytokinesis occurs at the end of both divisions and is not identified as the source of variation.
Both mitosis and meiosis involve formation of a spindle apparatus.
Chromatin condenses during prophase in both divisions.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares homologous chromosomes in mitosis and meiosis?
options: Homologous chromosomes form pairs in meiosis.
Homologous chromosomes form pairs in mitosis.
Sister chromatids separate during prophase in both divisions.
Crossing-over occurs in mitosis but not meiosis.
rationales: This is correct: homologous chromosomes form pairs in meiosis.
The comparison says homologous chromosomes do not form pairs in mitosis.
Sister chromatids separate during anaphase in mitosis and anaphase II in meiosis.
The comparison says crossing-over occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares the functions of mitosis and meiosis?
options: Mitosis occurs in germ line cells and meiosis in somatic cells.
Mitosis produces gametes and meiosis supports growth and maintenance.
Mitosis supports growth and maintenance; meiosis produces gametes in animals and spores in plants.
Both divisions produce four daughter cells for sexual reproduction.
rationales: The comparison gives the opposite locations: mitosis occurs in somatic cells and meiosis in germ line cells.
The functions are reversed: mitosis supports growth and maintenance, while meiosis produces reproductive cells or spores.
This is correct and matches the stated roles of the two divisions.
Mitosis produces two daughter cells, while meiosis produces four.

quiz.stem: What aligns to form a metaphase plate in meiosis, according to the comparison?
options: A single chromosome aligns at the metaphase plate.
Homologous pairs align at the metaphase plate.
Chromosomes do not align during either division.
Sister chromatids align only during telophase.
rationales: This describes mitosis in the comparison.
This is correct: homologous pairs align to form a metaphase plate in meiosis.
The comparison states that chromosomes or homologous pairs align during metaphase.
Telophase is not the stage when the metaphase plate forms.

quiz.stem: When does DNA replication occur before mitosis and meiosis?
rationales: This is correct: DNA replication occurs during interphase (S phase) before both divisions.
DNA replication occurs before both divisions, not only before mitosis.
DNA replication occurs before both divisions, not only before meiosis.
DNA replication occurs before the divisions, not after cytokinesis.

quiz.stem: A higher level of organization exhibits emergent properties when:
options: The sum of its parts is greater than the whole.
The individual parts are more important than the whole.
Its parts interact to perform more functions.
rationales: Parts functioning independently do not produce emergent properties of the higher level.
Emergent properties arise from interactions among parts, not from the sum being greater than the whole.
Emergent properties depend on how parts work together, rather than on individual parts being more important than the whole.
Interactions among parts can produce functions and properties not present in the parts individually.

quiz.stem: Which of the following demonstrates the levels of organization of the body, from simplest to most complex?
options: Cell → Organ → Tissue → Organelle → Organ system
Organelle → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system
Tissue → Cell → Organelle → Organ → Organ system
Organ system → Tissue → Cell → Organelle → Organ
rationales: This order incorrectly places organs before tissues and organelles after organs.
This correctly orders organization from organelle to cell to tissue to organ to organ system.
This order moves from tissue to cell to organelle, which is from more complex to simpler.
This order begins with the most complex level and does not proceed from simplest to most complex.

quiz.stem: At which level of organization gas exchange occurs between body and environment?
options: Organ system level in the respiratory system
rationales: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration but do not exchange gases between the body and its environment.
Alveolar cells participate in gas exchange, but the exchange with the environment is described at the respiratory system level.
Epithelial tissues line exchange surfaces, but tissue is not the level that represents the whole process between body and environment.
The respiratory system exchanges gases between the body and the environment.

quiz.stem: The epithelial tissue in the stomach wall is responsible for producing:
rationales: Stomach epithelial cells produce mucus, so this is true but incomplete.
Chief cells in the stomach epithelium produce pepsinogen, so this is true but incomplete.
Parietal cells in the stomach epithelium produce hydrochloric acid, so this is true but incomplete.
The stomach epithelium includes cells that produce mucus, pepsinogen, and hydrochloric acid.

quiz.stem: In the wall of stomach, which tissue also contains blood vessels and nerves?
rationales: The epithelial layer lines the stomach but is not the connective layer containing the vessels and nerves described here.
Muscle tissue enables stomach contractions but is not the tissue layer that contains the blood vessels and nerves.
The inner connective tissue, including the submucosa, contains blood vessels and nerves.
The outer connective tissue mainly forms an external covering and is not the layer typically identified for these vessels and nerves.

quiz.stem: In a leaf, which tissue is responsible for photosynthesis?
rationales: Xylem transports water and minerals rather than carrying out most leaf photosynthesis.
Mesophyll cells contain chloroplasts and are the principal photosynthetic tissue of a leaf.
The epidermis primarily protects the leaf and regulates exchange rather than performing most photosynthesis.
Phloem transports sugars from photosynthetic tissues to other parts of the plant.

quiz.stem: What is the primary function of the xylem tissue in a leaf?
options: To transport sugars to other parts
To transport water to parts of leaf
To control the opening and closing of stomata
rationales: Transporting sugars is primarily the function of phloem, not xylem.
Xylem transports water and minerals into and through the leaf.
Chlorophyll is produced or contained in photosynthetic cells, not synthesized by xylem as its primary function.
Guard cells control stomatal opening and closing, not xylem.

quiz.stem: Which of these is a function of the human skeletal system?
options: Storing minerals and producing blood cells
Filtering blood to remove waste products
rationales: The skeleton stores minerals and produces blood cells in bone marrow.
Removing carbon dioxide from blood is primarily a function of the respiratory system.
Filtering blood to remove wastes is primarily a function of the kidneys.
Breaking down food is primarily a function of the digestive system.

quiz.stem: Which structures are responsible for the transport of food in plant body?
rationales: Xylem transports water and minerals rather than food sugars.
Palisade mesophyll performs photosynthesis but does not transport food through the plant.
Phloem transports sugars and other organic nutrients throughout the plant.
Spongy mesophyll facilitates gas exchange and photosynthesis but does not transport food through the plant.

quiz.stem: In a plant, which of the following is the primary function of the flower?
rationales: Transporting water and minerals is mainly a function of xylem tissue.
Supporting leaf growth is not the primary function of a flower.
Flowers facilitate plant reproduction, including pollination and the formation of seeds.
Gas exchange is regulated primarily by stomata in leaves, not by flowers.

quiz.stem: Which description defines a tissue?
options: A group of similar cells working together
A group of molecules working together
A group of organs working together
A living entity made of organ systems
rationales: Correct: a tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform specific functions.
Incorrect: molecules combine in specific ways to make organelles, not tissues.
Incorrect: multiple organs working together make an organ system.
Incorrect: a living entity that functions independently is an organism.

quiz.stem: A structure made up of related tissues working together is a(n):
rationales: Incorrect: a cell is made when organelles assemble and interact.
Incorrect: a tissue is a group of similar cells.
Correct: related tissues working together make an organ.
Incorrect: multiple organs working together make an organ system.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the order from the smallest of these levels to the largest?
rationales: Correct: atoms form molecules, molecules form organelles, and organelles assemble in cells.
Incorrect: molecules are made of atoms, and organelles form before cells.
Incorrect: this sequence reverses the levels from cell down to atom.
Incorrect: molecules are made of atoms, and organelles are made from molecules.

quiz.stem: Which pair consists of animal organs?
rationales: Incorrect: xylem and phloem are examples of plant vascular tissues.
Incorrect: mitochondria and ribosomes are organelles.
Correct: the heart and lungs are examples of animal organs.
Incorrect: root system and shoot system are plant organ systems.

quiz.stem: Which plant tissue transports water and nutrients?
rationales: Incorrect: epidermal tissue protects the underlying parts of a plant.
Correct: vascular tissue, including xylem and phloem, transports water and nutrients.
Incorrect: muscle tissue enables movement in animals.
Incorrect: epithelial tissue covers body surfaces and lines cavities in animals.

quiz.stem: What is meant by an emergent property?
options: Tissues can perform only the functions of their individual cells.
Interactions between parts can produce functions not possible in the individual parts.
Higher levels are always simpler than lower levels.
Organ systems work independently of organs.
rationales: Incorrect: the section explains that tissues can have properties not present in their individual cells.
Correct: interactions among components can create new functions at a higher level.
Incorrect: higher levels of organization are increasingly complex.
Incorrect: organ systems consist of organs that work together.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of an animal organ system that breaks down food and absorbs nutrients?
rationales: Correct: the digestive system breaks down food and absorbs nutrients.
Incorrect: the circulatory system transports nutrients and oxygen through the body.
Incorrect: the root system anchors a plant and absorbs water and nutrients.
Incorrect: the shoot system supports the plant and conducts photosynthesis.

quiz.stem: Which choice is the highest level of organization in this list?
rationales: Incorrect: mitochondria are organelles.
Incorrect: cardiac muscle is a tissue.
Incorrect: the heart is an organ.
Correct: an organ system is above the organ level.

quiz.stem: Which leaf tissue contains cells rich in chloroplasts and is the site of photosynthesis?
rationales: Epidermal tissue forms the outer layer of the leaf rather than the main photosynthetic tissue.
Mesophyll tissue contains chloroplast-rich cells and is the site of photosynthesis.
Xylem conducts water and minerals to leaf cells.
Phloem transports sugars produced by photosynthesis.

quiz.stem: What does xylem tissue in a leaf do?
options: They transport sugars from the leaf.
They transport water and minerals to the leaf.
They open and close the stomata.
rationales: Phloem, not xylem, transports sugars from leaf cells.
Xylem conducts water and minerals from the stem to leaf cells.
Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata.
Fruits protect seeds; this is not a function of xylem.

quiz.stem: Which tissue has loosely arranged cells and air spaces that help gases diffuse through a leaf?
rationales: Palisade mesophyll has tightly packed elongated cells.
Spongy mesophyll has loosely arranged cells with air spaces that facilitate gas diffusion.
The lower epidermis contains guard cells and stomata, but it is not the tissue described.
Phloem transports products of photosynthesis rather than providing the described air spaces.

quiz.stem: Which structures surround the tiny pore called a stoma?
rationales: The upper epidermis is an outer leaf layer, not the pair of cells around a stoma.
A stoma is the tiny pore between two guard cells.
Xylem is a vascular tissue that transports water and minerals.
Palisade mesophyll is a photosynthetic tissue beneath the upper epidermis.

quiz.stem: Which plant organs anchor the plant in soil and can store nutrients?
rationales: Roots anchor the plant in soil and may store nutrients.
Stems support leaves, flowers, and fruits and transport materials.
Flowers are the reproductive part of a plant.
Leaves are the main sites of photosynthesis and transpiration.

quiz.stem: Which plant organ system includes stems, branches, leaves, and flowers?
rationales: The root system consists of roots.
The shoot system includes stems, branches, leaves, and flowers.
The section identifies the root and shoot systems as the two main plant organ systems.
Mesophyll is a leaf tissue, not an organ system.

quiz.stem: What is one function of the waxy cuticle covering the upper epidermis?
options: It reduces water loss and provides protection.
It transports sugars to the stem.
It absorbs water from the soil.
It produces air spaces in the leaf.
rationales: The cuticle reduces water loss and provides protection.
Phloem transports sugars from leaf cells to the stem.
Roots absorb water from the soil.
Air spaces occur between loosely arranged spongy mesophyll cells.

quiz.stem: Through which small pores does transpiration release water vapour from leaves?
rationales: Stomata are small pores through which water vapour is lost during transpiration.
Veins contain vascular tissue that transports materials through the leaf.
Chloroplasts are involved in photosynthesis, not pores for water-vapour loss.
The cuticle reduces water loss; it is not a pore.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the main function of the heart?
options: It pumps blood throughout the body.
It breaks down food using digestive enzymes.
It controls body functions through nerve impulses.
rationales: Correct: The heart pumps blood throughout the body.
Incorrect: The kidneys filter waste products from blood and produce urine.
Incorrect: The stomach breaks down food using digestive enzymes.
Incorrect: The nervous system coordinates and controls body functions through nerve impulses.

quiz.stem: Which is a function of the kidneys?
options: They filter waste products from blood and produce urine.
They absorb nutrients from digested food.
They exchange gases between the body and environment.
rationales: Incorrect: The liver produces bile.
Correct: The kidneys filter waste products from the blood and produce urine.
Incorrect: The intestines absorb nutrients from digested food.
Incorrect: The lungs are responsible for the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

quiz.stem: Which sequence correctly names the stomach's three smooth muscle layers, from outer to inner?
options: Outer longitudinal, middle circular, inner oblique
Outer circular, middle oblique, inner longitudinal
Outer oblique, middle longitudinal, inner circular
rationales: Correct: The stomach has an outer longitudinal, middle circular, and inner oblique layer.
Incorrect: This reverses and changes the stated order of the stomach muscle layers.
Incorrect: This is not the order given for the stomach's smooth muscle layers.
Incorrect: The section describes three layers of smooth muscles, not skeletal muscles.

quiz.stem: What does connective tissue beneath the stomach's epithelial tissue do?
options: It provides structural support and contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
It absorbs nutrients from digested food.
rationales: Correct: It provides structural support and contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
Incorrect: Insulin and glucagon are hormones produced by the pancreas.
Incorrect: The intestines absorb nutrients from digested food.
Incorrect: The kidneys produce urine.

quiz.stem: What is the stated role of the nervous system?
options: It coordinates and controls body functions through nerve impulses.
It stores minerals and produces blood cells.
It transports oxygen and nutrients through the body.
It mixes food with gastric juice.
rationales: Correct: The nervous system coordinates and controls body functions through nerve impulses.
Incorrect: Storing minerals and producing blood cells are functions of the skeletal system.
Incorrect: Transporting oxygen and nutrients throughout the body is a function of the blood circulatory system.
Incorrect: Smooth muscles in the stomach mix food with gastric juice.

quiz.stem: Which set of parts makes up the blood circulatory system?
rationales: Correct: The blood circulatory system includes the heart, blood vessels, and blood.
Incorrect: The brain and spinal cord are parts of the nervous system, while the lungs are part of the respiratory system.
Incorrect: Bones, cartilage, and tendons are listed as parts of the skeletal system.
Incorrect: The mouth and stomach are digestive organs, and the kidneys filter blood and produce urine.

quiz.stem: Which organ system is responsible for digestion of food and absorption of digested food?
rationales: Incorrect: The skeletal system provides structure, support, and protection, among other functions.
Correct: The digestive system digests food and absorbs digested food.
Incorrect: The respiratory system exchanges gases between the body and environment.
Incorrect: The muscular system allows movement and locomotion.

quiz.stem: Which organ is responsible for the partial digestion of proteins and also stores food?
rationales: Incorrect: The section describes the intestines as digesting food and absorbing nutrients.
Correct: The stomach partially digests proteins and stores food.
Incorrect: The liver filters blood, produces bile, and stores glucose.
Incorrect: The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and hormones such as insulin and glucagon.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes homeostasis?
options: The body maintains a stable internal environment despite external changes.
The body prevents all changes in the external environment.
Every organ works separately without coordination.
The body stops cells from using oxygen.
rationales: This is correct because homeostasis maintains stability inside the body despite changes outside it.
This is wrong because the body cannot prevent changes in the external environment.
This is wrong because organ systems coordinate their activities in homeostasis.
This is wrong because cells need oxygen for cellular respiration.

quiz.stem: Which system helps regulate body temperature by sweating?
rationales: This system supplies oxygen and expels carbon dioxide; it is not the system identified with sweating.
This is correct because the integumentary system helps regulate temperature through sweating.
This system distributes nutrients to cells; it is not the system identified with sweating.
This system supports and protects the body; it is not the system identified with sweating.

quiz.stem: Which substance does the pancreas release to lower a raised blood glucose level?
rationales: This is correct because the pancreas releases insulin, which lowers blood glucose towards normal.
This is wrong because oxygen is needed by cells but does not lower blood glucose.
This is wrong because carbon dioxide is expelled by the respiratory system and does not lower blood glucose.
This is wrong because mucus protects the stomach lining and does not lower blood glucose.

quiz.stem: What do muscles do when the body temperature falls below normal?
options: They help generate heat by shivering.
They release insulin into the blood.
rationales: This is correct because shivering generates heat and helps raise body temperature.
This is wrong because the pancreas releases insulin.
This is wrong because the respiratory system expels excess carbon dioxide.
This is wrong because the digestive system works for nutrient distribution to cells.

quiz.stem: How does the urinary system help maintain homeostasis?
options: It regulates water and salt balance and eliminates waste.
It secretes sweat to cool the body.
It supplies oxygen to the body.
It breaks down food in the stomach.
rationales: This is correct because the urinary system eliminates wastes and regulates water and salt balance.
This is wrong because sweating is a role of the integumentary system.
This is wrong because receiving oxygen is a role of the respiratory system.
This is wrong because the stomach is part of the digestive system.

quiz.stem: Which pair of systems works together to deliver oxygen to muscles during hard exercise?
rationales: This is correct because faster breathing and heartbeat help supply more oxygen to working muscles.
This is wrong because these systems are not the pair described as increasing oxygen delivery during exercise.
This is wrong because these systems are not the pair described as increasing oxygen delivery during exercise.
This is wrong because these systems are not the pair described as increasing oxygen delivery during exercise.

quiz.stem: Which system helps regulate body temperature and pH levels and carries necessary substances to cells?
rationales: This is wrong because the digestive system distributes nutrients to cells.
This is correct because the cardiovascular system helps regulate temperature and pH and supplies substances to cells.
This is wrong because the urinary system regulates water and salt balance and eliminates waste.
This is wrong because the muscular system helps with posture, support and movement.

quiz.stem: Why is maintaining a stable internal environment important for cells?
options: The body has no way to respond to a temperature change.
Cells may not function properly if their conditions move outside the normal range.
The pancreas stops producing all hormones.
rationales: This is wrong because the body has responses such as sweating and shivering.
This is correct because cells function properly only when conditions such as temperature and pH remain in a normal range.
This is wrong because homeostasis maintains internal conditions; it does not stabilise the external environment.
This is wrong because the section does not say homeostasis stops the pancreas from producing hormones.

quiz.stem: What is the primary function of carbohydrates?
rationales: Carbohydrates are a major source of energy for the body.
Carbohydrates are not generally enzymes; enzymes are mostly proteins.
Regulating body processes is not the primary function of carbohydrates.
Some carbohydrates are components of membranes, but this is not their primary function.

quiz.stem: How will you differentiate between monosaccharides and polysaccharides?
options: Monosaccharides are present in plant cell wall.
rationales: A monosaccharide consists of a single sugar unit, unlike a polysaccharide made of many sugar units.
Polysaccharides are not necessarily sweet, so sweetness does not distinguish them from monosaccharides.
Plant cell walls contain cellulose, a polysaccharide, so this does not define monosaccharides.
Many polysaccharides do not dissolve easily, and solubility is not the defining difference.

quiz.stem: What is true about cellulose?
options: It is digestible by human digestive system.
It provides structural support in plants.
rationales: Cellulose is not sweet in taste.
Humans cannot digest cellulose because they lack the enzyme needed to break it down.
Cellulose provides structural support in plant cell walls.
Cellulose is generally insoluble in water.

quiz.stem: Which of the following proteins is involved in oxygen transport?
rationales: Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose, not a protein that transports oxygen.
Haemoglobin binds and transports oxygen in the blood.
Collagen is a structural protein, not an oxygen-transport protein.
Keratin is a structural protein found in hair, nails, and skin, not an oxygen-transport protein.

quiz.stem: Which component of an amino acid determines its unique properties?
rationales: The amino group is common to amino acids and does not determine their unique properties.
The carboxyl group is common to amino acids and does not determine their unique properties.
The R group varies among amino acids and gives each one its distinctive properties.
Hydrogen is attached to the central carbon, but it is not the component that distinguishes amino acids.

quiz.stem: Which proteins are involved in defence against pathogens?
rationales: Antibodies recognize and help neutralize pathogens as part of immune defence.
Myosin is a motor protein involved in muscle contraction.
Fibrinogen helps blood clot, rather than directly defending against pathogens.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.

quiz.stem: Which of the following are the units of most lipids?
rationales: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, not most lipids.
Many lipids, such as triglycerides, are made from fatty acids and glycerol.
Nucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids, not lipids.
Simple sugars are carbohydrate units, not the units of most lipids.

quiz.stem: How do unsaturated fatty acids differ from saturated fatty acids?
options: They contain double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.
They are solid at room temperature.
They are found only in animal fats.
rationales: Unsaturated fatty acids have fewer hydrogen atoms than corresponding saturated fatty acids because of their double bonds.
Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.
Unsaturated fats are often liquid at room temperature, whereas many saturated fats are solid.
Unsaturated fatty acids occur in both plant and animal sources, not only animal fats.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of proteins?
rationales: Some proteins, such as haemoglobin, transport oxygen in the blood.
Genetic information is carried by nucleic acids such as DNA, not proteins.
Many proteins, including digestive enzymes, help break down food.
Antibodies are proteins that help defend the body against pathogens.

quiz.stem: Which components make up a nucleotide?
rationales: A nucleotide consists of a sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
Amino acids are protein building blocks and are not components of a nucleotide.
Fatty acids are lipid components and are not part of a nucleotide.
Proteins are not components of a nucleotide.

quiz.stem: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
rationales: Adenine is found in both RNA and DNA.
Thymine is found in DNA; RNA uses uracil instead.
Uracil is found in RNA and replaces thymine, which is used in DNA.
Guanine is found in both RNA and DNA.

quiz.stem: Which group of biomolecules includes DNA and RNA?
rationales: Carbohydrates are a separate group of biomolecules, not the group that includes DNA and RNA.
Proteins are made from amino acids and do not include DNA and RNA.
Lipids include molecules such as fats, not DNA and RNA.
Nucleic acids include both DNA and RNA.

quiz.stem: According to the table, where are carbohydrates found in the cell?
rationales: The table lists both the cytoplasm and cell membrane as locations for carbohydrates.
The table does not list the nucleus as a location for carbohydrates.
The table does not list ribosomes as a location for carbohydrates.
The table does not list the cell wall as a location for carbohydrates.

quiz.stem: Which function of lipids is given in the section?
options: They carry genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.
They store genetic information in the nucleoid region only.
rationales: This is the function of RNA given in the table.
Lipids act as heat insulators according to the table.
Making many cell structures is listed among the functions of proteins.
DNA is found in the nucleoid region of prokaryotes, but this is not a lipid function.

quiz.stem: What percentage of the dry mass of protoplasm is made up of proteins?
rationales: Proteins make up 50% of the dry mass in the table.
18% is the percentage given for nucleic acids.
15% is the percentage given for carbohydrates.
10% is the percentage given for lipids.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes anabolism?
options: Simpler substances combine to form complex substances.
Complex molecules break down into simpler ones.
Energy is released as complex molecules are formed.
rationales: Anabolism combines simpler substances to form complex substances and uses energy.
This describes catabolism, not anabolism.
Anabolism uses energy rather than releasing it as complex substances form.
Metabolism consists of chemical reactions, so this statement is incorrect.

quiz.stem: What happens during catabolism?
options: Complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones.
Simpler substances combine to form complex substances.
Energy is stored in the nucleus.
rationales: Energy is released during catabolism, rather than used to build complex substances.
Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy.
This describes anabolism.
The section does not describe energy being stored in the nucleus as catabolism.

quiz.stem: Which biomolecule carries genetic information from DNA to the ribosome for protein synthesis?
rationales: DNA carries genetic information, but the table says RNA carries it from DNA to the ribosome.
RNA carries genetic information from DNA to the ribosome for protein synthesis.
Carbohydrates are listed as energy sources and storage molecules.
Lipids are listed as energy storage molecules, heat insulators, and cell membrane components.

quiz.stem: What proportion of the dry mass of protoplasm is made up of biomolecules?

quiz.stem: Which of the following is a monosaccharide?
rationales: Glucose is a hexose monosaccharide.
Sucrose is a disaccharide made of glucose and fructose.
Starch is a polysaccharide made of glucose units.
Cellulose is a polysaccharide found in plant cell walls.

quiz.stem: Which monosaccharides join to form sucrose?
rationales: Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose.
Two glucose molecules make maltose, not sucrose.
Ribose and deoxyribose are pentose monosaccharides, not the units of sucrose.
Fructose and galactose are not the two units identified for sucrose.

quiz.stem: Which description best identifies polysaccharides?
options: They are made of a single sugar molecule.
They are made of hundreds to thousands of sugar units.
They are always tasteless and insoluble.
They are made of two monosaccharide units.
rationales: A single sugar molecule describes a monosaccharide.
Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharide units.
This describes polysaccharides' taste and solubility, but not their defining composition.
Two monosaccharide units describe a disaccharide.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes a role of starch?
options: It makes up the exoskeletons of insects.
It is the main sugar in milk.
rationales: Starch is a storage polysaccharide found in plants.
Oxygen transport is a role of haemoglobin, not starch.
Chitin is found in insect exoskeletons.
Lactose is the disaccharide found in milk and dairy products.

quiz.stem: Which carbohydrate provides support to plant cells?
rationales: Cellulose supports plant cells and the plant as a whole.
Glycogen is an animal storage polysaccharide, mainly stored in liver and muscles.
Sucrose is a disaccharide used to transport monosaccharides in plants.
Maltose is a disaccharide found in cereals.

quiz.stem: Which part of an amino acid varies between different amino acids?
rationales: The amino group is a shared part of the general amino-acid structure.
The carboxyl group is a shared part of the general amino-acid structure.
The R group varies and gives different amino acids different side groups.
The central carbon atom is part of the general structure and is not the variable side group.

quiz.stem: What are essential amino acids?
options: Amino acids that the body cannot synthesise
Amino acids that make up only enzymes
Amino acids made only by plants
Amino acids that cannot join to form proteins

Essential amino acids are not defined as units found only in enzymes.
The definition is about whether the human body can synthesise them, not whether plants make them.
