quiz.stem: According to the section, how many amino acids are non-essential?
rationales: Nine is the number of essential amino acids given in the section.
The section states that 11 amino acids can be synthesised in our bodies.
Twenty is the number of amino-acid types that participate in making most proteins.
About 170 types occur in organisms, not the number of non-essential amino acids.

quiz.stem: Which protein transports oxygen in the blood?
rationales: Keratin helps make structures such as hair and nails.
Fibrin helps blood clot after an injury.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Myosin is a component of muscle cells and helps with muscular contraction.

quiz.stem: Which protein group helps defend the body against harmful pathogens?
rationales: Collagen helps form structures such as cartilage.
Antibodies are part of the immune system and defend the body against harmful pathogens.
Insulin is a protein hormone, not the defence protein named in the section.
Actin is a component of muscle cells.

quiz.stem: What do enzymes do in organisms?
options: Make the side group of an amino acid
rationales: Enzymes catalyse biochemical reactions occurring in organisms.
Haemoglobin, rather than enzymes as a general group, is identified for oxygen transport.
The R group is part of an amino acid; enzymes do not make it.
Fibrin is identified as a blood-clotting protein.

quiz.stem: Where are the amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and R group attached in an amino acid?
options: They are the same in every amino acid.
They are attached to the central carbon atom.
They are made only of CH₃ groups.
They are the units that join to make amino acids.
rationales: These groups are not all described as being identical in every amino acid because the R group differs.

The R group can vary; glycine has H and alanine has CH₃.
Amino acids join to make proteins, not to make amino acids.

quiz.stem: Which protein helps form hair and nails?
rationales: Fibrin is involved in blood clotting.
Keratin helps make structures such as hair and nails.
Myosin is a muscle-cell protein involved in muscular contraction.
Insulin is a protein hormone that regulates body processes.

quiz.stem: Which description best identifies lipids?
options: They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
They are made only of amino acids.

rationales: This is incorrect because lipids are insoluble in water.
This is correct because it gives the defining solubility property of lipids.
This is incorrect because amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes glycerol?
options: One carbon atom with three hydroxyl groups
Three carbon atoms, each with a hydroxyl group
Three carbon atoms with no hydroxyl groups
A long hydrocarbon chain ending in COOH
rationales: This is incorrect because glycerol has three carbon atoms.
This is correct: glycerol is an alcohol having three carbon atoms, each with a hydroxyl group.
This is incorrect because each carbon in glycerol has a hydroxyl group.
This is incorrect because it describes a fatty acid.

quiz.stem: What feature identifies an unsaturated fatty acid?
options: They have one or more double bonds between carbon atoms.
They are always solid at room temperature.
rationales: This is correct because unsaturated fatty acids have one or more carbon-to-carbon double bonds.
This is incorrect because fatty acids are hydrocarbon chains containing carbon atoms.
This is incorrect because fatty acids have a carboxyl group at the end.
This is incorrect because unsaturated fatty acids are liquid at room temperature.

quiz.stem: What is the basic composition of fats and oils?
options: One glycerol and three fatty acids
One glycerol and two fatty acids
Three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid
One glycerol, one fatty acid and one amino acid
rationales: This is correct: fats and oils contain one glycerol and three fatty acids.
This is incorrect because one glycerol and two fatty acids plus a phosphate group describe a phospholipid.
This is incorrect because the section gives one glycerol and three fatty acids.
This is incorrect because amino acids are not listed as components of fats and oils.

quiz.stem: Which components make up a phospholipid molecule?
options: One glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group
One glycerol, three fatty acids and a phosphate group
Two glycerol molecules and one phosphate group
One glycerol and three amino acids
rationales: This is correct: a phospholipid consists of one glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group.
This is incorrect because three fatty acids are described for fats and oils, not phospholipids.
This is incorrect because the section specifies one glycerol.
This is incorrect because phospholipids contain fatty acids, not amino acids.

quiz.stem: What is a stated role of phospholipids?
options: They form the core of all membranes.
They carry oxygen in the blood.
They break down starch in the digestive system.
rationales: This is correct because phospholipids make the core of all membranes.
This is incorrect because oxygen transport is not the stated role of phospholipids.
This is incorrect because genetic information is not described as a lipid function.
This is incorrect because the section does not describe phospholipids as digestive enzymes.

quiz.stem: How do stored lipids help the body?
options: They are a long-term energy reserve.
They are the body's main source of genetic information.
They dissolve in water to form cell membranes.
They convert all vitamins into hormones.
rationales: This is correct because lipids stored as fats in adipose tissues are a long-term energy reserve.
This is incorrect because lipids are not described as the body's genetic information.
This is incorrect because lipids are insoluble in water.
This is incorrect because the section says lipids help absorb fat-soluble vitamins, not convert them into hormones.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares phospholipids with fats and oils?
options: A phospholipid has a phosphate group; a fat or oil has three fatty acids attached to glycerol.
A phospholipid has three fatty acids; a fat has two fatty acids and a phosphate group.
Both consist only of fatty acids.
A fat has a phosphate group, but a phospholipid does not.
rationales: This is correct: phospholipids have a phosphate group and two fatty acids, while fats and oils have three fatty acids.
This is incorrect because it reverses the structures described in the section.
This is incorrect because both groups also contain glycerol, and phospholipids have a phosphate group.
This is incorrect because the phosphate group is part of a phospholipid.

quiz.stem: Which pentose sugar is found in a DNA nucleotide?
rationales: Ribose is the pentose sugar in RNA, not DNA.
Deoxyribose is the pentose sugar in DNA nucleotides.
Glucose is a simple sugar, not the pentose sugar named for DNA.
Fructose is a simple sugar, not the pentose sugar named for DNA.

quiz.stem: Which pair of bases forms two hydrogen bonds in DNA?
rationales: Uracil is an RNA base; this is not the DNA pair described in the section.
Adenine pairs with thymine, and this pair has two hydrogen bonds.
Cytosine pairs with guanine, not thymine.
Guanine pairs with cytosine, not adenine.

quiz.stem: Which description best defines a gene?
options: It is a segment of DNA whose nucleotide sequence determines the synthesis of a protein.
It is a nucleotide that contains ribose.
It is the structure that transfers amino acids to ribosomes.
It is a pair of bases joined by hydrogen bonds.
rationales: A gene is a segment of DNA whose sequence determines the synthesis of a protein.
A ribose-containing nucleotide is a ribonucleotide, not a gene.
Transferring amino acids to ribosomes is the function of tRNA.
A pair of bases is part of DNA structure, but it is not the definition of a gene.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes RNA?
options: It is single-stranded and contains ribose.
It is double-stranded and contains deoxyribose.
It is single-stranded and contains deoxyribose.
It is double-stranded and contains ribose.
rationales: RNA is single-stranded, and its ribonucleotides contain ribose.
This describes the sugar of DNA, and DNA is a double helix.
RNA is single-stranded, but its sugar is ribose rather than deoxyribose.
RNA is single-stranded, not double-stranded.

quiz.stem: Which type of RNA transfers specific amino acids to ribosomes?
rationales: mRNA carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.
tRNA transfers specific amino acids to ribosomes.
rRNA forms structural and functional components of ribosomes.
DNA contains hereditary information; it is not one of the three types of RNA.

quiz.stem: Which shows the specific base pairing in DNA?
rationales: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine.
These are not the specific base pairs described for DNA.
These are not the specific base pairs described for DNA.
Uracil is found in RNA rather than DNA.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a gene?
options: A segment of DNA with a specific nucleotide sequence carrying information for a protein
A molecule made of joined amino acids
rationales: Correct: a gene is a specific DNA nucleotide sequence carrying information for a specific protein.
Incorrect: joined amino acids form a protein, not a gene.
Incorrect: the ribosome reads mRNA; it is not a gene.
Incorrect: a gene carries information used to make a protein, not a copy of one.

quiz.stem: What is the process called when a DNA sequence is copied into mRNA?
rationales: Incorrect: translation uses the mRNA sequence to make a protein.
Correct: transcription is the making of an mRNA copy of DNA.
Incorrect: proteins are not copied in this process.
Incorrect: diffusion is not the name of copying DNA information into mRNA.

quiz.stem: Which molecule carries the copied nucleotide sequence from DNA to the ribosome?
rationales: Correct: messenger RNA carries the nucleotide sequence to the ribosome.
Incorrect: amino acids are joined to form a protein; they do not carry the copied sequence.
Incorrect: a protein is the product of translation.
Incorrect: a chromosome contains DNA, but the copied sequence is carried to the ribosome by mRNA.

quiz.stem: Where does the mRNA sequence get read during protein formation?
rationales: Correct: the ribosome reads the mRNA sequence.

quiz.stem: Which process involves a ribosome reading mRNA and joining specific amino acids?
rationales: Incorrect: transcription makes an mRNA copy of DNA.
Correct: translation uses the mRNA sequence to join amino acids into a protein.
Incorrect: gene formation is not the process described.
Incorrect: this is not the textbook name for making a protein from mRNA.

quiz.stem: What is formed when a ribosome joins specific amino acids according to the mRNA sequence?
rationales: Correct: the joined amino acids form a protein.
Incorrect: a chromosome contains DNA and is not formed by joining amino acids.
Incorrect: a gene is a DNA sequence, not the product of translation.
Incorrect: a nucleotide is a component of DNA and RNA, not the product formed here.

quiz.stem: Primarily, all enzymes are:

Most enzymes are proteins, making this the best answer.
Carbohydrates are not the primary composition of enzymes.
Lipids are not the primary composition of enzymes.

quiz.stem: Which best defines an enzyme?
options: A chemical that breaks down food.
A protein that speeds up reactions.
rationales: Some enzymes break down food, but that does not define all enzymes.
Enzymes are not hormones, even though some hormones affect metabolism.
An enzyme is generally a protein that speeds up chemical reactions without being consumed.
Energy storage is not the defining function of an enzyme.

quiz.stem: What can happen if an enzyme is exposed to temperature that is higher than its optimal temperature?
options: Enzyme’s shape will change, potentially reducing its activity.
Enzyme will speed up the reaction and remain stable.
Enzyme will become a substrate itself.
rationales: Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme may lose activity rather than continuing to speed up.
High temperatures can alter an enzyme’s shape, including its active site, and reduce its activity.
An enzyme does not necessarily remain stable at temperatures above its optimum.
An enzyme catalyzes reactions and is not converted into a substrate.

quiz.stem: Enzymes are specific in their action because:

They work only at high temperatures.

Being a protein alone does not explain why an enzyme acts on specific substrates.
Enzymes are generally not consumed in the reactions they catalyze.
Enzymes do not work only at high temperatures; each has conditions under which it works best.

quiz.stem: Prosthetic groups are:
rationales: Not all enzymes require prosthetic groups to function.
Prosthetic groups are non-protein components, not proteins.

No shape changes occur in active site or substrate.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes metabolism?

Complex molecules are broken into simpler ones and energy is released.

It joins carbon dioxide and water to make glucose.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the role of an enzyme?

They are consumed as the reaction proceeds.

Incorrect: the section does not describe enzymes as predominantly lipids.

Incorrect: loose binding and possible release describe coenzymes.

quiz.stem: Which is the section’s example of an intracellular enzyme location?

Enzymes of cellular respiration work within cells.
Amylase breaks down starch into simple sugars.
Protease enzymes remove protein stains from clothes.

quiz.stem: Which industrial use of an enzyme matches the section?
options: Amylase is used to remove resistant starch residues in dish washing.

Coenzymes are used to produce white bread.

quiz.stem: What is an active site?

The product released after a reaction

The active site is reshaped by the substrate.

The product fits into the active site before the substrate.
The enzyme is consumed during catalysis.
rationales: Incorrect: a fixed active site is the feature of the lock-and-key model.

Incorrect: the model describes the substrate interacting with the enzyme, not the product binding first.

quiz.stem: Who proposed the lock-and-key model of enzyme action?

Incorrect: Gregor Mendel is not identified in this section as proposing either model.

quiz.stem: In which year was the induced fit model proposed?
rationales: Incorrect: 1894 is the year given for the lock-and-key model.

Incorrect: this year is not given for either model in the section.
Incorrect: this year is not given for either model in the section.

quiz.stem: What forms when the substrate fits into the enzyme's active site in the lock-and-key model?
rationales: Correct: the substrate and enzyme form an enzyme-substrate complex.

Incorrect: the product is formed after the enzyme catalyzes the reaction.
Incorrect: the substrate alone is not the complex; it must interact with the enzyme.

quiz.stem: After the enzyme-substrate complex forms, what happens in the lock-and-key model?

The enzyme's active site stays rigid in every interaction.
The substrate is released before interacting with the enzyme.
The product changes the active site before the substrate binds.

quiz.stem: At which temperature do most human enzymes have their optimum activity?

quiz.stem: What can happen when an enzyme is heated well above its optimum temperature?

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares the optimum pH conditions of pepsin and trypsin?

Pepsin works in an acidic medium and trypsin in an alkaline medium.

rationales: Incorrect: this reverses the conditions stated for the two enzymes.

Incorrect: the section gives different optimum pH values for different enzymes.

quiz.stem: What happens when substrate concentration becomes high enough to occupy all the enzyme active sites?
options: The reaction rate increases without limit.

Correct: once all active sites are occupied, additional substrate cannot find a free active site and the rate does not increase.
Incorrect: substrate does not change the enzyme into substrate.
Incorrect: adding substrate increases the rate at first; it does not immediately stop the reaction.

quiz.stem: According to the section, what causes enzyme denaturation at a temperature well above the optimum?
options: The active site is blocked by heat.
The heat breaks bonds in the enzyme molecule.
rationales: Incorrect: the section explains denaturation as a loss of enzyme structure, not simply a blocked active site.
Correct: heat breaks bonds in the enzyme molecule, causing its globular structure to be lost.
Incorrect: substrate concentration is not the stated cause of heat denaturation.
Incorrect: a change to neutral pH is not the stated cause of heat denaturation.

quiz.stem: How can a change in pH affect an enzyme?
options: It can change the ionization of amino acids at the active site.
It makes every enzyme work at pH 7.
It causes all enzymes to become saturated.
rationales: Correct: pH can affect the ionization of amino acids at the active site, slowing or blocking enzyme activity.
Incorrect: pH does not necessarily change the amount of substrate.
Incorrect: different enzymes have different optimum pH values.
Incorrect: saturation happens when enzyme active sites are occupied by substrate, not simply because pH changes.

quiz.stem: How does the reaction rate generally change as substrate concentration increases?
options: The reaction rate increases at first and then levels off.
The reaction rate immediately becomes zero.
The enzyme's optimum temperature rises with every substrate molecule.
The enzyme is denatured as soon as substrate concentration increases.
rationales: Correct: the rate increases as substrate concentration rises, then stops increasing when all active sites are occupied.
Incorrect: adding substrate initially increases the reaction rate rather than making it zero.
Incorrect: substrate concentration does not set the enzyme's optimum temperature.
Incorrect: increasing substrate concentration is not stated to denature the enzyme.

quiz.stem: How does a competitive inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?
options: It attaches to the active site and prevents the substrate from attaching.
It attaches to the substrate and carries it away.
It changes the substrate into an inhibitor.
It makes the enzyme produce more active sites.
rationales: Correct: it blocks the active site, so the substrate cannot attach.
Incorrect: competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate for the enzyme’s active site; they are not described as attaching to the substrate.
Incorrect: the inhibitor does not change the substrate into another substance.
Incorrect: competitive inhibition blocks the active site; it does not create more active sites.

quiz.stem: What happens during non-competitive inhibition?
options: It binds to the active site and blocks the substrate.
It attaches at another location and changes the enzyme’s shape.
It makes the substrate fit the active site more closely.
It breaks down the enzyme into its amino acids.
rationales: Incorrect: attaching to and blocking the active site is the description of competitive inhibition.
Correct: a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the shape of the enzyme and its active site.
Incorrect: the inhibitor changes the enzyme’s shape; it does not make the substrate fit better.
Incorrect: the section describes a shape change, not the enzyme being broken down.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of a competitive inhibitor given in this section?
rationales: Correct: the section gives antibiotics as examples of competitive inhibitors.
Incorrect: biotin is given as an example of an organic cofactor, not a competitive inhibitor.
Incorrect: NAD is given as an example of a coenzyme, not a competitive inhibitor.
Incorrect: magnesium ions are given as examples of inorganic cofactors, not competitive inhibitors.

quiz.stem: Why can a substrate no longer fit after a non-competitive inhibitor attaches?
options: It changes the shape of the enzyme’s active site.
It becomes a substrate for the enzyme.
It increases the similarity between the enzyme and substrate.
rationales: Incorrect: a non-competitive inhibitor does not attach to the active site to block it directly.
Correct: its attachment changes the enzyme’s shape, including the shape of the active site.
Incorrect: the inhibitor does not become a substrate.
Incorrect: the inhibitor changes the enzyme’s shape so the active site no longer fits the substrate.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes a competitive inhibitor?
options: It competes with the substrate for the same active site.
It attaches at a different location and changes enzyme shape.
It attaches to the substrate rather than the enzyme.
It binds only to the products of a reaction.
rationales: Correct: competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate to attach to the same active site.
Incorrect: this describes non-competitive inhibition.
Incorrect: the section says the inhibitor competes with the substrate to attach to the enzyme’s active site.
Incorrect: the section describes inhibitors attaching to enzymes, not only to reaction products.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of a non-competitive inhibitor mentioned in the section?
rationales: Correct: heavy metals such as mercury are given as examples of non-competitive inhibitors.
Incorrect: antibiotics are given as examples of competitive inhibitors.
Incorrect: substrates are the molecules inhibitors compete with; they are not given as inhibitors.
Incorrect: biotin is given as an example of a prosthetic group, not a non-competitive inhibitor.

quiz.stem: When we get energy from ATP, which bonds are broken?
rationales: ATP hydrolysis releases energy by breaking the terminal phosphate–phosphate bond.
C–H bonds are not the bonds whose hydrolysis releases ATP’s usable energy.
C–N bonds are not broken during ATP hydrolysis.
C–O bonds are not the bonds broken to release energy from ATP.

quiz.stem: Light reactions of photosynthesis occur in;
rationales: The plasma membrane is not where the photosynthetic light reactions occur in plant cells.
The cytoplasm is not the site of the light reactions.
The stroma is where the Calvin cycle occurs, not the light reactions.
The light reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.

quiz.stem: Which type of chlorophyll is most common in plants?
rationales: Chlorophyll a is the primary and most abundant photosynthetic pigment in plants.
Chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment and is less common than chlorophyll a.
Chlorophyll c is found in some algae, not as the most common chlorophyll in plants.
Chlorophyll d occurs in certain organisms but is not the most common plant chlorophyll.

quiz.stem: Which wavelengths of light are absorbed to maximum by chlorophylls?
rationales: Chlorophyll does not absorb green light strongly, so this is not the best pair.
Green light is poorly absorbed, making this pair incorrect.
Chlorophyll absorbs most strongly in the red and blue regions of the spectrum.
Chlorophyll reflects much green light rather than absorbing it maximally.

quiz.stem: When yeast ferments glucose, the products are;
rationales: Yeast fermentation produces ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide.
Water is not the characteristic product of alcoholic fermentation by yeast.
Lactic acid is produced by lactic acid fermentation, not typical yeast fermentation.
Carbon dioxide is produced, but water is not the other characteristic product; ethanol is.

quiz.stem: Where do the dark reactions of photosynthesis occur?
rationales: The Calvin cycle, often called the dark reactions, occurs in the chloroplast stroma.
Thylakoid membranes are the site of the light reactions, not the Calvin cycle.
The outer chloroplast membrane is not where the dark reactions occur.
The cytoplasm is not the site of the dark reactions in plant cells.

quiz.stem: Which molecule donates electrons in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?
rationales: NADPH carries electrons produced by the light reactions rather than donating the initial electrons to them.
Water is split during the light reactions and donates electrons to replace those lost by chlorophyll.
Oxygen is released as a product when water is split; it is not the electron donor.
Carbon dioxide is used in carbon fixation and does not donate electrons in the light reactions.

quiz.stem: Which process in aerobic respiration produces the most ATP?
rationales: Glycolysis produces only a small amount of ATP compared with oxidative phosphorylation.
The Krebs cycle produces some ATP, but far less than the electron transport chain.
The electron transport chain generates the most ATP during aerobic respiration.
Fermentation does not produce the most ATP and is not part of aerobic respiration.

quiz.stem: How many ATP molecules are the net profit from one glucose molecule during anaerobic respiration?
rationales: Anaerobic respiration through glycolysis yields a net two ATP molecules per glucose.
Four ATP are produced gross during glycolysis, but two are consumed, leaving a net of two.
Twelve ATP is not the net yield from anaerobic breakdown of one glucose molecule.
Thirty-six ATP is an outdated approximate yield for aerobic respiration, not anaerobic respiration.

quiz.stem: What is a common byproduct of anaerobic respiration in animal cells?
rationales: Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration and is not a common byproduct of anaerobic respiration in animal cells.
Water is not the characteristic byproduct of anaerobic respiration in animal cells.
Animal cells produce lactic acid (lactate) when they rely on anaerobic glycolysis.
Carbon dioxide is not the common byproduct of anaerobic respiration in animal cells.

quiz.stem: Which set of subunits makes up an ATP molecule?
options: Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
Adenine, glucose and two phosphate groups
Ribose and three phosphate groups only
Amino acid, ribose and three phosphate groups
rationales: This is correct: ATP contains adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
ATP contains ribose, not glucose, and has three phosphate groups.
This is incomplete because ATP also contains adenine.
ATP contains the nitrogen-containing base adenine, not an amino acid.

quiz.stem: What molecule is formed when ATP loses one phosphate group?
rationales: AMP has one phosphate group and is formed when ADP loses a phosphate group.
This is correct: loss of the outer phosphate changes ATP into ADP.
ATP is the starting molecule, not the product after it loses a phosphate group.
Pi is the released inorganic phosphate, not the remaining nucleotide.

quiz.stem: How much energy is released when one phosphate bond of ATP is broken, according to this section?
rationales: This is less than the amount stated in the section.
This is correct: the section gives about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.
This amount is not the value given for breaking one phosphate bond in the section.
This is one hundred times the stated energy release.

quiz.stem: What separates from ATP when its outer high-energy phosphate bond breaks?
rationales: Adenine is a base in the ATP molecule and is not the group released in this reaction.
Ribose is the sugar in ATP and is not released when the outer phosphate bond breaks.
This is correct: inorganic phosphate (Pi) separates from ATP.
Adenosine is the adenine-and-ribose part and is not released in this reaction.

quiz.stem: How do cells store energy from food in ATP?
options: Cells use energy from food to combine ADP with Pi
Cells use energy from food to remove adenine from ATP
ATP is made by breaking AMP into adenine
ADP combines with oxygen to form ATP
rationales: This is correct: cells use energy from food to combine ADP and Pi to form ATP.
The section describes joining ADP with Pi, not removing adenine from ATP.
This does not describe the section's explanation of how ATP is made.
The section states that ADP combines with Pi, not oxygen, to form ATP.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the ATP cycle in cells?
options: ATP is made during energy-consuming processes and broken down during energy-releasing processes
ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken down during energy-consuming processes
ATP is only used to build proteins
ATP transfers energy only outside cells
rationales: This reverses the relationship described in the section.
This is correct: energy-releasing processes make ATP, and energy-consuming processes break it down.
The section describes ATP as transferring energy between metabolic reactions, not only building proteins.
The section explains ATP as an energy currency used by cells, not as a molecule that transfers energy only outside them.

quiz.stem: Where do the light reactions of photosynthesis take place?
rationales: Correct: the light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
The stroma is where the dark reactions take place.
The section does not give the outer membrane as the site of light reactions.
The section places light reactions in chloroplast thylakoids, not the cytoplasm.

quiz.stem: Which high-energy molecules are made during the light reactions?
rationales: Correct: the light reactions use light energy to make ATP and NADPH.
Glucose is made using products of the light reactions; oxygen is released as a by-product.
Carbon dioxide and water are raw materials, not the high-energy molecules made in the light reactions.
Proteins and lipids are not identified as products of the light reactions.

quiz.stem: In which part of a chloroplast do the dark reactions take place?
rationales: Correct: the dark reactions take place in the stroma of chloroplasts.
The thylakoid membranes are the site of light reactions.
The cell wall is not the site of the dark reactions.
The nucleus is not the site of the dark reactions.

quiz.stem: Which substance is broken by light during the light reactions, releasing oxygen?
rationales: Correct: light breaks water molecules, and oxygen is released.
Carbon dioxide is used in the dark reactions to make carbohydrates.
Glucose is made from carbohydrates produced during the dark reactions; it is not broken to release oxygen.
NADP is reduced to NADPH; it is not the molecule broken to release oxygen.

quiz.stem: Which pigment is identified as the main pigment in the thylakoid membranes?
rationales: Correct: chlorophyll-a is the main pigment.
Chlorophyll-b is an accessory pigment.
Carotenoids are accessory pigments.
NADP is a coenzyme, not a pigment.

quiz.stem: What do the 3-carbon compounds use to become 3-carbon carbohydrates in the dark reactions?
rationales: Correct: they are reduced using ATP and hydrogen from NADPH.
Oxygen and water are not the materials used for this reduction in the section's summary.
Glucose is made from the 3-carbon carbohydrates, and light is used in the light reactions.
These are pigments, not the materials used to reduce the 3-carbon compounds.

quiz.stem: Which colours of light carry out more photosynthesis according to the section?
rationales: Correct: the section states that blue and red lights carry out more photosynthesis.
Green and yellow are not identified as the colours that carry out more photosynthesis.
The section says blue and red lights carry out more photosynthesis, not only green light.
The section does not identify only yellow light as carrying out more photosynthesis.

quiz.stem: What is one role of accessory pigments in photosynthesis?
options: Accessory pigments absorb wavelengths not absorbed by chlorophyll-a.
Accessory pigments make carbon dioxide in the stroma.
Accessory pigments replace water as the raw material.
Accessory pigments convert glucose into light.
rationales: Correct: wavelengths not absorbed by chlorophyll-a are absorbed by accessory pigments.
The section does not state that accessory pigments make carbon dioxide.
Water remains a raw material in photosynthesis; pigments do not replace it.
The section says pigments absorb sunlight and convert it into chemical energy, not that they convert glucose into light.

quiz.stem: Where does glycolysis occur?
rationales: Correct: glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect: the mitochondrial matrix is where the Krebs cycle occurs.
Incorrect: the inner mitochondrial membrane is where the electron transport chain occurs.
Incorrect: glycolysis does not occur in the nucleus.

quiz.stem: Which statement about glycolysis is correct?
options: It produces lactic acid in every cell.
rationales: Incorrect: oxygen is not required for glycolysis.
Incorrect: glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, not only in mitochondria.
Correct: glycolysis does not require oxygen and can also occur during anaerobic respiration.
Incorrect: glycolysis produces pyruvic acid, not lactic acid in every cell.

quiz.stem: Which products are formed when yeast carries out alcoholic fermentation?
rationales: Correct: yeast fermentation converts pyruvic acid into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Incorrect: lactic acid fermentation occurs in skeletal muscles, and oxygen is not a product here.
Incorrect: these are not the products of alcoholic fermentation.
Incorrect: these are not the products of alcoholic fermentation.

quiz.stem: Which substance is formed when skeletal muscles respire anaerobically?
rationales: Incorrect: ethyl alcohol is formed in alcoholic fermentation, such as in yeast.
Correct: during anaerobic respiration in skeletal muscles, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid.
Incorrect: acetyl coenzyme-A is formed before the Krebs cycle when oxygen is available.
Incorrect: FADH₂ is an energy-rich compound made during the Krebs cycle.

quiz.stem: On which cell structure does the electron transport chain occur?
rationales: Incorrect: glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect: the Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
Correct: the electron transport chain occurs on the inner membranes of mitochondria.
Incorrect: the section locates this process on the inner mitochondrial membranes.

quiz.stem: What forms when electrons and hydrogen ions combine with oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain?
rationales: Incorrect: carbon dioxide is produced during the breakdown of pyruvic acid in the Krebs cycle.
Correct: oxygen combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.
Incorrect: ethyl alcohol is a product of alcoholic fermentation.
Incorrect: lactic acid is formed during anaerobic respiration in muscles.

quiz.stem: According to the section's comparison table, what is the net ATP profit from anaerobic respiration?
rationales: Correct: the table gives a net profit of 02 ATP for anaerobic respiration.
Incorrect: the table does not give 4 ATP as the net profit.
Incorrect: the table gives 36 ATP for aerobic respiration, not anaerobic respiration.
Incorrect: anaerobic respiration releases some energy and gives a net profit of 2 ATP.

quiz.stem: Which is one use of respiratory energy (ATP) in the body?
rationales: Correct: ATP is used for muscle contractions and movement.
Incorrect: making oxygen in the lungs is not listed as a use of respiratory ATP.
Incorrect: absorbing sunlight is part of photosynthesis, not a listed use of respiratory ATP.
Incorrect: this is not one of the uses of respiratory energy listed in the section.

quiz.stem: Which of the following plant nutrients is required in large amount?
rationales: Iron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Zinc is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Potassium is a macronutrient required by plants in relatively large amounts.
Boron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.

quiz.stem: Which element is required by plants for the formation of chlorophyll?
rationales: Phosphorus is important in energy transfer and nucleic acids but is not the central element in chlorophyll.
Calcium supports cell walls and signaling but is not required as the central element in chlorophyll.
Magnesium is the central element in chlorophyll and is required for its formation.
Sulphur is found in some amino acids but is not the central element in chlorophyll.

quiz.stem: The primary function of root hairs is:
rationales: Root hairs do not primarily transport nutrients; their main role is absorbing water and minerals from soil.
Root hairs are not primarily used to store food.
Root hairs increase the root's surface area, improving absorption from the soil.
Root hairs do not primarily synthesize proteins.

quiz.stem: Root hairs absorb salts from soil by;
rationales: Diffusion may move substances down a concentration gradient but is not the main mechanism for uptake of mineral salts by root hairs.
Osmosis describes water movement across a selectively permeable membrane, not the uptake of dissolved salts.
Root hairs commonly take up mineral ions against their concentration gradient by active transport.
Filtration is not the mechanism by which root hairs take up mineral salts.

quiz.stem: Water moves from the soil into root cells by:
rationales: Water enters root cells by osmosis, moving across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential.
Active transport requires energy to move solutes and is not the process that brings water into root cells.
Diffusion is not the specific term for water movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
Bulk flow is movement of fluid driven by pressure differences and does not describe water entry into root cells at the membrane.

quiz.stem: The transpiration is regulated by;
rationales: Mesophyll cells are involved in photosynthesis and do not directly regulate stomatal opening.
Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata, thereby regulating transpiration.
Xylem transports water and minerals but does not regulate stomatal aperture.
Phloem transports sugars and does not regulate stomatal aperture.

quiz.stem: Under which condition, there will be high rate of transpiration?
rationales: High humidity reduces the water-vapor gradient between a leaf and the air, lowering transpiration.
Low light intensity generally promotes stomatal closure and reduces transpiration.
Wind removes the moist air around leaves, maintaining a steep water-vapor gradient and increasing transpiration.
Waterlogged soil can impair root function and does not generally create a high transpiration rate.

quiz.stem: Which ion plays a role in the opening of stomata?
rationales: Sodium ions are not the principal ions associated with stomatal opening in most plants.
Potassium ions accumulate in guard cells, lowering their water potential and promoting stomatal opening.
Calcium ions can act in guard-cell signaling, but potassium is the ion primarily associated with opening stomata.
Magnesium is not the main ion responsible for stomatal opening.

quiz.stem: In most plants the food is transported in the form of:
rationales: Glucose is generally converted into a transport form rather than transported as the main sugar in most plants.
Sucrose is the principal form in which food is transported through the phloem of most plants.
Starch is insoluble and is typically used for storage rather than long-distance transport.
Maltose is not the principal form in which food is transported in most plants.

quiz.stem: What is TRUE according to the pressure flow mechanism of food transport?
options: Water enters the source, creating pressure
Water is pulled from the sink
Movement of food in phloem is due to gravity
Solutes move from low to high concentration
rationales: At the source, sugar loading lowers water potential, so water enters the phloem and creates pressure that drives flow toward the sink.
Water does not generally get pulled from the sink to drive the pressure-flow mechanism; pressure is generated at the source.
Phloem transport is driven by pressure differences, not by gravity.
Solute loading at the source occurs against a concentration gradient in many cases, rather than by movement from low to high concentration as stated without qualification.

quiz.stem: Succulent organs are present in:
rationales: Xerophytes commonly have succulent organs that store water as an adaptation to dry conditions.
Hydrophytes are adapted to living in water and are not typically identified by succulent water-storing organs.
Mesophytes live in environments with moderate water availability and generally do not have succulent organs.
Some halophytes can be succulent, but succulent organs are most characteristically associated with xerophytes in this context.

quiz.stem: Which mineral is listed as a macronutrient in plants?
rationales: Iron is listed as a micronutrient.
Potassium is listed as a macronutrient.
Boron is listed as a micronutrient.
Zinc is listed as a micronutrient.

quiz.stem: Which role of nitrogen is stated in your textbook?
options: It is a component of proteins and chlorophyll.
It regulates the opening and closing of stomata.
It is needed to convert nitrates to ammonia.
It is involved in osmosis of water.
rationales: Nitrogen is a component of proteins and chlorophyll.
Potassium, not nitrogen, regulates the opening and closing of the stoma.
Molybdenum is a component of the enzyme that converts nitrates to ammonia.
Chlorine is involved in osmosis of water.

quiz.stem: Which mineral is a component of chlorophyll and activates many enzymes?
rationales: Iron is necessary for photosynthesis and activates many enzymes, but it is not identified as a chlorophyll component here.
Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and activates many enzymes.
Calcium activates enzymes and is a structural component of cell walls, but is not listed as a chlorophyll component.
Sulphur is a component of proteins, vitamins and enzymes, but is not listed as a chlorophyll component.

quiz.stem: In what form do plant roots absorb nitrogen, according to the section?
rationales: The section states that plant roots absorb nitrogen in the form of nitrates.
The section does not state that nitrogen is absorbed as phosphate ions.
The section does not state that nitrogen is absorbed as sulphate ions.
The section does not state that nitrogen is absorbed as chloride ions.

quiz.stem: What is the yellowing of leaves caused by insufficient chlorophyll called?
rationales: The section names yellowing caused by insufficient chlorophyll chlorosis.
Guttation is not the term used for yellowing of leaves in this section.
Transpiration is not the term used for yellowing of leaves in this section.
Germination is the beginning of growth from a seed, not yellowing of leaves.

quiz.stem: Which deficiencies can cause yellowing to appear first in older leaves?
rationales: Nitrogen deficiency can cause this pattern, but it is not the only one.
Magnesium deficiency can cause this pattern, but it is not the only one.
For either deficiency, the plant moves the element from older to younger leaves, so yellowing is first seen in old leaves.
Both deficiencies can cause yellowing to appear first in older leaves.

quiz.stem: Which root layer is the outermost covering?
options: The single outer layer of root cells
The broad zone just inside the epidermis
The innermost boundary of the cortex
A narrow layer inside the endodermis
rationales: Correct: the epidermis is the root's outermost covering.
Incorrect: the cortex lies just inside the epidermis.
Incorrect: the endodermis forms the innermost boundary of the cortex.
Incorrect: the pericycle lies on the inner side of the endodermis.

quiz.stem: Why do root hairs help roots absorb water and salts?
options: They produce food for the root.
They increase the root's surface area for absorption.
They carry food to the leaves.
They prevent water from entering the root.
rationales: Incorrect: food production is not given as the function of root hairs.
Correct: root hairs have a large surface area and contact soil water.
Incorrect: food transport is the role of phloem, not root hairs.
Incorrect: root hairs take in water from the soil rather than preventing its entry.

quiz.stem: Which process allows root hairs to take in more salts from the soil?
rationales: Incorrect: osmosis moves water, not salts, as described in this section.
Correct: the section states that root hairs take in more salts by active transport.
Incorrect: filtration is not the process described for salt uptake.
Incorrect: transpiration is not the process by which root hairs absorb salts.

quiz.stem: According to the definition in the section, in which direction does water move during osmosis?
options: From a region of higher solute concentration to a region of lower solute concentration
From a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration
From the root xylem directly into the soil
Only when the plant uses energy
rationales: Incorrect: the section describes water moving towards the region with higher solute concentration.
Correct: osmosis moves water from lower to higher solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane.
Incorrect: this is not the direction of water movement described for root uptake.
Incorrect: osmosis does not require energy.

quiz.stem: Which structure is the innermost boundary of the cortex?
rationales: Incorrect: the epidermis is the outermost root covering.
Incorrect: the cortex is the broad zone inside the epidermis.
Correct: the endodermis is the innermost boundary of the cortex.
Incorrect: the pericycle is on the inner side of the endodermis.

quiz.stem: After reaching the pericycle, where does water move next?
options: Water moves from the pericycle into the root xylem.
Water moves from the xylem into the soil.
Food moves from the pericycle into the root xylem.
Salts move from the root xylem into the cortex.
rationales: Correct: water moves from the pericycle into the root xylem.
Incorrect: the section describes water moving into the xylem, not out into soil.
Incorrect: the section describes water moving into the xylem, not food.
Incorrect: the stated route is from pericycle to xylem.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares the transport roles of xylem and phloem?
options: Xylem transports water and salts; phloem transports food.
Xylem transports food; phloem transports water and salts.
Both xylem and phloem transport only water.
Both xylem and phloem transport only food.
rationales: Correct: xylem carries water and salts, while phloem carries food.
Incorrect: this reverses the roles of the two tissues.
Incorrect: phloem is responsible for transporting food.
Incorrect: xylem transports water and salts, not only food.

quiz.stem: Which tissues form the vascular bundle in the root?
rationales: Incorrect: the epidermis is the outer covering of the root.
Incorrect: the cortex is a zone of cells inside the epidermis.
Correct: xylem and phloem together are called the vascular bundle.
Incorrect: root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells.

quiz.stem: After water evaporates from the moist walls of mesophyll cells, where do the water vapours move next?
options: Water vapours leave through the stomata
Water enters the xylem from the air spaces
Mineral salts evaporate from mesophyll cells
rationales: This is correct because water vapours move towards the stomata and then pass to the outside air.
This is incorrect because the described movement is from the mesophyll cell walls towards the stomata, not into the xylem.
This is incorrect because the section describes water vapour leaving the leaf, not glucose leaving through the cuticle.
This is incorrect because the section describes evaporation of water, not mineral salts.

quiz.stem: Which feature of guard cells is stated in the section?
options: They are the only epidermal cells that contain chloroplasts
Their outer walls are thicker than their inner walls
rationales: This is incorrect because the section says guard cells contain chloroplasts.
This is correct because guard cells are the only epidermal cells which contain chloroplasts.
This is incorrect because the section says the cell wall is thicker on the inside and thinner elsewhere.
This is incorrect because xylem vessels are not described as part of guard cells.

quiz.stem: What happens to potassium ions in guard cells during daytime?
options: Potassium ions move into guard cells
Potassium ions move from guard cells into epidermal cells
Guard cells lose all their chloroplasts
Water vapour changes into liquid water in the stoma
rationales: This is correct because guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport during daytime.
This is incorrect because the potassium ions move back to epidermal cells in the evening.
This is incorrect because the section does not say that guard cells lose their chloroplasts.
This is incorrect because the section describes water movement and evaporation, not condensation in the stoma.

quiz.stem: When the solute concentration of guard cells rises during daytime, how does water enter them?
options: Water moves from guard cells to epidermal cells by active transport
Water moves from epidermal cells to guard cells by osmosis
Water moves from xylem to the air by diffusion only
Water moves from the atmosphere into guard cells
rationales: This is incorrect because the section states that water enters guard cells, and it moves by osmosis rather than active transport.
This is correct because water moves from epidermal cells to guard cells by osmosis.
This is incorrect because it does not describe the stated movement into guard cells.
This is incorrect because the stated source of water is the surrounding epidermal cells.

quiz.stem: What is the effect of guard cells becoming turgid?
options: Guard cells become turgid and the stoma opens
Guard cells lose turgor and the stoma opens
Guard cells become turgid and the stoma closes
Guard cells stop containing water and remain open
rationales: This is correct because their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens.
This is incorrect because loss of turgor in the evening causes the stoma to close.
This is incorrect because turgid guard cells open the stoma, not close it.
This is incorrect because the section says water enters turgid guard cells.

quiz.stem: What effect does high humidity have on the rate of transpiration?
options: It increases the rate of transpiration
It decreases the rate of transpiration
It has no effect on transpiration
rationales: This is incorrect because high humidity is associated with a lower rate of transpiration.
This is correct because the higher the humidity, the lower the rate of transpiration.
This is incorrect because humidity is listed as a factor affecting transpiration.
This is incorrect because the section does not say that humidity directly closes every stoma.

quiz.stem: Why does wind speed up transpiration?
options: Wind carries away humid air surrounding leaves
Wind increases the number of stomata

options: The average of the data set
rationales: Incorrect: the highest value is the maximum, not the mode.
Incorrect: the average of the data set is the mean, not the mode.
Correct: if no values repeat, no value occurs more often than the others, so there is no mode.
Incorrect: the median is the middle value, not the mode.

quiz.stem: In a bar chart, what does the height or length of each bar represent?
options: The value of the corresponding category
The difference between the highest and lowest values
rationales: Incorrect: the number of categories is represented by the set of bars, not by each bar’s height or length.
Correct: each bar’s height or length represents the value for its corresponding category.
Incorrect: the average of all values is not what each individual bar represents.
Incorrect: the difference between the highest and lowest values is the range, not the meaning of a bar’s height or length.

quiz.stem: When constructing a bar chart, which axis usually represents the categories?
options: Both axes equally represent the categories
rationales: Incorrect: the vertical axis usually represents values or frequencies, not categories.
Correct: categories are usually listed along the horizontal x-axis in a bar chart.
Incorrect: the axes generally have different roles rather than equally representing categories.
Incorrect: one axis—usually the horizontal axis—represents the categories.

quiz.stem: A researcher uses statistical methods to study data about living organisms. Which field is the researcher using?
options: It applies statistical methods to biological sciences.
It studies only the structure of cells.
rationales: Correct: applying statistical methods to biological sciences is biostatistics.
Incorrect: biostatistics supports the analysis of evidence; it does not replace experiments with opinions.
Incorrect: biostatistics is not limited to studying cell structure.
Incorrect: financial transactions are not the focus of biostatistics.

quiz.stem: How does biostatistics help when a biological experiment is being planned?
options: To make sure collected data are relevant and sufficient for the research question.
To guarantee that every study gives the expected result.
To choose the final policy before studying the evidence.
rationales: Correct: it helps structure a study so its data can answer the research question.
Incorrect: careful planning cannot guarantee a particular result.
Incorrect: studies need data to answer research questions.
Incorrect: decisions should be informed by evidence, not chosen before the evidence is studied.

quiz.stem: What may analysing biological data help researchers discover?
options: It can reveal trends, correlations, and patterns in the data.
It changes the data so that the results look stronger.
It proves that every observed relationship is causal.
It removes the need to interpret results.
rationales: Correct: analysis can uncover trends, correlations, and patterns.
Incorrect: analysis should examine data, not alter it to strengthen a result.
Incorrect: a correlation alone does not prove that one factor caused another.
Incorrect: results still need to be interpreted meaningfully.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of biostatistics helping to interpret results?
options: Interpreting disease survey results to guide public health interventions.
Choosing a treatment without examining any evidence.
Predicting weather from plant names alone.
Counting laboratory equipment for an inventory.
rationales: Correct: interpreting disease prevalence results can guide public health interventions.
Incorrect: biostatistics uses evidence to inform decisions rather than ignore it.
Incorrect: the example does not use biological data to predict an outcome.
Incorrect: an equipment inventory is not an example of interpreting biological results.

quiz.stem: Which task is an example of predicting outcomes with biostatistics?
options: Using current data to model the likely spread of an infectious disease.
Changing the results of a completed study.
Listing the names of diseases alphabetically.
Selecting a vaccine without considering disease data.
rationales: Correct: models can use current data to predict how an infectious disease may spread.
Incorrect: results should not be changed to fit an expectation.
Incorrect: alphabetical listing is not prediction from data.
Incorrect: vaccine planning should use evidence about disease and health outcomes.

quiz.stem: Why is biostatistics useful in public health and policy making?
options: It provides evidence-based insights for health policies and guidelines.
It ensures that public health decisions need no evidence.
It is used only after a disease has disappeared.
It prevents researchers from comparing treatments.
rationales: Correct: evidence from statistical analysis can guide policies and health guidelines.
Incorrect: biostatistics helps decisions rely on evidence.
Incorrect: it can be used to study current health problems and plan responses.
Incorrect: biostatistics can support comparisons, including in clinical trials.

quiz.stem: Find the mean of 8, 10, 14, and 16.
rationales: Incorrect: the sum is 48, and 48 divided by 4 is not 10.
Incorrect: 14 is one of the data values, but it is not their mean.
Incorrect: 16 is the greatest value, not the mean.

quiz.stem: What is the median of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11?
rationales: Incorrect: 5 is the second value, not the middle value.
Correct: the ordered set has five values, so its third value, 7, is the median.
Incorrect: 9 is the fourth value, not the middle value.
Incorrect: 11 is the greatest value, not the middle value.

quiz.stem: Find the median of 4, 8, 6, 10.
rationales: Incorrect: after ordering, 4 is the first value.
Incorrect: 6 is one of the middle values, but the median is their average.
Correct: the ordered values are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the median is (6 + 8)/2 = 7.
Incorrect: 8 is one of the middle values, but the median is their average.

quiz.stem: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 4, 5?
rationales: Incorrect: 2 appears only once.
Correct: 3 appears twice, more often than any other value.
Incorrect: 4 appears only once.
Incorrect: 5 appears only once.

quiz.stem: Identify the mode or modes of 2, 2, 4, 4, 7.
rationales: Incorrect: 2 and 4 both occur more often than 7.
Correct: 2 and 4 each occur twice, the highest frequency, so both are modes.
Incorrect: 2 is a mode, but 4 also occurs twice.
Incorrect: 4 is a mode, but 2 also occurs twice.

quiz.stem: Which description gives the mode of a data set?
options: The middle value after arranging the data
The value that occurs most often
rationales: Incorrect: the smallest value is not necessarily the most frequent.
Incorrect: the largest value is not necessarily the most frequent.
Incorrect: this describes the median, not the mode.
Correct: the mode is the value that appears most frequently.

quiz.stem: A bar chart shows the numbers of four kinds of birds. What does the height of a bird’s bar represent?
options: The interval used on the axis
rationales: A category name is shown by the label, not by the bar’s height.
Correct: the bar’s height corresponds to the value for that category.
The number of bars shows how many categories there are, not a single bar’s height.
Axis intervals show the scale; they are not the value represented by a bar.

quiz.stem: When making a bar chart, where are the categories usually labelled?
rationales: Correct: the x-axis is labelled with the categories.
The y-axis is labelled with the values.
The axes have different roles: categories go on the x-axis and values on the y-axis.
The x-axis shows the categories.

quiz.stem: How should the value axis be marked when preparing a bar chart?
options: Use uneven intervals so the bars fit
Divide the y-axis into equal intervals
Put the categories on the y-axis
Make every bar a different width
rationales: Uneven intervals make comparisons misleading.
Correct: the scale should use equal intervals.
The categories are labelled on the x-axis.
Bars should have equal width and be spaced evenly.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes how bars should be drawn?
options: Bars should touch and have different widths
Bars should be equal in width and spaced evenly
Bars should all have the same height
Bars should be drawn without labels
rationales: The bars should be spaced evenly, and their widths should be equal.
Correct: bars have equal width and are spaced evenly.
Bar heights must correspond to the different category values.
Each bar should be labelled with its category name and value.

quiz.stem: What should you consider when choosing the scale for the y-axis?
options: The lowest value in the data
The highest value in the data
rationales: The lowest value alone does not determine a scale that covers all the data.
The number of categories is shown along the x-axis.
Correct: the scale should be based on the range of values, including the highest value.
Bar width does not determine the y-axis scale.

quiz.stem: What information should be written along the x-axis of a bar chart?
rationales: The values are shown on the y-axis and by the heights of the bars.
Correct: the x-axis is labelled with the categories.
A chart title describes the whole chart and is not the x-axis category labels.
The order may arrange categories but does not label them.

quiz.stem: Which action comes first when creating a bar chart using the section’s steps?
rationales: Correct: the first step is to gather the data to be represented.
Bars are drawn after organising the data, drawing and labelling axes, and choosing a scale.
Bars are labelled after they have been drawn.
The scale is chosen after gathering and organising the data and drawing the axes.

readiness.stem: Which branch of Biology focuses on the study of the structure and function of cells?
rationales: Cytology studies the structure and function of cells.
Microbiology studies microorganisms rather than cells as a general biological unit.
Histology studies tissues, which are groups of cells.
Ecology studies relationships between organisms and their environment.

readiness.stem: Which of the following taxonomic ranks represents the broadest rank?
rationales: Species is the narrowest taxonomic rank listed, not the broadest.
Genus is broader than species but narrower than kingdom and domain.
Kingdom is broad, but domain is a broader rank.
Domain is the broadest taxonomic rank listed.

readiness.stem: The process of cellular respiration occurs in:
rationales: The nucleus does not serve as the main site of cellular respiration.
Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic cellular respiration.
Ribosomes synthesize proteins rather than carry out cellular respiration.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages molecules rather than carry out cellular respiration.

readiness.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?
rationales: M phase is primarily for chromosome separation and cell division, not maximum growth.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, rather than when maximum cell growth occurs.
G1 phase is the main growth phase in which the cell increases in size and carries out normal functions.
G2 phase involves further growth and preparation for mitosis, but maximum growth generally occurs in G1.

readiness.stem: A higher level of organization exhibits emergent properties when:
options: The sum of its parts is greater than the whole.
The individual parts are more important than the whole.
Its parts interact to perform more functions.
rationales: Parts functioning independently do not produce emergent properties of the higher level.
Emergent properties arise from interactions among parts, not from the sum being greater than the whole.
Emergent properties depend on how parts work together, rather than on individual parts being more important than the whole.
Interactions among parts can produce functions and properties not present in the parts individually.

readiness.stem: What is the primary function of carbohydrates?
rationales: Carbohydrates are a major source of energy for the body.
Carbohydrates are not generally enzymes; enzymes are mostly proteins.
Regulating body processes is not the primary function of carbohydrates.
Some carbohydrates are components of membranes, but this is not their primary function.
Most enzymes are not nucleic acids, although a few catalytic RNA molecules exist.
Most enzymes are proteins, making this the best answer.
Carbohydrates are not the primary composition of enzymes.
Lipids are not the primary composition of enzymes.

readiness.stem: When we get energy from ATP, which bonds are broken?
rationales: ATP hydrolysis releases energy by breaking the terminal phosphate–phosphate bond.
C–H bonds are not the bonds whose hydrolysis releases ATP’s usable energy.
C–N bonds are not broken during ATP hydrolysis.
C–O bonds are not the bonds broken to release energy from ATP.

readiness.stem: Which of the following plant nutrients is required in large amount?
rationales: Iron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Zinc is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Potassium is a macronutrient required by plants in relatively large amounts.
Boron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.

readiness.stem: Which of the following organisms commonly reproduce by binary fission?
rationales: Yeast commonly reproduces by budding rather than binary fission.
Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission.
Rhizopus commonly reproduces by spores rather than binary fission.
Plants generally reproduce sexually or by vegetative propagation, not by binary fission.

readiness.stem: What is the primary purpose of biostatistics?
options: To apply statistical methods to biological sciences
rationales: Incorrect: financial data analysis is not the primary focus of biostatistics.
Correct: biostatistics applies statistical methods to biological and health-related sciences.
Incorrect: engineering models are not the primary subject of biostatistics.
Incorrect: studying historical events is the focus of history, not biostatistics.

mcqs.stem: Which step comes between making hypothesis and doing experiments?
rationales: Making deductions follows a hypothesis and helps guide experiments.
Making observations generally precedes forming a hypothesis.
Summarizing results occurs after experiments and analysis.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the scientific method?
rationales: The scientific method relies on evidence to evaluate explanations.
Formulating hypotheses is a key part of the scientific method.
A hypothesis is testable but is not guaranteed to be correct.
Rigorous testing is needed to assess a hypothesis.

mcqs.stem: Choose the correct sequence of steps of scientific method?

mcqs.stem: People who slept near smoky fire had less chance to suffer from malaria. Why?

Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled
rationales: Smoke does not kill Plasmodium in the blood.
The stated effect is not that fire heats the air enough to kill Plasmodium.
Smoke repels mosquitoes, reducing the chance that they transmit malaria.
Smoke does not kill Plasmodium inside mosquitoes as the relevant explanation.

mcqs.stem: Experiments are very important in scientific method because a researcher
options: Disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved
Is sure that he will prove the hypotheses
Gets a chance to work in the laboratory
rationales: Experiments do not guarantee correct results because they can be affected by error or limitations.
Experiments can disprove hypotheses or provide evidence supporting them, though they do not prove them with absolute certainty.
Researchers cannot be sure in advance that experiments will support a hypothesis.
Laboratory work may be part of an experiment, but it is not why experiments are important to the scientific method.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is the correct way for writing the scientific name of humans?

mcqs.stem: What does biodiversity mean?

The number of rocks in an area
The size of the largest organism

mcqs.stem: How is the biodiversity of an area measured?
options: Only the total number of organisms
The number of different kinds and the variation within each kind
Only the variation within one kind
The number of habitats in the world

This is correct because biodiversity is measured by considering the number of different kinds of organisms and the variation within each kind.
This is incorrect because biodiversity also considers the number of different kinds of organisms.
This is incorrect because the number of habitats alone is not the measure given in the section.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about biodiversity on Earth is correct?

Biodiversity is not evenly spread across Earth.
Polar regions always have more biodiversity than tropical regions.
Soil type has no effect on biodiversity.

written.text:
(a) Describe the diagnostic characteristics of the four kingdoms within the domain Eukarya.
(b) Discuss the challenges of classifying viruses within the traditional three domains of life.
modelAnswer: (a) Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular.
Plant-like protists are autotrophs; animal-like protists are heterotrophs, and fungus-like protists absorb nutrients from decaying organic matter.
Kingdom Fungi consists of heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; they absorb food from decaying matter.
Kingdom Plantae includes multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose; they prepare food through photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it within their bodies; they have no cell walls.
(b) Viruses are acellular; they are not made of cells and do not have organelles.
They cannot run metabolism.
For the synthesis of their proteins and to increase in number, viruses become parasites in organisms.
They lack any of the characteristics of the three domains of life.
Therefore, viruses are not included in the classification system.

written.text:
(a) Explain the rules and guidelines for suggesting scientific names to organisms.
(b) Q2.6. Discuss the challenges of classifying viruses within the traditional three domains of life.
modelAnswer: (a) Scientific names are taken from Latin.
Every scientific name has two parts: the genus name comes first, followed by the species name.
Every scientific name should be unique; the same name cannot be used for two different organisms.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, and the species name begins with a small letter.
When printed, the scientific name is typed in italics.
When handwritten, its two parts are underlined separately.
(b) Viruses are acellular and lack the cellular structure and organelles found in organisms of the three domains.
They cannot carry out all life processes independently.
They reproduce only inside host cells.
For these reasons, viruses do not fit easily into the traditional three-domain classification of cellular life.

written.text:
(a) Name the chemical compounds that make up:
(a) Cell membrane
(b) Fungal cell wall
(c) Plant cell wall
(d) Bacterial cell wall
(e) Ribosomes
(f) Chromosomes
(b) Explain the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.
modelAnswer: (a) (a) Cell membrane: proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates.
(b) Fungal cell wall: chitin.
(c) Plant cell wall: the primary wall is mainly cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.
(d) Bacterial cell wall: peptidoglycan.
(e) Ribosomes: almost equal amounts of proteins and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
(f) Chromosomes: DNA and proteins.
(b) The cell membrane is composed of proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates.
According to the fluid-mosaic model, the lipids make a fluid-like bilayer in which protein molecules are submerged.
The lipids and proteins can move laterally, so the mosaic pattern constantly changes.
Carbohydrates join proteins as glycoproteins or lipids as glycolipids.

written.text:
(a) Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall.
(b) Discuss the components of the nucleus.
modelAnswer: (a) The cell wall is a rigid, non-living wall around the cell membrane.
It provides shape, strength, protection and support to the protoplasm.
The plant cell wall has three layers: middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall.
The primary wall is mainly made of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly made of cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.
Plasmodesmata are channels in cell walls that allow the exchange of molecules between adjacent cells.
(b) The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which has many nuclear pores.
The inner jelly-like material is called nucleoplasm.
The nucleoplasm contains one or more nucleoli, where ribosomes are assembled.
It also contains chromatin, made of DNA and proteins; chromatin condenses into thick chromosomes when a cell starts dividing.
DNA contains genes that control cell activities and transmits characteristics to the next generation.

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membrane-bounded channels throughout the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes attached to its surface and functions in protein synthesis.

It provides structural support.
It also provides protection.

mcqs.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?
rationales: M phase is primarily for chromosome separation and cell division, not maximum growth.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, rather than when maximum cell growth occurs.
G1 phase is the main growth phase in which the cell increases in size and carries out normal functions.
G2 phase involves further growth and preparation for mitosis, but maximum growth generally occurs in G1.

mcqs.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?
rationales: Mitosis separates duplicated chromosomes but does not duplicate them.
G1 phase is mainly for cell growth and preparation for DNA synthesis.
G2 phase follows DNA duplication and prepares the cell for mitosis.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, duplicating the chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of mitosis?
options: It results in genetically identical daughter cells.
The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells.
It results in the formation of two daughter cells.
rationales: Mitosis commonly occurs in somatic cells.
Mitosis normally produces daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell and each other.
Mitosis preserves the chromosome number rather than halving it, so this is not a characteristic of mitosis.
Mitosis followed by cytokinesis results in two daughter cells.

mcqs.stem: At which stage of mitosis chromosomes line up in the centre?
rationales: In prophase, chromosomes condense and the spindle begins to form, but chromosomes have not yet lined up at the centre.
In metaphase, chromosomes align at the cell’s equatorial plane.
In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles.
In telophase, chromosomes are at the poles and new nuclei begin to form.

mcqs.stem: If you observe a cell in which nuclear membrane is reforming around two sets of chromosomes, what stage of cell cycle is this?
rationales: Anaphase is when sister chromatids move apart, before the nuclear membranes reform.
Telophase is when nuclear membranes reform around the two chromosome sets.
Prophase involves chromosome condensation and breakdown of the nuclear envelope, not its reformation.
Metaphase is when chromosomes align at the cell’s centre.

mcqs.stem: How does the centrosome contribute to mitosis?
rationales: The centrosome does not initiate DNA replication; DNA replication occurs during S phase.
The centrosome organizes microtubules to form the mitotic spindle.
The nuclear envelope reforms around chromosomes during telophase and is not formed by the centrosome.
Organelle duplication is not the centrosome’s role in mitosis.

mcqs.stem: Centrosomes make mitotic spindle in:
rationales: Animal cells typically use centrosomes to organize the mitotic spindle.
Most higher plant cells lack centrosomes and organize their spindle through other microtubule-organizing sites.
Prokaryotic cells do not undergo mitosis and do not have centrosomes.
This is not true of all cells because plant and prokaryotic cells do not use centrosomes to make a mitotic spindle.

mcqs.stem: An organism has 4 pairs of chromosomes. After meiosis-I, how many chromosomes and chromatids will be present in each daughter cell?
rationales: Each daughter cell has half the original chromosome number after meiosis I, so it does not have 8 chromosomes.
A starting cell with 8 chromosomes produces cells with 4 duplicated chromosomes after meiosis I, amounting to 8 chromatids per cell.
Each of the 4 chromosomes still consists of two sister chromatids after meiosis I, so there are 8 chromatids, not 4.
Each daughter cell has 4 chromosomes after meiosis I, not 8.

mcqs.stem: Which event is unique to meiosis but not mitosis?
rationales: DNA replication occurs before both mitosis and meiosis.
Chromosomes align during both mitosis and meiosis, although the details differ.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.
Nuclear division occurs in both mitosis and meiosis.

mcqs.stem: Why is meiosis-II necessary after meiosis-I?
rationales: Chromosomes are replicated before meiosis I, and meiosis II does not include another round of DNA replication.
The chromosome number is reduced during meiosis I, not meiosis II.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids that remained joined after meiosis I.
Genetic recombination mainly occurs through crossing over during prophase I, not meiosis II.

mcqs.stem: A cell has copied the DNA of each chromosome, but the total number of chromosomes has not changed. Which phase has just occurred?
rationales: G1 is mainly a growth and preparation phase before DNA replication.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, while the chromosome number remains the same.
G2 follows DNA replication and includes further growth and preparation for division.
M phase is the division phase, not the phase in which DNA is copied.

mcqs.stem: During which phase does a cell make proteins and organelles and grow in size?
rationales: G1 is the growth phase in which the cell makes proteins and organelles.
S phase is primarily for DNA replication.
G2 includes further growth and production of proteins needed for cell division.
G0 is a phase in which some cells stop dividing to perform specialized functions.

written.text: Enlist the events that occur during the G1 phase of interphase?
modelAnswer: During G1, the cell grows in size.
It makes proteins and organelles.
It makes enzymes required in S phase for DNA replication.
Answer: The cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and prepares enzymes for DNA replication.

written.text:
(a) Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
(b) Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
modelAnswer: (a) Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus and is divided into four phases.
During prophase, thread-like chromatin condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.
The nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and spindle fibres form.
During metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at the centromere and arrange along the equator, forming the metaphase plate.
During anaphase, spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart towards opposite poles.
During telophase, a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and results in two daughter cells.
(b) In prophase-I, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, exchanging portions of chromosomes.
In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator and form the metaphase plate.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate; one chromosome from each pair moves toward each opposite pole. Each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.
In telophase-I, spindles disappear, nuclear envelopes and nucleoli reform, and chromosomes uncoil into chromatin.
Cytokinesis occurs, producing two haploid daughter cells.
