written.text:
(a) Describe the significance of mitosis.
(b) Describe the significance of meiosis.
modelAnswer: (a) Growth occurs due to an increase in the number of cells.
Mitosis produces new cells that are identical to the original cells and plays a crucial role in growth.
Many cells constantly die in the body; mitosis forms new cells that are exact copies of the older cells to replace them.
Some animals regenerate parts of the body by forming new cells through mitosis in the cells of the remaining parts.
Mitosis is a means for asexual reproduction; for example, in Hydra it forms a bud that grows into a new individual.
(b) In animals, meiosis produces gametes with half the number of chromosomes.
During sexual reproduction, male and female gametes join to make a zygote, restoring the original number of chromosomes.
In flowering plants, meiosis produces spores with half the number of chromosomes; the gametes produced by the new generation join to make a zygote with a full set.
Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes, and each chromosome in the gametes carries a unique set of genes.
When diverse gametes combine, the zygote is genetically different from both parents, so meiosis contributes to genetic diversity.

mcqs.stem: A higher level of organization exhibits emergent properties when:
options: The sum of its parts is greater than the whole.
The individual parts are more important than the whole.
Its parts interact to perform more functions.
rationales: Parts functioning independently do not produce emergent properties of the higher level.
Emergent properties arise from interactions among parts, not from the sum being greater than the whole.
Emergent properties depend on how parts work together, rather than on individual parts being more important than the whole.
Interactions among parts can produce functions and properties not present in the parts individually.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following demonstrates the levels of organization of the body, from simplest to most complex?
options: Cell → Organ → Tissue → Organelle → Organ system
Organelle → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system
Tissue → Cell → Organelle → Organ → Organ system
Organ system → Tissue → Cell → Organelle → Organ
rationales: This order incorrectly places organs before tissues and organelles after organs.
This correctly orders organization from organelle to cell to tissue to organ to organ system.
This order moves from tissue to cell to organelle, which is from more complex to simpler.
This order begins with the most complex level and does not proceed from simplest to most complex.

mcqs.stem: At which level of organization gas exchange occurs between body and environment?
options: Organ system level in the respiratory system
rationales: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration but do not exchange gases between the body and its environment.
Alveolar cells participate in gas exchange, but the exchange with the environment is described at the respiratory system level.
Epithelial tissues line exchange surfaces, but tissue is not the level that represents the whole process between body and environment.
The respiratory system exchanges gases between the body and the environment.

mcqs.stem: The epithelial tissue in the stomach wall is responsible for producing:
rationales: Stomach epithelial cells produce mucus, so this is true but incomplete.
Chief cells in the stomach epithelium produce pepsinogen, so this is true but incomplete.
Parietal cells in the stomach epithelium produce hydrochloric acid, so this is true but incomplete.
The stomach epithelium includes cells that produce mucus, pepsinogen, and hydrochloric acid.

mcqs.stem: In the wall of stomach, which tissue also contains blood vessels and nerves?
rationales: The epithelial layer lines the stomach but is not the connective layer containing the vessels and nerves described here.
Muscle tissue enables stomach contractions but is not the tissue layer that contains the blood vessels and nerves.
The inner connective tissue, including the submucosa, contains blood vessels and nerves.
The outer connective tissue mainly forms an external covering and is not the layer typically identified for these vessels and nerves.

mcqs.stem: In a leaf, which tissue is responsible for photosynthesis?
rationales: Xylem transports water and minerals rather than carrying out most leaf photosynthesis.
Mesophyll cells contain chloroplasts and are the principal photosynthetic tissue of a leaf.
The epidermis primarily protects the leaf and regulates exchange rather than performing most photosynthesis.
Phloem transports sugars from photosynthetic tissues to other parts of the plant.

mcqs.stem: What is the primary function of the xylem tissue in a leaf?
options: To transport sugars to other parts
To transport water to parts of leaf
To control the opening and closing of stomata
rationales: Transporting sugars is primarily the function of phloem, not xylem.
Xylem transports water and minerals into and through the leaf.
Chlorophyll is produced or contained in photosynthetic cells, not synthesized by xylem as its primary function.
Guard cells control stomatal opening and closing, not xylem.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a function of the human skeletal system?
options: Storing minerals and producing blood cells
Filtering blood to remove waste products
rationales: The skeleton stores minerals and produces blood cells in bone marrow.
Removing carbon dioxide from blood is primarily a function of the respiratory system.
Filtering blood to remove wastes is primarily a function of the kidneys.
Breaking down food is primarily a function of the digestive system.

mcqs.stem: Which structures are responsible for the transport of food in plant body?
rationales: Xylem transports water and minerals rather than food sugars.
Palisade mesophyll performs photosynthesis but does not transport food through the plant.
Phloem transports sugars and other organic nutrients throughout the plant.
Spongy mesophyll facilitates gas exchange and photosynthesis but does not transport food through the plant.

mcqs.stem: In a plant, which of the following is the primary function of the flower?
rationales: Transporting water and minerals is mainly a function of xylem tissue.
Supporting leaf growth is not the primary function of a flower.
Flowers facilitate plant reproduction, including pollination and the formation of seeds.

mcqs.stem: Which description defines a tissue?

mcqs.stem: Primarily, all enzymes are:
rationales: Most enzymes are not nucleic acids, although a few catalytic RNA molecules exist.
Most enzymes are proteins, making this the best answer.
Carbohydrates are not the primary composition of enzymes.
Lipids are not the primary composition of enzymes.

mcqs.stem: Which best defines an enzyme?
options: A chemical that breaks down food.
A protein that speeds up reactions.
rationales: Some enzymes break down food, but that does not define all enzymes.
Enzymes are not hormones, even though some hormones affect metabolism.
An enzyme is generally a protein that speeds up chemical reactions without being consumed.
Energy storage is not the defining function of an enzyme.

mcqs.stem: What can happen if an enzyme is exposed to temperature that is higher than its optimal temperature?
options: Enzyme’s shape will change, potentially reducing its activity.
Enzyme will speed up the reaction and remain stable.
Enzyme will become a substrate itself.
rationales: Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme may lose activity rather than continuing to speed up.
High temperatures can alter an enzyme’s shape, including its active site, and reduce its activity.
An enzyme does not necessarily remain stable at temperatures above its optimum.
An enzyme catalyzes reactions and is not converted into a substrate.

mcqs.stem: Enzymes are specific in their action because:
options: Their active sites fit specific substrates.
They work only at high temperatures.
rationales: An enzyme’s active site has a shape and chemical properties suited to particular substrates, giving it specificity.
Being a protein alone does not explain why an enzyme acts on specific substrates.
Enzymes are generally not consumed in the reactions they catalyze.
Enzymes do not work only at high temperatures; each has conditions under which it works best.

mcqs.stem: Prosthetic groups are:
rationales: Not all enzymes require prosthetic groups to function.
Prosthetic groups are non-protein components, not proteins.
A prosthetic group is tightly bound rather than loosely attached to its enzyme.
Prosthetic groups are tightly bound non-protein components of enzymes.

mcqs.stem: How does increasing temperature affect enzyme activity?
rationales: Increasing temperature generally increases enzyme activity up to an optimum, after which activity can decline.
Temperature does not always decrease activity; moderate increases can speed enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
An enzyme does not become non-functional with every increase in temperature.
Temperature affects enzyme activity by changing reaction rates and, at high levels, enzyme structure.

mcqs.stem: How does competitive inhibitor affect enzyme action?
options: Attaches and blocks the active site.
rationales: A competitive inhibitor, rather than the substrate, binds to the enzyme’s active site.
Changing the enzyme’s shape is characteristic of some noncompetitive or allosteric inhibition, not competitive inhibition.
A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and prevents substrate binding.
Competitive inhibitors do not characteristically block cofactors.

mcqs.stem: An enzyme works best at a pH of 7.4. It is placed in an acidic solution with a pH of 4.0. How will this affect the enzyme?
options: The active site will be modified, reducing substrate binding.
The enzyme will catalyse reactions faster due to increased H ions.
The enzyme will gain additional active sites.
The substrate will become inactive in an acidic environment.
rationales: A pH far below the enzyme’s optimum can alter the active site and reduce substrate binding.
An acidic solution does not necessarily make the enzyme work faster; pH 4.0 is far from its stated optimum.
Acidity does not cause an enzyme to gain additional active sites.
The question describes an effect on the enzyme, and substrates are not universally rendered inactive by acidic conditions.

mcqs.stem: What is TRUE according to the induced fit model of enzyme action?
options: Enzyme's active site changes shape to bind the substrate.
Substrate changes shape to bind to active site.
No shape changes occur in active site or substrate.
Substrate attaches the enzyme at a site other that active site.
rationales: In the induced fit model, substrate binding induces a shape change in the enzyme’s active site.
The model primarily describes a change in the enzyme’s shape, not the substrate changing shape to fit.
The induced fit model involves a shape change in the active site.
The substrate binds at the active site in the induced fit model, not at a different site.

mcqs.stem: What is TRUE about the optimum pH values of the following enzymes of digestive system?
options: Pepsin works at low pH while trypsin works at high pH
Pepsin works at high pH while trypsin works at low pH
rationales: Pepsin functions best in the acidic stomach, while trypsin functions best in the more alkaline small intestine.
Pepsin does not work best at high pH, so both enzymes do not work best at high pH.
Trypsin does not work best at low pH, so both enzymes do not work best at low pH.
This reverses their usual optima: pepsin works at low pH and trypsin at higher pH.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes metabolism?
options: The sum of all chemical reactions within an organism to sustain life
The breakdown of food only in the stomach
The release of energy from sunlight only
The movement of substances into and out of cells
rationales: This is the definition of metabolism.
Metabolism includes many reactions in the organism, not only digestion in the stomach.
Sunlight is involved in photosynthesis, but metabolism includes all chemical reactions that sustain life.
Movement across cell membranes is not the definition of metabolism.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches catabolism?
options: Complex molecules are built from simpler ones and energy is consumed.
Complex molecules are broken into simpler ones and energy is released.
Water is removed from an organism without a chemical reaction.
Energy is released without any molecules changing.
rationales: This describes anabolism, which builds complex molecules and consumes energy.
Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy.
This does not describe the chemical breakdown of complex molecules.
Catabolism involves chemical reactions in which molecules are broken down.

written.text:

written.text:
(a) Explain the types and importance of anaerobic respiration.
(b) Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
modelAnswer: (a) Anaerobic respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen and incompletely oxidizes glucose, releasing less energy.
In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvic acid is broken down into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide; it occurs in yeast and some bacteria.
In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid; it occurs in the skeletal muscles of humans and other animals.
Early organisms respired anaerobically; anaerobes still use it, and muscles use it when oxygen supply is insufficient.
Fermentation is used to make cheese and yogurt, in brewing and baking, and in making soy sauce.
(b) ATP is a nucleotide made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds.
When the outer phosphate bond breaks, Pi separates and energy is released; ATP becomes ADP.
The breaking of one phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.
Cells use energy from food to combine ADP with Pi to form ATP.
ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken down during energy-consuming processes, so it transfers energy between metabolic reactions.

written.text:
(a) Q8.4. Explain the types and importance of anaerobic respiration.
(b) Outline the processes involved in photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: (a) Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose without oxygen and releases only a small amount of energy.
In animal muscle cells, it produces lactic acid.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces alcohol and carbon dioxide.
It supplies some ATP when oxygen is insufficient, enabling cells to continue activities.
Yeast fermentation is also used in making bread and alcoholic drinks.
(b) Photosynthesis occurs in two phases: light reactions and dark reactions.
Light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
Light energy is used to make ATP and NADPH; light also breaks water and oxygen is released.
Dark reactions take place in the stroma of chloroplasts.
Carbon dioxide is reduced using ATP and hydrogen from NADPH to make 3-carbon carbohydrates.
The 3-carbon carbohydrates are used to make glucose.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following plant nutrients is required in large amount?
rationales: Iron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Zinc is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Potassium is a macronutrient required by plants in relatively large amounts.
Boron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.

mcqs.stem: Which element is required by plants for the formation of chlorophyll?
rationales: Phosphorus is important in energy transfer and nucleic acids but is not the central element in chlorophyll.
Calcium supports cell walls and signaling but is not required as the central element in chlorophyll.
Magnesium is the central element in chlorophyll and is required for its formation.
Sulphur is found in some amino acids but is not the central element in chlorophyll.

mcqs.stem: The primary function of root hairs is:
rationales: Root hairs do not primarily transport nutrients; their main role is absorbing water and minerals from soil.
Root hairs are not primarily used to store food.
Root hairs increase the root's surface area, improving absorption from the soil.
Root hairs do not primarily synthesize proteins.

mcqs.stem: Root hairs absorb salts from soil by;
rationales: Diffusion may move substances down a concentration gradient but is not the main mechanism for uptake of mineral salts by root hairs.
Osmosis describes water movement across a selectively permeable membrane, not the uptake of dissolved salts.
Root hairs commonly take up mineral ions against their concentration gradient by active transport.
Filtration is not the mechanism by which root hairs take up mineral salts.

mcqs.stem: Water moves from the soil into root cells by:
rationales: Water enters root cells by osmosis, moving across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential.
Active transport requires energy to move solutes and is not the process that brings water into root cells.
Diffusion is not the specific term for water movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
Bulk flow is movement of fluid driven by pressure differences and does not describe water entry into root cells at the membrane.

mcqs.stem: The transpiration is regulated by;
rationales: Mesophyll cells are involved in photosynthesis and do not directly regulate stomatal opening.
Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata, thereby regulating transpiration.
Xylem transports water and minerals but does not regulate stomatal aperture.
Phloem transports sugars and does not regulate stomatal aperture.

mcqs.stem: Under which condition, there will be high rate of transpiration?
rationales: High humidity reduces the water-vapor gradient between a leaf and the air, lowering transpiration.
Low light intensity generally promotes stomatal closure and reduces transpiration.
Wind removes the moist air around leaves, maintaining a steep water-vapor gradient and increasing transpiration.
Waterlogged soil can impair root function and does not generally create a high transpiration rate.

mcqs.stem: Which ion plays a role in the opening of stomata?
rationales: Sodium ions are not the principal ions associated with stomatal opening in most plants.
Potassium ions accumulate in guard cells, lowering their water potential and promoting stomatal opening.
Calcium ions can act in guard-cell signaling, but potassium is the ion primarily associated with opening stomata.
Magnesium is not the main ion responsible for stomatal opening.

mcqs.stem: In most plants the food is transported in the form of:
rationales: Glucose is generally converted into a transport form rather than transported as the main sugar in most plants.
Sucrose is the principal form in which food is transported through the phloem of most plants.
Starch is insoluble and is typically used for storage rather than long-distance transport.
Maltose is not the principal form in which food is transported in most plants.

mcqs.stem: What is TRUE according to the pressure flow mechanism of food transport?
options: Water enters the source, creating pressure
Water is pulled from the sink
Movement of food in phloem is due to gravity
Solutes move from low to high concentration
rationales: At the source, sugar loading lowers water potential, so water enters the phloem and creates pressure that drives flow toward the sink.
Water does not generally get pulled from the sink to drive the pressure-flow mechanism; pressure is generated at the source.
Phloem transport is driven by pressure differences, not by gravity.
Solute loading at the source occurs against a concentration gradient in many cases, rather than by movement from low to high concentration as stated without qualification.

mcqs.stem: Succulent organs are present in:
rationales: Xerophytes commonly have succulent organs that store water as an adaptation to dry conditions.
Hydrophytes are adapted to living in water and are not typically identified by succulent water-storing organs.
Mesophytes live in environments with moderate water availability and generally do not have succulent organs.
Some halophytes can be succulent, but succulent organs are most characteristically associated with xerophytes in this context.

written.text:
(a) Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
(b) Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: (a) During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport.
Their solute concentration increases, so water moves from epidermal cells into guard cells by osmosis.
The guard cells become turgid; their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens.
In the evening, glucose concentration falls and potassium ions move back to epidermal cells.
Water moves out of the guard cells, they lose turgor, their inner sides touch and the stoma closes.
(b) Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: (a) Plants remove extra water during the day by transpiration.
Some plants, such as grasses, remove excess water at night by guttation.
In guttation, water droplets pass through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Some plants store wastes, including salts, as harmless crystals.
Other plants keep wastes in their leaves and get rid of them when the leaves fall; some excrete wastes through special pores by applying force.
(b) At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Q9.4. Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: (a) Many hydrophytes have broad leaves that float on the surface of water.
These leaves have a large number of stomata on their upper surfaces.
Water moves out through these stomata.
Halophytes absorb salts from outside and make their bodies hypertonic.
Excess salt can be stored in cells or excreted through salt glands on leaves.
(b) Root hairs absorb water from the soil by osmosis.
Mineral ions enter root hairs mainly by active transport.
Water and dissolved salts pass through the root tissues and enter the xylem.
They move upwards through xylem, helped by root pressure and the transpiration pull created by water loss from leaves.
Final answer: Water enters by osmosis and salts mainly by active transport; both are carried upwards in xylem.

written.text:
(a) Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
(b) Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
modelAnswer: (a) The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The gametophytes produce gametes, and pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.
The pollen tube grows to the ovule and carries two sperms into the embryo sac.
One sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.
The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.
A seed that gets suitable conditions can grow into the next sporophyte generation.
(b) During binary fission, the bacterial DNA replicates.
The daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides.
The cell membrane pinches in.
A new cell wall is synthesized in the middle.
Two identical daughter bacteria are produced.

written.text:
(a) Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
(b) Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.
modelAnswer: (a) The adult flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte (2n), which produces flowers.
Meiosis forms haploid spores. Microspores develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.
After pollination, a pollen tube grows to the embryo sac and carries the male gametes.
One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. This is double fertilization.
The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed, which germinates to form a new sporophyte.
(b) The diploid generation that produces spores is called the sporophyte generation.
The haploid generation that produces gametes is called the gametophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces spores, which grow into the gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte produces gametes, which unite to form a zygote that develops into the next sporophyte.

mcqs.stem: What is the primary purpose of biostatistics?
options: To apply statistical methods to biological sciences
rationales: Incorrect: financial data analysis is not the primary focus of biostatistics.
Correct: biostatistics applies statistical methods to biological and health-related sciences.
Incorrect: engineering models are not the primary subject of biostatistics.
Incorrect: studying historical events is the focus of history, not biostatistics.

mcqs.stem: In biostatistics, which method is used to predict future outcomes based on current data?
rationales: Incorrect: designing experiments helps collect data but does not itself predict outcomes from current data.
Incorrect: drawing charts presents data visually but does not itself predict future outcomes.
Incorrect: taking an average summarizes data but does not generally predict future outcomes.
Correct: analysing data can reveal patterns and trends that are used to predict future outcomes.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following best describes the mean of a data set?
options: The middle value when data is ordered
The sum of all values divided by the number of values
The difference between the highest and lowest values
rationales: Incorrect: the most frequently occurring value is the mode.
Incorrect: the middle value after ordering the data is the median.
Correct: the mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
Incorrect: the difference between the highest and lowest values is the range.

mcqs.stem: If the data set is 5, 8, 12, 15, 20, what is the median?
rationales: Incorrect: 8 is the second value, not the middle value in the ordered data set.
Correct: 12 is the middle value of the five ordered values.
Incorrect: 15 is the fourth value, not the middle value.
Incorrect: 20 is the largest value, not the middle value.

mcqs.stem: What is the mean of the data set: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11?
rationales: Incorrect: 7 is the smallest value, not the mean.
Incorrect: the values sum to 45, which divided by 5 gives 9, not 8.
Correct: the sum is 45 and 45 divided by 5 is 9.
Incorrect: 10 is one of the data values, but the mean is 9.

mcqs.stem: When the number of values in a data set is even, how is the median calculated?
options: By taking the average of the two middle values
By selecting the most frequent value
By adding all values and dividing by the total number of values
rationales: Incorrect: with an even number of values there are two middle values, so one cannot simply choose a single middle value.
Correct: the median is the average of the two middle values after the data are ordered.
Incorrect: selecting the most frequent value gives the mode.
Incorrect: adding all values and dividing by their count gives the mean.

mcqs.stem: In a data set with values 3, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, what is the mode?
rationales: Incorrect: 3 occurs twice, which ties with 9 rather than making 3 the sole mode.
Incorrect: 6 occurs only once, so it is not a mode.
Incorrect: 7 occurs only once, so it is not a mode.
Correct: both 3 and 9 occur twice, more often than any other value.

mcqs.stem: If a data set has no repeated values, what is the mode?
options: The average of the data set
rationales: Incorrect: the highest value is the maximum, not the mode.
Incorrect: the average of the data set is the mean, not the mode.
Correct: if no values repeat, no value occurs more often than the others, so there is no mode.
Incorrect: the median is the middle value, not the mode.

mcqs.stem: In a bar chart, what does the height or length of each bar represent?
options: The value of the corresponding category
The difference between the highest and lowest values
rationales: Incorrect: the number of categories is represented by the set of bars, not by each bar’s height or length.
Correct: each bar’s height or length represents the value for its corresponding category.
Incorrect: the average of all values is not what each individual bar represents.
Incorrect: the difference between the highest and lowest values is the range, not the meaning of a bar’s height or length.

mcqs.stem: When constructing a bar chart, which axis usually represents the categories?
options: Both axes equally represent the categories
rationales: Incorrect: the vertical axis usually represents values or frequencies, not categories.
Correct: categories are usually listed along the horizontal x-axis in a bar chart.
Incorrect: the axes generally have different roles rather than equally representing categories.
Incorrect: one axis—usually the horizontal axis—represents the categories.

mcqs.stem: A researcher uses statistical methods to study data about living organisms. Which field is the researcher using?
options: It applies statistical methods to biological sciences.
It studies only the structure of cells.
rationales: Correct: applying statistical methods to biological sciences is biostatistics.
Incorrect: biostatistics supports the analysis of evidence; it does not replace experiments with opinions.
Incorrect: biostatistics is not limited to studying cell structure.
Incorrect: financial transactions are not the focus of biostatistics.

mcqs.stem: How does biostatistics help when a biological experiment is being planned?
options: To make sure collected data are relevant and sufficient for the research question.
To guarantee that every study gives the expected result.
To choose the final policy before studying the evidence.
rationales: Correct: it helps structure a study so its data can answer the research question.
Incorrect: careful planning cannot guarantee a particular result.
Incorrect: studies need data to answer research questions.
Incorrect: decisions should be informed by evidence, not chosen before the evidence is studied.

mcqs.stem: Which branch of Biology focuses on the study of the structure and function of cells?
rationales: Cytology studies the structure and function of cells.
Microbiology studies microorganisms rather than cells as a general biological unit.
Histology studies tissues, which are groups of cells.
Ecology studies relationships between organisms and their environment.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following taxonomic ranks represents the broadest rank?
rationales: Species is the narrowest taxonomic rank listed, not the broadest.
Genus is broader than species but narrower than kingdom and domain.
Kingdom is broad, but domain is a broader rank.
Domain is the broadest taxonomic rank listed.

mcqs.stem: The process of cellular respiration occurs in:
rationales: The nucleus does not serve as the main site of cellular respiration.
Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic cellular respiration.
Ribosomes synthesize proteins rather than carry out cellular respiration.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages molecules rather than carry out cellular respiration.

mcqs.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?
rationales: M phase is primarily for chromosome separation and cell division, not maximum growth.
S phase is when DNA is replicated, rather than when maximum cell growth occurs.
G1 phase is the main growth phase in which the cell increases in size and carries out normal functions.
G2 phase involves further growth and preparation for mitosis, but maximum growth generally occurs in G1.

mcqs.stem: A higher level of organization exhibits emergent properties when:
options: The sum of its parts is greater than the whole.
The individual parts are more important than the whole.
Its parts interact to perform more functions.
rationales: Parts functioning independently do not produce emergent properties of the higher level.
Emergent properties arise from interactions among parts, not from the sum being greater than the whole.
Emergent properties depend on how parts work together, rather than on individual parts being more important than the whole.
Interactions among parts can produce functions and properties not present in the parts individually.

mcqs.stem: What is the primary function of carbohydrates?
rationales: Carbohydrates are a major source of energy for the body.
Carbohydrates are not generally enzymes; enzymes are mostly proteins.
Regulating body processes is not the primary function of carbohydrates.
Some carbohydrates are components of membranes, but this is not their primary function.

mcqs.stem: Primarily, all enzymes are:
rationales: Most enzymes are not nucleic acids, although a few catalytic RNA molecules exist.
Most enzymes are proteins, making this the best answer.
Carbohydrates are not the primary composition of enzymes.
Lipids are not the primary composition of enzymes.

mcqs.stem: When we get energy from ATP, which bonds are broken?
rationales: ATP hydrolysis releases energy by breaking the terminal phosphate–phosphate bond.
C–H bonds are not the bonds whose hydrolysis releases ATP’s usable energy.
C–N bonds are not broken during ATP hydrolysis.
C–O bonds are not the bonds broken to release energy from ATP.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following plant nutrients is required in large amount?
rationales: Iron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Zinc is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.
Potassium is a macronutrient required by plants in relatively large amounts.
Boron is a micronutrient needed in small amounts, not a large amount.

mcqs.stem: Which element is required by plants for the formation of chlorophyll?
rationales: Phosphorus is important in energy transfer and nucleic acids but is not the central element in chlorophyll.
Calcium supports cell walls and signaling but is not required as the central element in chlorophyll.
Magnesium is the central element in chlorophyll and is required for its formation.
Sulphur is found in some amino acids but is not the central element in chlorophyll.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following organisms commonly reproduce by binary fission?
rationales: Yeast commonly reproduces by budding rather than binary fission.
Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission.
Rhizopus commonly reproduces by spores rather than binary fission.
Plants generally reproduce sexually or by vegetative propagation, not by binary fission.

mcqs.stem: What is the primary method of reproduction in yeast?
rationales: Binary fission is not the primary method of reproduction in yeast.
Spore formation occurs in some fungi but is not yeast’s primary method of reproduction.
Yeast primarily reproduces asexually by budding.
Fragmentation is not the primary method of reproduction in yeast.

written.text:
(a) Discuss the functions of proteins.
(b) How does pH affect enzyme activity?
modelAnswer: (a) Proteins are an important part of all cell membranes.
Some proteins, such as collagen and keratin, make almost whole structures of cartilage, hair and nails.
Enzymes are proteins that catalyse all biochemical reactions occurring in organisms.
Some proteins are hormones that regulate body processes.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Actin and myosin are the main components of muscle cells and are responsible for muscular contractions.
Fibrin makes blood clot to prevent the loss of blood after an injury.
Antibodies defend the body against harmful pathogens.

mcqs.stem: The study of the processes of heredity and variation in living organisms is known as:

mcqs.stem: Which characteristics is unique to organisms in the domain Archaea?

mcqs.stem: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is primarily involved in the synthesis of:

mcqs.stem: In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?
rationales: Mitosis separates duplicated chromosomes but does not duplicate them.

S phase is when DNA is replicated, duplicating the chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following demonstrates the levels of organization of the body, from simplest to most complex?
options: Cell → Organ → Tissue → Organelle → Organ system
Organelle → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system
Tissue → Cell → Organelle → Organ → Organ system
Organ system → Tissue → Cell → Organelle → Organ
rationales: This order incorrectly places organs before tissues and organelles after organs.
This correctly orders organization from organelle to cell to tissue to organ to organ system.
This order moves from tissue to cell to organelle, which is from more complex to simpler.
This order begins with the most complex level and does not proceed from simplest to most complex.

mcqs.stem: How will you differentiate between monosaccharides and polysaccharides?
options: Monosaccharides are present in plant cell wall.
rationales: A monosaccharide consists of a single sugar unit, unlike a polysaccharide made of many sugar units.

mcqs.stem: Which best defines an enzyme?
options: A chemical that breaks down food.
A protein that speeds up reactions.

mcqs.stem: Light reactions of photosynthesis occur in;

mcqs.stem: The primary function of root hairs is:

mcqs.stem: Root hairs absorb salts from soil by;

Root hairs commonly take up mineral ions against their concentration gradient by active transport.
Filtration is not the mechanism by which root hairs take up mineral salts.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following statements is true about spore formation in fungi?
options: They produce spores during sexual reproduction

Spores can only grow into new fungi in dry environments
Spores are produced to withstand harsh conditions

Binary fission is a usual means of bacterial reproduction, not a special response to harsh conditions.

rubric.how: State that they are single sugar units and give an example.

rubric.description: (a) Describe disaccharides.
rubric.why: Disaccharides are made from two joined monosaccharides.
rubric.how: State that two monosaccharides are joined; examples include sucrose and maltose.

rubric.description: (a) Describe polysaccharides.
rubric.why: Polysaccharides consist of many sugar units.
rubric.how: State that many monosaccharides form a polysaccharide; examples include starch and cellulose.

rubric.description: (a) Explain the energy role.
rubric.why: Carbohydrates are an important energy source.
rubric.how: Mention energy release in respiration.

rubric.description: (a) Give storage and/or structural roles.
rubric.why: Storage and structural roles complete the account of carbohydrate roles.
rubric.how: Mention starch or glycogen storage and cellulose's structural role.

rubric.description: (b) Identifies enzyme composition and role.
rubric.why: The answer should state the nature of enzymes.
rubric.how: Describe enzymes as mainly proteins and biological catalysts.

rubric.description: (b) Explains their effect on reactions.
rubric.why: Catalysing reactions is their central function.
rubric.how: State that enzymes speed up chemical or metabolic reactions.

rubric.description: (b) States that enzymes are reusable.
rubric.why: Enzymes remain available after catalysing a reaction.
rubric.how: Explain that enzymes are not used up in the reaction.

rubric.description: (b) Gives another characteristic.
rubric.why: Specificity and conditions of activity are important characteristics.
rubric.how: Include enzyme specificity or the need for optimum conditions.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.
modelAnswer: (a) Plants remove extra water during the day by transpiration.
Some plants, such as grasses, remove excess water at night by guttation.
In guttation, water droplets pass through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Some plants store wastes, including salts, as harmless crystals.
Other plants keep wastes in their leaves and get rid of them when the leaves fall; some excrete wastes through special pores by applying force.
(b) The diploid generation that produces spores is called the sporophyte generation.
The haploid generation that produces gametes is called the gametophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces spores, which grow into the gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte produces gametes, which unite to form a zygote that develops into the next sporophyte.
written.followUp: Differentiate between: ii. Transpiration and guttation

rubric.description: (a) Explain that plants remove extra water by transpiration during the day.
rubric.why: The answer should give the main daytime method for removing extra water.
rubric.how: Name transpiration and associate it with daytime water removal.

rubric.description: (a) Explain that some plants remove water at night by guttation as droplets from leaf tips or edges.
rubric.why: Guttation is the other specific method for extra-water removal described in the section.
rubric.how: Name guttation and mention night-time droplets.

rubric.description: (a) State that plants may store wastes as harmless crystals.
rubric.why: The section gives harmless crystals as one way of dealing with other metabolic wastes, including salts.
rubric.how: Mention storage as harmless crystals.

rubric.description: (a) State that wastes stored in leaves are removed when the leaves fall.
rubric.why: Wastes stored in leaves leave the plant when those leaves fall.
rubric.how: Link waste storage in leaves to leaf fall.

rubric.description: (a) State that some plants excrete wastes through special pores by applying force.
rubric.why: Mentioning excretion through special pores completes the methods for waste removal.
rubric.how: Mention special pores and, where possible, force.

rubric.description: (b) Defines the sporophyte generation.
rubric.why: The ploidy and product define the sporophyte.
rubric.how: State that the diploid sporophyte produces spores.

rubric.description: (b) Defines the gametophyte generation.
rubric.why: The ploidy and product define the gametophyte.
rubric.how: State that the haploid gametophyte produces gametes.

rubric.description: (b) Explains how spores form the gametophyte.
rubric.why: This explains how one generation gives rise to the next.
rubric.how: Say spores grow into the gametophyte generation.

rubric.description: (b) Explains how gametes lead to a new sporophyte.
rubric.why: This completes the cycle by explaining how gametes lead to a new sporophyte.
rubric.how: Say gametes unite to form a zygote, which develops into the sporophyte.

mcqs.stem: Insulin made through bacteria is an example of the technique of:
rationales: Parasitology studies parasites and their relationships with hosts.
Biotechnology uses organisms or biological systems to produce useful products such as insulin.
Biochemistry studies chemical processes in living organisms, not specifically the production technique described.
Histology studies tissues and their microscopic structure.

mcqs.stem: Which of these statements is NOT related to bacteria?
rationales: Bacteria do not have a nucleus.
Many bacteria have cell walls containing peptidoglycan.
Many bacteria are heterotrophic, although some are autotrophic.
Bacteria do not have chloroplasts; some can photosynthesize using structures that are not chloroplasts.

mcqs.stem: Ribosomes are composed of:
rationales: Ribosomes are made of ribosomal RNA and proteins.
DNA is not a structural component of ribosomes.
Carbohydrates and lipids are not the primary components of ribosomes.
Ribosomes contain RNA, but carbohydrates are not their other main component.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of mitosis?
options: It results in genetically identical daughter cells.
The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells.
It results in the formation of two daughter cells.
rationales: Mitosis commonly occurs in somatic cells.
Mitosis normally produces daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell and each other.
Mitosis preserves the chromosome number rather than halving it, so this is not a characteristic of mitosis.
Mitosis followed by cytokinesis results in two daughter cells.

mcqs.stem: At which level of organization gas exchange occurs between body and environment?
options: Organ system level in the respiratory system
rationales: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration but do not exchange gases between the body and its environment.
Alveolar cells participate in gas exchange, but the exchange with the environment is described at the respiratory system level.
Epithelial tissues line exchange surfaces, but tissue is not the level that represents the whole process between body and environment.
The respiratory system exchanges gases between the body and the environment.

mcqs.stem: What is true about cellulose?
options: It is digestible by human digestive system.
It provides structural support in plants.
rationales: Cellulose is not sweet in taste.
Humans cannot digest cellulose because they lack the enzyme needed to break it down.
Cellulose provides structural support in plant cell walls.
Cellulose is generally insoluble in water.

mcqs.stem: What can happen if an enzyme is exposed to temperature that is higher than its optimal temperature?
options: Enzyme’s shape will change, potentially reducing its activity.
Enzyme will speed up the reaction and remain stable.
Enzyme will become a substrate itself.
rationales: Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme may lose activity rather than continuing to speed up.
High temperatures can alter an enzyme’s shape, including its active site, and reduce its activity.
An enzyme does not necessarily remain stable at temperatures above its optimum.
An enzyme catalyzes reactions and is not converted into a substrate.

mcqs.stem: Which type of chlorophyll is most common in plants?
rationales: Chlorophyll a is the primary and most abundant photosynthetic pigment in plants.
Chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment and is less common than chlorophyll a.
Chlorophyll c is found in some algae, not as the most common chlorophyll in plants.
Chlorophyll d occurs in certain organisms but is not the most common plant chlorophyll.

mcqs.stem: Water moves from the soil into root cells by:
rationales: Water enters root cells by osmosis, moving across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential.
Active transport requires energy to move solutes and is not the process that brings water into root cells.
Diffusion is not the specific term for water movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
Bulk flow is movement of fluid driven by pressure differences and does not describe water entry into root cells at the membrane.

mcqs.stem: The transpiration is regulated by;
rationales: Mesophyll cells are involved in photosynthesis and do not directly regulate stomatal opening.
Guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata, thereby regulating transpiration.
Xylem transports water and minerals but does not regulate stomatal aperture.
Phloem transports sugars and does not regulate stomatal aperture.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is an example of vegetative propagation through runners?
rationales: Potato propagates through tubers rather than runners.
Strawberry plants can propagate through aboveground runners.
Onion propagates through bulbs rather than runners.
Ginger propagates through underground rhizomes rather than runners.

mcqs.stem: Which plant propagates through tubers?
rationales: Onion propagates through bulbs.
Potato propagates through tubers.
Ginger propagates through rhizomes.
Garlic propagates through bulbs or cloves, not tubers.

written.text: Differentiate between Morphology and Physiology
modelAnswer: Morphology studies the form and external features of organisms.
Physiology studies the functions of organisms and their parts.
written.followUp: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the development of organisms from fertilization to birth or hatching?

rubric.description: State the meaning of Morphology.
rubric.why: A valid difference must state what Morphology examines.
rubric.how: Connect Morphology with form or external features.

rubric.description: State the meaning of Physiology.
rubric.why: The contrasting focus of Physiology completes the comparison.
rubric.how: Connect Physiology with functions of organisms or their parts.

written.text: What is the role of observation and experimentation in the scientific method?
modelAnswer: Observation helps a scientist notice a problem and collect information for forming a hypothesis.
Experimentation tests deductions made from the hypothesis and provides evidence to support, reject, or modify it.
written.followUp: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the development of organisms from fertilization to birth or hatching?

rubric.description: Explain the role of observation.
rubric.why: Observation provides the starting information for scientific investigation.
rubric.how: Say that observation helps identify a problem or collect information.

rubric.description: Explain the role of experimentation.
rubric.why: Experiments test the proposed explanation and provide evidence.
rubric.how: Say that experiments test deductions or a hypothesis.

written.text: Define Genetics, Anatomy, Palaeontology, Marine Biology and Pathology.
modelAnswer: Genetics is the branch of Biology that deals with the study of transfer of characteristics from parents to offspring. Anatomy is the branch of Biology that explores the internal physical structure of organisms, particularly humans. Palaeontology is the branch of Biology that deals with the study of fossils. Marine Biology is the branch of Biology that deals with the study of life in oceans. Pathology is the study of diseases, their causes, and effects.
written.followUp: Define Genetics, Anatomy, Palaeontology, Marine Biology and Pathology.

rubric.why: Rewards the definitions of Genetics and Anatomy, including their distinguishing ideas.
rubric.description: Genetics concerns the transfer of characteristics from parents to offspring; Anatomy concerns internal physical structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when both branch names and the key idea of each definition are present.

rubric.why: Rewards the definitions of Palaeontology, Marine Biology and Pathology.
rubric.description: Palaeontology studies fossils; Marine Biology studies life in oceans; Pathology studies diseases, their causes and effects.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when all three branch names and their defining subjects are present.

written.text: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the development of organisms from fertilization to birth or hatching?
modelAnswer: Embryology is the study of the process of development of organism from fertilized egg.
written.followUp: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the development of organisms from fertilization to birth or hatching?

rubric.why: Identifies the branch of Biology named in the answer.
rubric.description: The branch is Embryology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Embryology.

rubric.why: Checks that the response states what Embryology studies.
rubric.description: It studies the development of an organism from a fertilized egg.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the development-from-a-fertilized-egg idea.

written.text: List the three domains that encompass all living organisms.
modelAnswer: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
written.followUp: What are the shortcomings of the three-kingdom classification system?

rubric.description: Names Archaea and Bacteria.
rubric.why: These are two of the three domains.
rubric.how: List both prokaryotic domains.

rubric.description: Names Eukarya.
rubric.why: Eukarya completes the three-domain list.
rubric.how: Add Eukarya as the third domain.

written.text: What are the basic differences between archaea and bacteria?
modelAnswer: Archaea and bacteria are both prokaryotes.
Archaea have cell walls that do not contain peptidoglycan but are made of various polypeptides and proteins.
Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
Archaeal rRNA resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria, and their cell membranes contain unique lipids.
Some archaea live in extreme environments, whereas bacteria are found in all environments; many bacteria are beneficial decomposers.
written.followUp: What are the basic differences between archaea and bacteria?

rubric.description: State the different cell-wall composition.
rubric.why: The cell-wall difference is the clearest basic distinction between the two domains.
rubric.how: Write that archaeal cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan, while bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.

rubric.description: Give another difference between Archaea and Bacteria.
rubric.why: A second accurate distinction shows knowledge beyond cell-wall composition.
rubric.how: Add the rRNA difference, archaeal unique lipids/extreme environments, or a correct bacterial characteristic.

rubric.description: Present the comparison accurately.
rubric.why: The final answer must clearly compare the two groups without reversing their features.
rubric.how: Check that each characteristic is assigned to the correct domain.

written.text: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?
modelAnswer: Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
They increase the surface area for respiration.
written.followUp: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?

rubric.description: Identify the cristae as folds of the inner membrane.
rubric.why: Cristae are folds of the mitochondrial inner membrane.
rubric.how: Refer to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

rubric.description: Explain that they increase surface area for respiration.
rubric.why: The increased surface area explains their importance for respiration.
rubric.how: Link increased surface area to respiration.

written.text: How are chromatin and chromosomes related?
modelAnswer: Chromatin is made of DNA and proteins.
When a cell starts dividing, chromatin condenses and takes the shape of thick chromosomes.
written.followUp: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?

rubric.description: State that chromatin consists of DNA and proteins.
rubric.why: This identifies what chromatin is made of.
rubric.how: Name both DNA and proteins.

rubric.description: Explain that chromatin condenses into chromosomes when the cell starts dividing.
rubric.why: The change from chromatin to chromosomes directly answers the relationship.
rubric.how: Include condensation and chromosome formation.

written.text: What are the key events of anaphase in mitosis?
modelAnswer: The spindle fibres attached with chromosomes pull toward the poles.
The chromosome's sister chromatids separate.
Two similar sets of chromatids move towards the poles of the cell.
written.followUp: During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?

rubric.description: Describe the spindle-fibre action.
rubric.why: The spindle fibres' pulling action causes the chromosome sets to move.
rubric.how: State that spindle fibres pull towards the poles.

rubric.description: Describe chromatid separation.
rubric.why: Separation of sister chromatids is the defining event of anaphase.
rubric.how: State that sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles.

written.text: How is mitosis related to the process of regeneration?
modelAnswer: Some animals can regenerate parts of the body.
For this purpose, they form new cells by carrying out mitosis in the cells of the remaining parts.
written.followUp: During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?

rubric.description: State what mitosis produces.
rubric.why: Regeneration needs new cells to replace or rebuild the missing body part.
rubric.how: Explain that mitosis forms new cells.

rubric.description: Connect mitosis to regeneration.
rubric.why: This links mitosis to the rebuilding of a body part.
rubric.how: State that animals use mitosis in remaining cells to regenerate body parts.

written.text: Differentiate between the following: iii. Epidermal and mesophyll tissue
modelAnswer: Epidermal tissue forms the outermost layer of the leaf; the cuticle reduces water loss and stomata control gas exchange and water-vapour loss.
Mesophyll tissue lies between the upper and lower epidermis, contains chloroplast-rich cells, and is the site of photosynthesis.
written.followUp: What is the function of the palisade mesophyll in the leaf?

rubric.description: Describes epidermal tissue.
rubric.why: The location and a function distinguish epidermal tissue.
rubric.how: State that it is the outer layer and mention protection, the cuticle, or stomata.

rubric.description: Describes mesophyll tissue.
rubric.why: The mesophyll's position and function complete the comparison.
rubric.how: State that it lies between the epidermises and is the site of photosynthesis.

written.text: Differentiate between the following: iv. Palisade and spongy mesophyll
modelAnswer: Palisade mesophyll is located just beneath the upper epidermis and consists of tightly packed elongated cells.
Spongy mesophyll is below the palisade mesophyll and consists of loosely arranged cells with air spaces that facilitate diffusion of gases.
written.followUp: What is the function of the palisade mesophyll in the leaf?

rubric.description: Describes palisade mesophyll.
rubric.why: The palisade tissue is identified by its position and tightly packed cells.
rubric.how: Mention its position beneath the upper epidermis or its tightly packed elongated cells.

rubric.description: Describes spongy mesophyll.
rubric.why: The spongy tissue's air spaces are a key difference.
rubric.how: Mention its loose arrangement, air spaces, or role in gas diffusion.

written.text: What are the basic components of lipids? Draw their structures.
modelAnswer: Lipids are composed of glycerol and fatty acids.
Glycerol: CH₂OH–CHOH–CH₂OH.
Fatty acid: R–COOH, where R is a long hydrocarbon chain.
written.followUp: What are the basic components of lipids? Draw their structures.

rubric.description: Names glycerol and fatty acids as the basic components.
rubric.why: Naming both components shows knowledge of what lipids are composed of.
rubric.how: Write that lipids are composed of glycerol and fatty acids.

rubric.description: Gives structures for glycerol and a fatty acid.
rubric.why: The structures show the three-carbon glycerol and the fatty acid carboxyl group.
rubric.how: Draw or write glycerol as CH₂OH–CHOH–CH₂OH and a fatty acid as R–COOH.

written.text: Briefly describe the function of DNA.
modelAnswer: DNA contains the hereditary information in the form of a sequence of nucleotides.
This sequence determines the order of amino acids during protein synthesis.
During reproduction, DNA is passed from one generation to the next and carries hereditary information to the next generation.
written.followUp: What are the types of RNA? Write their functions.

rubric.description: State that DNA contains hereditary information in a nucleotide sequence.
rubric.why: This states what DNA contains and how its information is arranged.
rubric.how: Mention hereditary information and its sequence of nucleotides.

rubric.description: Explain the role of DNA information in protein synthesis or inheritance.
rubric.why: This explains how DNA information is used or passed on.
rubric.how: State that the sequence determines amino-acid order during protein synthesis, or that DNA passes hereditary information to the next generation.

written.text: Differentiate between: (a) Asexual and sexual reproduction
modelAnswer: Asexual reproduction does not involve the fusion of gametes.
Its offspring are genetically identical to the parents.
Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes.
Its offspring have variations among themselves and with the parents.
written.followUp: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.

rubric.description: Describe asexual reproduction.
rubric.why: The answer must distinguish asexual reproduction by whether gametes fuse.
rubric.how: State that it does not involve fusion of gametes and identify identical offspring.

rubric.description: Describe sexual reproduction.
rubric.why: The answer must distinguish sexual reproduction and its offspring.
rubric.how: Mention fusion of male and female gametes and variation in offspring.

written.text: Differentiate between: (b) Binary fission in bacteria and amoeba
modelAnswer: In bacteria, the DNA replicates and the daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides.
The cell membrane pinches in and a new cell wall is synthesized in the middle.
Two identical daughter bacteria are produced.
In Amoeba, the nucleus divides into two, followed by division of the cytoplasm.
Two daughter amoebae are formed.
written.followUp: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.

rubric.description: Describe DNA replication, membrane pinching, and cell-wall formation in bacteria.
rubric.why: The answer must give the bacterial sequence.
rubric.how: Include the bacterial cell structures and two daughter cells.

rubric.description: Describe nuclear division followed by cytoplasm division in Amoeba.
rubric.why: The answer must give the protist sequence.
rubric.how: State the order and the two daughter amoebae.

written.text: What is the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity?
modelAnswer: An increase in substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction.
At high substrate concentration, all active sites of the enzymes are occupied.
Any more substrate molecules do not find free active sites, so the reaction rate does not increase.
written.followUp: Provide two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH.

rubric.description: State that increasing substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction.
rubric.why: This states the initial effect of adding more substrate.
rubric.how: Explain that more substrate molecules can bind to enzyme active sites.

rubric.description: State that the rate levels off once all active sites are occupied.
rubric.why: This identifies why the rate eventually stops increasing.
rubric.how: Mention that additional substrate cannot find a free active site, so the rate does not increase.

written.text: Provide two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH.
modelAnswer: Pepsin in the stomach works in an acidic medium (pH 1.5 to 2.0).
Trypsin in the small intestine works in an alkaline medium (pH 7 to 8).
written.followUp: Provide two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH.

rubric.description: Give pepsin and its acidic optimum pH.
rubric.why: Pepsin is one example and its acidic optimum distinguishes it from trypsin.
rubric.how: State that pepsin works in an acidic medium, pH 1.5 to 2.0.

rubric.description: Give trypsin and its alkaline optimum pH.
rubric.why: Trypsin is the second example and works in an alkaline medium.
rubric.how: State that trypsin works in an alkaline medium, pH 7 to 8.

written.text: What are the end products of anaerobic respiration in animals and yeast?
modelAnswer: In animals, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid.
In yeast, pyruvic acid is converted into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.
written.followUp: Define anaerobic and aerobic respiration.

rubric.description: Give the animal-cell product.
rubric.why: Skeletal muscles of animals form lactic acid during anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Write lactic acid for animals.

rubric.description: Give the yeast products.
rubric.why: Yeast fermentation forms alcohol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Write ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide for yeast.

written.text: How do muscles respond to oxygen deficiency during intense exercise?
modelAnswer: When oxygen supply is insufficient, skeletal muscles carry out anaerobic respiration to get energy.
Pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid.
written.followUp: Define anaerobic and aerobic respiration.

rubric.description: Identify the process muscles use when oxygen is insufficient.
rubric.why: The muscles respond to insufficient oxygen by respiring anaerobically.
rubric.how: State that skeletal muscles carry out anaerobic respiration.

rubric.description: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in muscles.
rubric.why: Lactic acid is the product formed in muscle anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: State that pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid.

written.text: Write the importance of oxidation-reduction reactions.
modelAnswer: Oxidation-reduction reactions involve the transfer of electrons from one substance to another.
The energy released can be used by cells to make ATP.
written.followUp: What do ATP and ADP mean? What are the roles of these molecules for the cellular metabolism?

rubric.description: State that oxidation-reduction reactions involve electron transfer.
rubric.why: This identifies the electron transfer involved in oxidation-reduction reactions.
rubric.how: Mention the transfer of electrons between substances.

rubric.description: Explain their importance in releasing energy for ATP formation.
rubric.why: This connects these reactions to usable cellular energy.
rubric.how: State that released energy is used to make ATP or do cellular work.

written.text: How is the transpirational pull important in plants?
modelAnswer: Transpiration from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
It pulls water upwards through the xylem from the roots towards the leaves.
written.followUp: How is the transpirational pull important in plants?

rubric.description: Identify the source of the pull.
rubric.why: The answer must identify the pull created by transpiration.
rubric.how: State that transpiration from leaves creates a pulling force.

rubric.description: State the role of the pull.
rubric.why: The answer must explain what the pull does in the plant.
rubric.how: Explain that it draws water upwards through xylem from roots towards leaves.

written.text: Differentiate between: i. Xylem and phloem
modelAnswer: Xylem is a one-way passage for water and salts from roots to leaves.
Phloem is a two-way passage for food.
written.followUp: Differentiate between: i. Xylem and phloem

rubric.description: State what xylem transports and its direction.
rubric.why: This identifies the direction and materials transported by xylem.
rubric.how: Write that xylem carries water and salts one way, from roots to leaves.

rubric.description: State what phloem transports and its direction.
rubric.why: This identifies the direction and material transported by phloem.
rubric.how: Write that phloem carries food in two directions.

written.text: How do the plants of rubber and keekar excrete their wastes?
modelAnswer: Rubber plants excrete latex through special pores by applying force.
Keekar (Acacia) trees excrete gums through special pores by applying force.
written.followUp: Differentiate between: ii. Transpiration and guttation

rubric.description: Identify latex as the waste excreted by rubber plants.
rubric.why: Naming the waste excreted by rubber plants is one required part of the comparison.
rubric.how: Write that rubber plants excrete latex.

rubric.description: Identify gum as the waste excreted by keekar (Acacia) trees.

rubric.how: Write that keekar or Acacia trees excrete gum.

written.text:
(a) Explain the rules and guidelines for suggesting scientific names to organisms.
(b) Write a note on cell specialization.
modelAnswer: (a) Scientific names are taken from Latin.
Every scientific name has two parts: the genus name comes first, followed by the species name.
Every scientific name should be unique; the same name cannot be used for two different organisms.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, and the species name begins with a small letter.
When printed, the scientific name is typed in italics.
When handwritten, its two parts are underlined separately.
(b) Cells formed by cell division are initially similar.
After their formation, cells undergo specialization or differentiation.
During this process, they get special sizes, structures, and metabolic features and become specialized.
For example, mesophyll cells perform photosynthesis, neurons transmit nerve impulses, and red blood cells carry oxygen.
written.followUp: How does binomial nomenclature facilitate clear communication about organisms across different languages?

rubric.description: (a) State that scientific names use Latin words and have two parts.
rubric.why: These are the basic format and language requirements for a scientific name.
rubric.how: Mention Latin and the two-part structure.

rubric.description: (a) Give the correct order of the two parts.
rubric.why: The required order distinguishes the genus and species parts.
rubric.how: Write genus first, followed by species.

rubric.description: (a) State that each scientific name must be unique.

rubric.how: Explain that the same name cannot be used for two organisms.

rubric.description: (a) Give the capitalisation rule.
rubric.why: Correct capitalisation is an explicit naming rule.
rubric.how: Use a capital for genus and a small letter for species.

rubric.description: (a) State how printed and handwritten names are shown.
rubric.why: The written or printed form must follow the presentation rules.
rubric.how: Use italics in print and underline the two parts separately when handwriting.

rubric.description: (b) Explain the process.
rubric.why: The answer should explain when specialization occurs and identify the process.
rubric.how: State that cells formed by cell division later undergo specialization or differentiation.

rubric.description: (b) Describe the changes in cells.
rubric.why: These features explain how specialized cells become suited to their functions.
rubric.how: Mention special sizes, structures, and metabolic features.

rubric.description: (b) Give examples of specialized cells.
rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates specialization.
rubric.how: Include examples such as mesophyll cells for photosynthesis or neurons for transmitting impulses.

rubric.description: (b) Complete the answer with another example.
rubric.why: A further correct example earns the final mark.
rubric.how: State a further specialized cell and its function, such as red blood cells carrying oxygen.

written.text:
(a) Q6.2. Discuss the functions of proteins.
(b) Q7.2. Describe how temperature extremes can inhibit enzyme activity and lead to enzyme denaturation.
modelAnswer: (a) Proteins are needed for growth and repair and form structural materials such as collagen and keratin.
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, including digestion.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Antibodies help defend the body against pathogens.
Proteins also take part in movement, blood clotting and regulation; for example, myosin works in muscle and insulin is a protein hormone.
(b) At low temperatures, enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly.
Fewer successful collisions occur, so enzyme activity decreases.
Above the optimum temperature, excessive heat changes the shape of the enzyme, including its active site.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
modelAnswer: (a) Many hydrophytes have broad leaves that float on the surface of water.
These leaves have a large number of stomata on their upper surfaces.
Water moves out through these stomata.
Halophytes absorb salts from outside and make their bodies hypertonic.
Excess salt can be stored in cells or excreted through salt glands on leaves.
(b) The ovule acts as a megasporangium and contains a diploid megaspore mother cell.
The megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores.
Only one megaspore remains alive.
Inside the megaspore, mitosis forms eight haploid nuclei.
Two nuclei migrate to the centre and fuse to form a fusion nucleus.
One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the egg cell.
The resulting embryo sac has seven cells: one egg cell, one fusion nucleus, and five non-functional cells.

written.text: Describe the work of different scientists in discovering the cause of malaria.
modelAnswer: In 1878, Laveran examined the blood of a malarial patient and noticed microorganisms, which were named Plasmodium.
Biologists suggested the hypothesis: “Plasmodium is the cause of malaria”.
A. F. A. King suggested the hypothesis: “Mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium and so are involved in the spread of malaria.”
Ronald Ross allowed female Culex mosquitoes to bite a sparrow suffering from malaria.
He found that Plasmodium multiplied in the walls of the mosquito’s stomach and then moved into its salivary glands.
He allowed infected mosquitoes to bite healthy sparrows, which got malaria.
In 1898, Italian biologists allowed an infected Anopheles mosquito to bite a healthy man, who later became ill with malaria.

written.text: Describe the diagnostic characteristics of the four kingdoms within the domain Eukarya.
modelAnswer: Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular.

Kingdom Plantae includes multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose; they prepare food through photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it within their bodies; they have no cell walls.

written.text:

(b) Describe the Linnaean system of classification in detail, stating the seven taxonomic ranks and their relationships.
modelAnswer: (a) Both Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes.
Archaea have cell walls that do not contain peptidoglycan but are made of various polypeptides and proteins.
Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
Archaeal rRNA resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria, and archaeal cell membranes contain unique lipids.
Some archaea live in extreme environments, although they also exist in common environments such as soil and oceans.
Bacteria are found in all environments; some cause diseases, while many are beneficial, including decomposers that recycle nutrients.
(b) The Linnaean system arranges organisms in a taxonomic hierarchy.
The seven ranks, from broadest to most specific, are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
Each lower rank is more specific than the rank before it.
Thus, kingdom is the broadest rank and species is the most specific rank.

written.text:
(a) Describe the diagnostic characteristics of the four kingdoms within the domain Eukarya.
(b) Discuss the challenges of classifying viruses within the traditional three domains of life.
modelAnswer: (a) Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular.
Plant-like protists are autotrophs; animal-like protists are heterotrophs, and fungus-like protists absorb nutrients from decaying organic matter.
Kingdom Fungi consists of heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; they absorb food from decaying matter.
Kingdom Plantae includes multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose; they prepare food through photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it within their bodies; they have no cell walls.
(b) Viruses are acellular; they are not made of cells and do not have organelles.
They cannot run metabolism.
For the synthesis of their proteins and to increase in number, viruses become parasites in organisms.
They lack any of the characteristics of the three domains of life.
Therefore, viruses are not included in the classification system.

written.text:
(a) Explain the rules and guidelines for suggesting scientific names to organisms.
(b) Q2.6. Discuss the challenges of classifying viruses within the traditional three domains of life.
modelAnswer: (a) Scientific names are taken from Latin.
Every scientific name has two parts: the genus name comes first, followed by the species name.
Every scientific name should be unique; the same name cannot be used for two different organisms.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, and the species name begins with a small letter.
When printed, the scientific name is typed in italics.
When handwritten, its two parts are underlined separately.
(b) Viruses are acellular and lack the cellular structure and organelles found in organisms of the three domains.
They cannot carry out all life processes independently.
They reproduce only inside host cells.
For these reasons, viruses do not fit easily into the traditional three-domain classification of cellular life.

This is important because enzymes and structural proteins are needed for normal cell activities.

written.text:
(a) Name the chemical compounds that make up:
(a) Cell membrane
(b) Fungal cell wall
(c) Plant cell wall
(d) Bacterial cell wall
(e) Ribosomes
(f) Chromosomes
(b) Explain the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.
modelAnswer: (a) (a) Cell membrane: proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates.
(b) Fungal cell wall: chitin.
(c) Plant cell wall: the primary wall is mainly cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.
(d) Bacterial cell wall: peptidoglycan.
(e) Ribosomes: almost equal amounts of proteins and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
(f) Chromosomes: DNA and proteins.
(b) The cell membrane is composed of proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates.
According to the fluid-mosaic model, the lipids make a fluid-like bilayer in which protein molecules are submerged.
The lipids and proteins can move laterally, so the mosaic pattern constantly changes.
Carbohydrates join proteins as glycoproteins or lipids as glycolipids.
