written.text:
(a) Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall.
(b) Discuss the components of the nucleus.
modelAnswer: (a) The cell wall is a rigid, non-living wall around the cell membrane.
It provides shape, strength, protection and support to the protoplasm.
The plant cell wall has three layers: middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall.
The primary wall is mainly made of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly made of cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.
Plasmodesmata are channels in cell walls that allow the exchange of molecules between adjacent cells.
(b) The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which has many nuclear pores.
The inner jelly-like material is called nucleoplasm.
The nucleoplasm contains one or more nucleoli, where ribosomes are assembled.
It also contains chromatin, made of DNA and proteins; chromatin condenses into thick chromosomes when a cell starts dividing.
DNA contains genes that control cell activities and transmits characteristics to the next generation.

written.text: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
modelAnswer: Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus and is divided into four phases.
During prophase, thread-like chromatin condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.
The nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and spindle fibres form.
During metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at the centromere and arrange along the equator, forming the metaphase plate.
During anaphase, spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart towards opposite poles.
During telophase, a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and results in two daughter cells.

written.text: Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
modelAnswer: In prophase-I, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, exchanging portions of chromosomes.
In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator and form the metaphase plate.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate; one chromosome from each pair moves toward each opposite pole. Each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.
In telophase-I, spindles disappear, nuclear envelopes and nucleoli reform, and chromosomes uncoil into chromatin.
Cytokinesis occurs, producing two haploid daughter cells.

written.text: Describe the significance of meiosis.

written.text:
(a) Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
(b) Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
modelAnswer: (a) Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus and is divided into four phases.
During prophase, thread-like chromatin condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.
The nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and spindle fibres form.
During metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at the centromere and arrange along the equator, forming the metaphase plate.
During anaphase, spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart towards opposite poles.
During telophase, a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and results in two daughter cells.
(b) In prophase-I, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, exchanging portions of chromosomes.
In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator and form the metaphase plate.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate; one chromosome from each pair moves toward each opposite pole. Each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.
In telophase-I, spindles disappear, nuclear envelopes and nucleoli reform, and chromosomes uncoil into chromatin.
Cytokinesis occurs, producing two haploid daughter cells.

written.text: Evaluate the importance of organ systems working in harmony and predict the consequences of a failure in one system on the others.
modelAnswer: Organ systems consist of organs that work together to perform related functions.

If one system fails, the coordinated work of other systems can be disrupted.
As a result, the organism may not be able to function normally.

written.text: Describe the tissue composition of the stomach. How does each tissue contribute to the digestive function of the stomach?
modelAnswer: The inner wall of the stomach is made up of glandular epithelial tissue.
It secretes mucus, which protects the inner wall from acid, and gastric juice containing pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid.
Connective tissue lies beneath the epithelial tissue; it provides structural support and contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
There are three smooth muscle layers: outer longitudinal, middle circular, and inner oblique.
These muscles contract and relax to mix food with gastric juice.
The outer connective tissue encircles and supports the stomach.

written.text: How do the organ systems come together to form the human body?
modelAnswer: An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform particular functions.
The skeletal system provides structure, support, and protection and allows movement with the muscles.
The digestive system digests food and absorbs digested food, while the respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide.
The muscular system allows movement and locomotion.
The nervous system coordinates and controls body functions through nerve impulses.
The blood circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and waste products throughout the body.
Together, these organ systems perform the functions needed by the human body.

written.text: How does the human body maintain a stable internal temperature?
modelAnswer: When body temperature rises above normal, the temperature-regulating centre in the brain sends a message to sweat glands.
Sweating occurs and, as sweat evaporates, heat is lost and body temperature falls towards normal.
When body temperature falls, the centre sends a message to muscles, causing shivering.
Shivering generates heat and raises body temperature towards normal.

Organelles assemble and interact to make cells, the smallest units with characteristics of life.

Epidermal tissue is the outer layer; the cuticle reduces water loss and stomata control gas exchange and water-vapour loss.
Mesophyll tissue contains chloroplast-rich cells and is the site of photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll air spaces facilitate diffusion of gases.
Vascular tissue contains xylem, which conducts water and minerals to leaf cells, and phloem, which transports sugars from leaf cells to the stem.

In this condition, any more substrate molecules do not find free active sites. This state is called saturation of active sites and reaction rate does not increase.
written.followUp: What is the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity?

rubric.why: Increasing substrate concentration initially increases the reaction rate.
rubric.description: State the effect of increasing substrate concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an increase in substrate concentration increases the reaction rate.

rubric.why: At saturation, active sites are occupied and further substrate does not increase the reaction rate.
rubric.description: Explain the effect at high substrate concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that active sites become occupied (saturated), so further substrate does not increase the reaction rate.

written.text: Give two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH values.
modelAnswer: For example, pepsin in stomach works in acidic medium (pH 1.5 to 2.0) while trypsin in small intestine works in alkaline medium (pH 7 to 8).

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying trypsin as working in an alkaline medium in the small intestine, with pH 7 to 8.

written.text: What do you mean by optimum temperature and optimum pH?
modelAnswer: Each enzyme works at maximum rate at a specific temperature called optimum temperature. They show maximum activity at a specific pH, called their optimum pH.

rubric.why: Optimum pH is the specific pH at which an enzyme shows maximum activity.
rubric.description: Define optimum pH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an enzyme shows maximum activity at a specific pH called its optimum pH.

written.text: Which type of enzyme inhibitors inhibit enzymes without attaching to the active site?
modelAnswer: Some enzyme inhibitors do not have similarity to the substrate. They do not attach to the active site of enzyme. Rather, they attach to some other location of enzyme.

rubric.description: State where the inhibitor attaches.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the inhibitor attaches to another location on the enzyme rather than the active site.

written.text: Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibition.
modelAnswer: Some inhibitors resemble the enzyme’s substrate. They compete with the substrate to attach to the active site of enzyme. Some enzyme inhibitors do not have similarity to the substrate. They do not attach to the active site of enzyme. Rather, they attach to some other location of enzyme.

written.text:
(a) Describe the characteristics of enzymes.
(b) Describe how temperature extremes can inhibit enzyme activity and lead to enzyme denaturation.
modelAnswer: (a) Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed.
They are predominantly proteins, typically containing 100 to 1,000 amino acids.
They have a three-dimensional globular structure that allows them to form active sites that bind specifically to substrates.
Enzymes are highly specific to the reactions they catalyse and to the nature of their substrates.
Some enzymes require non-protein cofactors; enzymes may function inside or outside cells, work in sequences, and have uses in different industries.
(b) When temperature rises to a certain limit, heat adds in the movement of molecules, so the rate of enzyme action increases.
When temperature is raised well above the optimum temperature, heat breaks the bonds in the enzyme molecule.
The globular structure of the enzyme is lost; this is called denaturation of enzyme.
It results in a rapid decrease in the rate of enzyme action.

written.text:
(a) Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.
(b) How does pH affect enzyme activity?
modelAnswer: (a) In the lock-and-key model, the active site of the enzyme has a fixed structure.
The substrate molecule fits precisely into it to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
The enzyme catalyzes the reaction and the substrate is transformed into product or products, which are released.
In the induced fit model, the active site of the enzyme is not rigid.
When the substrate interacts with the enzyme, its active site is reshaped to perform its function.
(b) Enzymes are sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration (pH) of the fluid in which they work.
They show maximum activity at a specific pH, called their optimum pH.
Change in pH can affect the ionization of the amino acids at the active site of enzyme.
It slows down enzyme activity or blocks it completely.
Pepsin in stomach works in acidic medium (pH 1.5 to 2.0), while trypsin in small intestine works in alkaline medium (pH 7 to 8).

written.text:
(a) Q7.5. Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.
(b) Q7.1. Describe the characteristics of enzymes.
modelAnswer: (a) In the Lock-and-Key model, the enzyme’s active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate.
The substrate fits into this active site like a key fits into a lock.
In the Induced Fit model, the active site is flexible and changes shape as the substrate binds.
Both models show specific substrate binding and formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.
After the reaction, products leave the enzyme and the enzyme can be used again.

Diagram to draw and label: show two side-by-side enzyme models. Label the first “Lock-and-Key”: a fixed active site, a matching substrate, and the enzyme-substrate complex. Label the second “Induced Fit”: an initially flexible active site, the substrate, and the changed active site around the bound substrate. Add arrows showing substrate binding and product release.
(b) Enzymes are biological catalysts and are primarily proteins.
They speed up chemical reactions, including metabolic reactions.
They are not consumed in the reactions and can be used again.
Enzymes are specific because each active site fits particular substrate(s).
Each enzyme works best at an optimum temperature and pH.

written.text: What do ATP and ADP mean? What are the roles of these molecules for the cellular metabolism?
modelAnswer: ATP means adenosine triphosphate and ADP means adenosine diphosphate.
When ATP breaks down, ADP and Pi are formed and energy is released for cell processes.
Cells use energy from food to combine ADP with Pi to form ATP.

written.text: Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
modelAnswer: ATP is a nucleotide made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds.
When the outer phosphate bond breaks, Pi separates and energy is released; ATP becomes ADP.
The breaking of one phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.
Cells use energy from food to combine ADP with Pi to form ATP.
ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken down during energy-consuming processes, so it transfers energy between metabolic reactions.

written.text: Outline the processes involved in photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis occurs in two phases: light reactions and dark reactions.
Light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
Light energy is used to make ATP and NADPH; light also breaks water and oxygen is released.
Dark reactions take place in the stroma of chloroplasts.
Carbon dioxide is reduced using ATP and hydrogen from NADPH to make 3-carbon carbohydrates.
The 3-carbon carbohydrates are used to make glucose.

written.text: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: one glucose molecule is broken into two pyruvic acid molecules, with two ATP and two NADH formed.
When oxygen is available, pyruvic acid moves to the mitochondrial matrix and is converted into acetyl coenzyme-A.
In the Krebs cycle, acetyl coenzyme-A is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide, forming ATP, NADH and FADH₂.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner membranes of mitochondria; electron flow releases energy used to make ATP.
At the end of the chain, electrons and hydrogen ions combine with oxygen to form water.

written.text: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and NADH.
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is further broken down; the Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and transfers energy to carriers.
Electrons pass along the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with hydrogen to form water.
Most ATP is produced during the electron transport chain.

written.text:
(a) Explain the types and importance of anaerobic respiration.
(b) Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
modelAnswer: (a) Anaerobic respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen and incompletely oxidizes glucose, releasing less energy.
In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvic acid is broken down into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide; it occurs in yeast and some bacteria.
In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid; it occurs in the skeletal muscles of humans and other animals.
Early organisms respired anaerobically; anaerobes still use it, and muscles use it when oxygen supply is insufficient.
Fermentation is used to make cheese and yogurt, in brewing and baking, and in making soy sauce.
(b) ATP is a nucleotide made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds.
When the outer phosphate bond breaks, Pi separates and energy is released; ATP becomes ADP.
The breaking of one phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.
Cells use energy from food to combine ADP with Pi to form ATP.
ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken down during energy-consuming processes, so it transfers energy between metabolic reactions.

modelAnswer: (a) Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose without oxygen and releases only a small amount of energy.

written.text: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
modelAnswer: During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport.
Their solute concentration increases, so water moves from epidermal cells into guard cells by osmosis.
The guard cells become turgid; their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens.
In the evening, glucose concentration falls and potassium ions move back to epidermal cells.
Water moves out of the guard cells, they lose turgor, their inner sides touch and the stoma closes.

written.text: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

written.text: Describe temperature, wind and humidity as the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Higher temperature generally increases transpiration because evaporation and diffusion of water vapour become faster.
Wind usually increases transpiration by carrying away moist air from around the leaves.
High humidity decreases transpiration because the air already contains much water vapour.
This reduces the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air.
Final answer: Higher temperature and wind usually increase transpiration, while high humidity decreases it.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is loaded into the phloem.
This lowers the water potential in the phloem, so water enters from nearby xylem by osmosis.
The entry of water raises the pressure in the phloem at the source.
Phloem sap moves down the pressure gradient towards a sink, where sucrose is unloaded for use or storage.
Water then moves out of the phloem, helping maintain the pressure difference between source and sink.
Final answer: Food moves in phloem from source to sink because water entry at the source creates a pressure gradient.

written.text: Explain osmotic adjustments in in hydrophytes, xerophytes and halophytes.

Xerophytes face water shortage; they can accumulate solutes in cells, lowering water potential and helping cells absorb or retain water.

They accumulate compatible solutes in their cytoplasm or store salts in vacuoles, helping maintain water uptake while limiting salt damage.
Final answer: Xerophytes and halophytes adjust cell solute concentrations to maintain water uptake; hydrophytes live where water is readily available.

written.text:
(a) Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
(b) Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: (a) During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport.
Their solute concentration increases, so water moves from epidermal cells into guard cells by osmosis.
The guard cells become turgid; their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens.
In the evening, glucose concentration falls and potassium ions move back to epidermal cells.
Water moves out of the guard cells, they lose turgor, their inner sides touch and the stoma closes.
(b) Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: (a) Plants remove extra water during the day by transpiration.
Some plants, such as grasses, remove excess water at night by guttation.
In guttation, water droplets pass through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Some plants store wastes, including salts, as harmless crystals.
Other plants keep wastes in their leaves and get rid of them when the leaves fall; some excrete wastes through special pores by applying force.
(b) At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

written.text: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
modelAnswer: The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The gametophytes produce gametes, and pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.
The pollen tube grows to the ovule and carries two sperms into the embryo sac.
One sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.
The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.
A seed that gets suitable conditions can grow into the next sporophyte generation.

written.text: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
modelAnswer: The adult flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte (2n), which produces flowers.
Meiosis forms haploid spores. Microspores develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.
After pollination, a pollen tube grows to the embryo sac and carries the male gametes.
One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. This is double fertilization.
The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed, which germinates to form a new sporophyte.

written.text: Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
modelAnswer: A diploid megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Usually three megaspores degenerate, leaving one functional megaspore.
The functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, forming eight haploid nuclei.
The nuclei arrange into a seven-celled embryo sac: an egg cell and two synergids at one end, three antipodal cells at the other end, and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

written.text: Name the four whorls present in a flower and tell the components of each whorl.
modelAnswer: Calyx: It is the outermost whorl. It is made of green leaf-like sepals. Corolla: It is the second whorl and made of petals. (a) Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
(b) Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
modelAnswer: (a) The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.

A seed that gets suitable conditions can grow into the next sporophyte generation.
(b) During binary fission, the bacterial DNA replicates.
The daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides.
The cell membrane pinches in.
A new cell wall is synthesized in the middle.
Two identical daughter bacteria are produced.

Meiosis forms haploid spores. Microspores develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.
After pollination, a pollen tube grows to the embryo sac and carries the male gametes.
One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. This is double fertilization.
The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed, which germinates to form a new sporophyte.
(b) The diploid generation that produces spores is called the sporophyte generation.
The haploid generation that produces gametes is called the gametophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces spores, which grow into the gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte produces gametes, which unite to form a zygote that develops into the next sporophyte.

written.text:
(a) Compare and contrast the domains Archaea and Bacteria, focusing on their key characteristics.
(b) Discuss the components of the nucleus.
modelAnswer: (a) Both Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes.
Archaea have cell walls that do not contain peptidoglycan but are made of various polypeptides and proteins.
Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
Archaeal rRNA resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria, and archaeal cell membranes contain unique lipids.
Some archaea live in extreme environments, although they also exist in common environments such as soil and oceans.
Bacteria are found in all environments; some cause diseases, while many are beneficial, including decomposers that recycle nutrients.
(b) The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which has many nuclear pores.
The inner jelly-like material is called nucleoplasm.
The nucleoplasm contains one or more nucleoli, where ribosomes are assembled.
It also contains chromatin, made of DNA and proteins; chromatin condenses into thick chromosomes when a cell starts dividing.
DNA contains genes that control cell activities and transmits characteristics to the next generation.

written.text:
(a) Discuss the functions of proteins.
(b) How does pH affect enzyme activity?
modelAnswer: (a) Proteins are an important part of all cell membranes.
Some proteins, such as collagen and keratin, make almost whole structures of cartilage, hair and nails.
Enzymes are proteins that catalyse all biochemical reactions occurring in organisms.
Some proteins are hormones that regulate body processes.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Actin and myosin are the main components of muscle cells and are responsible for muscular contractions.
Fibrin makes blood clot to prevent the loss of blood after an injury.
Antibodies defend the body against harmful pathogens.
(b) Enzymes are sensitive to hydrogen ion concentration (pH) of the fluid in which they work.
They show maximum activity at a specific pH, called their optimum pH.
Change in pH can affect the ionization of the amino acids at the active site of enzyme.
It slows down enzyme activity or blocks it completely.
Pepsin in stomach works in acidic medium (pH 1.5 to 2.0), while trypsin in small intestine works in alkaline medium (pH 7 to 8).

written.text:
(a) Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
(b) Describe the ways by which humans can grow new plants by using the vegetative parts of the parent plants?
modelAnswer: (a) During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport.
Their solute concentration increases, so water moves from epidermal cells into guard cells by osmosis.
The guard cells become turgid; their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens.
In the evening, glucose concentration falls and potassium ions move back to epidermal cells.
Water moves out of the guard cells, they lose turgor, their inner sides touch and the stoma closes.
(b) Artificial propagation includes techniques such as cutting, grafting and tissue culture.
In cutting, a piece of stem or root is cut from a plant and used to grow a new plant.
In grafting, a bud or small stem of one plant is attached to the roots or stems of a second plant.
Grafting enables the beneficial characteristics of two plants to be combined.

written.text:
(a) Describe the diagnostic characteristics of the four kingdoms within the domain Eukarya.
(b) Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall.
modelAnswer: (a) Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular.
Plant-like protists are autotrophs; animal-like protists are heterotrophs, and fungus-like protists absorb nutrients from decaying organic matter.
Kingdom Fungi consists of heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; they absorb food from decaying matter.
Kingdom Plantae includes multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose; they prepare food through photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it within their bodies; they have no cell walls.
(b) The plant cell wall is a rigid structure made of cellulose.
It provides structural support.
It also provides protection.

written.text:
(a) Q6.1. Write a comprehensive note on the structures and roles of the three classes of carbohydrates.
(b) Q7.1. Describe the characteristics of enzymes.
modelAnswer: (a) Carbohydrates are organic compounds made mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Monosaccharides are single sugar units; examples include glucose and fructose.
Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join; examples include sucrose and maltose.
Polysaccharides are long chains of many monosaccharides; examples include starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Carbohydrates provide energy for cellular activities, and glucose is used in respiration.
Starch in plants and glycogen in animals store energy.
Cellulose forms plant cell walls and provides structural support.
(b) Enzymes are biological catalysts and are primarily proteins.
They speed up chemical reactions, including metabolic reactions.
They are not consumed in the reactions and can be used again.
Enzymes are specific because each active site fits particular substrate(s).
Each enzyme works best at an optimum temperature and pH.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.
modelAnswer: (a) Plants remove extra water during the day by transpiration.
Some plants, such as grasses, remove excess water at night by guttation.
In guttation, water droplets pass through small pores at the tips or edges of leaves.
Some plants store wastes, including salts, as harmless crystals.
Other plants keep wastes in their leaves and get rid of them when the leaves fall; some excrete wastes through special pores by applying force.
(b) The diploid generation that produces spores is called the sporophyte generation.
The haploid generation that produces gametes is called the gametophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces spores, which grow into the gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte produces gametes, which unite to form a zygote that develops into the next sporophyte.

written.text:
(a) Explain the rules and guidelines for suggesting scientific names to organisms.
(b) Write a note on cell specialization.
modelAnswer: (a) Scientific names are taken from Latin.
Every scientific name has two parts: the genus name comes first, followed by the species name.
Every scientific name should be unique; the same name cannot be used for two different organisms.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, and the species name begins with a small letter.
When printed, the scientific name is typed in italics.
When handwritten, its two parts are underlined separately.
(b) Cells formed by cell division are initially similar.
After their formation, cells undergo specialization or differentiation.
During this process, they get special sizes, structures, and metabolic features and become specialized.
For example, mesophyll cells perform photosynthesis, neurons transmit nerve impulses, and red blood cells carry oxygen.

written.text:
(a) Q6.2. Discuss the functions of proteins.
(b) Q7.2. Describe how temperature extremes can inhibit enzyme activity and lead to enzyme denaturation.
modelAnswer: (a) Proteins are needed for growth and repair and form structural materials such as collagen and keratin.
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, including digestion.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Antibodies help defend the body against pathogens.
Proteins also take part in movement, blood clotting and regulation; for example, myosin works in muscle and insulin is a protein hormone.
(b) At low temperatures, enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly.
Fewer successful collisions occur, so enzyme activity decreases.
Above the optimum temperature, excessive heat changes the shape of the enzyme, including its active site.
The substrate can no longer fit properly; the enzyme is denatured and its activity is greatly reduced or stops.

written.text:
(a) How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?
(b) Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
modelAnswer: (a) Many hydrophytes have broad leaves that float on the surface of water.
These leaves have a large number of stomata on their upper surfaces.
Water moves out through these stomata.
Halophytes absorb salts from outside and make their bodies hypertonic.
Excess salt can be stored in cells or excreted through salt glands on leaves.
(b) The ovule acts as a megasporangium and contains a diploid megaspore mother cell.
The megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores.
Only one megaspore remains alive.
Inside the megaspore, mitosis forms eight haploid nuclei.
Two nuclei migrate to the centre and fuse to form a fusion nucleus.
One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the egg cell.
The resulting embryo sac has seven cells: one egg cell, one fusion nucleus, and five non-functional cells.
